In $m$-player games, the same framework gives a significantly simplified proof of the recent $O(\sqrt{m}\log n\log T)$ regret bound due to Ha.

AI.tldr: Optimistic Hedge has horizon-independent O(n log n) regret in two-player general-sum games for a suitable learning rate, but in games with three or more players some player's regret can be exponential in the number of actions; the upper bound uses a temporal approximation framework that also gives a simpler proof of Ha's O(sqrt(m) log n log T) bound.
AI.motivation: Whether Optimistic Hedge achieves constant regret polynomial in the game size was a longstanding open question, since Ha's bound is non-constructive and its dependence on the number of actions n is not explicit.
AI.method: Lower bounds come from explicit m-player games with n actions per player; the upper bound uses a temporal approximation framework that approximates losses over time-localized windows by well-behaved functions, starting from the RVU bound of Daskalakis, Fishelson and Golowich.
AI.result: In two-player games a suitable learning rate gives O(n log n) regret independent of the horizon; in three-player games, for any learning rate up to an absolute constant and large enough T, some player's regret is 2^Omega(n); for every m at least 3 regret can be 2^Omega(mn), and for learning rates above 2^-Omega(mn) it grows linearly in T; the framework gives a much simpler proof of the O(sqrt(m) log n log T) regret bound.
AI.conclusion: The number of players decides whether Optimistic Hedge admits polynomial constant regret, and the temporal approximation framework simplifies the analysis of Optimistic Hedge.

title: Server-Side Sparse Assignment for Federated Mixture-of-Experts
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE Information Theory Workshop (ITW 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly recognized for their remarkable capabilities; federated learning (FL) offers a promising framework for collaboratively fine-tuning LLMs on edge devices while achieving data privacy. However, edge devices are inherently heterogeneous: clients may exhibit diverse data distributions and resource constraints, including limited memory and computation budgets. Recent federated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address these challenges by using sparse expert activation or partial expert loading. However, existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-specific relevant experts from partial observations. We propose $S^3$-MoE, a server-side sparse expert assignment framework that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit--explore mechanism. We also establish relevance-estimation error and exact Top-$K$ recovery guarantees. Experiments using a CNN-based MoE on CIFAR-100 show that $S^3$-MoE recovers task-dependent client--expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection across clients. Compared with Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client access to all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, $S^3$-MoE achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy while loading only $5$ experts per client.

AI.tldr: S3-MoE is a server-side sparse expert assignment method for federated mixture-of-experts fine-tuning that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations; on CIFAR-100 with a CNN-based MoE it reaches 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy than Full-20 FedAvg while loading only 5 experts per client.
AI.motivation: Edge clients are heterogeneous in data and in memory and compute budgets, and existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-relevant experts.
AI.method: The server estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit-explore mechanism, with relevance-estimation error and exact Top-K recovery guarantees established.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 with a CNN-based MoE, S3-MoE recovers task-dependent client-expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection; it achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy than Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, while loading only 5 experts per client.
AI.conclusion: Server-side assignment from partial observations can reach higher accuracy with far fewer experts loaded per client, backed by theoretical recovery guarantees.

title: A Night at the LLM Zoo: Data Conditioned Flow Matching for Generating Pretrained LLM Weights
summary: A challenge to Weight Space Learning as it expands from task specific and vision models to Large Language Models (LLMs) is the absence of a well curated and analyzed LLM population. To address this, we train such a model zoo for application to Weight Space Generation by systematically varying the data mixture composition between web text, books, mathematics, coding, and French across populations of 51M, 124M, and 355M parameter GPT-2 Models, each tier with count N = 100. We analyze these populations by cosine similarity, functional diversity, Leave-One-Mixture-Out modeling, and variance decomposition. We show that the zoo contains diverse models whose variation is structured by training mixture composition. We embed the training mixture composition to condition a Flow Matching model of complete pretrained LLM weights in Gram-PCA compressed weight space. By demonstrating zero-shot generalization to held out mixtures, measuring Continuous Ranked Probability Score skill, as well as finding minimal changes in downstream test-set perplexity and general capability benchmark scores, we show that our generator generalizes on the simplex of data mixtures to produce models that perform similarly to those in the zoo ex nihilo. Finally, we produce all source code and artifacts to support the continued expansion of Weight Space Learning and Generation into the LLM domain.

AI.tldr: The authors train 100 GPT-2 models in each of three sizes (51M, 124M, 355M parameters) on varied data mixtures and use a data-conditioned Flow Matching model to generate complete pretrained weights for held-out mixtures, which perform similarly to zoo models on perplexity and benchmark scores.
AI.motivation: Weight Space Learning has lacked a well-curated and analysed LLM population, which is needed to extend it from task-specific and vision models to large language models.
AI.method: Models are trained with systematically varied mixtures of web text, books, mathematics, coding and French, and the population is analysed by cosine similarity, functional diversity, Leave-One-Mixture-Out modelling and variance decomposition; the mixture composition conditions a Flow Matching model of full weights in Gram-PCA compressed weight space.
AI.result: The generator shows zero-shot generalization to held-out mixtures, measured by Continuous Ranked Probability Score skill, with minimal changes in downstream test-set perplexity and general capability benchmark scores relative to zoo models.
AI.conclusion: The generator generalizes across the simplex of data mixtures to produce models that perform similarly to zoo models trained directly, and source code and artifacts are released to support weight space learning for LLMs.

title: Regulating Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Operators with Fixed and Adaptive Penalties: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
summary: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) operators may exploit consumer surplus through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them. We study how penalty-based regulation of an AMoD operator in a multimodal mobility system can limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability. We model regulation as an outer control loop that acts on a learning-based operator. Static regulation with fixed penalties is formulated as a Markov Decision Process for an operator that jointly controls pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game in which a regulator periodically adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop. Operator and regulator policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. In experiments with real-world Manhattan data, fixed surge pricing penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%. For regional service availability, dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity. The gains in service availability are strongest when spare fleet capacity exists, whereas service deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets. The learned regulator policy responds by reducing penalties where limited fleet capacity restricts compliance. The results identify trade-offs between regulatory targets, operator profitability, and traveler utility.

AI.tldr: Using graph-based multi-agent RL on real Manhattan data, the paper shows that fixed surge-pricing penalties cut the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%, and dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity.
AI.motivation: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand operators may exploit consumers through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them.
AI.method: Static regulation with fixed penalties is an MDP for an operator controlling pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation is a partially observable stochastic game in which a regulator adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop; both policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning.
AI.result: Fixed surge penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%; dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over equal-mean fixed penalties; service availability gains are strongest with spare fleet capacity, while deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets, and the learned regulator reduces penalties where limited capacity restricts compliance.
AI.conclusion: The results identify trade-offs among regulatory targets, operator profitability and traveler utility in multimodal mobility regulation.

title: Machine Learning for Live-Birth Prediction After IVF/ICSI From Structured Clinical Data: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Critical Appraisal
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables; supplementary material (26 pages) in ancillary files. Data and code: this https URL. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
summary: Machine-learning models predicting live birth after in vitro fertilisation (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) from routine clinical data report performance from near chance to near perfect. We systematically reviewed these models under PRISMA 2020, searching OpenAlex, Scopus and Web of Science to 22 October 2026, appraised them with PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI, and pooled their discrimination with random-effects meta-analysis on the logit scale. We define what fixes the meaning of a model's output (decision point, endpoint, unit of analysis, data source) and map the 48 included studies by model family, decision point and validation design. Models evaluated only internally pooled to an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.814, against 0.756 (95% prediction interval 0.546-0.889) for models evaluated on a later period or another centre, and 0.764 for studies not at high risk of bias; neither difference was significant, and heterogeneity was extreme. Models whose decision point was not stated pooled to 0.910, the only significant moderator in meta-regression. Against logistic regression fitted to the same data, the best machine-learning model gained a pooled 0.056 AUC (95% CI 0.017-0.090). Of 48 studies, 47 were at high or unclear risk of bias, only four assessed the calibration slope, and no model has evidence of clinical impact. The certainty of the pooled evidence is low to very low; the gains that survive validation came from staging predictions to decision points and local calibration, not deeper architectures. We provide a TRIPOD+AI-mapped checklist, a benchmark specification and a research agenda.

AI.tldr: A PRISMA 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis of 48 studies finds that machine-learning models predicting IVF or ICSI live birth from structured clinical data pool to AUC 0.814 when evaluated only internally and 0.756 on later-period or other-centre validation, with extreme heterogeneity and low to very low certainty of evidence.
AI.motivation: Reported performance of machine-learning models for live birth after IVF or ICSI ranges from near chance to near perfect, so the validity and meaning of these models' outputs is unclear.
AI.method: The authors searched OpenAlex, Scopus and Web of Science under PRISMA 2020, appraised studies with PROBAST+AI and TRIPOD+AI, pooled discrimination with random-effects meta-analysis on the logit scale, and mapped studies by model family, decision point and validation design.
AI.result: Internally evaluated models pool to AUC 0.814, against 0.756 (95% prediction interval 0.546-0.889) for later-period or other-centre validation and 0.764 for studies not at high risk of bias, and neither difference is significant; models whose decision point was not stated pool to 0.910, the only significant meta-regression moderator; the best ML model gains a pooled 0.056 AUC (95% CI 0.017-0.090) over logistic regression on the same data; 47 of 48 studies are at high or unclear risk of bias, and only four assess calibration slope.
AI.conclusion: No model has evidence of clinical impact, and the authors supply a TRIPOD+AI-mapped checklist, a benchmark specification and a research agenda, arguing that the gains surviving validation came from staging predictions to decision points and local calibration rather than deeper architectures.

title: Data-Driven Modeling of Molten Chloride Corrosion Using Static Test Data
summary: Molten chloride corrosion has been studied for decades, yet reliable prediction across different alloys, salts, and test conditions remains difficult. In this work, 291 static molten chloride corrosion experiments reported in the literature were compiled into a structured dataset and used to develop an interpretable machine-learning framework for corrosion-rate predictions. To better represent the differences in salt condition across studies, a Chloride Salt Preparation Index (CSPI) was introduced to bring the reported salt-treatment method, atmosphere control, and pre-exposure impurity condition on a common numerical scale. A blended tree-based ensemble provided the most consistent predictive performance, achieving a cross-validated \(R^2\) of 0.85 and an MAE of 0.41 mg cm\(^{-2}\) day\(^{-1}\). The graded CSPI retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and emerged as the dominant model descriptor. Global sensitivity and SHAP analyses further identified exposure time, temperature, and alloy chemistry as important contributors to the model predictions, with several observed trends consistent with the established molten-chloride corrosion behavior. The conformal prediction intervals were well calibrated, providing an estimate of prediction uncertainty in addition to the point prediction. Overall, the framework demonstrates that historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable, and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, while also highlighting where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed to improve future molten-salt corrosion models.

AI.tldr: A blended tree-based ensemble trained on 291 literature static molten chloride corrosion experiments predicts corrosion rate with cross-validated R2 of 0.85 and MAE of 0.41 mg cm-2 day-1, with a graded Chloride Salt Preparation Index emerging as the dominant descriptor.
AI.motivation: Reliable prediction of molten chloride corrosion across alloys, salts and test conditions remains difficult, and salt-preparation conditions differ between studies in ways that are hard to compare.
AI.method: The 291 experiments are compiled into a structured dataset; a Chloride Salt Preparation Index encodes salt treatment, atmosphere control and pre-exposure impurity condition on one numerical scale; a blended tree-based ensemble is used with global sensitivity analysis, SHAP analysis and conformal prediction intervals.
AI.result: The ensemble achieves cross-validated R2 of 0.85 and MAE of 0.41 mg cm-2 day-1; the graded index retained more useful information than a simple purified/unpurified classification and is the dominant descriptor; exposure time, temperature and alloy chemistry are also important contributors, and the conformal prediction intervals are well calibrated.
AI.conclusion: Historical corrosion data can support quantitative, interpretable and uncertainty-aware prediction when experimental context is represented explicitly, and the work highlights where more consistent reporting and targeted experiments are needed.

title: Scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification for Cancer Histopathology: Calibrated Uncertainty Under Distribution Shift
summary: Reliable uncertainty quantification is essential for clinical deployment of cancer diagnosis models, yet neural networks and variational Gaussian process methods can produce overconfident predictions, particularly under the distribution shifts that arise when models trained at one hospital are applied at another. We present a scalable Bayesian Gaussian Process Classification (GPC) framework that operates on frozen pathology foundation model embeddings (Phikon) and combines accelerated Randomly Pivoted Cholesky (RPCholesky) for low-rank kernel factorization, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction. This makes HMC posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation tractable at N approximately 300,000 training points, enabling HC-based low-rank GPC on substantially larger datasets than prior MCMC-based demonstrations. We evaluate on two histopathology benchmarks for breast cancer metastasis detection: PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, where the latter tests calibration under hospital-level distribution shift. Compared to stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, our method improves calibration and predictive performance - reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% - with the largest gains appearing under distribution shift, suggesting that HMC-based posterior sampling provides more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification.

AI.tldr: A scalable Bayesian Gaussian process classifier on frozen Phikon pathology embeddings, using accelerated randomly pivoted Cholesky factorization and HMC, reduces expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90% relative to stochastic variational GP and neural baselines for breast cancer metastasis detection, with the largest gains under hospital-level shift.
AI.motivation: Neural networks and variational GP methods can be overconfident, particularly when a model trained at one hospital is applied at another, which is a problem for clinical deployment.
AI.method: Accelerated RPCholesky low-rank kernel factorization, HMC with non-centered parameterization for posterior sampling in the low-rank latent representation at about 300,000 training points, and a pivots-as-inducing-points scheme for prediction.
AI.result: On PCam and CAMELYON17-WILDS, compared with stochastic variational GP and neural network baselines, the method improves calibration and predictive performance, reducing expected calibration error by up to 88% and false negative rate by up to 90%, with the largest gains under distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: HMC-based posterior sampling gives more trustworthy uncertainty estimates for cross-site pathology classification, and the method makes HMC-based low-rank GPC feasible on much larger datasets than prior MCMC demonstrations.

title: Teaching Agents the "Principle", Not the "Reward"
summary: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong performance in many tasks by letting agents learn from nothing more than a reward signal. However, in more complex tasks, agents still struggle to learn good, generalizable policies, even with carefully designed rewards and abundant samples. We argue that this difficulty stems from the reward decoding burden: designers encode their knowledge of the desired behavior into rewards and penalties, and agents must infer this knowledge from long sequences of noisy scalars. To address this burden, we propose prescriptive policy learning (PPL), which directly teaches agents higher-level knowledge about the tasks, termed principles of behavior, such as how to maintain balance, how to accumulate energy, and how to land smoothly. Through appropriately selected key quantities and references, PPL can directly indicate at every step whether the agent follows the principles and to what extent. Our experiments show that agents can learn good, generalizable policies without any reward. Taught only simple heuristic principles, PPL agents outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples. Their policies also transfer directly to harder settings and keep performing well, demonstrating their strong generalization ability. In summary, PPL provides a new approach in which rough knowledge of the desired behavior is enough for agents to learn good, generalizable policies, even when the system dynamics cannot be accurately modeled.

AI.tldr: Prescriptive policy learning teaches RL agents high-level principles of behaviour, such as maintaining balance or landing smoothly, instead of relying on reward signals; agents taught only simple heuristic principles outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples and transfer to harder settings.
AI.motivation: Agents struggle to learn good, generalizable policies in complex tasks even with carefully designed rewards, because they must infer the designer's knowledge from long sequences of noisy scalar rewards.
AI.method: Prescriptive policy learning (PPL) uses appropriately selected key quantities and references to indicate at every step whether the agent follows the principles of behaviour and to what extent.
AI.result: Agents learn good, generalizable policies without any reward; PPL agents outperform reward-based methods with far fewer samples, and their policies transfer directly to harder settings and keep performing well.
AI.conclusion: Rough knowledge of the desired behaviour is enough for agents to learn good, generalizable policies, even when system dynamics cannot be accurately modelled.

title: Depth or Description? When a One-Step Latent Score Replaces Lookahead in Proactive Information Acquisition
summary: A proactive agent must decide what to ask before it acts. Exact lookahead values combinations of questions but is expensive and leans on a fitted model; a one-step score is cheap but can miss them. Our main finding: the need for depth often lies in how the hidden cause is described. A one-step score on the label can be blind to an interaction among answers. A score on a suitable latent cause is not, and where that latent encodes the decision it replaces most of depth at a fraction of the search. Described differently, the same problem can defeat the score while exact values do not move, so keep the latent small and check it against exact values. Probabilities learned from one language model's answers do not carry to another unless planning allows for both; those read from tokens are worth only a few labels.

AI.tldr: For proactive information acquisition, a one-step score on a suitable latent cause can replace most of the depth of exact lookahead at a fraction of the search cost, provided the latent is kept small and checked against exact values; probabilities learned from one language model's answers transfer to another only if planning allows for both.
AI.motivation: Exact lookahead values combinations of questions but is expensive and relies on a fitted model, while a one-step score on the label is cheap but can be blind to interactions among answers.
AI.method: The one-step score is computed on a latent representation of the hidden cause rather than on the label, the latent is kept small and checked against exact lookahead values, and probabilities learned from different language models' answers are compared for transfer.
AI.result: A one-step score on a suitable latent cause is not blind to answer interactions and, where the latent encodes the decision, replaces most of the depth at a fraction of the search; the same problem can defeat a label-level score while exact values do not move; probabilities learned from one language model's answers do not carry to another unless planning allows for both, and those read from tokens are worth only a few labels.
AI.conclusion: How the hidden cause is described, rather than search depth alone, determines whether depth is needed, so the latent should be validated against exact values.

title: A Survey of Nonlinear Filtering Methods for Data Assimilation and Recent Advances in Generative AI-Enabled Score Filters
summary: Many real-world applications, such as numerical weather prediction or wildfire tracking, involve modeling highly nonlinear dynamical systems that are chaotic and influenced by various sources of uncertainty. To improve model prediction accuracy and reduce such uncertainties, data assimilation (DA) combines the dynamical model with partial, noisy observations to estimate the evolution of the system's state. Doing so depends on solving the optimal filtering problem: computing the conditional distribution of a hidden state given a sequence of observations. Classical approaches fail along three distinct axes: Kalman-based methods assume Gaussian posteriors and produce biased estimates under nonlinear observation operators; particle-based methods represent distributions with weighted samples and collapse in high dimensions due to the curse of dimensionality; and kernel-based methods move beyond discrete particle representations but cannot maintain their density approximation affordably as dimension grows. The Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) avoids all three constraints by encoding the filtering density in a score function and approximating that score with a training-free Monte Carlo estimator, enabling stable filtering in high-dimensional, chaotic systems. This survey traces EnSF's mathematical foundations, establishes it as the state of the art for non-Gaussian, high-dimensional filtering, and examines fourteen extensions that expand its operational reach. Twelve of the fourteen extensions preserve this training-free Monte Carlo estimator at the core of the update, with only two departing from it to achieve planetary-scale deployment.

AI.tldr: This survey traces the mathematical foundations of the Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF), a training-free Monte Carlo score-based method for nonlinear data assimilation, and reviews fourteen extensions of it. It argues that EnSF is the state of the art for non-Gaussian, high-dimensional filtering.
AI.motivation: Optimal filtering for chaotic, nonlinear systems is hard. Kalman methods assume Gaussian posteriors and are biased under nonlinear observation operators, particle methods collapse in high dimensions, and kernel methods cannot maintain their density approximation affordably as dimension grows.
AI.method: A review of the Ensemble Score Filter, which encodes the filtering density in a score function approximated by a training-free Monte Carlo estimator, together with a survey of fourteen extensions that expand its operational reach.
AI.result: Twelve of the fourteen extensions keep the training-free Monte Carlo estimator at the core of the update, and only two depart from it to achieve planetary-scale deployment.
AI.conclusion: EnSF and its extensions enable stable filtering in high-dimensional chaotic systems, and the survey presents them as the state of the art for non-Gaussian, high-dimensional filtering.

title: Structural Conditional Independence Test via Neural Quantile Resolution
comment: Accepted at IEEE ICDM 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Conditional independence testing is difficult when dependence is weak, localized, or expressed through distributional changes rather than a global mean shift. Existing tests usually return a scalar statistic or p-value, which summarizes evidence against independence but does not describe where the conditional law changes. We propose QRCIT, a quantile-resolution conditional independence test that compares P(X|Z) and P(X|Y,Z) through a quantile deformation learned by a shared model. A lightweight residual quantile-flow model first learns the baseline conditional quantile law and then learns the additional deformation induced by Y, yielding a global predictive-gain statistic with conditional-randomization calibration and an inspectable deformation field over context and quantile level. We also introduce the Structural Dependency Benchmark (SDB), which evaluates dependence structures motivated by real applications, such as context-local, tail-only, sign-reversing, moving-ridge, and mean-neutral patterns. Across synthetic post-nonlinear (PNL) and SDB benchmarks, QRCIT improves detection of structured alternatives, with empirical Type-I behavior evaluated across settings. Higher quantile resolution improves merged-SDB power at moderate sample sizes, while diagnostics restricted to known affected regions improve detection of localized dependence. On Sachs, METABRIC breast cancer, and CCLE/PLX4720, QRCIT provides competitive real-data performance and interpretable deformation patterns. These results support quantile-resolved conditional-law deformation as a practical framework for testing and diagnosing structured conditional dependence.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes QRCIT, a conditional independence test that compares P(X|Z) and P(X|Y,Z) through a learned quantile deformation, yielding a global statistic and an inspectable deformation field. It also introduces the Structural Dependency Benchmark (SDB).
AI.motivation: Existing conditional independence tests return a scalar statistic or p-value, which shows evidence against independence but does not describe where the conditional law changes, and they struggle when dependence is weak, localized or expressed through distributional changes.
AI.method: A residual quantile-flow model first learns the baseline conditional quantile law and then the additional deformation induced by Y, giving a global predictive-gain statistic calibrated by conditional randomization. The new SDB benchmark covers context-local, tail-only, sign-reversing, moving-ridge and mean-neutral dependence patterns.
AI.result: On synthetic post-nonlinear and SDB benchmarks QRCIT improves detection of structured alternatives, and higher quantile resolution improves merged-SDB power at moderate sample sizes. Diagnostics restricted to known affected regions improve detection of localized dependence. On Sachs, METABRIC breast cancer and CCLE/PLX4720 it is competitive and gives interpretable deformation patterns, with empirical Type-I behaviour evaluated across settings.
AI.conclusion: Quantile-resolved conditional-law deformation is presented as a practical framework for testing and diagnosing structured conditional dependence.

title: Meta-Frieren: Beyond Single Level Online Learning
summary: We study a two-stage online optimization problem: at each round, a meta-learner first selects an agent-environment pair, then the chosen agent interacts with the environment, and receives a reward. We introduce Meta-Frieren, a general framework for maximizing cumulative reward in this setting. Our analysis yields a simple UCB-style criterion for meta-level selection and recovers prior guarantees as special cases while extending them to broader settings. We instantiate Meta-Frieren with GP-UCB under Bayesian and frequentist assumptions. We also derive, to our knowledge, the first high-probability regret bound for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling, specialize it to finite and parametric function classes, and integrate it into Meta-Frieren. Experiments support our theoretical results and demonstrate that Meta-Frieren can be successfully applied to hyperparameter optimization across multiple model classes.

AI.tldr: Meta-Frieren is a framework for a two-stage online problem in which a meta-learner first selects an agent-environment pair and the chosen agent then interacts with the environment. It uses a UCB-style meta-level criterion and is applied to hyperparameter optimization.
AI.motivation: The framework aims to extend prior guarantees for this setting, which they recover as special cases. The authors also note that no high-probability regret bound for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling was available to their knowledge.
AI.method: A UCB-style criterion for meta-level selection, instantiated with GP-UCB under Bayesian and frequentist assumptions, plus a high-probability regret bound for Feel-Good Thompson Sampling specialized to finite and parametric function classes and integrated into the framework.
AI.result: Experiments support the theoretical results and show that Meta-Frieren can be successfully applied to hyperparameter optimization across multiple model classes. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Meta-Frieren gives a general approach to maximizing cumulative reward when the agent-environment pair is chosen online, and it unifies and extends prior guarantees.

title: Backbone-Informed Adaptation after EEG Pretraining: A Capacity-Controlled Study
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures. Code available at this https URL
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models learn representations that combine information across channels and time. This structure motivates adapters that model the same relationships during downstream learning. However, it is not clear whether such a design outperforms other candidate adapters. Moreover, in order to arrive at a fair comparison between candidate adapters, we also need to consider their trainable parameters. Here, we ask whether a backbone-informed (native) adapter makes better use of a given capacity by comparing it against a token-wise multilayer perceptron control that transforms each feature vector independently. We approximately match their trainable parameter counts and keep the pretrained encoder fixed. Across two EEG foundation models and tasks covering emotion recognition, sleep staging, and EEG event classification, the native adapter shows no consistent advantage. For one backbone, differences between the designs are small relative to variation across runs. For the other, the token-wise control performs better on emotion recognition and EEG event classification. On sleep staging, the native adapter's advantage over the token-wise control is reduced when we also train the component that processes sequences of EEG segments. The relative performance of the two adapters depends on the backbone, task, and downstream training protocol. These findings motivate evaluating backbone-informed adapters against capacity-matched alternatives.

AI.tldr: The paper compares a backbone-informed (native) adapter against a parameter-matched token-wise MLP control for downstream learning after EEG foundation-model pretraining. The native adapter shows no consistent advantage.
AI.motivation: EEG foundation models combine information across channels and time, which motivates adapters that model the same relationships, but it is unclear whether such adapters outperform other candidate designs once trainable parameter counts are matched.
AI.method: A capacity-controlled comparison in which the native adapter and a token-wise MLP control have approximately matched trainable parameter counts and the pretrained encoder is kept fixed. Two EEG foundation models are tested on emotion recognition, sleep staging and EEG event classification.
AI.result: The native adapter shows no consistent advantage. For one backbone the differences are small relative to run-to-run variation. For the other, the token-wise control performs better on emotion recognition and EEG event classification. On sleep staging the native adapter's advantage shrinks when the component that processes sequences of EEG segments is also trained.
AI.conclusion: The relative performance of the adapters depends on backbone, task and downstream training protocol, so backbone-informed adapters should be evaluated against capacity-matched alternatives.

title: TrustMix: Graceful Degradation for Pretrained Models under Distribution Shift
summary: Predicting beyond the training domain necessarily requires assumptions about how the ground truth extrapolates, yet in most neural networks these assumptions are made only implicit through the architecture. We propose TrustMix, a lightweight post-hoc method that makes a pretrained model's extrapolative behaviour explicit and controllable. TrustMix combines the predictive distribution produced by a pretrained model with a user-specified fallback distribution $p_0(y|x)$, such that as the out-of-distribution (OOD) deviation statistic grows, we collapse towards $p_0(y|x)$. TrustMix provides graceful degradation: the predictive distribution converges toward the fallback distribution as the OOD signal grows. The fallback distribution $p_0(y|x)$ can reflect domain knowledge, if available, or rely on a domain-agnostic stationarity assumption. TrustMix does not require retraining of the base model and can be applied to both regression and classification problems. We evaluated TrustMix on several synthetic and real-world distribution shifts, including tabular, image, and natural language processing tasks. We tested TrustMix on datasets such as CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet and on numerous architectures including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers. TrustMix remains competitive in-distribution while improving predictive uncertainty under distribution shift, with gains in predictive likelihood for regression and calibration for classification. Finally, we showed that TrustMix can provide useful predictive distributions for decision-making applications by utilizing it as a surrogate for Bayesian Optimisation.

AI.tldr: TrustMix is a lightweight post-hoc method that mixes a pretrained model's predictive distribution with a user-specified fallback distribution, shifting toward the fallback as an out-of-distribution deviation statistic grows. It requires no retraining of the base model.
AI.motivation: Neural networks make assumptions about extrapolation beyond the training domain only implicitly, through their architecture, so their behaviour under distribution shift is not explicitly controlled.
AI.method: The predictive distribution of a pretrained model is combined with a fallback distribution p0(y|x), collapsing toward the fallback as the OOD statistic grows. The fallback can encode domain knowledge or a domain-agnostic stationarity assumption, and the method applies to both regression and classification.
AI.result: Evaluated on synthetic and real-world shifts across tabular, image and NLP tasks, with CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, CNNs and Transformers. It stays competitive in distribution, improves predictive likelihood for regression and calibration for classification under shift, and serves as a surrogate for Bayesian optimisation.
AI.conclusion: TrustMix gives explicit, controllable graceful degradation for pretrained models under distribution shift, and its predictive distributions can support decision-making.

title: Structured Machine Theory of Mind from Agent Trajectories
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 10/2026. 37 pages. OpenReview: this https URL. Code: this https URL
summary: Predictive models of human behavior trained on large-scale trajectory data optimize for statistical accuracy without representing the mental states that causally generate behavior. Such models support prediction but not principled intervention: they cannot answer how an agent's behavior would change if its beliefs or preferences were different. We introduce Structured Machine Theory of Mind (SMToM), a framework that attributes explicit, independently supervised belief and desire representations from observed trajectories within a Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) causal structure. The central architectural element is a goal head that consumes only the predicted mental-state channels and a current-trajectory embedding; counterfactual intervention on beliefs and desires is a direct operation. We instantiate SMToM on a controlled pedestrian navigation domain where ground-truth mental states are known by construction, enabling evaluation of attribution accuracy, local channel interventions, and trajectory-level counterfactual diagnostics. The resulting model, BDIBottleneck, improves over trajectory-only and unsupervised-context neural baselines. It is also competitive with a matched auxiliary-supervised context baseline while providing an editable mental-state interface that the unbottlenecked baseline lacks. Counterfactual experiments on desires confirm that substituting an agent's inferred preferences with a different activity type coherently shifts predicted destinations toward relevant locations. Counterfactual experiments on beliefs confirm that marking a location as unavailable in the agent's belief state reduces its predicted probability as a destination, though in a complex way. These results demonstrate, in a controlled navigation setting, that explicit BDI-structured supervision is a viable foundation for interpretable and counterfactual analysis of longitudinal trajectory data.

AI.tldr: Structured Machine Theory of Mind (SMToM) attributes explicit belief and desire representations from agent trajectories within a Belief-Desire-Intention causal structure. The BDIBottleneck model routes predictions through a goal head that supports counterfactual intervention on mental states.
AI.motivation: Predictive models of behaviour trained on trajectory data optimize statistical accuracy without representing the mental states that cause behaviour, so they support prediction but not principled intervention on beliefs or preferences.
AI.method: The SMToM framework uses independently supervised belief and desire representations and a goal head that consumes only the predicted mental-state channels and a current-trajectory embedding. It is instantiated on a controlled pedestrian navigation domain where ground-truth mental states are known by construction.
AI.result: BDIBottleneck improves over trajectory-only and unsupervised-context neural baselines and is competitive with a matched auxiliary-supervised context baseline, while offering an editable mental-state interface. Substituting inferred desires coherently shifts predicted destinations, and marking a location as unavailable in beliefs reduces its predicted destination probability in a complex way.
AI.conclusion: Explicit BDI-structured supervision is a viable foundation for interpretable and counterfactual analysis of longitudinal trajectory data, demonstrated in a controlled navigation setting.

title: Canonical Correlation Neural Networks
summary: Relational inductive biases such as grids or graphs allow neural networks with fewer trainable parameters and improved generalization, but require a known structure beforehand. When no structure is available, the covariance matrix provides a principled substitute, and coVariance Neural Networks (VNNs) have shown that using it yields models that are theoretically grounded in Principal Component Analysis, stable to finite-sample estimation errors and parameter-efficient. This framework, however, is limited to single-view data, whereas many applications observe the same phenomenon through multiple views, each with its own in-view covariance and a cross-view covariance linking them. To incorporate these matrices as inductive biases in a principled way, we introduce CAnonical correlation NEural networks (CANEs), architectures that use in-view and cross-view covariances as distinct relational biases to solve downstream tasks. Via spectral analysis, CANEs draw analogies with Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA), a classical technique to project two-view data onto a correlated subspace. However, while CCA's objective is to compute shared view representations, CANEs are trained to solve a downstream task directly. We bound their output error under finite-sample covariance perturbations and show that it depends on controllable Lipschitz constants of the learned filters in place of the singular-value gap that governs the stability of CCA, thus guaranteeing better robustness. Experiments on seven datasets from brain imaging and motion sensing show that CANEs match or outperform single-view, two-view and CCA-based baselines, often with fewer parameters, and retain their performance when covariances are re-estimated from fewer samples.

AI.tldr: Canonical Correlation Neural Networks (CANEs) use in-view and cross-view covariance matrices as distinct relational inductive biases for multi-view data and are trained directly on downstream tasks. They draw spectral analogies with CCA while offering better robustness guarantees.
AI.motivation: Covariance-based VNNs handle only single-view data, whereas many applications observe the same phenomenon through multiple views, each with its own in-view covariance and a cross-view covariance linking them. CCA computes shared representations rather than solving a downstream task directly.
AI.method: CANEs use in-view and cross-view covariances as relational biases, with spectral analysis drawing analogies to CCA. Output error is bounded under finite-sample covariance perturbations in terms of controllable Lipschitz constants of the learned filters.
AI.result: On seven datasets from brain imaging and motion sensing, CANEs match or outperform single-view, two-view and CCA-based baselines, often with fewer parameters, and retain their performance when covariances are re-estimated from fewer samples.
AI.conclusion: The error bound depends on filter Lipschitz constants in place of the singular-value gap that governs CCA stability, which the authors present as better robustness for multi-view covariance-based networks.

title: Fractional physics-informed neural networks to model social media virality
summary: Existing models of social media virality either prescribe the functional form of engagement growth or assume a fixed mechanism by which past activity influences future engagement. We present a fractional physics-informed neural network that learns both the temporal memory and nonlinear growth dynamics of social media engagement, using symbolic regression to translate the learned dynamics into interpretable equations. Synthetic experiments at the deployment resolution of 24 hourly observations demonstrate that the fractional order and reaction law can be jointly recovered from clean data. Under observation noise, however, the standard pointwise physics residual drives the fractional order toward its lower bound through a scale artifact. We address this failure using a fully whitened residual that propagates observation noise through the fractional operator. Applying the framework to 348 posts from X (formerly Twitter), we find that a single-window model estimates strongly memory-dependent dynamics but fails to accurately reconstruct held-out trajectories. Partitioning the 24-hour window into four teacher-forced segments substantially improves performance, yielding segment-specific fractional orders that increase from 0.23 to 0.99 and interpretable growth laws for each phase. The segmented model reconstructs 64% of held-out trajectories within a mean squared error of 0.01, compared with 44% for the strongest of nine classical baselines. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of fractional physics-informed equation discovery to uncover interpretable engagement dynamics while highlighting the importance of noise-aware estimation and temporal segmentation.

AI.tldr: A fractional physics-informed neural network learns the temporal memory and nonlinear growth dynamics of social media engagement and uses symbolic regression to turn them into interpretable equations. Applied to 348 X posts, a four-segment model reconstructs 64% of held-out trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing virality models either prescribe the functional form of engagement growth or assume a fixed mechanism for how past activity influences future engagement, and under observation noise the standard pointwise physics residual drives the fractional order to its lower bound.
AI.method: A fractional PINN with symbolic regression, plus a fully whitened residual that propagates observation noise through the fractional operator to address the scale artifact. The 24-hour window is partitioned into four teacher-forced segments.
AI.result: On clean synthetic data the fractional order and reaction law are jointly recovered. On 348 X posts a single-window model estimates strongly memory-dependent dynamics but fails to reconstruct held-out trajectories accurately, whereas the segmented model yields fractional orders rising from 0.23 to 0.99 and reconstructs 64% of held-out trajectories within MSE 0.01, compared with 44% for the strongest of nine classical baselines.
AI.conclusion: Fractional physics-informed equation discovery can uncover interpretable engagement dynamics, provided that noise-aware estimation and temporal segmentation are used.

title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: this https URL

AI.tldr: TileQuant is a training-free mixed-precision post-training quantization method for LLMs that assigns 16-bit or 8-bit precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles instead of whole columns. It reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput.
AI.motivation: Uniform PTQ ignores uneven weight sensitivity, column-wise mixed precision retains whole columns and so also protects less sensitive weights, and runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead.
AI.method: Tiles are scored offline by input-activation-aware statistics from forward passes or by gradient-informed loss sensitivity. Within each projection's retention budget the highest-scoring tiles stay at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit, and a kernel reuses compact weight buffers for integer and 16-bit computation.
AI.result: TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval and question answering it preserves quality, and on multiple tasks it surpasses both quantized and original models.
AI.conclusion: Selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution is a practical route to mixed-precision LLM quantization.

title: Loopback Transformer: Towards a Unified View of Residual Looped Transformers
comment: 31 pages, 9 figures. Code: this https URL ; Project page: this https URL
summary: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters (excluding token embeddings and the output head) at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It also has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B. At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean among the standard Transformer and seven looped residual designs.

AI.tldr: The Loopback Transformer reads individual block updates on a separate path from the stack input, so geometric decay sets total update weight and attention allocates it. It reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformers with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by sharing blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how repeated computation is reused, and a full block output couples the input history with its new update.
AI.method: A depth-memory view of residual connections in which the stack input is kept on a separate path and individual block updates are read. Geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight across updates.
AI.result: On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B, and at 191M, 374M and 778M it has the lowest validation loss and highest thirteen-task mean among standard Transformers and seven looped residual designs.
AI.conclusion: Separate controls for input strength, total update weight and allocation across updates give looped Transformers a more principled design, which the tested scales support.

title: Neural Compression over Equivalence Classes: Exact Gauges and Functional Rate-Distortion
summary: Neural networks admit many parameterizations of the same or nearly the same function, but deployment typically stores whichever parameter vector training happens to produce. We show that this representational freedom can itself be used for compression. Rather than redesigning the codec, we search over exact function-preserving transformations and controlled functional perturbations, using the unchanged physical compressor itself to select cheaper representations. Exact gauge families provide a zero-distortion reference under the strict audit; allowing small functional changes exposes much larger rate-distortion gains. Across SmolLM2 and Qwen3, our method reduces Zstandard-compressed checkpoint size by up to 23.4\%, with similar relative reductions under gzip, Brotli, and ZipNN, establishing trained-network representational freedom as a practical storage resource.

AI.tldr: The paper searches over exact function-preserving transformations and small functional perturbations of trained networks, using the unchanged compressor to pick the cheapest parameter representation. It cuts Zstandard-compressed checkpoint size by up to 23.4% on SmolLM2 and Qwen3.
AI.motivation: Deployment usually stores whichever parameter vector training happens to produce, although neural networks admit many parameterizations of the same or nearly the same function.
AI.method: A search over exact gauge families, which give a zero-distortion reference under a strict audit, and controlled functional perturbations, using the physical compressor itself to select cheaper representations without redesigning the codec.
AI.result: Checkpoint size under Zstandard falls by up to 23.4% across SmolLM2 and Qwen3, with similar relative reductions under gzip, Brotli and ZipNN. Allowing small functional changes exposes much larger rate-distortion gains than exact gauge families alone.
AI.conclusion: Trained-network representational freedom is established as a practical storage resource.

title: MAC-v2: Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels
comment: 9 pages (12 pages of appendix & references), submitted to ICLR 2027
summary: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.

AI.tldr: MAC-v2 performs long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels in offline RL, using a reconstruction-free latent world model trained with action chunking. It achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines on visual benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Pixel-based long-horizon value expansion is substantially harder than in state-based environments, because the agent must learn both representation and dynamics and errors from either accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories.
AI.method: A reconstruction-free latent world model trained with prediction and control objectives, so control-irrelevant visual details need not be encoded, combined with action chunking to reduce the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion.
AI.result: Across visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Analyses show that long-horizon value expansion is critical, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon model-based value expansion with latent learning and action chunking is presented as an effective framework for pixel-based offline RL.

title: KG-Neighbor: Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Construction for Embedding Visualization
summary: In embedding visualizations, nearby instances are interpreted as semantically related, although neighborhoods derived from input embeddings may not reflect content relationships. Neighborhood-based dimensionality reduction (DR) methods can propagate this limitation by optimizing layouts from embedding-based neighborhood graphs. We propose Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Graph Construction (KGN), which represents relational knowledge derived from each instance as a set of knowledge graph (KG) triples. It uses the degree of triple sharing as pairwise semantic evidence to adjust embedding distances and reconstruct the top-k neighborhood graph; neither KG extraction nor neighborhood construction uses class labels. We also introduce IDProfile (IDP), which interprets residual mismatches by independently assessing whether the source content supports the assigned class label and the neighborhood-majority class. Across eight text and image dataset-encoder conditions, we characterize KGN over the full guidance-strength sweep and four KG similarity measures. Across this sweep, the maximum NMI and LT_2D each exceed the corresponding kNN baseline in all eight conditions, with the largest gains reaching 0.68 and 1.35, respectively. The gains and the extent of neighborhood reconfiguration vary across conditions and are larger under encoder conditions with lower kNN baseline scores. The IDP analysis shows that the largest reductions are concentrated in Placement Issue candidates, whereas Label Issue and Unresolved Case instances account for a larger share of the remaining review set. These results indicate that KGN can narrow the evaluated gap between embedding-based neighborhoods and content-supported semantic relations, while IDP shows that a residual mismatch should not automatically be interpreted as a projection failure.

AI.tldr: KGN builds the neighbourhood graph for embedding visualizations from knowledge-graph triple sharing rather than from embedding distance alone, and IDProfile diagnoses residual mismatches. Across eight dataset-encoder conditions the maximum NMI and LT_2D exceed the kNN baseline.
AI.motivation: Nearby points in embedding visualizations are read as semantically related, but neighbourhoods derived from input embeddings may not reflect content relationships, and neighbourhood-based dimensionality reduction methods propagate this limitation.
AI.method: KGN represents knowledge from each instance as KG triples, uses the degree of triple sharing as pairwise semantic evidence to adjust embedding distances, and reconstructs the top-k neighbourhood graph without class labels. IDProfile independently assesses whether the source content supports the assigned class label and the neighbourhood-majority class.
AI.result: Across eight text and image dataset-encoder conditions the maximum NMI and LT_2D each exceed the kNN baseline in all eight, with the largest gains reaching 0.68 and 1.35. Gains are larger under encoders with lower kNN baseline scores, and the largest IDP reductions are concentrated in Placement Issue candidates.
AI.conclusion: KGN can narrow the evaluated gap between embedding-based neighbourhoods and content-supported semantic relations, and a residual mismatch should not automatically be read as a projection failure.

title: Using Transformers for Teaching and Learning via Symbolic Distillation of Neural A-life Agents
summary: Neural networks controlling behavior of A-life agents can evolve over multiple generations. While effective in making the agents survive, such networks are generally opaque to a human observer. Furthermore, the neural weights cannot be transferred between agents with different neural architectures. Distilling such neural networks into compact symbolic policies can help humans understand agent behavior in A-life. Additionally, it allows the agents to share their knowledge in a compact fashion, improving population-level learning. Distilling a neural policy into a symbolic policy is typically performed by searching the space of symbolic policies to find one that approximates the neural policy. However, even with a domain-specific language the space of policies can be large, necessitating incomplete stochastic search such as genetic algorithms. Yet the distillation remains computationally expensive. We propose to instead use a transformer pre-trained on readily available random percept-action data. Doing so speeds up distillation substantially. We derive the transformer architecture via a neural architecture search. Empirical results compare different distillation methods and the influence of the symbolic space on A-life population dynamics through self-reflection and teaching and learning.

AI.tldr: The paper uses a transformer pretrained on readily available random percept-action data, with its architecture derived by neural architecture search, to distil neural controllers of A-life agents into compact symbolic policies. The abstract reports that this speeds up distillation substantially.
AI.motivation: Neural controllers of evolved A-life agents are opaque to human observers and their weights cannot be transferred between agents with different architectures, while searching the space of symbolic policies is computationally expensive even with genetic algorithms.
AI.method: A transformer pretrained on random percept-action data, with its architecture derived via neural architecture search, is used in place of search over symbolic policies to distil neural policies into symbolic ones.
AI.result: Empirical results compare different distillation methods and show how the symbolic space influences A-life population dynamics through self-reflection and teaching and learning. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained transformers can make symbolic distillation of A-life controllers practical, supporting both human understanding of agent behaviour and knowledge sharing across the population.

title: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference
summary: Sparsity and quantization reduce the cost of attention by skipping interactions and lowering the precision of those retained. However, useful interactions differ in their precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal. We therefore introduce TriAttention, which assigns query-key (QK) tiles to skipping, 4-bit, or 8-bit computation, using 4-bit to retain quantization-tolerant interactions at lower cost. To represent compactly, we encode each head's computation regions with two diagonal-distance boundaries, keeping policy storage independent of context length. Offline calibration then evaluates candidate boundary pairs using normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs. Using these measurements, a model-wide allocator selects each head's boundaries to minimize calibration error under a shared computation budget. During prefill, the selected boundaries generate precision-grouped traversals for a fused kernel that skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized attention output. The quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are then reused in a compressed key-value (KV) cache for decoding, reducing repeated reads of prompt data. Experiments show that TriAttention achieves end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over the Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Meanwhile, TriAttention maintains quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks. These results show how a compact retention-and-precision policy translates local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access. The implementation is this https URL.

AI.tldr: TriAttention assigns query-key tiles to skipping, 4-bit or 8-bit computation using two diagonal-distance boundaries per head, executed by a fused kernel. It reports end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline while keeping quality comparable to the original models.
AI.motivation: Sparsity and quantization each reduce attention cost, but useful interactions differ in precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal.
AI.method: Per-head boundary pairs are selected offline by normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs, under a model-wide allocator with a shared computation budget. A fused kernel skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized output, and the quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are reused in a compressed KV cache for decoding.
AI.result: End-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Quality is comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks.
AI.conclusion: A compact retention-and-precision policy can translate local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access.

title: Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood Learning: A Genetic Algorithm for Instance-Dependent k Optimization in Nearest Neighbor Classification
summary: The number of neighbours k is the central hyperparameter of the k-nearest neighbour (k-NN) classifier and is usually selected globally through cross-validation or evolutionary search. However, the bias-variance trade-off is inherently local: dense and noise-free regions may favour small neighbourhoods, whereas sparse or noisy regions may require larger ones. Since global-k optimization is one-dimensional, replacing exhaustive search with a genetic algorithm offers little computational advantage. We therefore optimize an instance-dependent neighbourhood policy instead. We propose EANK (Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood K), which uses a low-dimensional policy to map local neighbourhood descriptors, including density, label entropy, vote margin, and concentration, to an adaptive number of neighbours k(x). A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes this policy using leave-one-out accuracy with a neighbourhood-smoothness penalty. Precomputed neighbour votes reduce fitness evaluation costs. We investigate theoretical properties of the method, including dominance over global-k solutions on the training criterion, evolutionary convergence, policy regularity, and generalization guarantees. Experiments on synthetic data with spatially heterogeneous structure and twelve public datasets evaluate predictive performance, robustness, and computational cost. Under nested cross-validation, EANK achieves competitive performance relative to tuned global-k baselines and improves upon the default k=5. We also examine the gap between training and test performance to assess the practical value of adaptive neighbourhood selection.

AI.tldr: EANK uses a real-coded elitist genetic algorithm to optimize a low-dimensional policy that maps local neighbourhood descriptors to an adaptive number of neighbours k(x) for k-NN classification. Under nested cross-validation it is competitive with tuned global-k baselines.
AI.motivation: The bias-variance trade-off is local, so one global k may suit neither dense and noise-free regions nor sparse or noisy ones, while global-k search is one-dimensional and a genetic algorithm offers little advantage over exhaustive search for it.
AI.method: The policy is optimized with leave-one-out accuracy and a neighbourhood-smoothness penalty, using descriptors that include density, label entropy, vote margin and concentration, with precomputed neighbour votes to reduce fitness evaluation cost.
AI.result: Under nested cross-validation EANK is competitive with tuned global-k baselines and improves on the default k=5. Experiments on synthetic heterogeneous data and twelve public datasets evaluate performance, robustness and computational cost, and the gap between training and test performance is examined.
AI.conclusion: Instance-dependent neighbourhood selection has practical value, with theoretical properties including dominance over global-k solutions on the training criterion and generalization guarantees reported.

title: Reweighting is not Harmless: Understanding the Role of Dataset Characteristics
summary: Reweighting is a widely used pre-processing method for promoting discrimination-free model behavior by assigning different weights to data points during model training. While it is often credited with improving fairness, particularly by mitigating systematic underestimation for underrepresented groups, it can also introduce unintended harms under certain data conditions. Using controlled simulations that vary group size and baseline event prevalence, we show how reweighting can yield misleading improvements in fairness by reducing underestimation for one group while introducing it for another. Across 3,000 simulated datasets with event prevalence of 7-14%, reweighting improved parity in positive classification and false negative rates (FNR) between groups, but did so partly by decreasing positive classifications and increasing FNR for the group with higher baseline prevalence. These effects were most pronounced when that group was a minority: its FNR rose by 6 percentage points, approximately 82 additional missed cases per 10,000 group members, and roughly three-quarters of the improvement in FNR parity came from this increase rather than from gains for the other group. The pattern held across six classifiers, from logistic regression to neural networks, while overall accuracy was essentially unchanged, leaving the shift invisible in aggregate performance metrics. These findings mirror patterns reported in real-world applications and underscore the critical role of data characteristics in shaping the impact of this fairness intervention. While reweighting may create desirable outcomes in some applications, practitioners should critically evaluate it relative to their problem area and goals. Specifically, when the goal is to reduce underestimation in one group without introducing underestimation in another, reweighting may not be the appropriate approach.

AI.tldr: Controlled simulations show that reweighting, a common fairness pre-processing method, can reduce underestimation for one group while introducing it for another, so fairness metrics can improve while missed cases rise for a minority group.
AI.motivation: Reweighting is credited with improving fairness, particularly by mitigating systematic underestimation for underrepresented groups, but its unintended harms under certain data conditions are less understood.
AI.method: Controlled simulations of 3,000 datasets with event prevalence of 7-14%, varying group size and baseline event prevalence, evaluated across six classifiers from logistic regression to neural networks.
AI.result: Reweighting improved positive-classification and false-negative-rate parity between groups, partly by decreasing positive classifications and increasing FNR for the group with higher baseline prevalence. When that group was a minority its FNR rose by 6 percentage points, about 82 extra missed cases per 10,000 members, and roughly three-quarters of the FNR parity gain came from this increase, while overall accuracy was essentially unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Reweighting may not be appropriate when the goal is to reduce underestimation in one group without introducing it in another, so practitioners should evaluate it against their problem and goals.

title: Energy Measurement and Optimization of TinyML in Resource-Constrained Embedded Systems: A Systematic Mapping Study
summary: The rapid expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased the volume of data generated at the network edge, where many devices operate under severe memory, processing, and energy constraints. In this context, Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) enables machine learning (ML) tasks to be executed on microcontrollers, smart sensors, and other resource-constrained platforms. However, the literature remains heterogeneous regarding the algorithms evaluated, energy-measurement methods, reported metrics, influencing factors, and optimization strategies. This study presents a systematic mapping of energy-aware TinyML research. It identifies the main models and learning approaches, classifies energy-evaluation methodologies and metrics, examines the technical factors affecting energy consumption, and organizes the reported optimization techniques into a structured taxonomy. The findings highlight the frequent use of convolutional and lightweight architectures, direct measurements and analytical estimations, and factors related to model architecture, hardware, communication, numerical precision, and input characteristics. The optimization strategies were grouped into model compression, hardware-aware design, system and communication optimization, and data and processing optimization. The results also reveal limited standardization in experimental platforms, measurement procedures, and reporting practices, limiting reproducibility and direct comparison across studies. This mapping provides an updated overview of the field and guidance for developing and evaluating more energy-efficient TinyML solutions.

AI.tldr: A systematic mapping study of energy-aware TinyML research that classifies models, energy-evaluation methods and metrics, influencing factors and optimization techniques into a structured taxonomy. It finds limited standardization of platforms, measurement procedures and reporting.
AI.motivation: The TinyML energy literature is heterogeneous in algorithms evaluated, energy measurement methods, reported metrics and optimization strategies, which limits reproducibility and direct comparison across studies.
AI.method: A systematic mapping of energy-aware TinyML research that identifies the main models and learning approaches, classifies energy-evaluation methodologies and metrics, examines technical factors affecting consumption, and organizes reported optimization techniques into a taxonomy.
AI.result: The studies frequently use convolutional and lightweight architectures and both direct measurements and analytical estimations. Influencing factors include model architecture, hardware, communication, numerical precision and input characteristics. Optimizations are grouped into model compression, hardware-aware design, system and communication optimization, and data and processing optimization.
AI.conclusion: The mapping gives an updated overview of the field and guidance for developing and evaluating more energy-efficient TinyML solutions, while the limited standardization of experimental practice remains a barrier to comparison.

title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model
