comment: Accepted at Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026, Findings Track. 10 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables
summary: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $\theta$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.

AI.tldr: A decoder-only transformer with 34.6M parameters, pretrained on 1.4B coded primary-care events, shows that colorectal cancer prediction AUROC rises from 0.551 at a 2-year lookback to 0.590 at 18 years and then plateaus. The paper argues that time-context is a design axis distinct from token-context.
AI.motivation: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens, so how far back in calendar time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown.
AI.method: Pretraining on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London, then fine-tuning to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, and a simulation examined RoPE aliasing over elapsed time.
AI.result: AUROC rose from 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years and then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years. An XGBoost baseline converged to the same level, with peak AUROC 0.589. The simulation suggests that RoPE over elapsed time aliases beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency.
AI.conclusion: Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported, and the aliasing result motivates retuning the RoPE theta.

title: Satisficing as competitive Bayesian weighting: a minimal model of goal-directed choice under an unattained target
summary: Animals and humans often do not maximize; they act relative to goals (aspiration levels) that are frequently not yet met. How can a goal that is not (yet) realized organize choice? Deacon (2012) calls such absence-referenced organization \emph{ententional}, and García-Valdecasas and Deacon (2024) argue that ends are best understood as constraints rather than as particular states. We examine this idea in a minimal formal setting: Risk-sensitive Satisficing (RS), a bandit learning rule that values each action by its share of past trials multiplied by its surplus or shortfall relative to an aspiration level. We show that RS can be rewritten as a Bayesian-like estimator, Attention Competitive Bayes (ACB), in which the aspiration level is the prior mean of every action and the finite budget of trials sets how strongly evidence can override it. Two consequences follow. First, actions that are no longer sampled are partially overridden by the goal rather than by past observations: their estimates relax toward the aspiration level without any data being discarded. This ``pseudo-forgetting'' distinguishes ACB from models with an explicit forgetting rate. Second, when the aspiration is unattainable, exploration does not settle; in Bernoulli bandit simulations, adjusting the aspiration level from evidence reduced regret (expected loss). ACB offers an analyzable model in which an unattained goal and a limited attentional resource jointly constrain behavior, and it yields testable predictions about how organisms revalue options they have abandoned.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes Risk-sensitive Satisficing (RS) as a Bayesian-like estimator, Attention Competitive Bayes (ACB), in which the aspiration level is the prior mean of every action and the finite trial budget sets how strongly evidence can override it. It explains how an unattained goal can organize choice in a bandit setting.
AI.motivation: Animals and humans act relative to goals that are often not yet met, and it is unclear how such absence-referenced goals can organize choice in a formal model.
AI.method: RS values each bandit action by its share of past trials multiplied by its surplus or shortfall relative to an aspiration level. It is rewritten as ACB, in which the aspiration is the prior mean and the finite budget of trials sets how strongly evidence overrides it.
AI.result: Unsampled actions relax toward the aspiration level without any data being discarded, a pseudo-forgetting effect distinct from models with an explicit forgetting rate. When the aspiration is unattainable, exploration does not settle, and in Bernoulli bandit simulations adjusting the aspiration level from evidence reduced regret.
AI.conclusion: ACB is an analyzable model in which an unattained goal and a limited attentional resource jointly constrain behaviour, and it yields testable predictions about how organisms revalue options they have abandoned.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Resource Allocation in Integrated Sensing and Communication
summary: In vehicular integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) networks, each service-provider vehicle uses a limited power budget to serve multiple sensing targets and communication receivers. Maximizing the communication sum-rate subject to sensing signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) constraints is nonconvex, and iterative optimization is costly to rerun for every network layout. This paper proposes a graph neural network (GNN)-based power allocation algorithm, termed GNN-ISAC. Concretely, GNN-ISAC addresses the aforementioned problem by considering two distinct edge types in the graph representation, one capturing the inter-provider interference, the other representing the intra-provider power-budget sharing. GNN-ISAC is trained without labels using a sensing-penalized sum-rate loss. We also adapt the weighted mean-square error minimization (WMMSE) algorithm to this problem by introducing a sensing-power reservation step. Simulation results show that GNN-ISAC achieves communication sum-rates close to WMMSE with low sensing-link violation rates and much less computation. It also outperforms an existing heterogeneous GNN and a channel-blind baseline, and generalizes to larger networks without retraining.

AI.tldr: Proposes GNN-ISAC, a label-free graph neural network for power allocation in vehicular integrated sensing and communication that maximizes communication sum-rate under sensing SINR constraints. It reaches sum-rates close to WMMSE with few sensing violations and much less computation.
AI.motivation: Sum-rate maximization with sensing SINR constraints is nonconvex, and iterative optimization must be rerun for every network layout, which is costly. Existing heterogeneous GNNs and channel-blind baselines are the comparison points.
AI.method: A GNN with two edge types, one for inter-provider interference and one for intra-provider power-budget sharing, trained without labels using a sensing-penalized sum-rate loss. The authors also adapt WMMSE with a sensing-power reservation step.
AI.result: GNN-ISAC reaches communication sum-rates close to WMMSE with low sensing-link violation rates and much less computation. It outperforms an existing heterogeneous GNN and a channel-blind baseline, and generalizes to larger networks without retraining.
AI.conclusion: A label-free GNN can replace per-layout iterative optimization for power allocation in vehicular ISAC, trading a small sum-rate gap for large computational savings and scalability to larger networks.

title: Scenario Augmentation for Rare Financial Events via Multimodal Latent Diffusion
summary: Extreme market movements are scarce, heterogeneous, and difficult to learn from imbalanced historical data. We study whether generative augmentation can improve the representation and classification of CVaR-labeled rare financial windows while retaining the complementary structure exposed by different financial representations. Each market window is expressed through three aligned modalities: structured market variables, a spatial image transformation, and a sequence of portfolio returns. Separate variational autoencoders map the modalities to compact latent codes, and a class-conditional diffusion model learns their joint latent distribution. Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) provides a risk-aware definition of rare windows and directs generation toward the minority regime. Across four window lengths on U.S. technology equities, the resulting synthetic samples improve fidelity and support relative to tabular diffusion baselines. An XGBoost classifier trained with real and generated samples attains AUCs of 0.953 - 0.960, exceeding both tabular generators and the corresponding real-only baselines. These results show that multimodal latent generation can provide useful synthetic stress scenarios for data-scarce financial risk models.

AI.tldr: Proposes a multimodal latent diffusion method that generates synthetic CVaR-defined rare financial windows to augment scarce tail-risk data. An XGBoost classifier trained on real plus generated samples reaches AUCs of 0.953 to 0.960.
AI.motivation: Extreme market movements are scarce and heterogeneous, which makes rare-window learning hard on imbalanced data. Tabular diffusion baselines do not exploit the complementary structure of different financial representations.
AI.method: Three aligned modalities (structured market variables, a spatial image transformation, and a sequence of portfolio returns) are each encoded by a VAE. A class-conditional diffusion model learns their joint latent distribution, with CVaR defining rare windows and steering generation toward the minority regime.
AI.result: Across four window lengths on U.S. technology equities, synthetic samples improve fidelity and support over tabular diffusion baselines. XGBoost trained with real and generated samples attains AUCs of 0.953 to 0.960, exceeding both the tabular generators and the real-only baselines.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal latent generation can produce useful synthetic stress scenarios for data-scarce financial risk models, pointing to generative augmentation as a route to better rare-event classification.

title: How do Transformers Perform Low-Level Control In-Context?
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, Accepted to the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026)
summary: One of the remarkable abilities of Transformer-based neural networks is in-context learning. This motivates us to think about "in-context" control. Can we control a system knowing only (1) that it belongs to a particular family of systems and (2) some data on system evolution (provided as the context trajectory) but no specific parameter information? Specifically, we investigate the ability of Transformer-models to perform "in-context" control of unstable, nonlinear dynamical systems, where context consists only of the unforced system dynamics. We leverage a multi-head, GPT-2-style architecture, and we evaluate performance for two classical nonlinear systems -- the cartpole system and the two-link acrobot system, where the system parameters are unknown to the Transformer. We consider a setting where trajectories from an expert controller are available at training time but not at inference time. Here, we identify training techniques that are essential to train Transformers to perform low-level control. Through an analysis over checkpoints, we show that in-context control is possible, and the learned policy performance generally improves as context increases. Furthermore, the Transformer models can generalize to stabilize systems that are out-of-distribution.

AI.tldr: Studies whether a GPT-2-style Transformer can perform low-level in-context control of unstable nonlinear systems, using only context trajectories of the unforced dynamics. It shows in-context control of cartpole and acrobot systems whose parameters are unknown to the model.
AI.motivation: Controllers usually need parameter knowledge or per-system training, whereas in-context learning suggests a model might infer control from system dynamics alone. Whether Transformers can do this for unstable nonlinear control was an open question.
AI.method: A multi-head GPT-2-style Transformer is trained on expert-controller trajectories that are available at training time but not at inference. The authors identify training techniques that are essential for low-level control and analyze performance across checkpoints.
AI.result: In-context control is possible on the cartpole and the two-link acrobot, and the learned policy generally improves as the context grows. The models can also stabilize systems that are out of distribution.
AI.conclusion: Transformers can acquire in-context low-level control of unstable nonlinear dynamics without parameter information, suggesting that in-context learning can support closed-loop control and not only prediction.

title: Provably Efficient Representation Learning for Low-Rank CMDPs
summary: We study representation learning in low-rank Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs), where both value and reward functions are approximated by a set of unknown representation vectors, and the transition dynamics admit a low-rank factorization. The objective is to maximize expected cumulative rewards while complying with constraints on the expected cumulative utility. To achieve this, we propose \texttt{MFRLC} (Model-Free Representation Learning for Low-Rank CMDP), a model-free algorithm that uses a primal-dual scheme to effectively balance reward regret and constraint violations. To the best of our knowledge, \texttt{MFRLC} is the first representation-learning method for low-rank CMDPs that combines the Least-Squares Value Iteration with Upper Confidence Bound (LSVI-UCB) and primal-dual techniques. \texttt{MFRLC} further enhances value function estimation with bonuses for function approximation and learns the mapping from representations to value functions directly, avoiding explicit estimation of the transition kernel. We prove that, with high probability, \texttt{MFRLC} achieves $\widetilde O(K^{3/4})$ reward regret and cumulative constraint violation over $K$ deployment rounds, independent of the size of the state space. To our knowledge, these are the first sublinear regret and violation guarantees for CMDPs with unknown features.

AI.tldr: Proposes MFRLC, a model-free primal-dual algorithm for representation learning in low-rank constrained MDPs. It achieves O~(K^{3/4}) reward regret and constraint violation over K rounds, independent of the state-space size.
AI.motivation: Existing work on low-rank CMDPs does not offer representation learning with unknown features that avoids estimating the transition kernel, and sublinear guarantees for such settings were not previously available.
AI.method: MFRLC combines LSVI-UCB with primal-dual optimization to balance reward regret against constraint violation. It adds bonuses for function approximation and learns a direct mapping from representations to value functions, avoiding explicit transition-kernel estimation.
AI.result: With high probability, MFRLC achieves O~(K^{3/4}) reward regret and cumulative constraint violation, independent of the state-space size. The authors state these are the first sublinear regret and violation guarantees for CMDPs with unknown features.
AI.conclusion: The work gives the first sublinear guarantees for constrained RL with unknown representations in the low-rank setting, showing that model-free representation learning can be combined with constraint handling.

title: WeightLoop: Weight-Space Programming with Experimental Feedback
summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) shows that language models can reason about and rewrite neural network weights; recursive self-improvement (RSI) motivates feedback-driven improvement. Models guiding experiments receive concrete feedback: completed assays reveal prediction errors and inform what to test next. We introduce WeightLoop, a framework that turns experimental feedback into persistent updates to deployed predictors. GPT-6 Astra inspects a task specification and the model implementation, then writes a bounded, reusable parameter-editing program. As new measurements arrive, the program identifies prediction discrepancies, validates candidate edits using observed outcomes, and writes the selected changes back to the original model. The editor remains fixed while the predictor evolves, enabling repeated updates without further LLM calls or gradient retraining while preserving the original inference interface. In offline replay, targeted edits improve mean ranking utility in seven of eight endpoint-budget settings (all eight versus random edits) and mean final discovery across three sequential tasks. WeightLoop connects WSP with an RSI-inspired improvement loop, making experimental evidence a direct driver of model change and subsequent decisions.

AI.tldr: Introduces WeightLoop, a framework that turns experimental feedback into persistent, validated edits to the weights of a deployed predictor, using a fixed and reusable editing program. In offline replay it improves ranking utility and discovery over random edits.
AI.motivation: Weight-space programming shows that language models can rewrite network weights, and recursive self-improvement motivates feedback-driven updates, but deployed predictors do not learn from completed experiments. Repeated LLM calls or gradient retraining would be costly.
AI.method: GPT-6 Astra inspects the task specification and the model implementation, then writes a bounded, reusable parameter-editing program. As measurements arrive, the program finds prediction discrepancies, validates candidate edits against observed outcomes, and writes the selected changes back to the original model.
AI.result: In offline replay, targeted edits improve mean ranking utility in seven of eight endpoint-budget settings (all eight versus random edits), and improve mean final discovery across three sequential tasks.
AI.conclusion: Experimental evidence can directly drive persistent changes to a deployed model without further LLM calls or gradient retraining, linking weight-space programming with a recursive improvement loop.

title: Rethinking Data Selection: The Importance of Coverage over Difficulty in LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Selecting high-quality training data can reduce computation cost for LLM fine-tuning. Prior work on data selection developed a variety of difficulty-based scores, motivated by the intuition that harder examples are more informative. While effective for smaller classification models, we find that such methods often fail to outperform random selection for LLM fine-tuning. Our analysis reveals that random selection performs better because it is more representative of the underlying input space---i.e., has better coverage. To validate the importance of coverage, we implement a simple clustering-based selection method which selects data that is more representative of the underlying input distribution. On a set of diverse single-domain tasks, this method yields performance at or above that of random selection. On the diverse, multi-domain Tülu 3 mixture, where random sampling no longer guarantees a balanced subset, our method outperforms all methods. Overall, our results indicate that prioritizing coverage over difficulty leads to more effective data selection for LLM fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Shows that difficulty-based data selection often fails to beat random selection for LLM fine-tuning, and that the reason is coverage. A simple clustering-based selection that favors representative data matches or beats random selection on single-domain tasks and outperforms all methods on the Tulu 3 mixture.
AI.motivation: Difficulty-based scores work for smaller classification models, but their benefit for LLM fine-tuning is unclear, and random selection is a strong baseline that they often fail to beat.
AI.method: The authors analyze why random selection performs better, attributing it to better coverage of the input space. They then implement a simple clustering-based selection method that picks data more representative of the underlying input distribution.
AI.result: On diverse single-domain tasks, the clustering method yields performance at or above random selection. On the multi-domain Tulu 3 mixture, where random sampling does not guarantee a balanced subset, it outperforms all methods.
AI.conclusion: Prioritizing coverage over difficulty leads to more effective data selection for LLM fine-tuning than difficulty-based scoring.

title: Permanent and Transient Representations for Continual Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) agents struggle to adapt to new situations while retaining prior knowledge, leading to a stability-plasticity trade-off. One approach to solving this problem is by using complementary learning systems: one for slow, long-term learning and another for quick, transient adaptation. Anand & Precup (2023) instantiated this idea using permanent and transient value functions, but used the same features in both systems. Intuitively, long-term learning should rely more on parametric representations for broad generalization, while transient learning would be best served by non-parametric representations for situation-specific adaptation. In this paper, we explore this idea both theoretically and empirically. By introducing a novel non-parametric approximation for estimating the transient value function in complex tasks, we demonstrate that our method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic, underscoring the effectiveness of our system-level decomposition.

AI.tldr: Proposes a continual RL method that pairs slow permanent value functions built on parametric features with fast transient value functions built on a novel non-parametric approximation. It enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic.
AI.motivation: Continual RL agents face a stability-plasticity trade-off. Anand and Precup (2023) used complementary permanent and transient value functions but shared the same features in both, although long-term and transient learning are better served by different representations.
AI.method: The permanent value function uses parametric representations for broad generalization, while the transient value function uses a new non-parametric approximation for situation-specific adaptation. The paper examines this system-level decomposition both theoretically and empirically.
AI.result: The method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and on Craftax-Classic.
AI.conclusion: Assigning different representation types to the two complementary learning systems is an effective decomposition for continual RL, supporting both stability and fast adaptation.

title: AtlasULP: Domain-aware Universal Link Prediction via Relation Atlas
summary: Link prediction (LP) is a widely applied task in graph learning. Conventional LP approaches typically follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring independent training for each graph and incurring high computational and maintenance costs in large-scale applications. Motivated by these limitations, recent work explores Universal Link Prediction (ULP), aiming to enable training-free inference on arbitrary unseen graphs. However, existing methods primarily rely on subgraph sampling strategies to construct universal representations, which are unable to capture higher-order information due to the exponential growth of higher-order neighborhoods. As a result, they often under-perform on graphs where long-range signals are essential, such as biological networks. Moreover, their prediction models are typically domain-agnostic and lack the ability to adapt to different graph domains, leading to limited generalization. To address these challenges, we propose an Atlas-based Universal Link Prediction framework (AtlasULP), which introduces the relation atlas to capture structural associations between node pairs from both global and local perspectives, enabling a comprehensive characterization of connectivity signals across diverse graph domains. Building upon this representation, we develop a domain-guided prompting ULP model, which generates domain-aware prompt tokens from contextual structures and performs prompt-guided in-context prediction for adaptive link inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AtlasULP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse graph domains.

AI.tldr: Proposes AtlasULP, a training-free universal link prediction framework that uses a relation atlas for global and local structural signals and domain-guided prompt tokens for in-context prediction. It consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across graph domains.
AI.motivation: Dataset-specific link predictors must be retrained for each graph. Existing universal methods rely on subgraph sampling, which cannot capture higher-order information, so they underperform where long-range signals matter, such as biological networks, and their predictors ignore domain differences.
AI.method: A relation atlas captures structural associations between node pairs from global and local perspectives. A domain-guided prompting model generates domain-aware prompt tokens from contextual structures and performs prompt-guided in-context prediction for adaptive link inference.
AI.result: AtlasULP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse graph domains in extensive experiments. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A relation atlas combined with domain-guided prompting enables adaptive, training-free link prediction that generalizes across graph domains.

title: Acoustic Anomaly Detection for Early Identification of Drill Jamming
comment: Accepted for publication at IEEE INDIN 2026. 8 pages, 6 figures. (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted
summary: In the context of Industry 4.0, predictive maintenance is essential to minimize unplanned downtime and ensure operational safety. In machining processes, drill jamming is a critical failure that compromises both workpiece quality and tool integrity. This work proposes an acoustic anomaly detection system using ultrasonic sensors to identify pre-failure patterns in Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machining. We release a public dataset of time- and frequency-domain acoustic features from 17 drills, and benchmark semi-supervised autoencoder-based normality modelling against supervised XGBoost classification using Leave-One-Drill-Out validation. The results demonstrate that the Autoencoder is highly effective for industrial safety, achieving a Recall of 1.00 and a consolidated F1-score of 0.81. Furthermore, the threshold-independent analysis shows that the Autoencoder better separates normal and pre-failure acoustic patterns, achieving a consolidated AUC of 0.8294, compared with 0.7559 for the supervised model under inter-tool covariate shift. In contrast, the supervised XGBoost achieved an average F1-score of 0.55 and failed to detect failures in some of the evaluated drills. The findings highlight that the ultrasonic spectrum provides a reliable window for identifying incipient mechanical instabilities, and the AE model offers a robust safety envelope by anticipating all jamming events across the tested drill bits.

AI.tldr: Presents an ultrasonic acoustic anomaly detection system for drill jamming in CNC machining, benchmarking a semi-supervised autoencoder against supervised XGBoost. The autoencoder achieves a Recall of 1.00 and a consolidated F1-score of 0.81.
AI.motivation: Drill jamming damages both workpiece quality and tool integrity, and predictive maintenance is needed to minimize unplanned downtime. Supervised classifiers may generalize poorly across individual tools.
AI.method: Time- and frequency-domain acoustic features from 17 drills form a released public dataset. Semi-supervised autoencoder normality modelling is benchmarked against supervised XGBoost classification using Leave-One-Drill-Out validation.
AI.result: The autoencoder achieves Recall 1.00 and consolidated F1-score 0.81, with consolidated AUC 0.8294 versus 0.7559 for the supervised model under inter-tool covariate shift. XGBoost averages an F1-score of 0.55 and fails to detect failures on some drills.
AI.conclusion: The ultrasonic spectrum is a reliable window for incipient mechanical instabilities, and the autoencoder offers a robust safety envelope by anticipating all jamming events across the tested drill bits.

title: Test-Time Self-Play: Scaling without a Verifier
summary: Test-time scaling methods spend additional compute at deployment to improve a large language model's performance on a hard target problem. Most methods rely on a verifier that scores candidate solutions for correctness, using it to select among or refine the model's outputs. In many deployment regimes, however, a strong verifier on the target problem is unavailable. We introduce Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), an approach to test-time scaling using asymmetric self-play without reliance on a verifier. On a difficulty-calibrated subset of LiveCodeBench v6, TTSP is the best-performing method at every verifier strength we evaluate, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as the verifier weakens; in the no-verifier limit, TTSP yields a 35\% absolute improvement in mean@8. The gains hold across a range of verifier strengths, except when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.

AI.tldr: Proposes Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), a verifier-free test-time scaling method based on asymmetric self-play. On a difficulty-calibrated LiveCodeBench v6 subset it is the best method at every verifier strength evaluated, with a 35% absolute mean@8 improvement in the no-verifier limit.
AI.motivation: Test-time scaling usually relies on a verifier to select or refine outputs, but a strong verifier on the target problem is often unavailable, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as verifiers weaken.
AI.method: Asymmetric self-play is used at test time, so candidate solutions are improved without a verifier scoring them for correctness.
AI.result: TTSP is the best-performing method at every verifier strength evaluated, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as the verifier weakens. In the no-verifier limit it yields a 35% absolute improvement in mean@8. Gains hold across verifier strengths except when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.
AI.conclusion: Test-time self-play offers a way to scale compute on hard problems without a verifier, but it fails when the base policy almost never produces a correct answer.

title: When Scores Conflict with Preferences: Pre-Alignment Diagnosis and Adaptive Correction of Constraint Drift in DPO
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Corresponding author: Yan Yan
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is increasingly used in settings where pairwise preferences coexist with pointwise criteria such as response length, answer correctness, or safety scores. When the two disagree, standard DPO treats pairs whose preferred output scores worse on the pointwise criterion (conflict pairs) in the same way as the remaining (matching) pairs. We characterize a systematic failure mode, constraint drift: for sufficiently small updates, conflict pairs tend to increase constraint cost while matching pairs tend to repair it, and the net change depends on their balance. This balance yields a closed-form pre-alignment diagnostic, $\rho^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$, computable from dataset statistics, that indicates whether a dataset is self-correcting or requires intervention. Building on this diagnostic, we propose Conflict-aware DPO (CoDPO), which down-weights conflict pairs with a strength set from $\rho^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ rather than tuned, and adds an adaptive margin shift that addresses residual drift during training. Empirically, drift grows monotonically with conflict exposure on the conflict-dominated domains, and the intervention decision given by $\rho^{*}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ matches the observed drift on every domain, including one that it identifies as self-correcting. On all four domains of the main comparison, CoDPO reduces drift while largely preserving the preference learning of vanilla DPO. Compared with hard filtering and recent constrained and multi-objective baselines, CoDPO also achieves a more favorable drift-preference trade-off.

AI.tldr: Identifies constraint drift in DPO, where pairs whose preferred output scores worse on a pointwise criterion push constraint cost up, and proposes CoDPO, which down-weights these conflict pairs. CoDPO reduces drift while largely preserving vanilla DPO's preference learning on four domains.
AI.motivation: When pairwise preferences disagree with pointwise criteria such as length, correctness or safety, standard DPO treats conflict pairs the same as matching pairs, and this can increase constraint cost.
AI.method: A closed-form pre-alignment diagnostic, rho*_eq, computed from dataset statistics indicates whether a dataset is self-correcting or needs intervention. CoDPO down-weights conflict pairs with a strength set from this diagnostic rather than tuned by hand, and adds an adaptive margin shift to correct residual drift during training.
AI.result: Drift grows monotonically with conflict exposure on conflict-dominated domains, and the diagnostic's intervention decision matches observed drift on every domain, including one it identifies as self-correcting. On all four main domains CoDPO reduces drift while largely preserving preference learning, and it gives a more favorable drift-preference trade-off than hard filtering and recent constrained or multi-objective baselines.
AI.conclusion: The diagnostic indicates before training whether a preference dataset needs correction, and CoDPO offers an untuned, principled way to reduce constraint drift.

title: Adversarial Multiplicity: Cherry-Picked Models and the Limits of Disclosure
summary: Predictive multiplicity -- where similarly accurate models disagree on individual predictions -- can be leveraged to optimize secondary metrics (e.g., fairness) without loss in predictive performance. However, exploiting multiplicity opens the opportunity for motivated parties (or coding agents gaming their objectives) to steer predictions toward their own ends, such as in litigation or consumer disputes with automated decision-making tools. In these adversarial multiplicity settings, we distinguish soft manipulation, where parties optimize over innocuous model choices (e.g., hyperparameter tuning, feature engineering), from hard manipulation, where parties directly perturb model parameters. We find a sufficiently flexible model can be manipulated to reverse any individual prediction with minimal change in predictive performance while passing black-box audits, making hard manipulation viable in most regulatory settings. Soft manipulation has smaller effects but can pass white-box audits requiring full access to code and data. Even aggregate estimates can be manipulated: a model's estimated effect of climate change on wildfires can be fully reversed by hard edits and soft search. We find the Reconcile algorithm typically resolves most disagreements between models, but more often in favor of the manipulator when the opposing model is chosen adversarially compared to at random. We map which manipulations can plausibly pass existing regulations and disclosure policies, and recommend mitigations such as pre-registration, proof of model training, sensitivity analyses, multi-metric evaluations, and committing to versioned public models.

AI.tldr: Shows that predictive multiplicity lets motivated parties manipulate individual predictions and even aggregate estimates, through soft and hard manipulation that can pass existing audits. The authors map which manipulations could plausibly pass current regulations and disclosure policies and recommend mitigations.
AI.motivation: Predictive multiplicity, where similarly accurate models disagree on individual predictions, can be exploited to optimize secondary metrics such as fairness, but the same flexibility opens the door to adversarial steering in litigation or consumer disputes.
AI.method: Soft manipulation optimizes over innocuous model choices such as hyperparameters and feature engineering, while hard manipulation directly perturbs model parameters. The authors test manipulation against black-box and white-box audits and examine the Reconcile algorithm when the opposing model is chosen adversarially versus at random.
AI.result: A sufficiently flexible model can be manipulated to reverse any individual prediction with minimal change in predictive performance while passing black-box audits. Soft manipulation has smaller effects but can pass white-box audits. Even an aggregate estimate, the effect of climate change on wildfires, can be fully reversed by hard edits and soft search. Reconcile usually resolves disagreements, but more often in the manipulator's favor when the opposing model is adversarial.
AI.conclusion: Existing audits and disclosure policies can be defeated, so mitigations such as pre-registration, proof of model training, sensitivity analyses, multi-metric evaluation and committing to versioned public models are needed.

title: Spectral symmetry fingerprints in equivariant representations
summary: Symmetry governs the organization of physical structures, while symmetry breaking reveals their transformations. In geometric deep learning, symmetry imposes rank constraints on equivariant representations, limiting the expressive capacity of equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs). Here we show that these constraints can instead be exploited: the singular-value spectra of equivariant representations provide a unified fingerprint of structural symmetry. We introduce spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP), which enable discrete point-group identification through rank-template matching and continuous symmetry analysis by quantifying spectral energy beyond target rank constraints. SymFP is orientation invariant and architecture agnostic, enabling a parameter-free GNN implementation. Its spectra can be reused across multiple target groups, and the resulting leakage scores satisfy subgroup monotonicity. Across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies, SymFP accurately identifies point groups, tracks controlled symmetry breaking and reveals local and degree-resolved symmetry changes that can be obscured by global geometric measures. These results establish the spectral structure of equivariant representations as a general framework for characterizing symmetry across physical systems.

AI.tldr: Introduces spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP), which use the singular-value spectra of equivariant representations to identify point groups and quantify symmetry breaking. It accurately identifies point groups across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies.
AI.motivation: The rank constraints that symmetry imposes on equivariant representations are usually seen as limiting the expressivity of equivariant GNNs, and global geometric measures can obscure local and degree-resolved symmetry changes.
AI.method: The singular-value spectra of equivariant representations serve as a symmetry fingerprint. Discrete point groups are identified by rank-template matching, and continuous symmetry is quantified by spectral energy beyond target rank constraints. SymFP is orientation invariant and architecture agnostic, enables a parameter-free GNN implementation, and its leakage scores satisfy subgroup monotonicity.
AI.result: SymFP accurately identifies point groups across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies, tracks controlled symmetry breaking, and reveals local and degree-resolved symmetry changes that global geometric measures can obscure.
AI.conclusion: The spectral structure of equivariant representations is a general framework for characterizing symmetry across physical systems, turning the rank constraints that symmetry imposes into a diagnostic signal.

title: IMUDINO: Self-distilled Foundation Model for Inertial Sensing
summary: We present IMUDINO, the first foundation model (FM) for inertial sensing to achieve competitive performance across diverse sensing tasks including human activity recognition (HAR), health, motion capture, and odometry. Prior inertial FMs often focus on one subfield of inertial sensing and sometimes underperform state-of-the-art supervised methods (e.g., in HAR), making their scope considerably narrower than FMs for vision and natural language. Moreover, they often require fixed input length and sampling rate, and generalize poorly to unseen sensor locations. To build a general-purpose foundation model for inertial sensing, we adapt the DINO self-supervised learning (SSL) paradigm to inertial data through a set of semantics-preserving motion transformations that simulate variations in motion pattern and sensor setup. For model architecture, we use a plain transformer encoder with frequency-aware positional encoding that natively supports varying input length and sampling rate. This simple setup proved remarkably effective for learning global and dense features generalizable across users, sensor setups, tasks, and, in the case of robot odometry, embodiments. We hope IMUDINO can serve as a backbone for inertial sensing and kickstart the development of general-purpose inertial FMs.

AI.tldr: Presents IMUDINO, a foundation model for inertial sensing that adapts DINO self-supervised learning with motion transformations and a plain transformer with frequency-aware positional encoding. It achieves competitive performance across activity recognition, health, motion capture and odometry.
AI.motivation: Prior inertial foundation models often cover only one subfield, sometimes underperform state-of-the-art supervised methods such as in HAR, need fixed input lengths and sampling rates, and generalize poorly to unseen sensor locations.
AI.method: DINO self-supervised learning is adapted to inertial data through semantics-preserving motion transformations that simulate variation in motion pattern and sensor setup. A plain transformer encoder with frequency-aware positional encoding natively handles varying input length and sampling rate.
AI.result: The model learns global and dense features that generalize across users, sensor setups, tasks and, in the case of robot odometry, embodiments. The abstract reports competitive performance but gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The simple setup is a candidate backbone for inertial sensing and could help start the development of general-purpose inertial foundation models.

title: Two-stage residual learning for calibrated uncertainty in solar irradiance forecasts
summary: Accurate forecasting of renewable generation requires not only point predictions but also reliable estimates of the uncertainty attached to them, particularly at extended horizons. Machine learning models are increasingly used to predict solar output, but they typically report a single value and capture the associated uncertainty poorly. The standard remedy is to train a model to predict the parameters of an assumed probability distribution directly. Here we develop an alternative two-stage method, motivated by synthetic solar signal generation, in which the forecast error is modeled separately from the expected irradiance. A first long short-term memory (LSTM) network predicts the expected global horizontal irradiance, and a second network models the distribution of the forecast error, which is added back to the mean to give both the forecast and its uncertainty. Using historical weather data from the National Solar Radiation Database and a probability integral transform evaluation, we show that explicitly modeling the error brings the predicted standard deviation markedly closer to the historical value, reducing the deviation between the two by 34.6 percent for a standalone LSTM and by 56.5 percent when the LSTM is coupled to Gaussian process regression, the most reliable of the configurations tested. Because the method models the total forecast error directly, it captures the full predictive uncertainty that matters for decisions, rather than only the model contribution that dropout-based approaches estimate.

AI.tldr: Proposes a two-stage method for calibrated uncertainty in solar irradiance forecasts, where an LSTM predicts expected irradiance and a second network models the forecast error distribution. Explicit error modelling brings the predicted standard deviation closer to the historical value, reducing the gap by 34.6% for a standalone LSTM and 56.5% for an LSTM coupled with Gaussian process regression.
AI.motivation: Machine learning solar forecasts usually report a single value and capture uncertainty poorly, especially at extended horizons. The standard remedy of training a model to predict the parameters of an assumed distribution directly is the usual alternative.
AI.method: A first LSTM predicts the expected global horizontal irradiance. A second network models the distribution of the forecast error, which is added back to the mean to give both the forecast and its uncertainty. Evaluation uses National Solar Radiation Database weather data and a probability integral transform analysis.
AI.result: Modelling the error explicitly brings the predicted standard deviation markedly closer to the historical value, reducing the deviation by 34.6% for a standalone LSTM and by 56.5% when the LSTM is coupled to Gaussian process regression, the most reliable configuration tested.
AI.conclusion: Modelling the total forecast error directly captures the full predictive uncertainty that matters for decisions, whereas dropout-based approaches estimate only the model contribution.

title: Echoes of Error: Residual-Directional Local Rollout Consistency for Timeseries Forecasting
summary: In time-series forecasting, rollout errors are not merely one-step fitting discrepancies: once fed back into the evolving state, they can perturb future predictions. We formalize this effect through local rollout consistency, which compares the next prediction produced under teacher forcing with that produced under free running. In principle, this consistency can be enforced directly by tracking the residual-induced perturbation of the next state. In practice, however, the residual-to-state alignment operator is often difficult to design when the input state and output block have different dimensions, heterogeneous components, or architecture-dependent layouts. We therefore use a first-order local surrogate that penalizes the Jacobian-vector product of the predictor along the actual feedback perturbation, suppressing precisely the directions through which self-generated errors remain visible to future predictions. We further give the same loss a geometric interpretation near a predictive manifold: by controlling residual-induced directions that probe the normal bundle, the objective yields theoretical conditions under which free-running trajectories remain inside a stability tube around the manifold. Experiments on time series forecasting tasks support this view, showing that the proposed regularization improves predictive accuracy. More broadly, our results suggest a training principle for time-series forecasters and sequential predictors: a model should not only make small one-step errors, but also learn not to let its own errors echo into the future. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes a residual-directional regularizer that penalizes the Jacobian-vector product of the predictor along the actual feedback perturbation, so that self-generated rollout errors do not echo into future predictions. Experiments on time-series forecasting tasks show improved predictive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Rollout errors fed back into the evolving state can perturb future predictions. Enforcing consistency between teacher-forced and free-running predictions directly is hard when input and output dimensions or architectures differ.
AI.method: A first-order local surrogate penalizes the Jacobian-vector product of the predictor along the actual feedback perturbation, suppressing the directions through which self-generated errors remain visible to future predictions. A geometric interpretation near a predictive manifold gives conditions under which free-running trajectories stay inside a stability tube.
AI.result: Experiments on time-series forecasting tasks support the view that the proposed regularization improves predictive accuracy. The abstract gives no specific numbers or datasets.
AI.conclusion: A forecaster should learn not only to make small one-step errors but also to keep its own errors from echoing into the future, a general training principle for time-series and sequential predictors.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Kernel Machines: A Comprehensive Analysis
summary: Kernel machines are an important class of models in machine learning. However, the question of how robust modern kernel machines are to adversarial examples has not been studied comprehensively. In this paper, we provide a thorough empirical investigation of the adversarial robustness of kernel-based models for both binary and multiclass classification tasks, via white-box and black-box evasion attacks. We evaluate the native robustness of kernel machines, random feature classifiers, and the relatively newer Recursive Feature Machines. In addition, we provide an algorithm for approximate adversarial training of kernel machines. Our experiments on classification tasks on image and tabular datasets strongly indicate that kernel machines are natively more robust than neural networks, i.e., their performance degrades more gracefully against adversarial perturbations.

AI.tldr: Empirically studies the adversarial robustness of kernel machines, random feature classifiers and Recursive Feature Machines under white-box and black-box evasion attacks. Kernel machines are natively more robust than neural networks, degrading more gracefully under adversarial perturbations.
AI.motivation: The adversarial robustness of modern kernel machines has not been studied comprehensively, even though they are an important class of models for binary and multiclass classification.
AI.method: Thorough white-box and black-box evasion attacks are applied to kernel machines, random feature classifiers and Recursive Feature Machines on image and tabular datasets. The authors also provide an algorithm for approximate adversarial training of kernel machines.
AI.result: On classification tasks with image and tabular datasets, kernel machines are natively more robust than neural networks, with performance degrading more gracefully against adversarial perturbations.
AI.conclusion: Kernel-based models are a more robust alternative to neural networks under evasion attacks, and the paper also offers an approximate adversarial training algorithm for them.

title: Learning Multi-Agent Orchestration:Higher-Order Interactions in Policy Improvement
summary: Learned orchestration has emerged as a promising paradigm for large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems, in which a central orchestrator selects agents and controls the information they receive throughout a task. Despite rapid empirical progress, existing methods train the orchestrator by crediting each decision with its own advantage, implicitly assuming that the other decisions in the episode stay fixed. This assumption fails in orchestration, where the contribution of each decision to the final outcome depends on the decisions preceding it, so the gain of a joint update is not the sum of its per-decision effects. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{IAPO}, an interaction-aware policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for interactions among decisions. Specifically, IAPO exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into the effects of individual decisions and their interactions, which we prove can account for half of the attainable gain, and then optimizes both from sampled trajectories while certifying that every update is an improvement. On long-input versions of GSM8K, MATH, DROP, MBPP and HumanEval, against fifteen published multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, IAPO's deployed plans reach the strongest system's accuracy with fewer tokens, and removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 points of accuracy on code.

AI.tldr: Proposes IAPO, an interaction-aware policy optimization framework for learned orchestration of LLM multi-agent systems, which decomposes performance differences into individual decision effects and their interactions. On long-input GSM8K, MATH, DROP, MBPP and HumanEval, its plans reach the strongest of fifteen baselines' accuracy with fewer tokens.
AI.motivation: Existing methods train the orchestrator by crediting each decision with its own advantage, implicitly assuming the other decisions stay fixed. In orchestration, each decision's contribution depends on the decisions preceding it, so the gain of a joint update is not the sum of per-decision effects.
AI.method: IAPO exactly decomposes the performance difference between two policies into the effects of individual decisions and their interactions, and optimizes both from sampled trajectories while certifying that every update is an improvement. The authors prove the interaction term can account for half of the attainable gain.
AI.result: Against fifteen published multi-agent and workflow-search systems on the same 7B executor, IAPO's deployed plans reach the strongest system's accuracy with fewer tokens. Removing the interaction term costs 7 to 17 accuracy points on code.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for interactions among orchestration decisions matters, since ignoring them costs substantial accuracy on code tasks, which makes interaction-aware credit assignment important for learned orchestrators.

title: RLGPA: A Reinforcement Learning-Guided Granularity Planning Attack for Decision-Based Sparse Adversarial Examples
summary: Decision-based sparse attacks must reduce perturbation support using only the victim's predicted label. The best restoration strategy varies as support contracts: coarse removal works early, while tail states need finer, history-aware tests. We propose RLGPA, an online reinforcement learning method that schedules support-reduction executors and their granularity under a hard query budget. A masked Dueling Double DQN selects among seven stable policy--scale actions; each action produces support-relative restoration groups that are rebuilt after every macro decision. A feasibility-preserving executor commits only adversarial restorations and feeds support gain and query cost back to the planner. Under the matched top-1-label oracle, RLGPA reaches 61\% targeted ASR at sparsity 0.01 on CIFAR-10 (vs. 25\% SparseEvo, 0\% Pointwise), and 75.5\%/73.0\% on ResNet50/ViT at sparsity 0.005 (vs. 29.0\%/15.5\%). A fixed-probe test reduces median \(L_0\) from 165 to 23 after 40 images without any update. State-blind and state-shuffled controls degrade significantly, confirming that the learned policy uses attack state; the main gains come from state-conditioned executor scheduling and dynamic repartition. The source code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes RLGPA, an online reinforcement learning method that schedules support-reduction executors and their granularity under a hard query budget for decision-based sparse adversarial attacks. It reaches 61% targeted ASR at sparsity 0.01 on CIFAR-10, versus 25% for SparseEvo and 0% for Pointwise.
AI.motivation: Decision-based sparse attacks must shrink perturbation support using only the victim's predicted label, and the best restoration strategy varies as the support contracts: coarse removal works early, while tail states need finer, history-aware tests.
AI.method: A masked Dueling Double DQN selects among seven stable policy-scale actions, each producing support-relative restoration groups that are rebuilt after every macro decision. A feasibility-preserving executor commits only adversarial restorations and feeds support gain and query cost back to the planner.
AI.result: Under the matched top-1-label oracle, RLGPA reaches 61% targeted ASR at sparsity 0.01 on CIFAR-10 (versus 25% for SparseEvo and 0% for Pointwise), and 75.5% and 73.0% on ResNet50 and ViT at sparsity 0.005 (versus 29.0% and 15.5%). A fixed-probe test reduces median L0 from 165 to 23 after 40 images without any update. State-blind and state-shuffled controls degrade significantly.
AI.conclusion: The main gains come from state-conditioned executor scheduling and dynamic repartition, confirming that the learned policy uses attack state.

title: Understanding Data Influence in Transportation Networks: A Physics-Constrained Influence-Function Framework
summary: Understanding how individual training observations influence model predictions is important for developing reliable and interpretable data-driven transportation systems. Existing influence-function methods, however, are primarily formulated for unconstrained learning and do not explicitly account for physical constraints that couple different components of a transportation network. Under such constraints, perturbing a training observation can affect model parameters and predictions only through physically feasible directions, potentially changing how its influence propagates across the network. This paper develops a hard physics-informed influence-function framework for constrained learning, in which training-data influence is characterized within the physically feasible space defined by network constraints. The analytical results reveal how physical constraints alter the magnitude, direction, and spatial distribution of training-sample influence relative to conventional influence measures. Using traffic prediction under flow-conservation constraints as a case study, we show that influential observations identified by the proposed framework differ systematically from those identified by classical influence functions. Through orthogonal decomposition, we quantitatively characterize how much of a perturbation in the training data is propagated through the network via the flow-conservation constraints and how much is removed by the constraint projection. The proposed influence framework provides a physically consistent approach for evaluating training-data influence in constrained transportation learning problems, with potential applications to data diagnostics, sensor evaluation, and targeted data collection.

AI.tldr: Proposes a hard physics-informed influence-function framework that characterizes training-data influence within the physically feasible space defined by network constraints. Using traffic prediction under flow-conservation constraints, it shows that influential observations differ systematically from those found by classical influence functions.
AI.motivation: Existing influence-function methods are formulated for unconstrained learning and ignore physical constraints that couple network components, so a perturbation can affect predictions only through physically feasible directions, which changes how influence propagates.
AI.method: Training-data influence is characterized within the physically feasible space defined by network constraints. An orthogonal decomposition quantifies how much of a training-data perturbation propagates through the network via flow-conservation constraints and how much is removed by the constraint projection.
AI.result: The analysis shows how physical constraints alter the magnitude, direction and spatial distribution of training-sample influence relative to conventional influence measures. Under flow-conservation constraints in traffic prediction, the influential observations identified by the framework differ systematically from those identified by classical influence functions.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives a physically consistent way to evaluate training-data influence in constrained transportation learning, with potential uses in data diagnostics, sensor evaluation and targeted data collection.

title: Provable Zeroth-Order Safe Exploration for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
summary: Safe reinforcement learning from human feedback (Safe-RLHF) seeks to improve helpfulness while satisfying harmlessness constraints. Existing primal-dual approaches can converge to feasible policies but do not prevent constraint violations during training. We study a stronger requirement, safe exploration for RLHF, under which every policy executed during training, including auxiliary exploration policies, remains feasible. We propose Zeroth-Order Log-Barrier Policy Gradient (ZO-LBPG), a reward-model-free method that optimizes a log-barrier objective using zeroth-order estimates derived directly from human preferences. To ensure safety under noisy feedback, we combine conservative constraint margin estimates with coupled rollouts and an adaptive step size that prevents updates from crossing constraint boundaries. We prove that, with high probability, all iterates and exploration policies remain strictly feasible, and that ZO-LBPG globally converges to an approximately optimal constrained policy. We establish a sample complexity of $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-6}+d^3\varepsilon^{-5})$ trajectories and $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-8}+d^5\varepsilon^{-7})$ human queries. Experiments on a synthetic CMDP and a language-model alignment task corroborate the training-time safety guarantees.

AI.tldr: Proposes ZO-LBPG, a reward-model-free zeroth-order log-barrier policy gradient method for Safe-RLHF that keeps every policy executed during training, including exploration policies, strictly feasible. It proves high-probability feasibility and global convergence to an approximately optimal constrained policy.
AI.motivation: Existing primal-dual Safe-RLHF approaches converge to feasible policies but do not prevent constraint violations during training, so safe exploration is not guaranteed.
AI.method: A log-barrier policy gradient driven by zeroth-order estimates derived directly from human preferences, combined with conservative constraint margin estimates, coupled rollouts and an adaptive step size that stops updates from crossing constraint boundaries.
AI.result: With high probability all iterates and exploration policies remain strictly feasible, and the method globally converges to an approximately optimal constrained policy, with sample complexity O~(eps^-6 + d^3 eps^-5) trajectories and O~(eps^-8 + d^5 eps^-7) human queries. Experiments on a synthetic CMDP and a language-model alignment task corroborate the training-time safety guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Safe exploration during RLHF can be obtained with provable guarantees and without a reward model, so safety holds throughout training rather than only at convergence.

title: MambaTG: Candidate-Aware State Space Modeling for Future Link Prediction on Temporal Graphs
summary: Future link prediction on temporal graphs involves both repeated interactions between previously connected node pairs and first-time interactions between pairs with no prior interaction. While repeated-edge prediction can exploit direct pairwise evidence, unseen-edge prediction must generalize beyond historical recurrence. Existing temporal graph models often exploit signals tied to recurring interactions or historical overlap, which are highly informative for repeated edges but become limited or unavailable for unseen edges, contributing to substantial performance degradation on unseen-edge prediction. Based on this observation, we identify two complementary signals for modeling sequential dynamics beyond historical recurrence: (1) historical-sequence evolution, which captures dependencies among the source node's chronologically ordered interactions, and (2) candidate--history compatibility, which captures how well a candidate fits the source node's evolving history. Based on the decomposition, we propose MambaTG, a candidate-aware Mamba-based framework that jointly models these two signals. Mamba provides a natural mechanism for this design: its selective recurrence captures the evolution of ordered interaction histories, while its input-dependent state transitions allow the history state to adapt to different candidate inputs. Extensive experiments on 13 temporal graph datasets against 13 representative baselines show that MambaTG achieves strong and consistent performance across both repeated and unseen edges while remaining computationally efficient.

AI.tldr: Proposes MambaTG, a candidate-aware Mamba framework that jointly models historical-sequence evolution and candidate-history compatibility for future link prediction on temporal graphs. It performs strongly on both repeated and unseen edges while remaining computationally efficient.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal graph models exploit recurrence or historical-overlap signals that help repeated edges but become limited for unseen edges, causing substantial performance degradation on unseen-edge prediction.
AI.method: Decomposes the problem into two complementary signals; selective Mamba recurrence captures the evolution of ordered interaction histories, and input-dependent state transitions let the history state adapt to each candidate.
AI.result: Evaluated on 13 temporal graph datasets against 13 representative baselines, achieving strong and consistent performance across both repeated and unseen edges.
AI.conclusion: Modelling sequential dynamics beyond historical recurrence, with candidate-aware state transitions, addresses the unseen-edge weakness of temporal graph models at efficient cost.

title: ACSeL: Adaptive Configuration Search for Hardware-Constrained LLM Inference
summary: Serving large language models (LLMs) under tight memory and latency service-level objectives (SLOs), including on edge devices, requires jointly selecting the model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and mixed-precision quantization recipes. Exhaustive search over this combinatorially large space is infeasible. Unlike data-center serving, which often prioritizes throughput or generation speed, resource-constrained deployments typically set memory and latency budgets as constraints and then seek the configuration with the highest generation quality among feasible ones. To this end, we propose ACSeL, a framework that identifies configurations predicted to satisfy deployment constraints while achieving high predicted generation quality. To enable efficient quality estimation, we use Relative Model Quality Degradation (RMQD), a proxy based on the divergence between the candidate and reference models' next-token distributions over a small calibration corpus. Across the evaluated model sizes and precisions, RMQD is inexpensive to evaluate and strongly correlated with downstream benchmark performance. ACSeL combines (i) a lightweight quality surrogate that predicts RMQD directly from a configuration; (ii) Few-shot Median Calibration (FMC), which calibrates operator-profile-based latency estimates using a small number of end-to-end profiles; and (iii) a structured search algorithm BandPareto for exploring layerwise mixed-precision configurations. Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation and an NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge platform show that FMC substantially improves deployment feasibility, while BandPareto + FMC achieves the highest feasibility and the lowest RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations in the evaluation set.

AI.tldr: Proposes ACSeL, a framework that searches for LLM serving configurations (model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, mixed-precision recipe) predicted to meet memory and latency constraints while maximising generation quality. Quality is estimated with a cheap proxy, RMQD.
AI.motivation: Serving LLMs under tight memory and latency SLOs, including on edge devices, requires joint configuration choices in a combinatorially large space where exhaustive search is infeasible, and throughput-oriented data-centre methods do not fit constrained deployments.
AI.method: Combines a lightweight quality surrogate that predicts RMQD from a configuration, Few-shot Median Calibration (FMC) that calibrates operator-profile latency estimates with a few end-to-end profiles, and the BandPareto structured search over layerwise mixed-precision configurations. RMQD is the divergence between candidate and reference next-token distributions on a small calibration corpus.
AI.result: On an NVIDIA RTX A6000 and an NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge platform, FMC substantially improves deployment feasibility, and BandPareto with FMC achieves the highest feasibility and the lowest RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations.
AI.conclusion: A cheap quality proxy that correlates with downstream benchmarks, together with calibrated latency estimates, makes it efficient to find feasible high-quality LLM configurations on resource-constrained hardware.

title: Binding Paraphrased Instructions to Encountered Objects in sLLM Agents under Partial Observability
summary: Reliable deployment of LLM agents requires grounding diverse user expressions in their environments. Although RL-finetuned smaller large language model (sLLM) agents rival larger prompted LLMs on embodied tasks, their robustness to instruction paraphrases remains unclear. We introduce ALFWorld-Para to evaluate this robustness under controlled paraphrases, revealing 21-52% declines in success rates (SRs), predominantly driven by object synonyms. Despite retaining knowledge of synonym referents, agents often fail to take the corresponding objects even after observing them, exposing a gap between referential knowledge and object binding. Partial observability further complicates binding, as referents may remain unseen or have already been encountered under different labels. To address this challenge, we propose BINDIntent, a training-free framework that probabilistically binds referring expressions to observed labels using semantic proximity and estimated persistence against unseen candidates. Without additional training or LLM calls, BINDIntent improves synonym-paraphrase success of RL-finetuned sLLMs by 17.5-49.1 percentage points (pp) with only 0.4 ms of CPU overhead per step. It also raises GiGPO-7B's overall SR from 61.8% to 77.4%, surpassing a prompted 24B LLM. Code and benchmark are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces ALFWorld-Para to test the paraphrase robustness of RL-finetuned small LLM agents, and BINDIntent, a training-free framework that binds paraphrased referring expressions to observed object labels. It raises the overall success rate of GiGPO-7B from 61.8% to 77.4%.
AI.motivation: RL-finetuned sLLM agents rival larger prompted LLMs on embodied tasks, but their robustness to instruction paraphrases is unclear, and partial observability complicates binding expressions to objects that were already encountered under other labels.
AI.method: BINDIntent probabilistically binds referring expressions to observed labels using semantic proximity and estimated persistence against unseen candidates, with no additional training and no extra LLM calls.
AI.result: Paraphrases cause 21-52% declines in success rate on ALFWorld-Para, mostly from object synonyms. BINDIntent improves synonym-paraphrase success of RL-finetuned sLLMs by 17.5-49.1 percentage points with 0.4 ms of CPU overhead per step, and lifts GiGPO-7B overall SR from 61.8% to 77.4%, surpassing a prompted 24B LLM.
AI.conclusion: The failure lies in binding referential knowledge to observed objects rather than in missing knowledge, and a lightweight training-free binding step recovers much of the loss.

title: Monotone Viability Learning for Offline Safe Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline safe reinforcement learning requires reliable long-horizon safety estimates from fixed data. Learning Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) viability in this setting calls for semantic preservation, convergence, and numerical stability. To address these challenges, we propose Monotone Viability Learning (MoViL), which learns viable sets from offline transitions through monotone finite-horizon set recursion. The recursion preserves finite-horizon safety semantics and converges to the infinite-horizon viability kernel. Binary supervision maintains a fixed target scale across horizons, avoiding discount-induced numerical attenuation. We further establish sufficient conditions for recovering behavior-supported viable subsets. The learned viability estimates are used to certify actions at deployment. Dubins car experiments validate the numerical accuracy of the learned viable sets. Evaluations on safe RL benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art reward-cost performance. MoViL satisfies the average cost constraint on every task and achieves the lowest average cost among the compared methods. These results highlight MoViL's potential to extend long-horizon HJ viability analysis to safety-critical systems where reliable dynamics models are unavailable and online exploration is unsafe.

AI.tldr: Proposes MoViL, which learns Hamilton-Jacobi viability sets for offline safe RL through a monotone finite-horizon set recursion that converges to the infinite-horizon viability kernel. It satisfies the average cost constraint on every benchmark task and reports state-of-the-art reward-cost performance.
AI.motivation: Offline safe RL needs reliable long-horizon safety estimates from fixed data, and learning HJ viability requires semantic preservation, convergence and numerical stability at once.
AI.method: Monotone finite-horizon set recursion over offline transitions, with binary supervision that keeps a fixed target scale across horizons to avoid discount-induced numerical attenuation; the learned viable sets certify actions at deployment.
AI.result: Dubins car experiments validate the numerical accuracy of the learned viable sets. On safe RL benchmarks MoViL satisfies the average cost constraint on every task and achieves the lowest average cost among the compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Monotone viability learning can extend long-horizon HJ viability analysis to safety-critical systems where reliable dynamics models are unavailable and online exploration is unsafe.

title: Online Learning with Ordered Experts (via Two-point Feedback)
summary: We study adversarial online learning with expert recommendations in a totally ordered action space, where the experts' recommendations may change and be reordered arbitrarily. Our focus is two-point feedback: on each round the learner plays two current recommendations, observes both, and pays their average. We study two problems. In the separated monotone problem, the loss is the sum of a hidden nondecreasing component and a hidden nonincreasing component, and a query reveals the two components separately. In the BV problem, the losses are bounded and have bounded variation (BV) along the order, and a query reveals only the loss. In the separated monotone problem, two paid observations achieve \[ O\bigl(\log(|\cF|T)\sqrt{T\log|\cF|}\bigr) \] regret against the best of $|\cF|$ experts, within a logarithmic factor of the classical full-information bound. For the BV problem, we obtain $\wtO(\sqrt T+|\cF|)$ regret. We give an application in dynamic pricing with expert advice, showing that two-option menus matches the full information rate up to $\log$ factors. The main technical ingredient is a marginal-preserving endpoint flow estimator. Two observations reveal a loss increment along the order; random paths supply telescoping identities that turn this local information into unbiased loss estimates for all current recommendations. A reversible pair sampler preserves the learner's intended marginal at both played actions. The estimator's second-moment and stability bounds support online updates for both feedback models.

AI.tldr: Studies adversarial online learning with expert recommendations in a totally ordered action space under two-point feedback, where the learner plays two recommendations and pays their average. It gives regret within a logarithmic factor of full-information bounds for the separated monotone problem and O~(sqrt(T) + |F|) regret for the BV problem.
AI.motivation: Expert recommendations can change and be reordered arbitrarily, and the learner observes only two-point feedback, so classical full-information guarantees do not directly apply.
AI.method: A marginal-preserving endpoint flow estimator: two observations reveal a loss increment along the order, random paths give telescoping identities that turn this into unbiased loss estimates for all current recommendations, and a reversible pair sampler preserves the intended marginal at both played actions.
AI.result: For the separated monotone problem, O(log(|F|T) sqrt(T log|F|)) regret against the best of |F| experts, within a logarithmic factor of the full-information bound. For the BV problem, O~(sqrt(T) + |F|) regret. In dynamic pricing with expert advice, two-option menus match the full-information rate up to log factors.
AI.conclusion: For these structured problems, two paid observations per round are nearly as informative as full information, and the estimator's moment and stability bounds support online updates under both feedback models.

title: Measuring the Marginal Value of Verifier-Based RL Beyond Supervised Fine-Tuning
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Code and artifacts: this https URL
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is usually evaluated as an alternative to supervised fine-tuning (SFT), or as a stage that follows it, with the implicit assumption that the RL stage contributes gains of its own. We measure that contribution directly, in a controlled setting where both stages can be run to completion and compared exactly. We built gpu-train-debug, a deterministic benchmark of 1,877 synthetic GPU and LLM training failure diagnosis tasks across 30 archetypes, graded by a programmatic verifier with partial credit, and calibrated so that a mid-tier model scores in a 0.60 to 0.75 band.
