A pilot produced a surprise: 1,200 gold demonstrations nearly solved the benchmark (SFT 0.785 on the hard split), while 15 steps of GRPO from the base model did not move it (0.314 vs 0.311 base). We therefore amended the study, in writing and before the full run, to ask the sharper question: what does verifier-based RL add beyond demonstrations? At the pre-registered scale (60 GRPO steps, learning rate 1e-6), the answer is: no detectable improvement in-distribution (+0.22 points, 95% CI [-0.06, +0.51]), and a modest but measurable improvement under distribution shift (+0.33 points on a held-out OOD split, CI [+0.02, +0.68]). SFT accounted for most of the available improvement, while verifier-based RL produced only modest additional gains under distribution shift. The residual errors SFT leaves are mostly systematic, identical across samples, which likely reduces the within-group learning signal available to GRPO. A full 60-step cold-start GRPO arm confirms the pilot at the full horizon. The whole study cost $8.69 of compute and is fully reproducible from archived generations, frozen configs, and tagged code.

AI.tldr: Measures the marginal contribution of verifier-based RL (GRPO) beyond supervised fine-tuning, using a deterministic benchmark of 1,877 GPU and LLM training failure diagnosis tasks. SFT accounts for most of the available gain, and RL adds no detectable in-distribution improvement and only a modest gain under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: RLVR is usually evaluated as an alternative to SFT or as a stage after it, with an implicit assumption that the RL stage adds its own gains, which had not been measured directly in a controlled setting.
AI.method: Built gpu-train-debug, 1,877 synthetic tasks across 30 archetypes graded by a programmatic verifier with partial credit and calibrated so a mid-tier model scores 0.60 to 0.75; compared SFT on 1,200 gold demonstrations with 60 GRPO steps at learning rate 1e-6, using a pre-registered scale after the study was amended before the full run.
AI.result: SFT reaches 0.785 on the hard split, while a 15-step GRPO pilot from the base model did not move it (0.314 vs 0.311 base). At the pre-registered scale GRPO gives +0.22 points in-distribution (95% CI [-0.06, +0.51]) and +0.33 points on a held-out OOD split (CI [+0.02, +0.68]), for a total compute cost of 8.69 USD.
AI.conclusion: Most of the improvement comes from demonstrations, and the residual SFT errors are mostly systematic and identical across samples, which likely shrinks the within-group learning signal available to GRPO.

title: WaSP: Wasserstein Data Synthesis Pipeline for Solver-Free Operator Learning
summary: Neural operators offer fast surrogates for solving PDEs, but training them typically requires expensive input-solution pairs. Two solver-free alternatives include physics-informed learning and training on manufactured data. Physics-informed learning approximates solutions by minimizing PDE residuals. While the residual norm must be strong enough to control solution error, stronger norms increase mini-batch variance and hinder optimization. Manufactured data constructs input-solution pairs for learning by applying the PDE operator to artificial solutions. However, the resulting training distribution can be mutually singular with the target distribution, yielding poor accuracy on the target distribution. We introduce the Wasserstein Data Synthesis Pipeline (WaSP), which trains on manufactured input-solution pairs while gradually mitigating the distribution shift. WaSP synthesizes new pairs by applying the learned operator to a path of intermediate distributions converging to the target input distribution. Training proceeds in stages along this path. At each stage, the previous surrogate generates solutions, and the exact PDE operator derives corresponding inputs, yielding training pairs for the next surrogate. Theoretically, we prove a stepwise error-propagation bound for the distribution shift introduced during synthesis. Empirically, WaSP reduces solution error by $3.9\times$ to $9.5\times$ compared to existing solver-free methods on PDEs such as Allen-Cahn, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, and Ginzburg-Landau, and better reproduces the two chaotic systems' statistical observables.

AI.tldr: Proposes WaSP, a solver-free neural operator training method that trains on manufactured input-solution pairs while gradually moving the training distribution toward the target input distribution. It reduces solution error by 3.9x to 9.5x compared with existing solver-free methods.
AI.motivation: Neural operators normally need expensive input-solution pairs, physics-informed training is limited by the strength of residual norms and mini-batch variance, and manufactured data can be mutually singular with the target distribution, giving poor target accuracy.
AI.method: The Wasserstein Data Synthesis Pipeline trains in stages along a path of intermediate distributions converging to the target input distribution; at each stage the previous surrogate generates solutions and the exact PDE operator derives matching inputs for the next surrogate.
AI.result: Reduces solution error by 3.9x to 9.5x relative to existing solver-free methods on Allen-Cahn, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Ginzburg-Landau equations, and better reproduces the statistical observables of two chaotic systems. A stepwise error-propagation bound for the synthesis-induced distribution shift is proved.
AI.conclusion: Gradually mitigating the distribution shift during synthesis makes manufactured data a practical solver-free route to accurate neural operators, including for chaotic systems.

title: Simple Meta-Learning for HPO and CASH Using Performance Representations
summary: Bayesian optimization for Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) and Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter Optimization (CASH) often relies on explicit hyperparameter encodings as surrogate inputs. In high-dimensional search spaces, however, such representations can make it difficult for standard surrogates to learn useful performance models. We instead study an alternative meta-learning representation that describes each configuration directly as its historical performance across prior tasks. This representation can be paired directly with standard surrogate models. Our scope is the iterative selection component of AutoML, deciding which configuration to evaluate next from a fixed candidate set, rather than a complete framework with features such as runtime estimation, cost-aware budgeting and ensembling. We further apply this representation to maximal marginal relevance (MMR), a diversity-based re-ranking criterion from recommender systems, as a posterior-free acquisition rule. When selecting and optimising across multiple models on the TabArena benchmark, the performance-based representation paired with a linear Bayesian ridge regression model outperforms dedicated meta-learning baselines, achieving the same tuned performance in roughly half the number of trials. For single-model HPO, it remains a competitive second. Across both benchmarks this method closely matches or improves on regret at a fraction of the complexity and cost, requiring no pre-training or tuning and scaling independently of search space dimensionality. Code for reproducing our results is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Represents each hyperparameter configuration by its historical performance across prior tasks and pairs this representation with standard surrogates for HPO and CASH. On TabArena it reaches the same tuned performance in roughly half the trials, with no pre-training or tuning required.
AI.motivation: Explicit hyperparameter encodings make it hard for standard Bayesian optimisation surrogates to learn useful performance models in high-dimensional search spaces.
AI.method: A performance-based configuration representation used with standard surrogates for the iterative selection step over a fixed candidate set; it is also applied to maximal marginal relevance as a posterior-free acquisition rule.
AI.result: On TabArena for multi-model selection and optimisation, the performance-based representation with Bayesian ridge regression outperforms dedicated meta-learning baselines and reaches the same tuned performance in roughly half the trials; for single-model HPO it is a competitive second. Across both benchmarks regret is closely matched or improved.
AI.conclusion: A simple performance-based representation gives competitive regret at a fraction of the complexity and cost, and it scales independently of search-space dimensionality.

title: An Information Bottleneck for Post-hoc Memorization Mitigation in LLMs
summary: Recent studies have shown that large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce copyrighted training data, raising serious privacy and intellectual property concerns. In this work, we investigate whether memorization can be mitigated without modifying or retraining the underlying model through an information bottleneck. We propose a modular plug-and-play framework that inserts a nonparametric variational information bottleneck (NVIB) between a frozen LLM backbone and its language modeling head. By compressing the final hidden representations before token prediction, the proposed bottleneck aims to preserve general linguistic knowledge while filtering out highly specific memorized sequences. We evaluate our approach on memorization extraction tasks involving book passages and on standard language modeling benchmarks to measure the trade-off between memorization reduction and downstream utility. Our experiments show that the NVIB layer substantially reduces extractability while maintaining competitive performance on benchmark tasks. These results suggest that adding an information bottleneck offers a practical and architecture agnostic direction for post-hoc memorization mitigation in pretrained LLMs.

AI.tldr: Inserts a nonparametric variational information bottleneck between a frozen LLM backbone and its language modelling head to reduce the extractability of memorised training data without retraining. It substantially reduces extractability while keeping competitive benchmark performance.
AI.motivation: LLMs can memorise and reproduce copyrighted training data, raising privacy and intellectual property concerns, and existing mitigation generally requires modifying or retraining the model.
AI.method: A modular plug-and-play NVIB layer compresses the final hidden representations before token prediction, aiming to keep general linguistic knowledge while filtering highly specific memorised sequences; the design is architecture agnostic.
AI.result: On book-passage memorisation extraction and standard language modelling benchmarks, the NVIB layer substantially reduces extractability while maintaining competitive benchmark performance, and the trade-off between memorisation reduction and utility is measured.
AI.conclusion: An information bottleneck is presented as a practical, architecture-agnostic direction for post-hoc memorisation mitigation in pretrained LLMs.

title: Calibrated Target Noise Recovers Curvature from the Gradients
summary: Estimating curvature information from gradients alone is a fundamental problem in machine learning. The challenge becomes particularly acute in settings where only aggregate mini-batch gradients are available, yet curvature information is still required for applications such as preconditioning in optimisation, sampling, and early stopping. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that a simple target-perturbation scheme suffices to recover such curvature information from gradients alone. Our method injects zero-mean noise into the targets, with variance calibrated to the local output curvature. The covariance of the resulting noisy batch gradients then recovers practical curvature matrices, without requiring per-sample gradients, second-order derivatives, or other internal network quantities. For a broad class of non-linear models, our scheme recovers the Generalised Gauss--Newton (GGN) matrix; for feed-forward ReLU networks, it additionally recovers the diagonal blocks of the population Hessian. We demonstrate that the resulting estimator is simple, lightweight, provably optimal, and easy to integrate into existing training pipelines. Experiments demonstrate accurate curvature recovery, faster optimisation when the estimator is used for preconditioning, and the utility of the estimated GGN for early stopping.

AI.tldr: Shows that injecting zero-mean target noise, with variance calibrated to the local output curvature, makes the covariance of noisy batch gradients recover practical curvature matrices from gradients alone. For feed-forward ReLU networks it also recovers diagonal blocks of the population Hessian.
AI.motivation: Curvature information is needed for preconditioning, sampling and early stopping, but when only aggregate mini-batch gradients are available, standard curvature computation requires per-sample gradients or second-order derivatives.
AI.method: A target-perturbation scheme adds zero-mean noise to the targets with variance calibrated to the local output curvature; the covariance of the resulting noisy batch gradients serves as the estimate, with no per-sample gradients, second derivatives or internal network quantities.
AI.result: For a broad class of non-linear models the scheme recovers the Generalised Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix, and for feed-forward ReLU networks it also recovers diagonal blocks of the population Hessian. Experiments show accurate curvature recovery, faster optimisation when used for preconditioning, and utility of the estimated GGN for early stopping.
AI.conclusion: The estimator is simple, lightweight and easy to add to existing training pipelines, and the authors describe it as provably optimal.

title: Instrumental Variables in Continuous-Time Stochastic Processes
summary: Causal questions often arise in systems that evolve in continuous time. While instrumental variable (IV) methods provide a principled approach to identify causal effects in static or discrete-time settings, even in the presence of unobserved confounding, they do not yet extend to continuous-time dynamics. In this work, we develop an IV framework for stationary continuous-time stochastic processes parameterized by stochastic differential equations (SDE), where the instrument itself takes the form of a stochastic process. We encode the structural sparsity and causal effects directly at the infinitesimal level of the drift, and contrast these assumptions with the IV assumptions on the discretized version of the same process. Based on these structural assumptions, we derive moment restrictions using path-valued instruments. We show how these restrictions simplify for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes and present an identification condition together with a corresponding consistent estimation method. Finally, we extend our estimation framework to nonlinear causal effects by expressing the path-based moment restrictions leveraging the signature kernel. Empirically, our method recovers causal effects in confounded continuous-time systems where maximum-likelihood-based estimation and discrete-time IV methods are systematically biased.

AI.tldr: Develops an instrumental variable framework for stationary continuous-time stochastic processes defined by SDEs, where the instrument is itself a stochastic process, and derives moment restrictions from path-valued instruments. It recovers causal effects in confounded continuous-time systems where maximum likelihood and discrete-time IV estimators are biased.
AI.motivation: IV methods identify causal effects in static or discrete-time settings, even with unobserved confounding, but they do not extend to continuous-time dynamics.
AI.method: Encodes structural sparsity and causal effects at the infinitesimal level of the drift and contrasts these assumptions with the IV assumptions on the discretised process; the path-based moment restrictions are simplified for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes and extended to nonlinear effects through the signature kernel.
AI.result: Gives an identification condition and a consistent estimation method; empirically the approach recovers causal effects in confounded continuous-time systems where maximum-likelihood and discrete-time IV methods are systematically biased.
AI.conclusion: Instrumental-variable identification is extended to continuous-time stochastic processes, with assumptions stated at the level of the drift and distinct from those of the discretised process.

title: $O(1/n)$ Convergence Rate for RVI $Q$-Learning
summary: We establish finite-time convergence guarantee for synchronous relative value iteration (RVI) $Q$-learning for finite weakly communicating Markov decision processes (MDPs). For stochastic Krasnosel'ski\uı--Mann iterations driven by a non-expansive, linearly regular map on a finite-dimensional normed space, we establish last-iterate mean-squared residual bounds under martingale-difference noise whose conditional second moment grows at most linearly with the squared residual. Suitable polynomial stepsizes of order $n^{-a}$ yield an $O(n^{-a})$ rate for $0<a\leq1$. We verify linear regularity and the noise condition for the centered Bellman operator for finite weakly communicating MDPs. Applying the general result gives an $O(n^{-1})$ bound on the mean-squared Bellman span residual of RVI $Q$-learning iterates when a suitable stepsize sequence is used. The positive gap between optimal and suboptimal stationary deterministic policies then yields an $O(n^{-1})$ bound on the expected suboptimality of the greedy policy. Consequently, $O(\epsilon^{-1})$ synchronous iterations suffice for an $\epsilon$-optimal policy in expectation. These guarantees are instance-dependent, with constants that depend on the hitting-time parameters and the suboptimality gap of the second-best policy.

AI.tldr: Establishes finite-time convergence for synchronous relative value iteration (RVI) Q-learning on finite weakly communicating MDPs, with an O(1/n) mean-squared Bellman span residual. It implies that O(eps^-1) synchronous iterations suffice for an eps-optimal policy in expectation.
AI.motivation: Finite-time guarantees for RVI Q-learning on weakly communicating MDPs were needed, and the analysis builds on stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann iterations under noise.
AI.method: Proves last-iterate mean-squared residual bounds for stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann iterations driven by a non-expansive, linearly regular map under martingale-difference noise whose conditional second moment grows at most linearly with the squared residual; polynomial stepsizes of order n^-a are used, and linear regularity and the noise condition are verified for the centred Bellman operator.
AI.result: Stepsizes of order n^-a give an O(n^-a) rate for 0 < a <= 1. With a suitable stepsize, the mean-squared Bellman span residual of RVI Q-learning iterates is O(n^-1), and the expected suboptimality of the greedy policy is O(n^-1), using the positive gap between optimal and suboptimal stationary deterministic policies.
AI.conclusion: The guarantees are instance-dependent, with constants that depend on hitting-time parameters and on the suboptimality gap of the second-best policy.

title: Non-Parametric Mutual Information Estimation with Vine Copulas
comment: Accepted at the conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: We introduce VINE: a non-parametric mutual information (MI) estimator based on simplified D-vine copulas. Approximating the joint density with a simplified D-vine allows the density ratio to simplify to a product of pair copulas, which we can estimate non-parametrically. This structural simplification yields VINE, a flexible and computationally efficient MI estimator. We compare VINE against SotA neural MI estimators on a range of datasets, both under settings where the simplified D-vine assumption holds and where it is violated, demonstrating competitive accuracy at a lower computational cost for low- to medium-dimensional datasets.

AI.tldr: Introduces VINE, a non-parametric mutual information estimator based on simplified D-vine copulas, in which the density ratio factorises into a product of pair copulas estimated non-parametrically. It gives competitive accuracy at lower computational cost than neural MI estimators on low- to medium-dimensional data.
AI.motivation: Neural MI estimators are the state of the art but are comparatively costly, and the work seeks a flexible, computationally efficient alternative.
AI.method: Approximates the joint density with a simplified D-vine, so that the density ratio simplifies to a product of pair copulas that are estimated non-parametrically.
AI.result: Compared with state-of-the-art neural MI estimators on datasets where the simplified D-vine assumption holds and where it is violated, VINE shows competitive accuracy at a lower computational cost for low- to medium-dimensional datasets.
AI.conclusion: The structural simplification yields an efficient MI estimator that is best suited to low- to medium-dimensional problems.

title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
summary: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

AI.tldr: Proposes DP-Learner, an equivariant Transformer that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space, for electronic-structure Hamiltonian prediction. It also introduces the MP-HAM-110K dataset.
AI.motivation: Most equivariant Hamiltonian models propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, which mismatches the direct-product representation of Hamiltonian blocks, fragments contiguous blocks, needs many transformations and aligns poorly with efficient hardware.
AI.method: Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left-right products and contractions that preserve SO(3), SU(2) and spatial-inversion equivariance without Clebsch-Gordan decomposition; instantiated as a Transformer with invariant scalar routing over matrix units, directional propagation, attention and environment-embedded context.
AI.result: MP-HAM-110K contains more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements, with Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. On MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC, DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.
AI.conclusion: Operating natively in the direct-product space resolves the representation mismatch and improves both accuracy and efficiency for Hamiltonian prediction.

title: Evaluating Language Model Features for Zero-Shot Time-Series Anomaly Detection Under Isolation Assumption
summary: Time-Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamentally challenging task: it is unsupervised, requires high local precision capabilities, and suffers from limited labelled data. Recent work has explored adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to time-series via cross-modal transfer. However, existing approaches are poorly suited to Multivariate TSAD (MTSAD), as tokenisation often obscures fine-grained temporal and variables structures, and most methods optimise auxiliary objectives such as forecasting or reconstruction. We posit that these surrogate objectives become unreliable as model capacity increases. Highly expressive models risk reconstructing or forecasting anomalies, undermining the foundations of both strategies. Instead, we propose to use LLMs purely as feature extractors and directly analyse their induced feature spaces. In this work, investigate the ability of LLMs to provide useful representations for MTSADs in a zero-shot setting through classification. To this end, we study the separability of the extracted features, under the assumption that anomalous features should be isolated from normal ones. We analyse their temporal and contextual discriminative ability using simple step-wise tokenisation schemes, with one time-step per token, which preserve fine-grained local information. Their usability for MTSAD is assessed using an unsupervised Isolation Forest, enabling a direct evaluation of the resulting representation quality. We further investigate whether the observed performance can be attributed to the language-related pre-training of the LLMs or arises independently of it. Our results provide empirical insight into the ability of LLMs to represent multivariate time-series for anomaly detection and highlight broader applications of cross-modal foundation models.

AI.tldr: Uses LLMs purely as frozen feature extractors with step-wise tokenisation, one time-step per token, for zero-shot multivariate time-series anomaly detection, and tests separability of the features with an unsupervised Isolation Forest. It also asks whether the performance depends on language pre-training.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-for-time-series methods rely on forecasting or reconstruction objectives that become unreliable as model capacity grows, and tokenisation obscures fine-grained temporal and variable structure in multivariate settings.
AI.method: Analyses the feature spaces induced by LLMs under one-time-step-per-token schemes for their temporal and contextual discriminative ability, assesses anomaly separability with Isolation Forest, and compares against models with and without language-related pre-training.
AI.result: The abstract reports empirical insight into how well LLMs represent multivariate time series for anomaly detection, but it gives no specific numbers, datasets or baselines and does not state whether the performance comes from language pre-training.
AI.conclusion: LLM features can serve as representations for multivariate anomaly detection, which points to broader applications of cross-modal foundation models.

title: Reinforcing What the Student Has Learned: Teacher-Guided On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model reasoning through dense teacher feedback on student-generated this http URL first observe an amplitude disparity in this feedback: on math reasoning responses, style-related positions exhibit 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher--student log-probability difference of mathematical this http URL OPD updates by these discrepancies thus directs much of the update strength toward matching the teacher's expression. We instead take the student's own pretrained base as a reference: the student--base difference records the token preferences acquired during post-training and provides supervision that does not depend on the student's distance from the teacher. Building on this reference, we propose Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation (SD-OPD), which uses centered student--base differences as update coefficients, keeps each coefficient only when its sign agrees with centered teacher--student feedback, and recomputes the student signal every training round. Across 5 teacher--student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes SD-OPD, which uses centred student-minus-base log-probability differences as update coefficients, keeping them only where their sign agrees with centred teacher-student feedback. It improves six-task math avg@16 pass@1 over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points across five Qwen3 configurations.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation gives dense teacher feedback, but on math responses style-related positions show 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher-student log-probability difference of mathematical positions, so updates are dominated by matching the teacher's expression.
AI.method: Uses the student's own pretrained base as a reference: the student-base difference records token preferences acquired during post-training and supplies supervision independent of the student's distance from the teacher; centred student-base differences serve as coefficients, kept only when their sign agrees with centred teacher-student feedback, and recomputed every round.
AI.result: Across 5 teacher-student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves the six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Using the student's base model as the reference redirects distillation updates toward mathematical reasoning rather than the teacher's expression.

title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). 23 pages, 10 figures, including supplementary material. The first three authors contributed equally. BILBY-PRO dataset: this https URL ; BILBY-MD code: this https URL
summary: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.

AI.tldr: Introduces BILBY-PRO, a 220-case benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, and BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation. Only 8 of 55 statically solved designs pass all of its checks, so static refolding success does not establish dynamical fidelity.
AI.motivation: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function depends on conformational ensembles and transitions.
AI.method: BILBY-PRO is systematically derived from PROSITE-linked structures and used to evaluate six recent scaffold-generation models; BILBY-MD compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations, applied to statically solved MotifBench designs.
AI.result: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, while ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy the MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks; compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more often.
AI.conclusion: Target coverage, unique-solution yield and MD-supported dynamical fidelity are three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation, and static refolding success alone does not establish the dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold.

title: Comparing Classification and Feature Learning by Analyzing Their Loss Functions in Normalized Spaces with Different Scale Factors
summary: Classification and feature learning are two closely interrelated fundamental tasks. Feature learning in supervised settings is typically achieved by training classification models, under the common assumption that higher classification accuracy implies better feature quality. In this paper, we first point out that classification accuracy reflects the sample-wise local properties of a model on a dataset, whereas feature learning aims to learn features with good dataset-level global properties, such as intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. From the first principle of feature learning, we redesign the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, a counterpart of the cross-entropy (CE) loss used in classification. Then, in normalized feature space, we analyze the minima of the BCE and CE losses and show that both can lead to neural collapse, where sample features from different classes become maximally compact and maximally separated. More importantly, by investigating the convergence behaviors of the two losses as the scale factor $\gamma$ varies in the normalized space, we reveal how classification accuracy and feature quality change differently across spaces of different sizes. Under a fixed training strategy, a very large $\gamma$ achieves perfect classification accuracy but slows convergence toward the ideal feature geometry, whereas a very small $\gamma$ makes classification highly sensitive to small perturbations. A moderate $\gamma$ is therefore necessary for simultaneously achieving reliable classification and well-structured features. Extensive experiments validate these findings and demonstrate that BCE loss exhibits advantages in long-tail and open-set recognitions, as it better aligns with the global requirements of feature learning.

AI.tldr: Redesigns binary cross-entropy (BCE) as a feature-learning counterpart to cross-entropy and analyses both losses in normalised feature space as a scale factor gamma varies. A moderate gamma is needed to get reliable classification and well-structured features together, and BCE shows advantages in long-tail and open-set recognition.
AI.motivation: Classification accuracy reflects sample-wise local properties, whereas feature learning needs dataset-level global properties such as intra-class compactness and inter-class separability, so accuracy alone does not indicate feature quality.
AI.method: From first principles of feature learning the authors redesign BCE, then analyse the minima and convergence behaviour of BCE and CE in normalised feature space as the scale factor gamma changes.
AI.result: Both losses can lead to neural collapse. A very large gamma gives perfect classification accuracy but slows convergence toward the ideal feature geometry, while a very small gamma makes classification highly sensitive to small perturbations. Extensive experiments show BCE has advantages in long-tail and open-set recognition.
AI.conclusion: A moderate scale factor is necessary to balance reliable classification and feature quality, and BCE aligns better with the global requirements of feature learning.

title: Ordering Multivariate Time Series by Volatility Memory: A Temporal Convolutional Approach to Volatility Heredity
summary: Volatility dynamics can carry information about temporal relationships that is not apparent in the conditional mean. Extracting this information is difficult because the persistence of each variable can obscure its dependence on other variables. This paper presents QS-TCN, a method for ordering multivariate time series that combines statistical estimates of volatility memory with temporal convolutional learning. Persistence estimates obtained by quasi-maximum likelihood and temporal modes extracted by the Matrix Pencil method define structured filters within the network. Together with learned filters, they represent the history of the target and support comparisons of directional evidence between variables. These comparisons are combined into a global order of precedence, which does not identify a causal graph. The method is evaluated on synthetic systems with linear and nonlinear volatility interactions and on the Finance and fMRI benchmarks, whose reference relations are known. Across the four synthetic volatility regimes studied, QS-TCN reaches a higher mean ordering quality than an external lead--lag ordering and its squared-input adaptation, although the gain over the adaptation is uncertain in two regimes. Applications to currency, gold and cryptocurrency markets are reported descriptively.

AI.tldr: Proposes QS-TCN, a temporal convolutional network that orders multivariate time series by volatility memory, using quasi-maximum-likelihood persistence estimates and Matrix Pencil temporal modes as structured filters. It produces a global order of precedence rather than a causal graph.
AI.motivation: Volatility dynamics carry temporal relationships that are not visible in the conditional mean, but each variable's persistence can obscure its dependence on other variables.
AI.method: Persistence estimates from quasi-maximum likelihood and temporal modes from the Matrix Pencil method define structured filters within the network, alongside learned filters that represent the target's history; directional evidence between variables is compared and combined into a global order.
AI.result: On four synthetic volatility regimes QS-TCN reaches higher mean ordering quality than an external lead-lag ordering and its squared-input adaptation, although the gain over the adaptation is uncertain in two regimes. It is evaluated on the Finance and fMRI benchmarks with known reference relations, and applications to currency, gold and cryptocurrency markets are reported descriptively.
AI.conclusion: The method gives a descriptive precedence ordering of volatility-linked series rather than a causal graph, and its gains over the baselines are not uniform across regimes.

title: ConvPE: Convolutional Position Embedding Improves Transformers
summary: ConvPE (Convolutional Position Embedding) improves both the performance and efficiency of Transformer models in language modeling, long-context extension, and vision. It injects a windowed, content-dependent bias into attention scores through a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states. As a lightweight plug-in, ConvPE is compatible with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation. It also supports high-dimensional position embeddings via high-dimensional convolutions. In a reproduction, ConvPE outperforms five 1D baselines and eight 2D baselines. The code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ConvPE adds a windowed, content-dependent bias to attention scores through a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of hidden states, improving performance and efficiency of Transformers in language modeling, long-context extension and vision.
AI.motivation: The abstract states no explicit gap; it targets Transformer position embeddings, aiming for gains in both performance and efficiency while remaining compatible with RoPE, attention masks and KV concatenation.
AI.method: A causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states produces a windowed, content-dependent bias added to attention scores; it works as a plug-in and extends to high-dimensional position embeddings via high-dimensional convolutions.
AI.result: In a reproduction, ConvPE outperforms five 1D baselines and eight 2D baselines; the abstract reports improvements in language modeling, long-context extension and vision.
AI.conclusion: ConvPE is a lightweight, compatible position-embedding plug-in that improves Transformers in both accuracy and efficiency, and its code is publicly available.

title: Foresee to Trade: Forecast-Augmented Policy Optimization for Portfolio Management
summary: Online investment services must translate asset opportunities into investment outcomes for users' accounts, yet the same market opportunity can warrant different account actions. We study how supervision from future asset opportunities can strengthen account-level trading decisions and propose Forecast-Augmented Relative Policy Optimization (FRPO). FRPO separately supervises asset opportunities and account decisions through a jointly learned representation: a Financial State Head (FSH) learns future relative-return targets to provide asset-level opportunity supervision, while Same-Path Group-Relative Optimization compares trading trajectories under the same market path and initial account to provide account-level relative-outcome supervision. An Adaptive Gate coordinates auxiliary supervision using predictive variance and gradient alignment. FSH is used only during training; inference uses the encoder and policy for trading. Across DJIA30, TOPIX Core30, and three investment-style portfolios, ten-seed evaluations show that FRPO achieves the highest mean cumulative and annualized returns among the compared methods in all five settings. These results support strengthening investment agents' trading decisions through joint supervision from asset opportunities and trading outcomes.

AI.tldr: FRPO trains trading agents with auxiliary supervision from future asset opportunities and account-level relative outcomes, and reports the highest mean cumulative and annualized returns among compared methods in all five portfolio settings tested.
AI.motivation: The same market opportunity can warrant different account actions, so the paper argues that supervision from future asset opportunities can strengthen account-level trading decisions.
AI.method: A Financial State Head learns future relative-return targets for asset-level supervision during training only; Same-Path Group-Relative Optimization compares trajectories under the same market path and initial account for account-level supervision; an Adaptive Gate weights the auxiliary supervision using predictive variance and gradient alignment; inference uses only the encoder and policy.
AI.result: Over DJIA30, TOPIX Core30 and three investment-style portfolios, with ten-seed evaluations, FRPO achieves the highest mean cumulative and annualized returns among compared methods in all five settings.
AI.conclusion: Joint supervision from asset opportunities and trading outcomes can strengthen the trading decisions of investment agents.

title: Neural Collapse on Imbalanced Datasets and Open-Set Scenario
summary: Neural collapse (NC) describes the elegant geometric structure that sample features and classifier vectors exhibit when a classification model's loss reaches its minimum. Class imbalance, however, generally distorts standard NC. In this paper, we theoretically reformulate NC on imbalanced datasets and in open-set settings. Our analysis is based on an optimization problem over class-wise averaged losses, rather than the global averaged losses used in prior NC studies. We prove that when class-wise averaged losses attain their minima, standard NC is achieved on balanced or imbalanced datasets, for both cross-entropy (CE) and binary cross-entropy (BCE) losses. We further extend the analysis to an open-set-inspired scenario, where some classes contain no training samples yet are still assigned classifier vectors in the losses. We find that in this scenario, when class-wise averaged losses reach their minima, standard NC still emerges on the known classes with training samples, while the classifier vectors of unknown classes without training samples overlap with each other and become orthogonal to those of the known classes. Finally, we analyze Softmax- and Sigmoid-based contrastive losses re-balanced by inverse sample frequency, proving that at their minima on balanced or imbalanced datasets, sample features of different classes likewise form standard NC.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates neural collapse for class-imbalanced and open-set settings using class-wise averaged losses, and proves that standard NC emerges on balanced or imbalanced data for CE and BCE losses.
AI.motivation: Class imbalance generally distorts standard NC, and prior NC analyses use global averaged losses rather than class-wise ones; open-set settings, where some classes have no training samples, were not covered.
AI.method: The analysis studies an optimization problem over class-wise averaged losses, extends it to open-set-inspired settings where classes without training samples still receive classifier vectors, and analyzes Softmax- and Sigmoid-based contrastive losses re-balanced by inverse sample frequency.
AI.result: At minima of the class-wise averaged losses, standard NC holds on balanced or imbalanced data for CE and BCE; in the open-set scenario, known classes still exhibit NC while the classifier vectors of unknown classes overlap with each other and are orthogonal to those of known classes; the re-balanced contrastive losses also yield standard NC.
AI.conclusion: Under class-wise averaged losses, NC persists under class imbalance and in open-set settings, clarifying the theory behind imbalanced and open-set training.

title: Optimal Learning in Games with Arbitrary Delays: Best-of-Both-Worlds for Self-Play and Adversarial Opponents
summary: We study learning in zero-sum games with delayed feedback. We introduce Multi-Anchor Optimistic Online Mirror Descent (MAO-OMD), a single algorithm which obtains optimal fast rates in self-play on smooth games, while simultaneously maintaining minimax optimal guarantees against arbitrary opponents. In particular, in smooth zero-sum games with arbitrary and unknown feedback delays, MAO-OMD obtains $O(\sigma_{\max}+1)$ social and individual regrets when used by both players, where $\sigma_{\max}$ denotes the maximum number of outstanding gradients, while also guaranteeing minimax optimal $O(\sqrt{T+d_{\mathrm{tot}}})$ individual regret against arbitrary opponents, where $d_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total delay. Moreover, we show that these optimal rates cannot be obtained simultaneously using the standard black-box reduction to the undelayed setting. We also extend our results to multi-player games, and to games with player-dependent delay sequences.

AI.tldr: MAO-OMD is a single algorithm for delayed-feedback zero-sum games that attains optimal O(sigma_max+1) regret in self-play on smooth games and minimax optimal O(sqrt(T+d_tot)) individual regret against arbitrary opponents.
AI.motivation: Learning in zero-sum games with delayed feedback needs fast rates in self-play as well as worst-case guarantees against adversaries, and the abstract notes that the standard black-box reduction to the undelayed setting cannot achieve both simultaneously.
AI.method: Multi-Anchor Optimistic Online Mirror Descent (MAO-OMD), a single algorithm used by both players, applied to smooth zero-sum games with arbitrary unknown feedback delays; extended to multi-player games and to player-dependent delay sequences.
AI.result: In self-play, both players obtain O(sigma_max+1) social and individual regrets, where sigma_max is the maximum number of outstanding gradients; against arbitrary opponents, individual regret is O(sqrt(T+d_tot)), where d_tot is the total delay.
AI.conclusion: A single algorithm can attain optimal rates both in self-play and against adversaries under arbitrary delays, rates that the black-box reduction cannot deliver simultaneously.

title: Adapters as Data: The Latent Space of LoRAs
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Neural Network Artifacts as a New Data Modality
summary: LoRA adapters are usually treated as finished artifacts rather than as a data modality. Prior work has shown that LoRA adapters populate a low-dimensional manifold that a linear PCA basis already organizes well enough to support different operations such as sampling, editing, and inversion. We ask what a learned, nonlinear latent adds beyond this. We train a transformer autoencoder on the same population of LoRA identity adapters, mapping each into a latent space and compare every operation against the identical operation applied directly to the raw adapter weights. The latent preserves the capabilities already available in weight space, sampling diverse identities and editing individual attributes. Beyond preservation, we show that the latent is far more robust to displacement than weight space, degrading into distorted but still valid faces rather than texture. Fixed-dimensional weight-space representations cannot natively host adapters of more than one rank, so we extend our sequential autoencoder to hold mixed-rank adapters within one shared latent. This gives a path toward treating adapter weights of varying architecture as a single, general modality rather than one tied to a fixed rank, and points to a learned, nonlinear latent as the mechanism that could carry this generalization further, toward heterogeneous populations of adapters.

AI.tldr: The paper trains a transformer autoencoder on LoRA identity adapters to build a nonlinear latent space that preserves the sampling and editing abilities of weight space, is more robust to displacement, and is extended to mixed-rank adapters.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed a linear PCA basis already organizes the LoRA adapter manifold for sampling, editing and inversion; the paper asks what a learned nonlinear latent adds, and fixed-dimensional weight-space representations cannot host adapters of more than one rank.
AI.method: A transformer autoencoder is trained on the same population of LoRA identity adapters and each operation is compared against the identical operation on raw weights; a sequential autoencoder is extended to hold mixed-rank adapters in one shared latent.
AI.result: The latent preserves sampling diverse identities and editing individual attributes; it is far more robust to displacement than weight space, degrading into distorted but still valid faces rather than texture.
AI.conclusion: A learned nonlinear latent is a path toward treating adapters of varying architecture as a single general modality, with potential extension to heterogeneous adapter populations.

title: PBPO: Prefix-Block Policy Optimization for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) commonly decode responses by proceeding autoregressively across blocks while iteratively denoising multiple tokens within each block. This structure makes block-level policy optimization a natural adaptation of autoregressive policy optimization. However, the exact likelihood of a completed block is intractable because it marginalizes over the intermediate states and reveal orders of the denoising process. To realize the block-level formulation, we construct a prefix-block state and use a single model evaluation to define a factorized one-step surrogate for the block likelihood. The resulting block surrogate ratio is a product of its token surrogate ratios, allowing variation at individual positions to propagate across the entire block before clipping. We therefore introduce Prefix-Block Policy Optimization (PBPO), which preserves block-level conditioning but applies surrogate importance weighting and clipping separately to each token. PBPO further diversifies repeated updates by resampling corrupted views of the prompt and revealed prefix, a design motivated by masked-dLLM pre-training. Under our analysis assumptions, block-product weighting amplifies the variance of gradient contributions relative to token-local weighting. Across two LLaDA-family initializations, six benchmarks, and three generation lengths, PBPO achieves competitive performance against existing dLLM RL methods.

AI.tldr: PBPO is a block-level policy optimization method for diffusion LLMs that applies importance weighting and clipping per token within a prefix-block state, and is competitive with existing dLLM RL methods on two LLaDA-family initializations.
AI.motivation: The exact likelihood of a completed block in a diffusion LLM is intractable because it marginalizes over intermediate states and reveal orders, so block-level policy optimization needs a tractable surrogate.
AI.method: A prefix-block state and a single model evaluation define a factorized one-step surrogate for the block likelihood, whose ratio is the product of token surrogate ratios; clipping is applied to each token separately, and repeated updates resample corrupted views of the prompt and revealed prefix.
AI.result: Across two LLaDA-family initializations, six benchmarks and three generation lengths, PBPO achieves competitive performance against existing dLLM RL methods; under the paper's analysis assumptions, block-product weighting amplifies gradient variance relative to token-local weighting.
AI.conclusion: Block-level conditioning with per-token surrogate weighting is a workable RL approach for dLLMs, with a variance cost relative to token-local weighting.

title: EnergyBench: a live, gate-aligned benchmark of day-ahead forecasts for European power markets
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, 7 tables. Live benchmark at this https URL
summary: Energy forecasting models are usually compared on backtests and fixed public datasets. Backtests can use data that did not yet exist when the forecast would have been made, and a fixed test set, reused across studies and possibly contained in the pretraining data of foundation models, invites overfitting to the benchmark. EnergyBench evaluates every entry live instead. Each day at 11:30 CET/CEST, thirty minutes before the day-ahead (SDAC) gate closes, every model forecasts the next day's price, wind and solar generation and load on the 15-minute grid for six bidding zones (BE, NL, FR, DE-LU, DK1, DK2). Unlike existing live benchmarks, EnergyBench runs the models itself, on one information set that it freezes at the cut-off and publishes, including three numerical weather prediction models, so that foundation models can be compared with and without the same weather covariates under the actual market deadline. Errors are pooled per series against a seasonal-naive baseline, and models are ranked by a Bradley-Terry rating on the Elo scale with a day-bootstrap interval. The field spans baselines, linear and gradient-boosted models on the frozen weather, eighteen time-series foundation models from eleven families, ensembles, and the grid operators' own forecasts. Over the first thirty-two live days, the covariates reduced the error of each of the ten foundation models run with and without them by 37-51% on matched races (64-73% on wind, 48-61% on solar). Used zero-shot, these models match or outperform a LightGBM model trained on the same covariates. Model size, from 3M to 331M parameters, has a much smaller effect, and median ensembles of the covariate models rank highest. The grid operators' pre-gate forecasts remain ahead on wind and solar, where the best single foundation models have 16-22% more error; on load the gap is 4-6%, within the intervals.

AI.tldr: EnergyBench is a live benchmark in which every model forecasts day-ahead price, wind, solar and load for six European bidding zones before the SDAC gate closes, ranked by Bradley-Terry ratings; the grid operators' own forecasts remain ahead on wind and solar.
AI.motivation: Backtests can use data unavailable at forecast time, and fixed public test sets may appear in foundation-model pretraining data, inviting overfitting; existing live benchmarks do not run the models themselves on one frozen information set.
AI.method: Each day at 11:30 CET/CEST every model forecasts the next day's price, wind, solar and load on a 15-minute grid for six bidding zones, using one frozen and published information set that includes three NWP models; errors are pooled per series against a seasonal-naive baseline and models are ranked by a Bradley-Terry rating on the Elo scale with a day-bootstrap interval.
AI.result: Over the first 32 live days, the covariates reduced the error of each of ten foundation models by 37-51% on matched races (64-73% on wind, 48-61% on solar); used zero-shot, these models match or outperform a LightGBM model trained on the same covariates; model size from 3M to 331M parameters has a much smaller effect; median ensembles of covariate models rank highest; the best single foundation models have 16-22% more error than the grid operators on wind and solar, and 4-6% more on load, within the intervals.
AI.conclusion: Weather covariates matter more than model size for these forecasts, and the grid operators' pre-gate forecasts still lead on wind and solar, while the load gap lies within the uncertainty.

title: Computation, not weight access: large language models as auditors of clinical prediction networks
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Code, simulated networks, prompts and replies: this https URL
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have been reported to read, edit and write the weights of small neural networks, raising the prospect of auditing clinical prediction models from their files alone. Public demonstrations, however, mixed reading raw weights with running code. We separated these conditions in internally pre-specified simulation experiments. Tanh networks of 105 to 38,401 weights were trained on simulated cohorts of patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage, each with a planted relationship or none, and one network was trained on labels that under-recorded deaths in a subgroup. GPT-6 Astra and four other GPT models answered single prompts under a default or an explicit system instruction, either with the weights in the prompt and no tools, or with a calculation-only tool that exposed the weights (white box) or only the network's predictions (black box). Without tools, Astra recovered planted relationships in 353-weight networks but became unreliable at 3,457 weights, and under the default instruction it declined 11 of 12 audit and repair tasks as unidentifiable; the explicit instruction removed these refusals. With the tool, it recovered the planted relationship in all 29 runs on networks of up to 38,401 weights, raised no false alarm in 15 runs on null networks, and found the biased subgroup in 6 of 6 runs. Black-box access performed as well as white-box access, and other GPT-6 models read as accurately. A well-designed script matched the comparator models on the audit and the best LLM repair. For auditing these networks, what mattered was computation and elicitation, not access to the weights.

AI.tldr: In simulated clinical prediction networks, GPT-6 Astra recovers planted relationships and a biased subgroup when given a calculation-only tool, and black-box access performs as well as white-box access, so computation and elicitation matter more than weight access.
AI.motivation: Public demonstrations of LLMs reading and editing network weights mixed reading raw weights with running code, so it was unclear whether clinical prediction models can be audited from their files alone.
AI.method: Tanh networks of 105 to 38,401 weights were trained on simulated subarachnoid haemorrhage cohorts with a planted relationship or none, and one network was trained on labels that under-recorded deaths in a subgroup; GPT-6 Astra and four other GPT models answered single prompts with the weights in the prompt and no tools, or with a calculation-only tool exposing either the weights (white box) or only the predictions (black box), under a default or an explicit system instruction.
AI.result: Without tools, Astra recovered planted relationships in 353-weight networks but became unreliable at 3,457 weights, and under the default instruction declined 11 of 12 audit and repair tasks; the explicit instruction removed these refusals. With the tool, it recovered the planted relationship in all 29 runs on networks of up to 38,401 weights, raised no false alarm in 15 runs on null networks, and found the biased subgroup in 6 of 6 runs; black-box access matched white-box access, and a well-designed script matched the comparator models.
AI.conclusion: For auditing these networks, computation and elicitation matter more than access to the weights, so auditing clinical prediction models does not require exposing their parameters.

title: When, Where, How: Active In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) adapt to a new task only through the labeled rows in their context. However, labels are expensive to acquire in real-world scenarios due to the need for highly specific domain knowledge to ensure high-quality data. Active in-context learning transfers classical acquisition rules to this setting, in which the model that guides acquisition changes with every label added. We ask how the value of diversity, predictive uncertainty and target-aware information gain changes as a frozen TFM acquires more context. For that, we study Target-Aware Nearest Neighbor (TANN) acquisition and the Expected Predictive Information Gain in Context (EPIC) and evaluate them against classical rules. Our study across twenty benchmarks with two well-established TFMs and classical GBDTs highlights three findings: (i) When: diversity-based acquisition is best during the first acquisition iterations; (ii) Where: labeling pool rows that serve the target inputs via a simple target-aware nearest-neighbor rule matters substantially; (iii) How: EPIC yields the best models at the label budget, retains on average 80--87% of the chance-corrected full-data performance with only 5-10% of the pool labeled on the eight benchmarks with the largest pools, and selects labels that also improve the predictive performance of gradient-boosted decision trees.

AI.tldr: The paper studies active in-context learning for tabular foundation models and finds that diversity works best in early acquisition, target-aware nearest-neighbor selection matters, and EPIC gives the best models at a fixed label budget.
AI.motivation: Labels are expensive, and tabular foundation models adapt only through the labeled rows in their context; classical acquisition rules must be reconsidered because the model guiding acquisition changes with every label added.
AI.method: The study evaluates Target-Aware Nearest Neighbor (TANN) acquisition and Expected Predictive Information Gain in Context (EPIC) against classical acquisition rules across twenty benchmarks, using two tabular foundation models with a frozen model acquiring context, and classical GBDTs as comparators.
AI.result: Diversity-based acquisition is best during the first acquisition iterations; labeling pool rows that serve the target inputs via a simple target-aware nearest-neighbor rule matters substantially; EPIC yields the best models at the label budget, retaining on average 80-87% of chance-corrected full-data performance with only 5-10% of the pool labeled on the eight benchmarks with the largest pools, and its selected labels also improve gradient-boosted decision trees.
AI.conclusion: The acquisition rule should change as the context grows, and target-aware information gain (EPIC) selects labels that benefit both the tabular foundation models and GBDTs.

title: DISCERN: Distributional Synthetic Replay for Retain-Free Incremental Machine Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a trained model without retraining from scratch. In real deployments, however, deletion requests arrive over time, calling for incremental class unlearning (ICU): classes are removed sequentially, previously forgotten knowledge must remain forgotten, and the remaining classes must be preserved. We present DIstributional SynthetiC rEplay for Retain-free iNcremental unlearning (DISCERN), an intervention-based class unlearning method that replaces access to the retain set with synthetic embeddings sampled from per-class parametric distributions. Unlike prototype-based replay, which assumes an isotropic Gaussian around each class centroid, DISCERN fits Euclidean (Gaussian, Laplace, Student's $t$) and directional (von Mises--Fisher, Fisher--Bingham) families to each class and selects among them through statistical tests and, when none of them accepts, cross-validated log-likelihood. This design is motivated by the architecture-dependent latent geometry: transformer embeddings lie approximately on a hypersphere and concentrate around class directions, unlike those of convolutional networks. We evaluate DISCERN against seven retain-free baselines on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with two convolutional and two transformer backbones, under single-class, multi-class, and incremental unlearning. DISCERN is competitive when classes are removed at once and is the most stable method in ICU on transformers: on ViT-B/16, after 20 sequential deletions it retains a harmonic mean of $0.797$, whereas the strongest method in the simultaneous setting drops from $0.918$ to $0.048$. A paired ablation shows that per-class distribution selection substantially reduces the resurfacing of previously forgotten classes, acting as a stabilizer of accumulated forgetting rather than a uniform improvement.

AI.tldr: DISCERN is a retain-free incremental class unlearning method that replaces retain data with synthetic embeddings sampled from per-class parametric distributions, and it is the most stable method on transformers across sequential deletions.
AI.motivation: Deletion requests arrive over time, so incremental class unlearning must keep forgotten classes forgotten while preserving the rest; existing retain-free replay such as prototype-based replay assumes an isotropic Gaussian around each class centroid.
AI.method: DISCERN fits Euclidean (Gaussian, Laplace, Student's t) and directional (von Mises-Fisher, Fisher-Bingham) families to each class and selects among them with statistical tests and, when none is accepted, cross-validated log-likelihood, motivated by transformer embeddings lying approximately on a hypersphere.
AI.result: On ViT-B/16, after 20 sequential deletions DISCERN retains a harmonic mean of 0.797, whereas the strongest method in the simultaneous setting drops from 0.918 to 0.048; it is competitive when classes are removed at once; it was evaluated against seven retain-free baselines on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with two convolutional and two transformer backbones; a paired ablation shows per-class distribution selection substantially reduces resurfacing of forgotten classes.
AI.conclusion: Per-class distribution selection acts as a stabilizer of accumulated forgetting rather than a uniform improvement, which matters most in incremental unlearning.

title: Same Answer, Different Future: Matched Predictions Do Not Imply Matched Belief Updating in Language Models
summary: Language models can produce similar probabilistic predictions after observing outcomes, reading summaries, receiving instructions, or undergoing activation interventions. Whether these routes induce equivalent belief states remains unclear: agreement in current predictions does not establish how a model will respond to subsequent evidence. We investigate this distinction in a Bernoulli inference task with an analytic Bayesian reference. Across three open-weight language models, we prepare states through four textual routes and two activation-level interventions, measure both next-outcome continuations and explicit probabilistic estimates, and append identical new evidence from each prepared state. We quantify the persistence of the initial belief through its effective evidence weight, the number of new observations it is worth. We find that the format of evidence decides which readouts express its content: outcome sequences primarily affect continuations, whereas summaries and stated rates primarily affect explicit estimates. Moreover, effective weights differ substantially across routes, with summaries receiving weights that scale weakly with their stated observation counts and elicitation questions changing inferred weights by orders of magnitude. In a one-shot steering setting, an intervention that reproduces a natural record's immediate prediction loses most of its effect under subsequent evidence. These results show that agreement in current readouts is insufficient to establish equivalence in belief updating: how a belief is acquired and how it is read jointly determine its subsequent dynamics.

AI.tldr: Across three open-weight language models, the paper shows that matched current predictions can hide different belief states, because the route by which a belief is formed and the readout used determine how the model updates on later evidence.
AI.motivation: Agreement in current predictions does not establish how a model will respond to subsequent evidence, so it is unclear whether different routes to a belief induce equivalent belief states.
AI.method: In a Bernoulli inference task with an analytic Bayesian reference, beliefs are prepared through four textual routes and two activation-level interventions, identical new evidence is appended, and the effective evidence weight, the number of new observations the initial belief is worth, quantifies its persistence.
AI.result: Outcome sequences mainly affect continuations, while summaries and stated rates mainly affect explicit estimates; effective weights differ substantially across routes, with summaries receiving weights that scale weakly with their stated observation counts, and elicitation questions changing inferred weights by orders of magnitude; in a one-shot steering setting, an intervention that reproduces a natural record's immediate prediction loses most of its effect under subsequent evidence.
AI.conclusion: Agreement in current readouts is insufficient to establish equivalent belief updating, because how a belief is acquired and how it is read jointly determine its subsequent dynamics.

title: Flux as a Codec: Zero-Shot Lossy Compression with Flux
summary: We propose FluxC, a zero-shot codec that uses Flux as a compression prior. Although DiffC has shown that pretrained diffusion models can serve as zero-shot codecs, we ask how the choice of coding path and reconstruction method affects rate--distortion--perception behavior. We analyze FluxC along three axes: coding cost and bit allocation, reconstruction method, and low rate distortion. At matched signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), we show that the path choice does not affect the ideal information rate, but changes how bits are allocated across time steps. For reconstruction, we compare ancestral sampling, one-step ODE reconstruction, and many-step ODE reconstruction. Our analysis shows that ODE-based reconstruction can achieve lower distortion than ancestral sampling, especially in the low rate regime. Experiments on Gaussian sources and natural images support this prediction. Moreover, FluxC performs competitively with, and in some cases outperforms, recent neural image compression methods, suggesting that Flux can serve as a principled zero-shot codec.

AI.tldr: FluxC uses the pretrained Flux model as a zero-shot lossy codec and finds that ODE-based reconstruction achieves lower distortion than ancestral sampling, especially at low rates, performing competitively with recent neural image compression methods.
AI.motivation: DiffC has shown that pretrained diffusion models can serve as zero-shot codecs, but how the choice of coding path and reconstruction method affects rate-distortion-perception behavior was open.
AI.method: FluxC is analyzed along three axes: coding cost and bit allocation, reconstruction method (ancestral sampling, one-step ODE and many-step ODE reconstruction), and low-rate distortion, at matched signal-to-noise ratio, using Gaussian sources and natural images.
AI.result: At matched SNR, the path choice does not affect the ideal information rate but changes how bits are allocated across time steps; ODE-based reconstruction achieves lower distortion than ancestral sampling, especially in the low-rate regime; FluxC performs competitively with, and in some cases outperforms, recent neural image compression methods.
AI.conclusion: Flux can serve as a principled zero-shot codec, and ODE-based reconstruction is the preferable choice when distortion matters.

title: AttnSR: Attention Step Reward for Long-Horizon Agentic RL
comment: 20 pages, 4 figures, including appendices. Code: this https URL
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents make multi-step decisions, yet outcome-reward-only reinforcement learning provides little direct supervision for individual steps. We introduce AttnSR, a step-level reward augmentation method that derives reward allocations from policy attention extracted during training replay, without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts. AttnSR traces backward through the policy model attention graph to estimate the relevance of earlier steps to the final response. The terminal step, measured relative to a running baseline, determines whether these rewards reinforce or penalize the selected steps. In a controlled Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct study, AttnSR consistently outperforms the PPO baseline across all evaluated checkpoints on ALFWorld, raising final held-out success from 91.2% to 97.1%. The ablation experiment shows that the benefit depends on how intermediate rewards are assigned, rather than simple accumulation of step rewards over time. AttnSR also improves ScienceWorld at every checkpoint while cutting environment interactions by 29.9%. These results support policy attention as a practical prior for step-level reward allocation in long-horizon agentic RL. Code is available at this https URL .

AI.tldr: AttnSR derives step-level rewards from policy attention traced backward during training replay, without a separate reward model or extra rollouts, and raises final held-out ALFWorld success on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct from 91.2% to 97.1% over PPO.
AI.motivation: Outcome-reward-only RL gives little direct supervision for individual steps in long-horizon LLM agents, and step-level rewards usually require a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts.
AI.method: AttnSR traces backward through the policy model's attention graph to estimate the relevance of earlier steps to the final response; the terminal step, measured relative to a running baseline, determines whether these rewards reinforce or penalize the selected steps.
AI.result: In a controlled Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct study, AttnSR consistently outperforms the PPO baseline across all evaluated checkpoints on ALFWorld, raising final held-out success from 91.2% to 97.1%; it also improves ScienceWorld at every checkpoint while cutting environment interactions by 29.9%; an ablation shows the benefit depends on how intermediate rewards are assigned rather than on simple accumulation of step rewards.
AI.conclusion: Policy attention is a practical prior for step-level reward allocation in long-horizon agentic RL.

title: The Blindfolded Controller: Decision Model-Guided Training for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework for continuous improvement through interaction with an environment. However, RL agents struggle against tasks that offer exploration challenges and sparse rewards, because learning efficient policies from scratch is slow and sample-inefficient. In contrast, decision models (DMs), given a description of the environment and task, can perform well in sparse-reward tasks, but, as they do not learn from reward, they are not able to improve towards the optimal solution. In this paper, we present Decision Model-Guided Training (DMGT), a technique that uses a DM with a description of the environment and task to initialise an RL policy, combining the DM's ability to act without training with RL's ability to improve from reward. Instead of exploring from scratch, the agent reaches the goal and receives reward from its first episodes, and RL then improves its policy beyond what the DM achieves. We demonstrate through experiments on seven tasks that our approach outperforms RL in all seven and DM in five. In addition, we provide comprehensive guidelines, derived from ablation studies, for describing an environment and task to a DM.

AI.tldr: DMGT initializes an RL policy with a decision model given the environment and task description, so the agent reaches the goal from its first episodes and RL then improves beyond the decision model; it outperforms RL on all seven tested tasks and the decision model on five.
AI.motivation: RL is slow and sample-inefficient on tasks with exploration challenges and sparse rewards when learning from scratch, while decision models perform well on sparse-reward tasks but cannot improve toward the optimum because they do not learn from reward.
AI.method: Decision Model-Guided Training (DMGT) uses a decision model, given a description of the environment and task, to initialize an RL policy, which then learns from reward; the ablations yield guidelines for describing an environment and task to a decision model.
AI.result: Across seven tasks, DMGT outperforms RL in all seven and the decision model in five.
AI.conclusion: Initializing RL from a decision model combines acting without training with reward-driven improvement, and the ablation-derived guidelines help in describing tasks to decision models.

title: Leakage- and Label-Aware Benchmarking of Class-Imbalance Strategies for Multimodal Chest X-Ray and EHR Classification
summary: Benchmarks of class-imbalance strategies for multimodal chest X-ray (CXR) and electronic health record (EHR) prediction are often evaluated on record-level splits of cohorts in which one patient contributes several radiographs. We audit such a benchmark on 29,083 MIMIC-CXR radiographs of 10,479 patients with eight diagnosis targets.
