First, the record-split benchmark was misleading: a lookup table that copies the label of a development-set radiograph with the same EHR vector nearly matched the best model, and on unseen patients every model fell to the level of predicting every case positive. Second, tracing the labels back to MIMIC-IV explained why: each patient's labels are keyword matches on the diagnosis codes of a single admission, copied, with one EHR vector per patient, to all of the patient's radiographs, so about a third of the radiographs carry labels that differ from the codes of their own admission. Third, under patient-separated evaluation with admission-aligned and rule-refined labels, the initial conclusions do not hold: in the evaluated configurations no imbalance strategy raised the observed mean macro F2 over no augmentation by more than 0.01, tuned tree ensembles showed no consistent advantage over tuned logistic regression, and the released EHR variables stayed at the level of the all-positive baseline, whereas the diagnostic history available at imaging time and image embeddings exceeded it, including, with rule-refined labels, a CheXpert-trained encoder that never saw these radiographs; RAD-DINO had seen 96.6% of them during self-supervised pretraining. Adding either encoder to the diagnostic history gave no statistically significant F2 gain; exploratory AUROC gains were significant with RAD-DINO but not with DenseNet. We provide reusable diagnostics, a leakage-aware protocol and a checklist.

AI.tldr: An audit of a multimodal chest X-ray and EHR class-imbalance benchmark on MIMIC-CXR finds that record-level splits and leaky labels misled earlier conclusions; under patient-separated evaluation, no imbalance strategy raised macro F2 by more than 0.01 over no augmentation.
AI.motivation: Benchmarks of class-imbalance strategies for multimodal chest X-ray and EHR prediction use record-level splits of cohorts in which one patient contributes several radiographs, which can leak information across splits.
AI.method: The authors audit the benchmark on 29,083 MIMIC-CXR radiographs of 10,479 patients with eight diagnosis targets, trace the labels back to the MIMIC-IV diagnosis codes, and re-evaluate under patient-separated evaluation with admission-aligned and rule-refined labels.
AI.result: Under record-level splits, a lookup table copying labels from development radiographs with the same EHR vector nearly matched the best model, and on unseen patients every model fell to the all-positive level; about a third of radiographs carry labels that differ from the codes of their own admission; under the corrected evaluation, no imbalance strategy raised the observed mean macro F2 over no augmentation by more than 0.01, tuned tree ensembles showed no consistent advantage over tuned logistic regression, and the released EHR variables stayed at the all-positive baseline, while the diagnostic history at imaging time and image embeddings exceeded it, including a CheXpert-trained encoder with rule-refined labels; RAD-DINO had seen 96.6% of the radiographs in pretraining; adding either encoder to the diagnostic history gave no statistically significant F2 gain.
AI.conclusion: The initial benchmark conclusions do not hold under leakage-aware, patient-separated evaluation, and the paper provides reusable diagnostics, a leakage-aware protocol and a checklist.

title: Invariance before structure: two modes of emergent compression in representation learning
comment: Extended abstract, UniReps workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Learned representations show striking invariance across biological and artificial neural networks, with different substrates and variations driven by drift, heterogeneity and initialisation. To understand this invariance, we propose Emergent Adaptive Representation Learning (EARL), a framework that distinguishes two modes of emergence in learned representations: state-space compression, where a learned representation gains predictive power over its own future beyond what the network's units can predict individually, and parameter-space compression, where networks with different micro-level parameters converge to the same representation. We formalise both as Fisher sensitivities and introduce ensemble-level information-theoretic measures for each. In a recurrent reservoir with a trained bottleneck, parameter-space compression rises within the first few epochs of training and partly independently of the task, whereas state-space compression rises about 30 epochs later and only when the network begins to learn the temporal structure of the task. These results suggest that invariance to the substrate and task-specific emergent structure are acquired in distinct phases of learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Emergent Adaptive Representation Learning (EARL), which separates state-space compression from parameter-space compression, and shows in a recurrent reservoir that parameter-space compression emerges within the first few epochs while state-space compression emerges about 30 epochs later.
AI.motivation: Learned representations show striking invariance across biological and artificial networks, and the paper seeks to explain this invariance by distinguishing two modes of emergence in learned representations.
AI.method: State-space compression is a representation gaining predictive power over its own future beyond what the units predict individually; parameter-space compression is networks with different micro-level parameters converging to the same representation; both are formalized as Fisher sensitivities with ensemble-level information-theoretic measures and studied in a recurrent reservoir with a trained bottleneck.
AI.result: Parameter-space compression rises within the first few epochs and partly independently of the task; state-space compression rises about 30 epochs later, and only when the network begins to learn the temporal structure of the task.
AI.conclusion: Invariance to the substrate and task-specific emergent structure are acquired in distinct phases of learning.

title: Tight Asymptotic Bounds on the Maximum Number of Linear Regions of Piecewise-Linear Kolmogorov--Arnold networks
summary: Schoots et al.~\citep{schoots2025relating} (AISTATS 2025) established a generally loose upper bound on the number of linear regions of continuous piecewise-linear (CPWL) Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs), without providing a lower bound. We consider a $T$-layer network with width vector $\mathbf n=(n_0,\ldots,n_T)$, input dimension $n_0=d$, output width $n_T=1$, and at most $k\geq2$ affine segments per edge. Our matching upper and lower bounds determine the tight growth order $\Theta_{\mathbf n}(k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}\rho_{\ell-1}})$ in $k$, where $\rho_{\ell-1}:=\min_{0\leq s\leq\ell-1}n_s$. When every hidden width is at least $d$, the tight order simplifies to $\Theta_{\mathbf n}(k^{dT})$. The upper bound of \citep{schoots2025relating} is $k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}n_{\ell-1}n_\ell}$. Our upper bound improves it by a factor of $\Theta_{\mathbf n}\!\left(k^{\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}n_{\ell-1}n_\ell-\sum_{\ell=1}^{T}\rho_{\ell-1}} \right)$, with strict asymptotic improvement whenever a hidden layer has width greater than one. We further compare CPWL KANs with rectified linear unit (ReLU) networks using dense parameterizations with at most $\Lambda$ parameters per model and the same fixed nonlinear depth $T$. Counting trainable knot locations and optimizing the widths and $k$, we prove that the maximum region count of CPWL KANs divided by that of ReLU networks is $\Theta_{d,T}(\Lambda^{d\lfloor T/2\rfloor})$ as $\Lambda\to\infty$, yielding a polynomial advantage for KANs when $T\geq2$. These tight bounds characterize the attainable geometric complexity of CPWL KANs, providing a foundation for understanding their expressive power and guiding architectural design.

AI.tldr: The paper gives matching upper and lower bounds on the maximum number of linear regions of piecewise-linear Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, tightening a previously loose upper bound and showing a polynomial advantage over ReLU networks when the depth is at least two.
AI.motivation: Schoots et al. (AISTATS 2025) established a generally loose upper bound on the number of linear regions of CPWL KANs without providing a lower bound.
AI.method: For a T-layer network with width vector n, input dimension d, output width 1 and at most k affine segments per edge, the authors derive matching bounds, with rho defined as the minimum width over the preceding layers; they also compare with dense ReLU networks with at most Lambda parameters at the same fixed depth, counting trainable knot locations and optimizing the widths and k.
AI.result: The tight growth order is Theta(k^(sum of rho over layers)) in k, which simplifies to k^(dT) when every hidden width is at least d; the new upper bound improves the earlier one by a factor that is strictly asymptotic whenever a hidden layer has width greater than one; the ratio of region counts of CPWL KANs to ReLU networks is Theta(Lambda^(d times floor(T/2))) as Lambda grows.
AI.conclusion: The bounds characterize the attainable geometric complexity of CPWL KANs and give a polynomial advantage over ReLU networks for T at least 2, guiding architectural design.

title: QRAE: Query-Relevant Attention Entropy for Context Compression in DeepSearch Agents
summary: DeepSearch LLM agents repeatedly search and carry retrieved sources into subsequent reasoning steps. This expanding context increases token consumption and latency, although many results do not contribute to later reasoning. We propose Query-Relevant Attention Entropy (QRAE), an online context compression method that uses sparse evidence-assessment heads to decide which intact retrieved chunks should persist across reasoning steps. It scores bounded candidate batches through paired prefills: a query-free control suppresses shared attention responses, while normalized entropy measures the breadth of the positive response within each chunk. High-scoring chunks enter a persistent evidence whitelist and are included in the reasoning context. Uncertain chunks remain outside the reasoning context but are retained in a candidate cache, where they can be retrieved for later reevaluation. QRAE requires neither an additional generative compression pass nor modification of the attention operator. Across multiple DeepSearch benchmarks and reasoning models, QRAE improves task success by an average of 2.35 percentage points and reduces end-to-end latency and reported token usage by an average of 30% and 45%, respectively. These benefits generalize to a model with nearly 100B parameters.

AI.tldr: QRAE compresses retrieved context in DeepSearch agents by keeping only the chunks that sparse evidence-assessment heads score as relevant, improving task success by an average of 2.35 percentage points while cutting latency by about 30% and reported token usage by about 45%.
AI.motivation: In DeepSearch agents, the expanding context of retrieved sources increases token consumption and latency, although many results do not contribute to later reasoning.
AI.method: Sparse evidence-assessment heads score bounded candidate batches through paired prefills, a query-free control suppressing shared attention responses and normalized entropy measuring the breadth of the positive response within each chunk; high-scoring chunks enter a persistent evidence whitelist, while uncertain chunks go to a candidate cache for later reevaluation; no extra generative compression pass or change to the attention operator is needed.
AI.result: Across multiple DeepSearch benchmarks and reasoning models, QRAE improves task success by an average of 2.35 percentage points and reduces end-to-end latency and reported token usage by an average of 30% and 45%, respectively; the benefits generalize to a model with nearly 100B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Attention-based online context selection can reduce the cost and latency of DeepSearch agents without an additional compression pass.

title: Towards Multiscale Molecular Representation Learning through Geometry-Based Fragmentation for Polymer Property Prediction
comment: 29 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in ACS Omega
summary: It is well established that molecular substructures can contribute unequally to chemical and physical properties, with specific motifs or side chains often playing dominant roles. Fragment-based representations have therefore emerged as an effective strategy for incorporating chemically meaningful inductive biases, as exemplified by molecular fingerprints and fragment-based attention mechanisms. However, many existing fragmentation-based machine learning methods rely on predefined chemical rules, which may yield suboptimal fragmentation for previously unseen or chemically unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations. To address these limitations, we formulate molecular fragmentation as a radius-constrained optimization problem inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters is not fixed a priori but emerges from the specified radius, and propose a geometry-based fragmentation method that partitions arbitrary molecular or material structures using largely geometric information, without relying on predefined chemical fragmentation rules. The method provides flexible control over fragment size, enabling the construction of multiscale fragment representations for scale-adaptive modeling. Building on this framework, we develop a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structural information and incorporate it into a multimodal machine learning model combining p-SMILES representations with three-dimensional (3D) conformational information. Experiments on a benchmark polymer dataset show that incorporating 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based exclusively on p-SMILES representations. Explainable artificial intelligence analyses further provide insights into the physical relevance of the learned representations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a radius-constrained, geometry-based molecular fragmentation method and a multimodal model that combines p-SMILES with 3D conformations, reporting improved prediction accuracy for several polymer properties over p-SMILES-only models.
AI.motivation: Predefined chemical fragmentation rules may give suboptimal fragmentations for unseen or unfamiliar structures and often overlook the importance of multiscale molecular representations.
AI.method: Fragmentation is formulated as a radius-constrained optimization inspired by the k-center formulation, where the number of clusters emerges from the radius, using largely geometric information; a geometric fragment-based attention mechanism that integrates multiscale structure is incorporated into a multimodal model combining p-SMILES with 3D conformational information.
AI.result: On a benchmark polymer dataset, adding 3D conformational information improves prediction accuracy for several properties over models based only on p-SMILES; explainable AI analyses provide insight into the physical relevance of the learned representations.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-based multiscale fragments with 3D information form a flexible inductive bias for polymer property prediction, with interpretable learned representations.

title: GTAFL: Addressing Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning in Medical Image
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics (JBHI). 13 pages. Code: this https URL
summary: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions. During the inference stage, an ensemble mechanism combines retrained expert classifiers to handle test data with unknown distributions. Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets manifest that our framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: GTAFL introduces test-agnostic long-tailed federated learning for medical images, combining adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, self-supervised learning and an ensemble, and outperforms other state-of-the-art methods on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing long-tailed federated learning methods assume the model will be evaluated on a uniform test distribution, whereas practical test data in healthcare is often unknown and unpredictable, which can cause model failures.
AI.method: During training, GTAFL uses adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces; at inference, an ensemble of the retrained expert classifiers handles test data with unknown distributions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on CIFAR10 and two medical datasets show that the framework outperforms other state-of-the-art methods; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Long-tailed federated learning for medical imaging should not assume a known test distribution, and GTAFL is offered as a framework for that setting.

title: Reproducing Kernel (Quasi-)Banach Spaces with the $\ell^p$ Coefficient Norms
summary: This paper advances the theory of reproducing kernel Banach spaces (RKBSs) by investigating the general $\ell^p$ regularization framework, with a particular focus on the non-convex regime $0<p<1$. While our preceding work established the foundation for RKBSs with the $\ell^1$ norm, the pursuit of stronger sparsity---closer to the $\ell^0$ pseudo-norm---naturally motivates this exploration into $\ell^p$ quasi-norms. For $0<p<1$, we construct reproducing kernel quasi-Banach spaces (RKQBSs) with $\ell^p$ quasi-norms and establish existence and sparsity results for interpolation and regularized learning under appropriate assumptions. We characterize the linear and relaxed representer theorems in terms of a generalized Lebesgue constant and derive bounds under kernel decay, sample spacing, and stability assumptions. For $p>1$, we construct RKBSs using a fixed countable dictionary, establish minimizer existence, and identify the optimal relaxed representer factor through an off-sample coefficient operator. These results reveal fundamental differences between the regimes $0<p<1$, $p=1$, and $p>1$. Numerical experiments compare the accuracy and sparsity of solutions for these three cases.

AI.tldr: Extends reproducing kernel Banach space theory to l^p coefficient norms, constructing reproducing kernel quasi-Banach spaces for 0<p<1 and RKBSs for p>1, with representer theorems and sparsity results that differ across the three regimes.
AI.motivation: Prior work covered only the l^1 norm, while stronger sparsity closer to the l^0 pseudo-norm calls for non-convex l^p quasi-norms with 0<p<1.
AI.method: For 0<p<1 the authors build reproducing kernel quasi-Banach spaces with l^p quasi-norms and analyze interpolation and regularized learning through a generalized Lebesgue constant under kernel decay, sample spacing and stability assumptions; for p>1 they build RKBSs from a fixed countable dictionary and identify the optimal relaxed representer factor through an off-sample coefficient operator.
AI.result: Existence and sparsity results are established for 0<p<1, and linear and relaxed representer theorems are characterized with bounds; numerical experiments compare accuracy and sparsity across the regimes 0<p<1, p=1 and p>1.
AI.conclusion: The three regimes differ fundamentally in representer theory and in the sparsity of solutions.

title: Should We Pay This Much for Robustness? Efficient Proxy Certificates with Marginal Guarantees
summary: Modern classifiers remain sensitive to small input perturbations, while strong model-agnostic robustness certificates such as randomized smoothing are often too expensive for deployment, requiring an extensive number (e.g. 2000) of model forward passes per input. We propose a framework that delegates certification to a cheap proxy function while statistically controlling its deviation from the original sound certificate. Given an exchangeable unlabeled calibration set, we tune the proxy via robust conformal risk control to guarantee a bounded marginal (rather than pointwise) false-approval rate: the probability, over future inputs, that the proxy accepts an input whose prediction is flipped due to perturbation. The resulting proxy certificate can be used either as a standalone marginal certificate or as a fallback mechanism that invokes the expensive certificate only when the proxy rejects. We provide both single-sample and sample-heavy calibration recipes. Empirically, as a standalone certificate our method reduces the test-time certification cost to a single model forward while retaining much of the certified performance of randomized smoothing at small radii, and as a fallback it recovers the certified ratio of randomized smoothing at a more modest speedup. This enables cheap yet effective robustness guarantees for larger architectures such as vision transformers and language models.

AI.tldr: Proposes certifying robustness with a cheap proxy function whose deviation from randomized smoothing is statistically controlled, giving a marginal rather than pointwise false-approval guarantee.
AI.motivation: Randomized smoothing gives strong model-agnostic robustness certificates but needs about 2000 forward passes per input, which is too costly for deployment.
AI.method: The proxy is tuned on an exchangeable unlabeled calibration set via robust conformal risk control to bound the marginal false-approval rate, and it is used either as a standalone certificate or as a fallback that invokes the expensive certificate only when the proxy rejects; single-sample and sample-heavy calibration recipes are given.
AI.result: As a standalone certificate it reduces test-time certification cost to a single forward pass while retaining much of the certified performance of randomized smoothing at small radii; as a fallback it recovers randomized smoothing's certified ratio at a more modest speedup.
AI.conclusion: The approach makes robustness guarantees affordable for larger architectures such as vision transformers and language models.

title: Performance metrics in machine learning: a scenario-based guide from the confusion matrix to calibration, regression and uncertainty
summary: Performance metrics can yield different conclusions from the same predictions. This methodological tutorial explains the effects of class prevalence, decision thresholds, aggregation rules and software conventions through controlled scenarios. Twenty-two confusion-matrix metrics are organized in a prevalence-coded map. Fifteen scenarios cover binary and multi-class classification, score discrimination, probability calibration, regression, uncertainty and consistency checks. Inputs are fixed in released files, and one factor is varied in each scenario. All 205 verification checks passed; 202 were independent and 3 were internal. An always-negative rule achieved an accuracy of 0.990 at a prevalence of 0.010, with balanced accuracy of 0.500. At fixed sensitivity and specificity, precision fell from 0.889 to 0.008 as prevalence fell from 0.5 to 0.001. Three probability variants shared a ROC-AUC of 0.825 but had calibration slopes of 2.08, 1.04 and 0.52. With 10 participants, participant-majority accuracy of 0.700 had a 95% interval of 0.348-0.933. Fold-averaged scores were falsely flagged as inconsistent under an inappropriate pooled-test-set model. A goal-based metric table and a reporting checklist are provided. The scenarios illustrate mechanisms and do not estimate their frequency in published studies. A literature audit and a real-data demonstration are specified as future protocols and were not executed.

AI.tldr: A methodological tutorial showing through fifteen controlled scenarios how class prevalence, thresholds, aggregation and software conventions change the conclusions drawn from the same predictions, with a prevalence-coded map of twenty-two confusion-matrix metrics.
AI.motivation: Performance metrics can lead to different conclusions from identical predictions, and the effects of prevalence, decision thresholds, aggregation rules and software defaults are not always clear to practitioners.
AI.method: Twenty-two confusion-matrix metrics are organized in a prevalence-coded map, and fifteen scenarios covering classification, score discrimination, calibration, regression, uncertainty and consistency checks each vary one factor while the inputs stay fixed in released files.
AI.result: All 205 verification checks passed (202 independent, 3 internal). An always-negative rule reached accuracy 0.990 at prevalence 0.010 with balanced accuracy 0.500; at fixed sensitivity and specificity precision fell from 0.889 to 0.008 as prevalence fell from 0.5 to 0.001; three probability variants shared ROC-AUC 0.825 with calibration slopes 2.08, 1.04 and 0.52; participant-majority accuracy of 0.700 from 10 participants had a 95% interval of 0.348 to 0.933.
AI.conclusion: The paper supplies a goal-based metric table and a reporting checklist; the scenarios illustrate mechanisms and do not estimate how often these pitfalls occur in published studies, and the literature audit and real-data demonstration remain future protocols that were not executed.

title: Can an LLM Actually Reason and Program about Neural Network's Weights or is it just memorization on steroids? Exploring "Weight-Space Programming"
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been reported to read and write the raw weights of neural networks directly, a capability termed weight-space programming. We ask whether the reading side of this capability reflects reasoning about weight flows or a combination of local arithmetic at the network's edges and memorized priors over public datasets. We test Claude Opus 5.5 on small convolutional networks of about 125,000 parameters trained on five image datasets, providing every weight as plain text with no tools, no forward passes, and no dataset or class names. The model performs accurate local calculations: batch-normalization statistics lead it to infer about three optimizer steps on networks stopped after three updates, and output-layer sign patterns recover the vehicle/animal split of CIFAR-10. The sessions report reading the first and last layers closely and sampling the middle, and several claims built on partial tracing fail verification, although we did not run a direct forward-pass test. Semantic judgments lean on familiar datasets: the model names CIFAR-10 for CIFAR-10 networks but also for all three fast-food networks, relabels KMNIST as MNIST, reads a 99.57%-accurate SAT-6 network as CIFAR-10 animal photos, and calls "frog" the output favored by a feature that fires most on trees. Permuting CIFAR-10's labels preserves the output split at the new indices, but every class pair the model interprets is then wrong, indicating reliance on remembered label order. These are exploratory results from mostly single runs. We conclude that zero-shot weight reading by this model is better described as local arithmetic plus dataset priors than as weight-flow tracing, and we provide a protocol for auditing future weight-space claims.

AI.tldr: Tests whether Claude Opus 5.5 can reason about neural network weights from raw text, concluding that its zero-shot weight reading is better described as local arithmetic plus dataset priors than as weight-flow tracing.
AI.motivation: LLMs have been reported to read and write raw network weights, and it is unclear whether this reflects reasoning about weight flows or memorized priors over public datasets.
AI.method: The model is given every weight of about 125,000-parameter convolutional networks trained on five image datasets as plain text, with no tools, no forward passes, and no dataset or class names; exploratory sessions probe batch-normalization inference, output-layer sign patterns and label permutations.
AI.result: The model infers about three optimizer steps from batch-normalization statistics and recovers the vehicle/animal split of CIFAR-10 from output-layer signs, but some claims built on partial tracing fail verification; it names CIFAR-10 for all three fast-food networks, reads a 99.57% accurate SAT-6 network as CIFAR-10 animal photos, and after permuting CIFAR-10 labels keeps the output split while every interpreted class pair is wrong.
AI.conclusion: The results point to reliance on remembered label order and dataset priors, and the authors provide a protocol for auditing future weight-space claims; they come from mostly single exploratory runs, and no direct forward-pass test was run.

title: Optimal Competitive Ratios for Chasing Convex Functions with Quadratic Growth
summary: Chasing convex function has attracted much attention in recent years, which can be formulated as a game between a learner and an adversary. In each round, the adversary reveals a convex function, and the learner selects a decision and incurs a hitting cost and a movement cost for changing its decision. The performance of the learner is measured by the \emph{competitive ratio}, which compares its cumulative cost with that of an optimal offline decision sequence. For Euclidean movement, existing upper and lower bounds for $\kappa$-well-conditioned functions exhibit a polynomial gap. For squared Euclidean movement, dimension-free competitive guarantees have been established under quadratic growth, but the optimal competitive ratio remains unclear. In this paper, we establish optimal dimension-free competitive ratios for convex function chasing under two types of movement costs. For Euclidean movement, we propose Clipped Proximal Descent (CPD), which combines a balanced proximal step with a clipped correction toward the current minimizer. CPD achieves an $O(\kappa^{1/3})$ competitive ratio for smooth convex functions satisfying quadratic growth, improving the previous $O(\sqrt{\kappa})$ upper bound and matching the existing $\Omega(\kappa^{1/3})$ lower bound. For squared Euclidean movement, we establish the exact optimal dimension-free competitive ratio for convex functions satisfying quadratic growth. Our result is based on a new tight competitive analysis of Regularized Online Balanced Descent (R-OBD) and a matching lower bound against randomized algorithms.

AI.tldr: Establishes optimal dimension-free competitive ratios for convex function chasing, giving an O(κ^{1/3}) ratio for Euclidean movement via Clipped Proximal Descent and the exact optimal ratio for squared Euclidean movement.
AI.motivation: For Euclidean movement, upper and lower bounds for κ-well-conditioned functions had a polynomial gap, and for squared Euclidean movement the optimal competitive ratio under quadratic growth was unknown.
AI.method: Clipped Proximal Descent (CPD) combines a balanced proximal step with a clipped correction toward the current minimizer; for squared Euclidean movement the analysis is a new tight competitive analysis of Regularized Online Balanced Descent (R-OBD).
AI.result: CPD achieves O(κ^{1/3}) for smooth convex functions with quadratic growth, improving the previous O(√κ) upper bound and matching the existing Ω(κ^{1/3}) lower bound; for squared Euclidean movement the exact optimal ratio is established and matched by a lower bound against randomized algorithms.
AI.conclusion: The results close the gap for both movement costs, giving optimal dimension-free guarantees under quadratic growth.

title: Value or Attention: Investigating Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for Graph Attention Networks
comment: Accepted at the XAI4Science Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival). 17 pages, 9 figures
summary: Graph Attention Networks (GATs) are increasingly used in domains where scientists need to read a model's reasoning, from medicine to materials science, yet the routing they learn remains opaque to most explainers. Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) follows the model's computation, but in an attention layer the relevance reaching a node is the sum of two mechanically different quantities: its content relevance through the value path and its routing relevance through the attention path. Existing rules either drop one or add them into a single number. We write a single product rule with free weights on the two factors that recovers current approaches as special cases. The value path measures what content a node supplied against a zero baseline; the attention path measures how the node shaped what was passed relative to its neighborhood, and its sign records whether the node's features moved the gating the way the prediction demanded. On a ground-truth classification task, we show that the same node receives negative, positive and near-zero relevance under three settings of the rule. The separated relevance maps yield a hypothesis about the model: it gains by not reading that node. We give reading rules for both paths and argue that they should be interpreted separately.

AI.tldr: Proposes a product-rule relevance propagation for graph attention networks that separates value-path content relevance from attention-path routing relevance, showing the same node can receive negative, positive or near-zero relevance under different settings of the rule.
AI.motivation: In attention layers, LRP sums content relevance through the value path and routing relevance through the attention path into one number, and existing rules either drop one path or merge the two.
AI.method: A single product rule with free weights on the two factors recovers current approaches as special cases; the value path measures what content a node supplied against a zero baseline, and the attention path measures how the node shaped what was passed relative to its neighborhood, with its sign recording whether the node moved the gating in the direction the prediction demanded.
AI.result: On a ground-truth classification task the same node receives negative, positive and near-zero relevance under three settings of the rule, and the separated relevance maps suggest the model gains by not reading that node.
AI.conclusion: The authors give reading rules for both paths and argue that they should be interpreted separately.

title: SAE Interprets MoE: Sparse AutoEncoders Reveal That MoE Experts Exhibit Human-Interpretable Fine-Grained Specialization
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a few of many experts, yet what an individual expert is responsible for remains unsettled. Existing analyses count how often an expert is selected on domain-labeled corpora, an instrument that fixes the taxonomy in advance, stays coarse, and records selection rather than contribution. We instead study specialization in feature space by training a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on the output of an MoE layer. Since this output is a router-weighted sum of expert outputs and the SAE encoder is affine, the pre-activation of every latent decomposes exactly over the experts. Aggregated over a corpus, this gives each expert a dominant set of latents whose activation it principally drives. On layers 4, 30 and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B, contribution is far more concentrated than gating, most latents have only one or two dominators, and the overlap between dominant sets concentrates on a few expert pairs. Auto-interpreting these sets reveals a division of labor below coarse domains, with distinct experts for Java and front-end web code, or for geometry and for arithmetic and polynomials, while the coarse domains themselves take very unequal numbers of experts. Our SAEs and code are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Trains sparse autoencoders on MoE layer outputs and shows that expert contributions are far more concentrated than gating, with experts specializing at a fine-grained, human-interpretable level below coarse domains.
AI.motivation: Existing analyses count how often experts are selected on domain-labeled corpora, which fixes the taxonomy in advance, stays coarse, and records selection rather than contribution.
AI.method: Because the MoE output is a router-weighted sum of expert outputs and the SAE encoder is affine, each latent pre-activation decomposes exactly over the experts; aggregating over a corpus gives each expert a dominant set of latents, studied on layers 4, 30 and 46 of Qwen3-30B-A3B.
AI.result: Contribution is much more concentrated than gating, most latents have only one or two dominators, and dominant-set overlaps concentrate on a few expert pairs; auto-interpretation reveals distinct experts for Java and front-end web code and for geometry versus arithmetic and polynomials.
AI.conclusion: Expert specialization operates below coarse domains, and the coarse domains receive very unequal numbers of experts.

title: Gradient Boosting for Efficient Rank Discovery in Tensor Network Kernel Machines
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Code available at: this https URL
summary: Tensor network kernel machines (TNKMs) combine nonlinear features with low-rank tensor representations to model complex relationships efficiently. However, selecting an appropriate tensor rank remains challenging, as conventional rank-search methods require training multiple candidate models, increasing computational costs. In this work, we focus on a canonical polyadic (CP) tensor network parameterization and propose GB-CPKM, a gradient boosting framework that builds a higher-capacity predictor by sequentially adding fixed-rank learners. This approach provides a new perspective on rank selection by incrementally increasing model capacity, with ensemble size selected based on validation performance rather than through explicit rank search. Experiments on real-world regression benchmarks show that GB-CPKM trains up to 6x faster and uses up to 2x less peak memory than a conventional rank-selection method based on cross-validation, while achieving comparable predictive performance. These results highlight the potential of gradient boosting to improve the computational efficiency and scalability of tensor-network learning.

AI.tldr: Proposes GB-CPKM, a gradient boosting framework for canonical polyadic tensor network kernel machines that selects rank by sequentially adding fixed-rank learners instead of running an explicit rank search.
AI.motivation: Selecting tensor rank for tensor network kernel machines is costly because conventional rank-search methods train multiple candidate models.
AI.method: Gradient boosting sequentially adds fixed-rank CP learners to build a higher-capacity predictor, with the ensemble size chosen by validation performance.
AI.result: On real-world regression benchmarks GB-CPKM trains up to 6x faster and uses up to 2x less peak memory than a cross-validation-based rank selection method, with comparable predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: Gradient boosting can improve the computational efficiency and scalability of tensor-network learning.

title: PersonaAgent: Retrieval-Augmented Transaction Anomaly Scoring with Refreshable Multi-Entity Persona Memory
summary: In large-scale payment networks, entities (card, merchant, etc.) and their interactions play a key role in transaction anomaly detection. However, transaction patterns between different entities usually change more frequently than the production model refresh schedule. Meanwhile, entity embedding tables suffer from high-cardinality and sparse interaction issues. To resolve the above challenges, we present PersonaAgent, an agentic transaction anomaly detection framework which represents the latest entity behavior signals as personas and saves them in a refreshable memory. Offline, a weekly scheduled batch job is used to extract the latest behavior signals and update them in the memory. At inference time, a lightweight adapter retrieves the corresponding entity behavior signals of each transaction from memory and uses them to augment the base anomaly classifier's scoring. Through comprehensive benchmarking with different anomaly detection models at Visa, PersonaAgent is able to score transactions efficiently (a 1,000-transaction CPU batch in 1-2 ms), lifting the PR-AUC by 0.65-6.58% and the production business metric by 8.93-14.24% relatively in deployment.

AI.tldr: Presents PersonaAgent, an agentic transaction anomaly detector that stores refreshable entity behavior personas in memory and retrieves them to augment a base classifier, deployed at Visa.
AI.motivation: Entity transaction patterns change more often than the production model refresh schedule, and entity embedding tables suffer from high cardinality and sparse interactions.
AI.method: A weekly batch job extracts the latest behavior signals into a refreshable persona memory offline; at inference a lightweight adapter retrieves each transaction's entity personas to augment the anomaly classifier's score.
AI.result: Benchmarking against several anomaly detection models at Visa shows relative PR-AUC gains of 0.65% to 6.58%, a relative production business metric gain of 8.93% to 14.24% in deployment, and scoring of a 1,000-transaction CPU batch in 1 to 2 ms.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers efficient, deployable augmentation of anomaly detection with fresher entity behavior signals.

title: How Far Can Untrained Neural Networks Go in Anomaly Detection? From Tables to Pixels
summary: Anomaly detection (AD) is often framed as a representation-learning problem, where strong performance is expected to require learned features or AD-specific optimization. However, this view can overlook the intrinsic separability of anomalies from normal references, even in the absence of learned representations. We therefore investigate how far untrained neural networks can go in anomaly detection. To this end, we propose PRISM, a framework combining fixed random nonlinear features with normal-reference Mahalanobis scoring for tabular detection and dense visual localization. Across 47 tabular datasets in ADBench, PRISM-T achieves the highest mean AUROC (86.4%) and the second-highest mean AUPRC (65.9%) among the compared methods. On MVTec AD and VisA, covering 27 visual categories, PRISM-V achieves mean image-level and pixel-level AUROCs of 90.4% and 96.4%, respectively. Notably, both models achieve these results without neural weight optimization or pretrained representations. A theoretical analysis further characterizes how nonlinear transformations affect the mean and covariance contributions to the Mahalanobis score gap, while empirical analyses examine the resulting score separability. These findings establish PRISM as both a competitive anomaly detector and a prior-to-learning baseline for assessing the added value of learned representations in anomaly detection.

AI.tldr: Shows that PRISM, which combines fixed random nonlinear features with normal-reference Mahalanobis scoring and no trained weights, is competitive with learned methods for tabular anomaly detection and visual localization.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection is often framed as representation learning, but this overlooks the intrinsic separability of anomalies from normal references even without learned features.
AI.method: PRISM applies untrained random nonlinear feature maps followed by Mahalanobis scoring against normal references, for tabular detection (PRISM-T) and dense visual localization (PRISM-V); a theoretical analysis examines how the nonlinearity affects the mean and covariance contributions to the score gap.
AI.result: Across 47 ADBench tabular datasets PRISM-T has the highest mean AUROC (86.4%) and second-highest mean AUPRC (65.9%) among compared methods; on MVTec AD and VisA, covering 27 visual categories, PRISM-V reaches mean image-level AUROC 90.4% and pixel-level AUROC 96.4%.
AI.conclusion: Without neural weight optimization or pretrained representations, PRISM serves as a competitive detector and as a prior-to-learning baseline for measuring what learned representations add.

title: Detecting Weather Fronts from Satellite Observations: What Does Reanalysis Add?
comment: Accepted to the 2nd Workshop on Advances in Representation Learning for Earth Observation at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Weather fronts are transition regions between air masses with contrasting thermodynamic properties and are associated with mid-latitude precipitation and severe weather. We investigate machine learning (ML) methods for detecting weather fronts and quantify the contribution of reanalysis data to performance. We compare two configurations of the same ML model for pixel-wise frontal classification over the North Atlantic and Europe: (1) using only geostationary infrared satellite observations, and (2) additionally using 28 ERA5 reanalysis fields. The satellite-only model achieves a neighbourhood critical success index at a 150 km tolerance (CSI@150) of $0.402$, which lies within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services. The satellite$+$ERA5 model achieves $0.575$, an improvement of $0.173$. Our analysis shows that low-level winds are the least predictable from the satellite representation ($R^2 = 0.23$, compared with $0.88$ for temperature), while removing winds or moisture causes the largest decreases in detection performance.

AI.tldr: Shows that adding 28 ERA5 reanalysis fields to geostationary infrared satellite inputs raises weather front detection skill from CSI@150 of 0.402 to 0.575.
AI.motivation: Weather fronts are linked to mid-latitude precipitation and severe weather, and it is unclear how much reanalysis data contributes to machine learning detection from satellites.
AI.method: The same ML model is compared in two configurations for pixel-wise frontal classification over the North Atlantic and Europe, one using only geostationary infrared observations and one adding 28 ERA5 fields.
AI.result: The satellite-only model reaches CSI@150 of 0.402, within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services, and the satellite plus ERA5 model reaches 0.575, a gain of 0.173; low-level winds are least predictable from satellites (R^2 0.23, versus 0.88 for temperature), and removing winds or moisture causes the largest drops in detection performance.
AI.conclusion: Reanalysis fields add substantial skill, and low-level wind and moisture information matter most for front detection.

title: Interpretable Multimodal MRI-Clinical Fusion for Functional Outcome Prediction After Acute Ischemic Stroke
summary: This study evaluates the added prognostic value of day-1 multimodal MRI for predicting three-month functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Sixty-six AIS patients with ADC, DWI, FLAIR, and clinical data were analyzed. Three-dimensional pretrained ResNet embeddings were extracted from each MRI modality, reduced using fold-isolated principal component analysis, and combined with structured clinical variables and ADC-derived lesion biomarkers. Linear support vector machines were evaluated using eight-fold stratified group cross-validation across MRI modality combinations. Clinical-only modeling achieved strong performance (AUC = $0.899 \pm 0.151$), while MRI-only models showed limited discrimination (AUC $\approx$ $0.67$-$0.73$). Among multimodal configurations, FLAIR-clinical fusion achieved the highest mean cross-validated performance (AUC = $0.948 \pm 0.061$), followed by ADC-clinical fusion (AUC = $0.941 \pm 0.094$). Full ADC-DWI-FLAIR fusion did not consistently outperform single-modality clinical fusion. Feature-importance analysis identified age, NIHSS subscores, ADC lesion burden, and learned FLAIR representations as key contributors, while qualitative FLAIR activation maps showed responses over lesion-like regions. These findings suggest that compact day-1 FLAIR and ADC representations provide complementary prognostic information beyond clinical variables and support interpretable, data-efficient outcome prediction in AIS.

AI.tldr: Finds that compact day-1 FLAIR and ADC representations add prognostic value beyond clinical variables for three-month functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke, with FLAIR-clinical fusion reaching the highest AUC.
AI.motivation: The added prognostic value of multimodal day-1 MRI beyond clinical data for functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke needs an interpretable evaluation.
AI.method: ADC, DWI and FLAIR embeddings from 3D pretrained ResNets are reduced with fold-isolated PCA, combined with structured clinical variables and ADC lesion biomarkers for 66 patients, and classified by linear support vector machines under eight-fold stratified group cross-validation.
AI.result: Clinical-only modeling reached AUC 0.899 ± 0.151 and MRI-only models 0.67 to 0.73; FLAIR-clinical fusion reached 0.948 ± 0.061 and ADC-clinical fusion 0.941 ± 0.094, while full ADC-DWI-FLAIR fusion did not consistently outperform single-modality clinical fusion.
AI.conclusion: Compact FLAIR and ADC representations provide complementary prognostic information, supporting interpretable, data-efficient outcome prediction after acute ischemic stroke.

title: BUMP: Brief Unexpected Mid-Interpolation Peak
summary: We identify an intriguing phenomenon when linearly interpolating between permutation-aligned neural networks: test accuracy briefly improves near the interpolation endpoints before dropping toward the midpoint, which we term BUMP (Brief Unexpected Mid-interpolation Peak). We observe that BUMP appears consistently across datasets, architectures, training regimes, and remains robust under substantial perturbations such as early checkpoints and extreme pruning. Moreover, controlled ablations suggest that it cannot be attributed to trivial regularization effects. While similar near-endpoint gains are visible in prior interpolation plots, they have not been explicitly documented or systematically and thoroughly analyzed. Leveraging this effect, we propose a simple, novel ensembling scheme: weight-prediction mixed ensembling that combines weight mixing with prediction-space mixing. Across our experiments, the resulting ensembling method consistently outperforms standard logit ensembling in test accuracy and yields improved calibration trade-off, highlighting complementary benefits of weight- and prediction-space mixing.

AI.tldr: Documents BUMP, a brief test accuracy peak near the endpoints when linearly interpolating permutation-aligned networks, and proposes weight-prediction mixed ensembling, which outperforms standard logit ensembling.
AI.motivation: Near-endpoint accuracy gains appear in prior interpolation plots but have not been explicitly documented or systematically analyzed.
AI.method: Linear interpolation between permutation-aligned networks is examined across datasets, architectures and training regimes, under perturbations such as early checkpoints and extreme pruning and with controlled ablations; the proposed ensemble combines weight mixing with prediction-space mixing.
AI.result: The peak appears consistently, stays robust under substantial perturbations and cannot be attributed to trivial regularization effects; weight-prediction mixed ensembling consistently outperforms standard logit ensembling in test accuracy and yields an improved calibration trade-off.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight complementary benefits of weight-space and prediction-space mixing.

title: Do sEMG Foundation Models Improve Cross-Subject Generalisation?
summary: sEMG Foundation Models aim to learn general purpose representations over diverse subjects and recording conditions that boost performance on a variety of downstream tasks. However, existing evaluations make it difficult to discern whether pretraining alone is sufficient to combat the cross-subject overfitting which makes machine learning on sEMG so challenging. We conduct a systematic evaluation of three sEMG foundation models across three gesture classification datasets under both intra-session and inter-subject splits, using three fine-tuning strategies designed to isolate the contribution of pretraining. We find that pretraining boosts performance when train and test samples are drawn from the same recording session, but this benefit largely disappears under inter-subject evaluation. In low subject count datasets, pretraining provides little to no benefit and classical ML baselines match or exceed foundation model performance.

AI.tldr: Systematically tests whether sEMG foundation models improve cross-subject generalization, finding that pretraining helps within a session but its benefit largely disappears under inter-subject evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations do not show whether pretraining alone can counter the cross-subject overfitting that makes machine learning on sEMG difficult.
AI.method: Three sEMG foundation models are evaluated on three gesture classification datasets under intra-session and inter-subject splits, using three fine-tuning strategies designed to isolate the contribution of pretraining.
AI.result: Pretraining boosts performance when training and test samples come from the same session, but this benefit largely vanishes under inter-subject evaluation; on low-subject-count datasets pretraining gives little to no benefit and classical ML baselines match or exceed foundation model performance.
AI.conclusion: Pretraining alone does not sufficiently solve cross-subject generalization for sEMG.

title: Beyond Quadratic Attention: Separable Gaussian Operators for ODE Vision Transformers
summary: Self-attention carries a quadratic cost in token count, which limits how far Vision Transformers can scale with input resolution. We introduce SSoG, a separable sum-of-Gaussians spatial operator that replaces dense self-attention with a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels, reducing the per-layer cost from $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ to subquadratic in $N$. Unlike dot-product self-attention, whose Lipschitz constant is unbounded outside a compact input domain, SSoG with fixed kernels is globally Lipschitz continuous, which, via the Picard--Lindelöf theorem, guarantees that the continuous-depth variant has a unique solution on the whole integration interval, a global guarantee that dense-attention counterparts lack in general. On CIFAR-100 at $224\times224$, in a matched discrete-Transformer setting and in the continuous setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 2.2--4.1 points across three model widths while using 8.8--16.6\% fewer parameters, with depth and training recipe held fixed. In a looped-Transformer setting, SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 5.4--8.1 points. We further probe inference-time scaling by evaluating on inputs up to $1024\times1024$ at matched batch size: in the continuous-depth (Neural ODE) architecture, SSoG reaches up to 154\% higher throughput and over 60\% lower peak memory than dense attention, with the gap widening as resolution grows, consistent with the difference in asymptotic cost. In the discrete and looped settings, SSoG also achieves over 30\% higher throughput than dense attention at this resolution. Together, these results establish SSoG as a practical, parameter-efficient, and theoretically grounded alternative to dense attention across discrete, weight-shared, and continuous-depth Transformer variants.

AI.tldr: Proposes SSoG, a separable sum-of-Gaussians operator that replaces dense self-attention in Vision Transformers, improving CIFAR-100 accuracy and inference throughput while being globally Lipschitz, which guarantees a unique solution for the continuous-depth variant.
AI.motivation: Self-attention costs grow quadratically with token count, which limits how far Vision Transformers scale with input resolution, and dot-product attention has an unbounded Lipschitz constant outside a compact input domain.
AI.method: SSoG uses a learned mixture of axis-factorized Gaussian kernels with subquadratic cost in N; with fixed kernels it is globally Lipschitz, which via the Picard-Lindelöf theorem guarantees a unique solution on the whole integration interval for the continuous-depth variant.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100 at 224x224 SSoG improves Top-1 accuracy by 2.2 to 4.1 points with 8.8% to 16.6% fewer parameters in matched discrete and continuous settings, and by 5.4 to 8.1 points in a looped-Transformer setting; at inputs up to 1024x1024 the Neural ODE variant reaches up to 154% higher throughput and over 60% lower peak memory than dense attention.
AI.conclusion: SSoG is presented as a practical, parameter-efficient and theoretically grounded alternative to dense attention across discrete, weight-shared and continuous-depth Transformers.

title: FewStepRL: Fine-tuning Few-step Diffusion Models with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models, but most RL objectives roll out the current policy at every iteration, and with a many-step sampler these rollouts typically dominate the cost of training. Few-step models cut this cost, yet they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives are built for an instantaneous velocity with a many-step sampler. We adapt RL objectives to few-step models systematically in three phases, namely a transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation. The transformation to $x$-space expresses each objective we consider through a common policy prediction, at the clean end by default and at an explicitly marked level for transition or flow-map objectives, so that objectives stated over densities, velocities or rewards become comparable. The decomposition writes the gradient of each of these objectives as the sum of a self-regression toward a reference and a reward augmentation, so that a method reduces, at the gradient level, to a choice of anchors and weights. The adaptation computes each anchor from a few-step model at the end of its transport or along its tangent, with the instantaneous velocity recovered from the network itself or from an auxiliary network. This yields few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL in one modular codebase. In our experiments, reward-gradient-based methods are the most effective when the reward is differentiable and its gradient is affordable; otherwise DiffusionNFT-style methods generally reach high rewards in relatively few iterations despite a sometimes higher per-iteration cost. Extra inference steps show no systematic aggregate benefit in our experiments, although selected outputs visibly improve with two to four times as many sampling steps as in training.

AI.tldr: Adapts reinforcement learning objectives to few-step diffusion models through a transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation, yielding few-step versions of five methods in one codebase.
AI.motivation: Few-step models model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives were built for instantaneous velocity with many-step samplers, and many-step rollouts dominate training cost.
AI.method: Each objective is expressed in x-space through a common policy prediction, its gradient is written as a self-regression toward a reference plus a reward augmentation, and each anchor is computed from a few-step model at the end of transport or along its tangent.
AI.result: Few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL are implemented; reward-gradient methods work best when the reward is differentiable and its gradient affordable, otherwise DiffusionNFT-style methods reach high rewards in relatively few iterations; extra inference steps show no systematic aggregate benefit, though selected outputs improve with two to four times as many sampling steps as in training.
AI.conclusion: The choice of method depends on reward differentiability and gradient cost, and extra sampling steps help only selected outputs.

title: Geometric Relevance Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating Focused Post-Training Supervision in Diffusion Docking
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures; accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 AI4DD Workshop
summary: Diffusion-based molecular docking requires learning a corrective score field across a broad corruption distribution, yet individual pose errors can differ substantially in their structural consequences. This creates a post-training conflict between preserving broad score-field coverage and concentrating supervision on corrections that appear more relevant to docking geometry. Using DiffDock, a fixed-budget study compares broad continuation with torsional supervision focused on Cartesian consequence or conditional target consistency, and with a broad/focused mixture. Evaluation separates fixed score fidelity, generated-pose quality, best-of-10 sampling capacity, and confidence-selected Top-1 docking performance. At <5 Angstrom, broad continuation had the highest mean Top-1 success among trained policies, and focused or mixed supervision showed no consistent advantage under the tested budget. The starting model had better fixed score fidelity, whereas the evaluated broad-continuation model had higher mean Top-1 success with the same aggregate best-of-10 recovery. Focusing supervision on structurally consequential or more consistently specified corrections did not consistently improve returned-pose success over broad continuation.

AI.tldr: Finds that focusing post-training supervision on structurally consequential torsional corrections does not beat broad continuation for DiffDock's returned-pose success.
AI.motivation: Diffusion docking must learn a score field over a broad corruption distribution, while concentrating supervision on docking-relevant corrections may conflict with preserving that coverage.
AI.method: A fixed-budget study of DiffDock compares broad continuation with torsional supervision focused on Cartesian consequence or conditional target consistency, and with a broad/focused mixture, evaluating score fidelity, generated-pose quality, best-of-10 capacity and confidence-selected Top-1 performance.
AI.result: At under 5 Angstrom, broad continuation had the highest mean Top-1 success among trained policies, while focused or mixed supervision showed no consistent advantage; the starting model had better fixed score fidelity, and both had the same aggregate best-of-10 recovery.
AI.conclusion: Focusing supervision on structurally consequential or more consistently specified corrections did not consistently improve returned-pose success over broad continuation under the tested budget.

title: Nowcasting of Tropical Cyclone Wind Fields and Intensity from Geostationary Imagery
comment: Accepted as a workshop paper at Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning, NeurIPS 2026
summary: High-resolution tropical cyclone surface wind speeds derived from synthetic aperture radar (SAR) observations can support storm structure and intensity modelling, but remain spatially and temporally sparse and unavailable near-real-time. Geostationary satellites capture cloud tops continuously in space and time, but do not directly resolve surface winds. Here, we present simple neural networks to predict 2D wind fields and storm-scale intensity metrics from geostationary imagery. Through a series of ablation studies, we find that joint prediction of 2D fields and scalar metrics from the model latent space improves the retrieval of the (radius of) maximum wind, especially for rapid intensification events.

AI.tldr: Presents simple neural networks that predict 2D tropical cyclone surface wind fields and storm intensity metrics from geostationary imagery, with joint prediction improving retrieval of the radius of maximum wind.
AI.motivation: SAR-derived surface winds are high-resolution but spatially and temporally sparse and not available in near-real-time, while geostationary satellites observe cloud tops continuously but do not directly resolve surface winds.
AI.method: Neural networks predict 2D wind fields and storm-scale intensity metrics from geostationary imagery, with ablation studies comparing joint prediction of fields and scalar metrics from the model latent space against alternatives.
AI.result: Joint prediction improves retrieval of the radius of maximum wind, especially for rapid intensification events.
AI.conclusion: Joint field and scalar prediction from a shared latent space is a useful design for nowcasting cyclone winds from geostationary imagery.

title: Scaling Neural Motor Decoding via Decoupled Behavioral Pretraining
summary: Recent neural decoding approaches achieve strong performance by training on large collections of paired neural-behavioral recordings, but such datasets are expensive, invasive, and difficult to scale. In contrast, behavioral data is abundant and easy to collect, raising the question of whether neural decoding can benefit from decoupling behavioral and neural representation learning. We introduce BEEMO, a flexible multi-session framework that enables training with arbitrary mixtures of paired neural-behavioral recordings and unpaired behavioral data. A behavior decoder learns movement dynamics directly from behavioral trajectories, while neural activity is incorporated through cross-attention layers when available, allowing behavioral and neural supervision to scale independently. Across multiple intracortical motor datasets and tasks in nonhuman primates, we show that incorporating unpaired behavioral data improves decoding performance, particularly when transferring to new tasks, and that adding even a small amount of behavioral data from the target task further improves transfer. By decoupling neural and behavioral data, we unlock a new dimension for scaling: unpaired behavioral data, which is substantially cheaper and easier to collect than paired neural recordings, can be used directly to improve decoding performance. We further show that behavior-only pretraining, without any neural pretraining, achieves performance comparable to models pretrained on substantially larger neural datasets. Together, our results suggest that scaling behavioral data offers a practical and cost-effective path toward neural decoding models that generalize across subjects and tasks. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces BEEMO, a multi-session framework that trains neural motor decoders on mixtures of paired neural-behavioral and unpaired behavioral data, showing that behavior-only pretraining rivals neural pretraining on substantially larger datasets.
AI.motivation: Strong neural decoders need large paired neural-behavioral recordings that are expensive, invasive and hard to scale, while behavioral data is abundant and easy to collect.
AI.method: A behavior decoder learns movement dynamics directly from behavioral trajectories, and neural activity is incorporated through cross-attention layers when available, so behavioral and neural supervision scale independently.
AI.result: Across intracortical motor datasets and tasks in nonhuman primates, unpaired behavioral data improves decoding, particularly when transferring to new tasks, and adding a small amount of target-task behavioral data further improves transfer; behavior-only pretraining achieves performance comparable to models pretrained on substantially larger neural datasets.
AI.conclusion: Scaling behavioral data offers a practical, cost-effective path toward neural decoders that generalize across subjects and tasks.

title: Accelerating Safe Reinforcement Learning with Massive Parallelism
summary: We investigate the problem of scaling safe reinforcement learning (safe RL) to massively parallel training regimes, where a large number of environments are exe- cuted with short rollout horizons. Although this setting improves data throughput and wall-clock efficiency, it creates a mismatch with constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), whose safety constraints are defined over full-episode cost returns. We address this mismatch by analyzing staggered environment resets as a phase-mixture distribution over short trajectory segments. This analysis charac- terizes the bias induced by phase coverage and motivates a phase-aggregated cost estimator that reconstructs episode-level cost estimates from short rollout batches. We further incorporate finite-sample uncertainty and distribution mismatch into a constraint-tightening framework, yielding a scalable Safe RL method compatible with on-policy optimization. Using an MJX-based implementation of Safety Gym, our experiments show that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to non-massively parallel implementations while substantially reducing wall-clock training time.

AI.tldr: Adapts safe reinforcement learning to massively parallel training with short rollouts by reconstructing episode-level cost estimates from staggered-reset phase mixtures, reaching performance comparable to non-parallel implementations with substantially less wall-clock time.
AI.motivation: Massively parallel short rollouts mismatch constrained Markov decision processes, whose safety constraints are defined over full-episode cost returns.
AI.method: Staggered environment resets are analyzed as a phase-mixture distribution over short trajectory segments, which motivates a phase-aggregated cost estimator built from short rollout batches; finite-sample uncertainty and distribution mismatch are added to a constraint-tightening framework compatible with on-policy optimization, implemented on an MJX-based Safety Gym.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves performance comparable to non-massively parallel implementations while substantially reducing wall-clock training time.
AI.conclusion: Reconstructing episode-level cost estimates from short rollout batches makes scalable on-policy safe RL practical.

title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression
summary: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.

AI.tldr: AutoCompress is a hardware-guided LLM pruning framework that uses differentiable architecture search with serving-engine cost models, so compression targets latency, throughput and memory rather than parameter count. It improves average accuracy over Minitron on eight benchmarks across three GPUs.
AI.motivation: Existing pruning workflows target parameter counts, so practitioners must manually choose model sizes that meet latency, throughput and GPU memory limits, since parameter count alone does not predict these metrics.
AI.method: AutoCompress embeds hardware and workload constraints in differentiable architecture search, jointly optimising global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput and memory measurements.
AI.result: Compared with Minitron, average accuracy across eight benchmarks improves by 6.57, 2.35 and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080 and H100 respectively; Nemotron 3.5 Super is compressed from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.
AI.conclusion: Compression should be driven by hardware and workload constraints rather than parameter count, and cost-model-guided search can meet deployment targets on both consumer and datacenter GPUs.

title: Dynamic Optimistic Constrained OCO with Memory via Delay Equivalence
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Online Convex Optimization with memory and time-varying constraints (COCO-M) is a recently-introduced framework that captures the dynamics of stateful online learning and non-stochastic control with budget constraints. Despite its expressive power, COCO-M remains largely understudied. In this work, we tackle this problem in its full scale, providing an optimistic algorithm that incorporates untrusted predictions to tame universal dynamic regret and cumulative constraint violation. Our analysis leverages a potent reduction from memory to delay and treats state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback. We establish the first bounds that adapt to both environment non-stationarity (path length $P_T$) and prediction accuracy, while lifting previous restrictive assumptions such as functional separability. En route to these results, we derive findings of independent interest for the memory-to-delay reduction, and for delayed OCO with time-varying constraints. The proposed framework ensures sublinear worst-case guarantees that improve with prediction accuracy, reaching $\mathcal O(1)$ regret under perfect predictions, with cumulative constraint violation (CCV) $\mathcal O(\sqrt{T})$ for unknown $P_T$ and $\mathcal O(\log T)$ for known or online observable $P_T$ , while recovering the optimal COCO rates when memory disappears.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an optimistic algorithm for online convex optimization with memory and time-varying constraints (COCO-M) that uses untrusted predictions. It gives the first bounds that adapt to both environment non-stationarity and prediction accuracy without functional separability assumptions.
AI.motivation: COCO-M captures stateful online learning and budgeted non-stochastic control but remains largely understudied, and earlier analyses relied on restrictive assumptions such as functional separability.
AI.method: The authors reduce memory to delay, treat state-dependent gradients as delayed feedback, and build an optimistic algorithm that uses untrusted predictions, with bounds stated in terms of the path length P_T.
AI.result: The guarantees are sublinear in the worst case and improve with prediction accuracy, reaching O(1) regret under perfect predictions; cumulative constraint violation is O(sqrt(T)) for unknown P_T and O(log T) for known or online observable P_T, and the optimal COCO rates are recovered when memory disappears.
AI.conclusion: The memory-to-delay reduction and the analysis of delayed OCO with time-varying constraints give a unified framework that adapts to both environment dynamics and prediction quality.

title: Interpretable many-body interaction laws for collective motion from few trajectories
summary: Models of collective motion usually reduce social interactions to pairwise forces, despite empirical evidence for many-body effects. We introduce the directional atomic cluster expansion (dACE), which adapts the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) of interatomic potentials to self-propelled agents. dACE provides a systematically improvable, exactly equivariant expansion of an agent's acceleration that splits uniquely into 1-, 2-, 3-body and higher contributions, along with a self term for the agent's own past motion that is fitted so that it does not absorb the interactions. On simulated collectives in two and three dimensions with known rules, dACE recovers the interaction law body order by body order from little data, while the neural model SocialNet, the current closest competitor, needs more data, has much larger errors on many-body or chiral rules and is restricted to 2D. On real data sets of tracked zebrafish and golden shiners, the laws learned by dACE agree better between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's. The learned laws are interpretable, and in the shiners the 3-body term opposes the pairwise response as neighbourhoods get dense. Finally, we show that next-step prediction accuracy mostly measures self-propulsion and noise rather than the interactions, and suggest more robust combinations of error measures for interaction learning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the directional atomic cluster expansion (dACE), an equivariant many-body expansion of agent acceleration for self-propelled agents. It recovers interaction laws body order by body order from little data and yields interpretable laws for collective motion.
AI.motivation: Collective-motion models usually reduce social interactions to pairwise forces despite evidence for many-body effects, and the closest neural competitor, SocialNet, needs more data, has larger errors on many-body rules, and is restricted to 2D.
AI.method: dACE adapts the atomic cluster expansion to self-propelled agents, splitting an agent's acceleration uniquely into 1-, 2-, 3-body and higher terms, plus a self term fitted so that it absorbs the agent's own past motion but not the interactions.
AI.result: On simulated 2D and 3D collectives with known rules, dACE recovers the law body order by body order from little data and outperforms SocialNet on many-body and chiral rules; on tracked zebrafish and golden shiner data, its laws agree better between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's, and in shiners the 3-body term opposes the pairwise response as neighbourhoods get dense.
AI.conclusion: Next-step prediction accuracy mostly measures self-propulsion and noise rather than interactions, so the authors recommend more robust combinations of error measures for interaction learning.

title: Discovering Learning Rules that Shape Others
summary: In general-sum games, self-interested learners can reach outcomes that are poor for everyone, which has motivated methods that shape the opponent's learning. Methods like Learning with Opponent-Learning Awareness (LOLA), which differentiates through the opponent's learning process, and Model-Free Opponent Shaping (M-FOS), which uses model-free optimisation methods for long-horizon opponent shaping, have enabled mutual cooperation and exploitation of learners.
