However, these methods require access to the opponent's parameters, policy, rewards or learning rule during deployment. In single-agent reinforcement learning, update rules discovered by meta-learning have achieved state-of-the-art results (e.g. DiscoRL). These rules are separate from the policy they train and read only the agent's own experience. We hereby extend this framework to general-sum settings by introducing Discovered Update Rule for Opponent Shaping (DUOS). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to discover an update rule for an agent in general-sum games. DUOS meta-trains the rule to maximise the agent's expected return over its lifetime, and updates an inner network using the agent's own experience. We show that our discovered rule exhibits behaviour consistent with opponent shaping without reading opponent policies or parameters, and ranks 1st in normalised mean score and 1st in self-play among tournament entrants.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DUOS, a method that meta-learns an update rule for an agent in general-sum games so that the agent shapes its opponents' learning. It is presented as the first method to discover an update rule for general-sum games and ranks first in a tournament.
AI.motivation: Opponent-shaping methods such as LOLA and M-FOS require access to the opponent's parameters, policy, rewards or learning rule during deployment, and meta-discovered update rules such as DiscoRL have so far been limited to single-agent reinforcement learning.
AI.method: DUOS meta-trains a rule that updates an inner network using only the agent's own experience, optimising the agent's expected return over its lifetime, so it needs no access to opponent policies or parameters.
AI.result: The discovered rule shows behaviour consistent with opponent shaping without reading opponent policies or parameters, and ranks first in normalised mean score and first in self-play among tournament entrants.
AI.conclusion: A meta-discovered update rule can induce opponent shaping in general-sum games without opponent information, extending the discovered-rule framework beyond single-agent reinforcement learning.

title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
summary: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.

AI.tldr: StrataFlux is a low-bit LLM inference framework that recovers accuracy lost to 2-4-bit weight and 2-3-bit KV-cache quantization by streaming higher-precision data from host RAM and solid-state drives, while keeping quantization's memory and speed advantages.
AI.motivation: Quantization reduces memory and bandwidth demands but can degrade accuracy, while offloading higher-precision data to slower tiers can stall generation.
AI.method: StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection and delivery; its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer.
AI.result: For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, WikiText-2 perplexity falls from 9.46 to 8.40 while keeping 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090; with 2-bit weights and KV cache, Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy rises from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use; at 128K context, 3-bit weights with 2-bit KV cache reach perplexity and speed comparable to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights with 8-bit KV cache, using about half the GPU memory.
AI.conclusion: GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, and offloading-tier latency need not dictate decoding speed.

title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
summary: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.

AI.tldr: Muir is a linear attention architecture that reallocates the gates of Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) using a sensitivity analysis, adds a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. It lowers perplexity relative to GDN-2 and Transformer baselines and trains faster.
AI.motivation: The authors show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes, and that slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms, so GDN-2's gate design wastes capacity and forces stronger erasure to suppress interference.
AI.method: Muir fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network, and uses a parallel update that stays numerically stable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units.
AI.result: Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer and raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points; at 1.34B it outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from a 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, keeps near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout, matches GDN-2 throughput, and trains 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.
AI.conclusion: Sensitivity-guided gate allocation and readout weighting can improve linear attention without losing throughput, with gains in long-context recall and training speed.

title: Module-Aware Optimization for Graph Neural Networks
summary: Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves $1.32\times$-$2.42\times$ validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: GraphMuon is a graph-aware variant of the Muon optimiser that orthogonalises updates in a metric defined by graph-propagated layer inputs. It reports 1.32x-2.42x validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large OGB benchmarks.
AI.motivation: For GNNs the effective geometry of a weight matrix depends on the graph-propagated representations it acts on, so an update that is well normalised as a matrix can be amplified when applied to propagated features, and vanilla Muon can suffer from this graph-induced amplification.
AI.method: GraphMuon performs orthogonalisation in a metric defined by the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs and normalises step sizes by the update's induced effect on the layer representation, giving a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step.
AI.result: GraphMuon achieves 1.32x-2.42x validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks; across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification and graph regression, it reaches lower time-to-target in 13 while staying competitive or superior in predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for graph geometry mitigates update amplification, so graph-aware matrix optimisers are a useful direction for GNN training.

title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data
summary: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an interpretable hybrid framework that fuses an LSTM-autoencoder reconstruction-error descriptor with statistical flight-history features and feeds them to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier for landing-phase safety-event prediction. It reports mean macro recall above 0.90 at all airports.
AI.motivation: Landing-phase safety events are rare within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data, and capturing coupled temporal behaviour while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts is a central modelling challenge.
AI.method: An LSTM autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows produces a continuous reconstruction-error descriptor, which is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and classified by a class-weighted XGBoost model into Normal, Speed High, Path High and Flaps Late windows; pooled and airport-specific learning are compared.
AI.result: On 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports, mean macro recall exceeds 0.90 at all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining; class weighting matters, continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives, and local specialisation helps at the two airports with larger datasets while pooled training helps at the smallest.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers interpretable rare-event detection and practical guidance on choosing local or pooled models according to airport-level data availability.

title: Synthesis of Ovarian Cancer Multi-Omics Datasets: A Biology-Informed Evaluation Framework
comment: Accepted at the GenAI4Health Workshop at NeurIPS 2026 and in the Findings track of ML4H 2026. Both acceptances are non-archival
summary: Paired multi-omic cancer cohorts are costly to assemble and difficult to share, motivating synthetic cohorts as a complementary resource. As generative model development accelerates, we shift the focus from proposing yet another architecture to defining evaluation criteria that determine whether synthetic data preserve biologically relevant structure. We introduce a biology-informed and patient-disjoint framework for evaluating the generation of paired RNA expression and copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and apply it to the longitudinal DECIDER high-grade serous ovarian cancer cohort. The framework assesses modality-specific fidelity and coherence between RNA and CNV pairs using agreement between real training and held-out data as a reference, alongside complementary training-data proximity diagnostics. We adapt three multi-omic integration architectures based on variational autoencoders to generate paired profiles. The model leading several fidelity and coherence measures also shows the strongest training-data proximity. The protocol and case study offer the community a reference for comparing future multi-omic generators.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a biology-informed, patient-disjoint framework for evaluating synthetic paired RNA expression and copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and applies it to the longitudinal DECIDER high-grade serous ovarian cancer cohort using three VAE-based multi-omic generators. It shifts the focus from new architectures to evaluation criteria.
AI.motivation: Paired multi-omic cancer cohorts are costly to assemble and difficult to share, and generative-model development lacks criteria for judging whether synthetic data preserve biologically relevant structure.
AI.method: The framework assesses modality-specific fidelity and RNA-CNV coherence, using agreement between real training and held-out data as the reference, alongside complementary training-data proximity diagnostics; three multi-omic integration architectures based on variational autoencoders are adapted to generate paired profiles.
AI.result: The model that leads several fidelity and coherence measures also shows the strongest training-data proximity.
AI.conclusion: The protocol and case study give the community a reference for comparing future multi-omic generators, and they show that fidelity gains can coincide with strong proximity to the training data.

title: Conformal Prediction for Time-Dependent PDEs
summary: Uncertainty quantification is crucial in scientific machine learning, where models inform safety-critical tasks such as flood forecasting, financial risk management, and thermal control in machines. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees, but in time-dependent settings common to physics and engineering, these guarantees can break down, leading to systematic undercoverage. We study this problem in the context of surrogate models for time-dependent physical systems described by partial differential equations. We prove that in a function space setting, distributions at arbitrarily close times can be mutually singular, making exact coverage guarantees impossible. We further show that in discretized settings, the total variation distance between distributions often saturates exponentially fast with the grid resolution, mandating restrictions on the spatial discretization to ensure coverage. Finally, for certain settings, we show how to use principled weighted conformal prediction to obtain finite-sample coverage guarantees over growing time horizons.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that conformal prediction coverage can break down for time-dependent PDE surrogate models, proving that distributions at arbitrarily close times can be mutually singular, and gives a weighted conformal method that obtains finite-sample coverage over growing time horizons in certain settings.
AI.motivation: Conformal prediction gives distribution-free coverage, but in time-dependent physical and engineering settings its guarantees can fail and lead to systematic undercoverage in safety-critical uses such as flood forecasting and thermal control.
AI.method: The authors study surrogate models for time-dependent systems described by partial differential equations in a function space setting and in discretised settings, measuring total variation distance against grid resolution, and apply principled weighted conformal prediction where it applies.
AI.result: Exact coverage guarantees are impossible in the function space setting; in discretised settings the total variation distance often saturates exponentially fast with grid resolution, so the spatial discretisation must be restricted to ensure coverage; for certain settings, weighted conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage guarantees over growing time horizons.
AI.conclusion: Time dependence requires care in conformal uncertainty quantification for scientific machine learning, and coverage depends on spatial discretisation and suitable weighting.

title: Spectral and Subspace Dynamics of LoRA in Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.

AI.tldr: The paper analyses how LoRA updates differ between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), and finds that group-mean baseline subtraction drives the contrast. It then tailors LoRA updates to each stage and reports the best performance among compared methods in most evaluated settings.
AI.motivation: LoRA is used in both SFT and RL, often under similar optimiser settings, yet how the two stages' dynamics manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimises remains unclear.
AI.method: The singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates are tracked on mathematical reasoning tasks, SFT and RL are interpolated one ingredient at a time, and a quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA explains the mechanism; the SFT configuration flattens the spectrum of the full update, while the RL configuration flattens the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span.
AI.result: RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; RL rotates singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates; group-mean baseline subtraction is identified as the source of both contrasts; the stage-specific configurations give the best performance among compared methods in most evaluated settings across multiple models.
AI.conclusion: The optimisation dynamics of SFT and RL differ in the LoRA increment, so stage-specific LoRA updates can improve results.

title: On the limitations of molecular representations
summary: Molecular representations such as fingerprints and learned embeddings play a central role in cheminformatics and small-molecule machine learning. They serve as the primary input for a diverse array of tasks, including clustering, dataset splitting, and virtual screening, yet their evaluation is often limited to downstream model performance on narrow benchmark tasks. We carried out a systematic investigation of the quality of molecular representations, finding that none of the state-of-the-art molecular embedding models capture graph structure, 3D shape, or ADMET endpoint similarity better than fingerprints or physicochemical descriptors. However, classical fingerprints also revealed their own material limitations. For example, we show that depending on the representation, between 225M and $\sim$4B molecules have non-unique representations in the 10.8B Enamine REAL database, with implications for virtual screening. Our findings provide an insight into the current limitations of molecular representations, outlining future research directions for the development of more robust encodings of small molecules.

AI.tldr: A systematic study finds that state-of-the-art molecular embedding models capture graph structure, 3D shape and ADMET endpoint similarity no better than fingerprints or physicochemical descriptors, and that classical fingerprints also have non-uniqueness limits at the scale of the Enamine REAL database.
AI.motivation: Molecular representations are the primary input for clustering, dataset splitting and virtual screening, yet their evaluation is often limited to downstream performance on narrow benchmark tasks.
AI.method: The authors systematically assess the quality of molecular representations, comparing learned embeddings with fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors on graph structure, 3D shape and ADMET endpoint similarity, and count non-unique representations across the 10.8B-molecule Enamine REAL database.
AI.result: None of the state-of-the-art molecular embedding models captures these properties better than fingerprints or physicochemical descriptors; depending on the representation, between 225M and about 4B molecules in the 10.8B Enamine REAL database have non-unique representations.
AI.conclusion: Current molecular representations have clear limitations, and more robust encodings are needed for virtual screening and related small-molecule tasks.

title: Data-driven discovery of intrinsic Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems
comment: 63 pages, 10 figures. Code and data availability statements are included in the manuscript
summary: Discovering continuous symmetries directly from differential-equation data can reveal geometric structure for model reduction and scientific machine learning without symbolic determining equations or a closed-form representation of the governing system. We formulate intrinsic Lie point-symmetry discovery as an operator-theoretic problem on sampled jet-space data. Admissible generators are identified from a sampled determining operator and separated from redundant, solution-dependent, and geometrically trivial directions. The framework combines prolongation, sequential subspace restrictions, and a fixed nonlinear dictionary linear in trainable coefficients. A rank-stabilization preflight test diagnoses systems whose represented intrinsic symmetry algebra does not stabilize under dictionary refinement. On a controlled differential-equation benchmark with an analytically known 11-dimensional represented intrinsic symmetry algebra, the method recovers the complete represented generator set, reproduces its Lie-bracket structure to numerical precision, and approximates a known generator beyond the training domain. Here we show that explicit intrinsic continuous-symmetry generators can be recovered from data obtained from exact or approximate differential systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an operator-theoretic method that discovers intrinsic Lie point symmetries directly from sampled jet-space data of differential equations, without symbolic determining equations. On a benchmark with a known 11-dimensional represented symmetry algebra it recovers the complete generator set.
AI.motivation: Continuous symmetries revealed from differential-equation data would support model reduction and scientific machine learning, but existing approaches typically need symbolic determining equations or a closed-form description of the governing system.
AI.method: Admissible generators are identified from a sampled determining operator, using prolongation, sequential subspace restrictions and a fixed nonlinear dictionary that is linear in trainable coefficients; redundant, solution-dependent and geometrically trivial directions are separated out, and a rank-stabilisation preflight test flags systems whose represented symmetry algebra does not stabilise under dictionary refinement.
AI.result: On a controlled differential-equation benchmark with an analytically known 11-dimensional represented intrinsic symmetry algebra, the method recovers the complete represented generator set, reproduces its Lie-bracket structure to numerical precision, and approximates a known generator beyond the training domain.
AI.conclusion: Explicit intrinsic symmetry generators can be recovered from data of exact or approximate differential systems, with the preflight test guarding against systems whose symmetry algebra does not stabilise.

title: A Hidden Markov Preference Model for Online Prediction of Adversary Actions
summary: A defender anticipating an attacker needs a probability distribution over the attacker's next action from information available before that action occurs. Two structures complicate this: the attacker's behavioral regime persists and can switch within an episode, and each action combines an operation with state-dependent arguments whose feasible values change over time. We capture both with a hidden Markov model whose latent state is the active regime and whose regime-conditioned action law is defined on a feasibility-masked tree of executable actions. The same likelihood forms the next-action distribution and updates the regime belief once the action is seen, and a partially observed prefix contributes its resolved local factors. Estimation separates into convex logistic fits that Baum-Welch reuses when regimes are unlabeled. We derive a reach-weighted nodewise KL expression for regime information, a sequence-wise log-loss bound for switching regime paths, and a uniform fallback guarantee. On the CAGE 2 cyber defense benchmark the filtered latent state is worth 0.8 nats per step, and after a controller switch the loss begins to fall in three steps against ten for a recurrent baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hidden Markov model that predicts an attacker's next action from a regime-conditioned distribution over a feasibility-masked tree of executable actions, and updates the regime belief as actions are observed. On the CAGE 2 cyber defence benchmark its loss falls within three steps after a controller switch, against ten for a recurrent baseline.
AI.motivation: Predicting attacker actions is complicated because the behavioural regime persists but can switch within an episode, and each action combines an operation with state-dependent arguments whose feasible values change over time.
AI.method: A hidden Markov model whose latent state is the active regime, with a regime-conditioned action law defined on a feasibility-masked tree of executable actions; estimation separates into convex logistic fits that Baum-Welch reuses when regimes are unlabelled, and the analysis gives a reach-weighted nodewise KL expression for regime information, a sequence-wise log-loss bound for switching regime paths and a uniform fallback guarantee.
AI.result: On the CAGE 2 benchmark the filtered latent state is worth 0.8 nats per step, and after a controller switch the loss begins to fall within three steps, against ten steps for a recurrent baseline.
AI.conclusion: Modelling latent regimes and feasibility constraints gives a principled next-action predictor for defenders that adapts quickly after behaviour changes.

title: Adversarial Training with Large Step Sizes: Implicit Bias, Optimization, and Sharpness
summary: Adversarial Training (AT) is an important method for improving model robustness. We study the dynamics of deterministic Gradient Descent (GD) in AT. Most existing works in this direction focus on the small or vanishing step sizes regime, where GD resembles a continuous-time flow. However, such step sizes can make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice. In this paper, we study the AT dynamics of GD with large constant step sizes. We first study GD in adversarial linear logistic regression, focusing on two aspects: where the model parameters converge (implicit bias) and how quickly the losses decrease (optimization). We then turn to neural networks training and study how the sharpness of losses evolve during AT. Our results advance the understanding of the behaviors of GD with large step sizes in AT and highlight three key differences from its behavior in Standard Training (ST): (i) the implicit bias gap between AT and ST, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes, (ii) different from ST, there is no uniform rate of convergence for the optimization error in AT, and (iii) sharpness can exhibit two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behavior observed in ST.

AI.tldr: The paper analyses deterministic gradient descent for adversarial training (AT) with large constant step sizes, showing that its implicit bias and optimisation behaviour differ from standard training and that loss sharpness follows a two-stage pattern. The analysis covers adversarial linear logistic regression and neural network training.
AI.motivation: Most AT theory assumes small or vanishing step sizes, where gradient descent resembles a continuous-time flow, yet such step sizes make training inefficient and are rarely used in practice.
AI.method: The authors study gradient descent with large constant step sizes in adversarial linear logistic regression, examining where the parameters converge and how fast the losses decrease, and then study how loss sharpness evolves during adversarial training of neural networks.
AI.result: The implicit bias gap between AT and standard training, previously established only for small step sizes, persists for arbitrarily large constant step sizes; unlike standard training, AT has no uniform convergence rate for the optimisation error; and sharpness can show two-stage dynamics that differ from the Edge-of-Stability behaviour seen in standard training.
AI.conclusion: Large-step AT differs from standard training in implicit bias, convergence and sharpness, so small-step theory does not transfer directly.

title: Towards interpreting any residual stream direction by scaling activation inversion
comment: Euan Ong and Jiahai Feng advised equally
summary: To interpret a direction in a language model's residual stream, we can look for text that strongly activates it. But when such text is found by scanning a corpus, it is limited to what that corpus contains. We develop Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models which map residual stream directions from a subject model to text exemplars that strongly activate those directions. Our objective is to maximise the cosine similarity of a supplied residual stream direction with the activations of the text generated by the MAEM. This label-free RL objective helps to scale MAEMs on diverse sources of residual stream directions. Empirically, we find the resultant metamodel produces informative exemplars: a Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search (at 10M tokens) on a majority of held-out languages/domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features. It also identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers the payloads of LoRA backdoors more often than corpus search, and can even verbalise some model workspace inner monologue. Unlike explanations produced by other metamodels (e.g. NLAs), MAEM exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model, making the MAEM objective a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.

AI.tldr: The paper trains Maximally-Activating Example Metamodels (MAEMs), language models that map a residual-stream direction to text exemplars that strongly activate it, using a label-free reinforcement learning objective. The exemplars can be verified with a forward pass on the subject model.
AI.motivation: Scanning a corpus for text that activates a residual-stream direction is limited to what that corpus contains, so interpretation is bounded by corpus coverage.
AI.method: MAEMs are trained to maximise the cosine similarity between a supplied residual-stream direction and the subject model's activations on the generated text, a label-free RL objective that scales across diverse sources of directions.
AI.result: A Qwen3.6-27B MAEM inverts held-out activations better than corpus search or a natural-language autoencoder (NLA), beats corpus search at 10M tokens on a majority of held-out languages and domains, and activates 89% of held-out SAE features; it identifies concepts behind steering vectors about as well as NLAs, recovers LoRA backdoor payloads more often than corpus search, and can verbalise some of a model's workspace inner monologue.
AI.conclusion: Because MAEM exemplars can be checked with a forward pass on the subject model, the MAEM objective is a grounded alternative for scaling the training of metamodels.

title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information
comment: 30 pages, 7 figures. Code available as ancillary files
summary: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $\alpha$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.

AI.tldr: The paper asks what finite experiments can certify about integrated information phi in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. It shows that behaviour can hide mechanism differences, that phi changes sharply across partition edges, and that one-sided lower bounds can be certified from finite data.
AI.motivation: Interpretability, AI auditing and machine-consciousness assessments rely on mechanism-level quantities that experiments see only through finite, partial and noisy interventions, so identifiability, continuity and certifiability need to be established.
AI.method: The authors answer exactly for the integrated information phi of integrated information theory in small stochastic networks with known ground truth, comparing recurrent and feed-forward networks with identical input-output laws, testing partial recordings and parity networks, and examining sensitivity of phi near partition edges.
AI.result: A recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials; units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers; infinitesimal mechanism changes across an edge change phi by 25-100% at 99% of the edges found in random networks; about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport phi by more than 20%; and the data certify phi above 1.004 bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms from about 10^7 controlled transitions, with false-certificate probability at most alpha.
AI.conclusion: Measurability of mechanism-level quantities is a design question with computable answers, and finite data certify lower bounds on phi on both sides of an edge rather than precise values.

title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration
summary: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.

AI.tldr: XStack is a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Agents must deliver a working JAX repository from a PyTorch one, and current agents remain unreliable on this task.
AI.motivation: Moving ML code between the PyTorch/NVIDIA and JAX/TPU ecosystems unlocks different hardware for researchers, and the task spans frameworks, hardware and whole repositories over a long horizon, which makes it a natural benchmark.
AI.method: Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository; an output passes if it meets grading criteria based on the source repository's published result, which the authors authenticate and calibrate.
AI.result: Claude Opus 5 passes 75% of tasks, GPT-5.6-sol passes 45%, and every other agent passes at most 40%.
AI.conclusion: Agent-driven repository migration across frameworks and hardware is still unreliable, and XStack is released to make progress toward it measurable.

title: User Embeddings are Superpositions of Interpretable Behavioral Modes
summary: User embeddings are central components of modern recommendation, personalization, and behavioral modeling systems. Though these embeddings can compactly encode rich behavioral information, they are inherently dense and opaque, limiting interpretability. To address this gap, we argue that user embeddings can be understood as sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioral modes. This structure is directly predicted by generative models of user behavior for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep-learning representations by the superposition hypothesis. Superimposed modes can naturally be recovered by sparse dictionary learning methods, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and recovered modes can be automatically named and queried in natural language. We validate mode recovery against known ground truth on synthetic data, where SAEs recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings. We then apply the method to classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets. We also show how the corresponding natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterization over embeddings never trained on text. The framework is post-hoc and model-agnostic, requiring no modification to the upstream embedding system.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that user embeddings are sparse superpositions of interpretable behavioural modes, and recovers these modes with sparse autoencoders, which can then be named and queried in natural language. The method is post-hoc and model-agnostic.
AI.motivation: User embeddings encode rich behavioural information compactly but are dense and opaque, which limits their interpretability in recommendation, personalisation and behavioural modelling systems.
AI.method: The authors argue that the structure is predicted by generative models of user behaviour for linear embeddings and extends approximately to deep representations via the superposition hypothesis; sparse dictionary methods such as sparse autoencoders recover the modes, which are then labelled automatically.
AI.result: On synthetic data with known ground truth, sparse autoencoders recover modes better than classical sparse baselines, including on transformer-encoded embeddings; on classical and transformer-based user embeddings from two real-world datasets, the natural-language labels enable zero-shot audience retrieval and characterisation over embeddings never trained on text.
AI.conclusion: Post-hoc sparse dictionary learning can make dense user embeddings interpretable and queryable without modifying the upstream embedding system.

title: Reading a neuron's tuning from its correlations with other neurons
comment: Code: this https URL. Reassignment to q-bio.NC as primary welcome
summary: What a neuron represents is usually established by relating its activity to a stimulus. We ask whether the same facts are contained in the correlation matrix of a recorded population, which keeps the pairwise relations among the neurons and discards the stimulus. A transformer that sees only the correlation matrix of 512 sampled neurons, with no labels and no reference population in its input, decodes the preferred orientation of mouse visual cortex neurons from in-vivo MICrONS responses to a mean error of 25° (uninformed: 45°; best constant guess: 41°) and their receptive-field position at R^2 = 0.23; on the digital-twin substrate, 20° and 0.48. Asked whether a neuron prefers horizontal or vertical, it is right for 79% of neurons in vivo and 87% on the twin, against 56% for the majority answer; it does not resolve the obliques. The ordering is recoverable because the relations between orientation classes are close to circulant, which fixes the class structure up to rotation and reflection; the rotation of the frame is recoverable only because of a departure from that symmetry. The departure survives equal representation of every orientation and disjoint training and test stimuli, and it is an anisotropy of the signal correlations: in V1 the neurons preferring the dominant orientation have the most similar responses to one another, and a model population with only that property recovers the frame. Across 33 mice of the Allen Brain Observatory, with relations from drifting gratings, orientation transfers to unseen animals only when a sampled population mixes animals; populations drawn from one animal are not decoded measurably below the best constant, a limit of the diversity of populations one animal provides. For receptive fields, what crosses animals is where each animal's imaged patch looks on the screen, not the layout of neurons within it.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a transformer given only the correlation matrix of a recorded neural population can decode the preferred orientation and receptive-field position of mouse visual cortex neurons well above chance. The orientation information is carried by the correlation structure itself, without stimulus labels.
AI.motivation: What a neuron represents is usually established by relating its activity to a stimulus; the authors ask whether the same facts are contained in the correlation matrix of a recorded population, which keeps pairwise relations among neurons and discards the stimulus.
AI.method: A transformer sees only the correlation matrix of 512 sampled neurons, with no labels and no reference population in its input, and is evaluated on MICrONS in vivo responses and a digital-twin substrate, with controls for equal representation of orientations, disjoint training and test stimuli, and 33 mice from the Allen Brain Observatory.
AI.result: Preferred orientation is decoded to a mean error of 25 degrees in vivo (uninformed 45, best constant guess 41) and 20 degrees on the twin; receptive-field position reaches R^2 = 0.23 in vivo and 0.48 on the twin; horizontal versus vertical preference is right for 79% of neurons in vivo and 87% on the twin, against 56% for the majority answer; orientation transfers to unseen animals only when a sampled population mixes animals.
AI.conclusion: Orientation structure is recoverable from correlations because of an anisotropy in signal correlations, and populations drawn from a single animal do not decode measurably above the best constant, so population diversity matters.

title: Capturing Membrane Dynamics and Spike Timing of Human Neurons at Scale using Neural Operators
summary: Characterizing the properties of neuronal cell types is central to understanding brain function. Yet, biophysically realistic neuron models remain difficult to scale to large populations while preserving the richness of cellular dynamics and within-cell-type variability. We present a cell-type-specific neural-operator framework for scalable neuronal population modeling. Rather than training separate surrogate models for individual neurons, the proposed framework learns a shared operator across multiple modeled neurons from the same cell type, conditioned on biologically interpretable electrophysiological features. Relative to the original single-neuron \texttt{NOBLE} setting, learning across heterogeneous neurons requires a richer electrophysiological conditioning representation and a training objective designed to preserve diverse spiking dynamics. This enables efficient generation of large ensembles of somatic voltage responses while preserving variability across cells and model configurations. We evaluate the approach using membrane dynamics metrics, action potential waveform metrics, spike timing accuracy, input-output firing relationships, and electrophysiological feature distributions. Our framework reproduces subthreshold membrane dynamics, spike waveforms, and firing-rate responses across major cortical inhibitory neuron types, while accurately preserving spike timing despite the sensitivity of threshold-crossing dynamics. The predicted electrophysiological feature distributions show strong agreement with detailed simulator outputs and human experimental recordings, including high explained variability in properties such as inter-spike intervals, firing frequency, action-potential shape, and post-spike recovery.

AI.tldr: Proposes a cell-type-specific neural-operator framework that learns one shared operator across many neurons of the same cell type, conditioned on electrophysiological features, to generate large ensembles of realistic somatic voltage responses. It reproduces membrane dynamics, spike waveforms, spike timing and firing-rate responses for major cortical inhibitory neuron types.
AI.motivation: Biophysically realistic neuron models are hard to scale to large populations while keeping rich cellular dynamics and within-cell-type variability, and the original NOBLE setting covers only single neurons.
AI.method: A shared neural operator trained across heterogeneous neurons of one cell type, conditioned on biologically interpretable electrophysiological features, with a richer conditioning representation and a training objective designed to preserve diverse spiking dynamics.
AI.result: Across major cortical inhibitory neuron types the framework reproduces subthreshold dynamics, spike waveforms and firing-rate responses and keeps spike timing accurate; predicted feature distributions agree strongly with detailed simulator outputs and human recordings, with high explained variability for inter-spike intervals, firing frequency, action-potential shape and post-spike recovery.
AI.conclusion: The framework generates large neuron ensembles efficiently while preserving variability across cells and model configurations, offering a scalable route to population-level neuron modeling.

title: BrainPFN: Amortized Brain-Behaviour Prediction via Prior-Data Fitted Networks
summary: The standard approach to predicting behavioral phenotypes from functional MRI is represented by Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) applied on functional connectivity (FC) matrices. However, this approach is limited: separate models must be fit and tuned for every score and cohort, they do not transfer across datasets, and accuracy degrades sharply when only a handful of subjects are available, as is typical of clinical or cognitive studies. Despite an increasing interest in developing brain foundation models, none has consistently outperformed KRR on behaviour prediction; most reported gains come from easier targets such as age, sex, or diagnosis rather than continuous behavioural scores. We introduce BrainPFN, a Prior Data Fitted Network for brain behaviour regression. BrainPFN is meta-trained on a domain-specific prior built from ~7k real FC matrices, from which we sample one billion synthetic training samples. At inference, a labelled context is simply passed through the network in a single forward pass, with no per-score or per-cohort refitting required. Across four independent cohorts, BrainPFN beats KRR on small sample prediction, and leads recent foundation models pre-trained at four to nine times larger scale. Our meta-training pool, aggregated from open repositories, is a fraction of the size of the corpora behind competing models, most of which sit behind restrictive data use agreements such as UK Biobank. We release this pool publicly alongside code and checkpoints, showing that a modest, openly available pool can match or beat models trained at Biobank scale.

AI.tldr: Introduces BrainPFN, a prior-data fitted network for brain-behaviour regression that predicts behavioural scores from functional connectivity in a single forward pass over a labelled context, with no per-score or per-cohort refitting. It beats kernel ridge regression on small samples and leads foundation models pre-trained at four to nine times larger scale.
AI.motivation: Kernel ridge regression on functional connectivity must be refitted for every score and cohort, does not transfer across datasets and degrades with few subjects, while brain foundation models have not consistently beaten it on behavioural prediction.
AI.method: BrainPFN is meta-trained on a domain-specific prior built from about 7k real FC matrices, from which one billion synthetic training samples are drawn, and at inference a labelled context is passed through the network directly.
AI.result: Across four independent cohorts BrainPFN beats kernel ridge regression on small-sample prediction and outperforms foundation models pre-trained at four to nine times larger scale; its openly aggregated meta-training pool is a fraction of the size of competing corpora, many of which sit behind restrictive agreements such as UK Biobank.
AI.conclusion: A modest, openly available meta-training pool can match or beat models trained at Biobank scale, and the released pool, code and checkpoints support data-efficient, reproducible brain-behaviour prediction.

title: ToroFit: Fitting Wedge Sums of Tori to High-Dimensional Data
summary: Data arising in scientific applications often exhibits complex nonlinear structure. Identifying and parameterizing said nonlinearities can enable better modeling, enhance predictive analysis, data interpolation, denoising, and anomaly detection. In this paper, we develop theoretical and computational methods to detect and parametrize Euclidean point cloud data lying near a wedge sum of tori. Specifically, we use persistent cohomology and cup products to identify the distinct toroidal components, and on each component, we optimize over low-energy multivariate trigonometric polynomials for best data fit. The ensuing optimization problem reduces to generalized ridge regression, which can be solved efficiently via standard techniques. We demonstrate the utility of the proposed framework in both synthetic and real datasets, including interpolation of low frame-rate recurrent videos, attractor recovery in quasiperiodic dynamical systems, and the parametrization of gene-space cycle data for parasites and humans.

AI.tldr: Presents ToroFit, a method that detects Euclidean point cloud data lying near a wedge sum of tori using persistent cohomology and cup products, then fits low-energy trigonometric polynomials to each toroidal component. The fitting reduces to generalized ridge regression and is demonstrated on synthetic and real datasets.
AI.motivation: Scientific data often has complex nonlinear structure, and identifying and parameterizing it enables better modeling, prediction, interpolation, denoising and anomaly detection.
AI.method: Persistent cohomology and cup products identify the distinct toroidal components, and on each component the method optimizes over low-energy multivariate trigonometric polynomials for best data fit.
AI.result: The optimization reduces to generalized ridge regression, which standard techniques solve efficiently; applications include interpolation of low frame-rate recurrent videos, attractor recovery in quasiperiodic dynamical systems, and parametrization of gene-space cycle data for parasites and humans.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives a theoretically grounded and computationally efficient way to detect and parametrize toroidal structure in high-dimensional data, with utility across synthetic and real scientific datasets.

title: Synthesizing symbolic models of human and machine reasoning at scale
summary: Symbolic models offer a powerful account of cognition, but their scope has historically been limited by the need for hand-engineering and computational tractability. We show how advances in artificial intelligence (AI) can scale symbolic modeling and help overcome these engineering limitations. We introduce Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS)---an approach for automated search of interpretable, deterministic symbolic programs that verifiably reproduce behavior---and apply it to model both human and machine behavior across hundreds of challenging reasoning problems. Analyzing these programs reveals that both people and machines tend to oversimplify, adopt rules that are partial explanations for their observations, and misinfer dependencies between problem features. These shared signatures are modulated by available resources, with reasoning effort predicting the extent to which machines simplify and explain their observations. Together, these results point to underlying mechanisms reminiscent of satisficing in both people and machines, and illustrate how BCSS offers a general approach for interpreting and comparing rule-based reasoning of humans and black-box AI systems.

AI.tldr: Introduces Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS), which automatically searches for interpretable deterministic symbolic programs that reproduce behavior, and applies it to hundreds of reasoning problems for both people and machines. The analysis finds that both oversimplify and adopt partial rules, with shared signatures modulated by reasoning effort.
AI.motivation: Symbolic models of cognition are limited by the need for hand-engineering and by computational tractability, which restricts their scope.
AI.method: BCSS performs automated search over interpretable deterministic symbolic programs that are verified to reproduce observed behavior, applied to human and black-box AI behavior across hundreds of challenging reasoning problems.
AI.result: People and machines tend to oversimplify, adopt rules that are only partial explanations of their observations, and misinfer dependencies between problem features; reasoning effort predicts how far machines simplify and explain their observations.
AI.conclusion: The shared signatures point to satisficing-like mechanisms in people and machines, and BCSS offers a general way to interpret and compare rule-based reasoning of humans and black-box AI systems.

title: Credibility Clustering for Experience Rating: An Automated Approach to Risk Group Allocation in Group Life Insurance
summary: In insurance, experience rating plays a crucial role in mitigating adverse selection by adjusting premiums according to historical claims experience. A key step in this process is the classification of insured collectives into homogeneous risk groups. Within group life insurance, this classification traditionally relies on manual decisions and arbitrary thresholds, which may lead to inefficiencies and inconsistent outcomes. This paper proposes a data-driven methodology for automating risk group allocation based on a combination of the multidimensional Bühlmann-Straub model and k-means clustering -- referred to as credibility clustering. By incorporating credibility weights, the method accounts for the varying statistical significance of experience data and ensuresthat risk classifications are both actuarially sound and practically implementable. Empirical results based on real-world group life insurance data from a major European insurer demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms the two k-means benchmark variants considered in the empirical application in terms of viability, temporal stability and accounting for statistical reliability.

AI.tldr: Proposes credibility clustering, which combines the multidimensional Bühlmann-Straub credibility model with k-means clustering to automate risk group allocation in group life insurance. On real data from a major European insurer it outperforms two k-means benchmarks in viability, temporal stability and handling of statistical reliability.
AI.motivation: Experience rating requires insured collectives to be grouped into homogeneous risk groups, but group life classification relies on manual decisions and arbitrary thresholds, which produce inefficient and inconsistent outcomes.
AI.method: The method combines the multidimensional Bühlmann-Straub model with k-means clustering and incorporates credibility weights, so that the varying statistical significance of experience data is taken into account.
AI.result: On real-world group life insurance data from a major European insurer, the method outperforms the two k-means benchmark variants in viability, temporal stability and accounting for statistical reliability.
AI.conclusion: Credibility clustering yields risk classifications that are both actuarially sound and practically implementable, offering an automated alternative to manual, threshold-based allocation.

title: PromptOps: Iterative Prompt Optimization for LLM-as-a-Judge Systems
comment: CONVERSATIONS 2026, International Symposium on Chatbots and Human-Centred AI, Preprint
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges for evaluating the behavior of chatbots and other AI systems. In deployment, however, their agreement with the intended human evaluation policy may degrade as user interactions and score distributions change. Existing automatic prompt optimization methods are primarily studied as one-shot procedures on static development sets and therefore provide limited guidance for maintaining LLM judges over time. We frame this problem as judge drift and introduce PromptOps, a closedloop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaaJ) systems. PromptOps separates four operational decisions: when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt. We instantiate the framework with five prompt optimization methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. Our experiments demonstrate that iterative prompt optimization can recalibrate LLM judges and recover performance after controlled shifts in the referencescore distribution. However, effective maintenance is inherently contextdependent: neither optimization algorithm choice nor update timing generalizes universally across settings. These findings establish prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an inherently iterative maintenance problem and demonstrate that PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing this process.

AI.tldr: Introduces PromptOps, a closed-loop framework for monitoring and iteratively recalibrating LLM-as-a-Judge systems against judge drift. Experiments show that iterative prompt optimization can recover judge performance after controlled shifts in the reference score distribution.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic prompt optimization is studied as a one-shot procedure on static development sets, which gives little guidance for keeping LLM judges aligned with the intended human evaluation policy as interactions and score distributions change.
AI.method: PromptOps separates four operational decisions (when to optimize, which optimization procedure to apply, which feedback records to use, and how to update the judge prompt) and instantiates them with five methods: GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection using either simulated annealing or a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator.
AI.result: Iterative optimization recalibrates LLM judges and recovers performance after controlled shifts in the reference score distribution, but neither the optimization algorithm nor the update timing generalizes universally across settings.
AI.conclusion: Maintaining deployed LLM judges is an inherently iterative and context-dependent maintenance problem, and PromptOps provides a practical abstraction for studying and implementing it.

title: Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines with Automatic Model Complexity Inference
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 1 algorithm. Code available at this https URL
summary: Tensor Network (TN) kernel machines accelerate supervised learning by using low-rank TNs to reduce computation and memory. However, most TN-based methods are deterministic with manually tuned ranks and feature dimensions, while the existing Bayesian TN kernel machine is restricted to the CANDECOMP/PARAFAC decomposition (CPD), whose single rank is shared by all modes. We extend this framework to the tensor train (TT) and propose Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines (BTT-KM), whose hierarchical ARD-type priors on the TT cores infer the TT ranks and feature dimensions from data. Since each TT core is coupled to the others only through its neighbors, its closed-form posterior update requires propagating the contributions of all other cores along the chain. Mean-field variational inference yields a Bayesian alternating least squares algorithm with the same computational complexity as its deterministic counterpart and a closed-form predictive distribution. A synthetic experiment illustrates that BTT-KM recovers the true TT ranks and feature dimensions from an over-parameterized initialization.

AI.tldr: Proposes Bayesian Tensor Train Kernel Machines (BTT-KM), which extends Bayesian tensor-network kernel machines from CP decomposition to the tensor train, with hierarchical ARD-type priors that infer TT ranks and feature dimensions from data. A synthetic experiment shows it recovers the true ranks and feature dimensions from an over-parameterized initialization.
AI.motivation: Most tensor-network kernel machines use manually tuned ranks and feature dimensions, and the existing Bayesian version is restricted to CP decomposition, whose single rank is shared by all modes.
AI.method: Hierarchical ARD-type priors are placed on the TT cores, and mean-field variational inference yields a Bayesian alternating least squares algorithm, with closed-form core updates that propagate the contributions of all other cores along the chain.
AI.result: On a synthetic experiment the model recovers the true TT ranks and feature dimensions from an over-parameterized initialization, and the algorithm has the same computational complexity as its deterministic counterpart.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian TT kernel machines remove manual rank tuning at deterministic-level cost and provide a closed-form predictive distribution.

title: A Proxy-Based Method for Measuring Racial Disparities in~Text-to-Image~Generators
summary: We present an automated method for auditing text-to-image generators for representational bias against ground-truth demographic benchmarks. Our approach adapts the racial proxy variables used in U.S. antidiscrimination law to provide a fine-grained comparative analysis of variations in racial representation in generated images. We classify each generated image by race and then compare the model's distribution to publicly available demographic benchmark data to identify patterns of over- and under-representation. We also measure skin tone using CIELAB values and calculate cosine similarity amongst groups of images in order to capture biases that don't show up in demographic comparisons such as differences in image quality across races and skin tones. We report on experiments testing three models (Imagen 4 Fast, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo, and Flux Schnell) using three categories of proxies (geographic, occupational, and surname) and 50 variants within each category. We find notable variation across the models as well as by proxy category. For example, Imagen 4 Fast overrepresents white classified images more than the other models tested and produces images with lighter, more homogeneous skin tones. Imagen 4 Fast also had the largest representational disparity for Black demographics among surname and geographical prompts. Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo produces results that overall diverge most from census data but yield the most diverse range of skin tones. Our method yields a generalizable and legally-grounded auditing tool that surfaces detailed information about model outputs without relying on implicit normative definitions of fairness.

AI.tldr: Presents an automated method for auditing text-to-image generators for racial representation bias, using racial proxy variables from U.S. antidiscrimination law (geographic, occupational and surname) and comparing generated images with public demographic benchmarks. Tests on Imagen 4 Fast, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo and Flux Schnell show notable variation across models and proxy categories.
AI.motivation: Auditing text-to-image models for representational bias requires fine-grained comparison against demographic benchmarks, without relying on implicit normative definitions of fairness.
AI.method: Each generated image is classified by race and the model's distribution is compared with public demographic benchmark data to find over- and under-representation; skin tone is measured in CIELAB and cosine similarity among image groups captures differences that demographic comparisons miss, across three proxy categories with 50 variants each.
AI.result: Imagen 4 Fast overrepresents white-classified images and produces lighter, more homogeneous skin tones, and has the largest Black representational disparity for surname and geographic prompts; Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo diverges most from census data but yields the most diverse range of skin tones.
AI.conclusion: The method is a generalizable, legally grounded auditing tool that surfaces detailed information about model outputs without relying on implicit normative definitions of fairness.

title: Context-Aware Automated NMR Structure Elucidation
summary: Machine learning approaches are rapidly revolutionizing the ability to analyze and extract structural insights from chemical data, enabling high-throughput chemical discovery. While existing data-driven approaches have shown remarkable promise for predicting chemical structures in the de novo setting, incorporating additional chemically informed context offers the opportunity to further improve these models' performance and extend their real-world utility. Here we provide a straightforward protocol to combine artificial-intelligence-based spectroscopic elucidation pipelines with contextual chemical data, e.g., known reactants or a desired product, by using automated retrosynthetic analysis to generate large training sets of molecules and contextual data in the form of synthetic precursors. We demonstrate our approach by showing that our recently introduced NMR structure elucidation framework can be trained to effectively leverage molecular precursor context. We show that when the chemical context provides useful information on the target molecule we obtain dramatically improved accuracy over using NMR spectra alone, obtaining Top-15 accuracies of up to 95.4% for molecules up to 40 heavy atoms spanning the full elemental range of organic chemistry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach is highly robust, such that even when the context provided is uncorrelated with the target, one still obtains accuracies commensurate with those of the original NMR structure elucidation framework. This approach provides an efficient route to improve a wide range of spectroscopic structure elucidation platforms using contextual data.

AI.tldr: Shows how to combine AI-based NMR structure elucidation with chemical context such as known reactants or a desired product, using automated retrosynthetic analysis to generate large training sets of molecules and synthetic precursors. Top-15 accuracy reaches up to 95.4% for molecules of up to 40 heavy atoms when the context is informative.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven spectroscopic elucidation predicts structures de novo and does not exploit available chemical context, which could improve accuracy and real-world utility.
AI.method: An automated protocol uses retrosynthetic analysis to create synthetic precursors as contextual data and trains the authors' recently introduced NMR structure elucidation framework to leverage precursor context.
AI.result: With informative context, Top-15 accuracy reaches 95.4% for molecules of up to 40 heavy atoms spanning the full elemental range of organic chemistry, far above spectra-only use; with context uncorrelated with the target, accuracy remains comparable to the original framework.
AI.conclusion: The approach is an efficient route to improve a wide range of spectroscopic structure elucidation platforms using contextual data, and it is robust when the context is uninformative.

title: FastAFD: When Does Attention-FFN Disaggregation Pay on Rack-Scale NVLink?
summary: Attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) separates attention from the experts of a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model and has been reported to raise decode throughput over colocated serving. Whether this advantage holds on rack-scale NVLink systems such as GB200 NVL72 remains unclear: prior results were obtained on other hardware, against narrower colocated baselines, or with analytical models, whereas production engines serve large MoE models on these systems with wide expert parallelism (wide EP). We build and tune FastAFD, an AFD engine for GB200 NVL72 that overlaps the MoE of one microbatch with the attention of the other, and compare it against the best vLLM wide EP setting. Experiments show that AFD has a throughput advantage of up to 1.17x over wide EP on Qwen3 and 1.16x on Qwen3.5, and matches it on MiniMax-M2.5. We derive an analytical model that predicts AFD throughput within 3% using only profiles of colocated vLLM, telling whether switching to AFD would pay off before deploying it. The model yields a concise insight: AFD's speedup factors into a batch gain (larger batches, since attention GPUs hold no expert weights), an overlap gain (shorter steps, since the MoE runs on the expert GPUs behind attention), and a disaggregation cost (the GPUs given to experts). AFD has the advantage when the two gains outweigh the cost. This view explains which models benefit from AFD, and shows that speculative decoding helps light-expert models most, where the enlarged overlap gain outweighs the larger disaggregation cost and adds a further 8% to AFD's advantage over wide EP. Looking ahead, serving the experts on accelerators that keep their weights in on-chip SRAM, such as the Groq LPX accelerators paired with Vera Rubin NVL72, would remove most of the disaggregation cost, raising the ideal speedup to 2.48x with speculative decoding. FastAFD is open source at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Builds FastAFD, an attention-FFN disaggregation engine for GB200 NVL72 that overlaps the MoE of one microbatch with the attention of another, and finds up to 1.17x throughput over the best vLLM wide expert-parallel setting on Qwen3 and 1.16x on Qwen3.5, with an analytical model that predicts AFD throughput within 3%.
AI.motivation: Whether attention-FFN disaggregation's decode throughput advantage holds on rack-scale NVLink systems was unclear, since prior results used other hardware, narrower colocated baselines or analytical models only.
AI.method: An AFD engine tuned for GB200 NVL72 is compared against the best vLLM wide EP setting, and an analytical model built only from colocated vLLM profiles predicts whether switching to AFD would pay off.
AI.result: AFD gives up to 1.17x over wide EP on Qwen3 and 1.16x on Qwen3.5 and matches it on MiniMax-M2.5; the model predicts throughput within 3%; speculative decoding adds a further 8% to AFD's advantage on light-expert models, and with Groq LPX accelerators paired with Vera Rubin NVL72 the ideal speedup rises to 2.48x with speculative decoding.
AI.conclusion: AFD's speedup factors into batch gain, overlap gain and disaggregation cost, so it pays off only when the gains outweigh the cost, and serving experts on SRAM-based accelerators would remove most of that cost.

title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
comment: Preprint. Code and benchmark: this https URL
summary: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. The tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in an existing source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier.
