Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. We release Multi-step SWE publicly at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5 to 15 dependent steps on one codebase in which the agent builds on its own earlier code. The strongest of nine frontier models solves only 18.5% of tasks, and 38 of the 69 tasks are unsolved by every model.
AI.motivation: Developers extend code that an agent wrote earlier, but most benchmarks score one task at a time and do not test whether agents can keep building on their own code over long horizons.
AI.method: Each step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward; tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in a source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier.
AI.result: Across nine frontier models the best solve rate is 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon work that builds on the agent's own code remains very hard for current coding agents, and the publicly released benchmark measures a capability that single-task benchmarks miss.

title: ShapleyOG: Fast Adaptive Shapley Value Estimation with Odd Gaussian Processes
summary: Shapley values are a central tool for attribution in machine learning. Since their exact computation requires evaluating the cooperative game to be explained on exponentially many player coalitions, they are typically estimated from a limited number of evaluations. Recently, ShaplEIG has shown that adaptively selecting the coalitions to evaluate substantially improves sample efficiency over classical estimators. This, however, comes at the cost of a sequential procedure that, in every iteration, refits a Gaussian process surrogate of the game and selects the coalition with the largest expected information gain about the Shapley values. The resulting computational overhead limits its applicability to costly games with low evaluation budgets. We present fast adaptive Shapley value estimation with Odd Gaussian Processes (ShapleyOG) to overcome this limitation. ShapleyOG leverages the fact that Shapley values depend only on the odd component of the game, and we show that under paired sampling a Gaussian process surrogate on this component alone yields the same Shapley value posterior and coalition selection criterion from half as many observations. Moreover, ShapleyOG refits the surrogate only on a sparse schedule and efficiently updates the selection criterion in between, and it extends quadrature-based computation schemes to the prior covariance of the Shapley values, which allows for exact or cheaper approximate computation. In extensive experiments on diverse games, ShapleyOG matches the estimation accuracy of ShaplEIG while reducing its overhead by up to three orders of magnitude. As a result, it outperforms state-of-the-art non-adaptive estimators at equal total computation time already when a single evaluation takes a tenth of a second and a budget of a few thousand evaluations suffices, thereby widening the regime in which adaptive coalition selection is applicable and pays off.

AI.tldr: Presents ShapleyOG, a fast adaptive Shapley value estimator that uses Odd Gaussian Processes to model only the odd component of the game, cutting the overhead of ShaplEIG by up to three orders of magnitude while matching its estimation accuracy. It outperforms non-adaptive estimators at equal computation time when one evaluation takes a tenth of a second.
AI.motivation: Adaptive coalition selection with ShaplEIG improves sample efficiency but refits a Gaussian process surrogate at every iteration, which is too costly for expensive games with low evaluation budgets.
AI.method: Under paired sampling, a Gaussian process surrogate on the odd component of the game yields the same Shapley value posterior and coalition selection criterion from half as many observations; the surrogate is refitted on a sparse schedule, the criterion is updated in between, and quadrature schemes are extended to the prior covariance of the Shapley values.
AI.result: ShapleyOG matches the estimation accuracy of ShaplEIG while reducing its overhead by up to three orders of magnitude, and outperforms state-of-the-art non-adaptive estimators at equal total computation time when a budget of a few thousand evaluations suffices.
AI.conclusion: The method widens the regime in which adaptive coalition selection is applicable and pays off for attribution in costly models.

title: Task-Calibrated Random Features via Influence-Based Error Cancellation
summary: Random features approximate kernel integrals by Monte Carlo, yet only selected frequency-sampling errors affect a downstream task. We propose Task-Calibrated Random Features (TCRF), which balance frequency moments constructed from task-specific influence using weights shared across kernel entries. Closed-form weights coincide with classical minimum-distance calibration; the contribution is a reusable, task-derived calibration space. We show that first-order variance equals the residual variance after projection onto this space. For kernel ridge regression, complete cancellation yields a non-Gaussian second-order limit. For kernel Stein discrepancy, a subset identity and disjoint-block variance decomposition eliminate the linear component of pilot noise. Positive exponential-tilting weights preserve the positive-semidefinite feature representation and support higher feasible calibration ranks. Paired experiments show improved approximation to exact kernel ridge regression at larger frequency budgets and to the exact empirical Stein discrepancy under a fixed alternative, even after accounting for a frequency-equivalent pilot budget. Gains are smaller with cross-validated ridge, landmark pilots require conservative rank selection, and near the Stein null allocating the pilot budget to additional ordinary frequencies is preferable.

AI.tldr: Proposes Task-Calibrated Random Features (TCRF), which balances frequency moments built from task-specific influence so that selected Monte Carlo frequency-sampling errors cancel in the kernel approximation. It improves approximation to exact kernel ridge regression and to the exact empirical kernel Stein discrepancy, with smaller gains under cross-validated ridge.
AI.motivation: Random features approximate kernel integrals by Monte Carlo, but only selected frequency-sampling errors affect a downstream task, so errors can be targeted rather than reduced uniformly.
AI.method: Calibration weights shared across kernel entries balance task-derived frequency moments; closed-form weights coincide with classical minimum-distance calibration, and positive exponential-tilting weights preserve the positive-semidefinite feature representation.
AI.result: First-order variance equals the residual variance after projection onto the calibration space; complete cancellation gives a non-Gaussian second-order limit for kernel ridge regression, and for kernel Stein discrepancy a subset identity and disjoint-block decomposition remove the linear pilot-noise component. Paired experiments show improved approximation at larger frequency budgets, even after accounting for a frequency-equivalent pilot budget, while landmark pilots require conservative rank selection.
AI.conclusion: The reusable, task-derived calibration space is the main contribution, and near the Stein null, allocating the pilot budget to additional ordinary frequencies is preferable.

title: Goal Revelation as a Bridge Between Information-Theoretic Empowerment and Capability-Based Human Power
comment: 19 pages, 3 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Power matters for AI safety. Optimal agents tend to acquire power across a wide range of objectives (instrumental convergence). As we embed AI agents into socio-technical systems, humans risk gradual disempowerment. Both concerns call for a formal, quantitative measure of power. Two such measures in the context of Markov games are information-theoretic empowerment, the capacity of the channel from an agent's actions to future states, and capability-based individual power, a measure of goal attainment built from the probabilities that a human would attain each goal in a family of candidates were they pursuing it. We show where the two meet. From individual power, Fano's inequality yields a floor $B(s)$. This floor is a lower bound on what we term goal revelation, the mutual information $\mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s)$ between the human's latent goal and the realised trajectory. Empowerment caps revelation from above, so that $B(s) \le \mathbb{I}(G;\xi \mid s) \le \mathbb{I}(\mathbf{A}_h \to \xi \mid s) \le \mathfrak{E}_h(s)$. Each quantity can be large while the one below it stays at zero, highlighting the following failure modes. An assistant maximising empowerment can prefer an interface offering broad influence over goal-irrelevant degrees of freedom to one that lets the human attain every goal they might hold. An assistant maximising revelation cannot tell a working interface from one rewired so that every goal yields the wrong outcome, since relabelling goals leaves mutual information unchanged while zeroing every attainment probability. Positive guarantees therefore come only from the attainment end of the chain. A satisfaction floor, computable from two statistics of interaction logs, offers a way to monitor the power users retain in a deployed system, and simulations in random environments show the three quantities are correlated but far from interchangeable.

AI.tldr: Links two formal measures of power in Markov games, information-theoretic empowerment and capability-based individual power, through goal revelation, the mutual information between a human's latent goal and the realised trajectory. Empowerment caps revelation from above and a Fano-based floor bounds it from below, but the three quantities are not interchangeable, so only the attainment-based satisfaction floor gives positive guarantees.
AI.motivation: AI safety needs formal, quantitative measures of power because optimal agents acquire power across many objectives and humans risk gradual disempowerment, yet the two existing measures had not been connected.
AI.method: From individual power, Fano's inequality yields a floor on goal revelation, which is sandwiched between that floor and empowerment in a chain of inequalities, and a satisfaction floor is computed from two statistics of interaction logs.
AI.result: An empowerment-maximizing assistant can prefer an interface with broad influence over goal-irrelevant degrees of freedom, and a revelation-maximizing assistant cannot tell a working interface from one rewired so that every goal yields the wrong outcome; simulations in random environments show the three quantities are correlated but far from interchangeable.
AI.conclusion: Positive guarantees come only from the attainment end of the chain, and the satisfaction floor offers a way to monitor the power users retain in a deployed system.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Stochastic Gradient Methods for Unbounded Problems
summary: Last-iterate convergence guarantees for stochastic gradient methods have attracted significant attention as practical implementations typically return the last iterate instead of an average of the iterates. In this paper, we study two approaches for analyzing the last-iterate convergence of proximal and projected stochastic gradient methods without bounded domain or bounded variance assumptions, where black-box variational inference serves as a running example. Under two related assumptions relaxing the bounded variance, we show near-optimal anytime rate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\sqrt{T})$ for the last iterate. Moreover, when the horizon $T$ is known, we remove the logarithmic factor and obtain the optimal order $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$, matching the order known under bounded variance or bounded domain assumptions.

AI.tldr: Analyzes last-iterate convergence of proximal and projected stochastic gradient methods without bounded-domain or bounded-variance assumptions, with black-box variational inference as a running example. It shows a near-optimal anytime rate of order 1/sqrt(T) up to a logarithmic factor for the last iterate, and removes that factor to obtain the optimal order when the horizon T is known.
AI.motivation: Practical implementations return the last iterate rather than an average of the iterates, but existing last-iterate guarantees typically assume bounded domains or bounded variance.
AI.method: Two related assumptions relax the bounded-variance requirement, and two analysis approaches are applied to proximal and projected stochastic gradient methods.
AI.result: The last iterate achieves a near-optimal anytime rate of order 1/sqrt(T) up to a logarithmic factor; when T is known the logarithmic factor is removed, giving order 1/sqrt(T), which matches the order known under bounded-variance or bounded-domain assumptions.
AI.conclusion: Last-iterate guarantees hold without bounded-domain or bounded-variance assumptions, so the optimal rate is available in these unbounded settings when the horizon is known.

title: From What Is Used to What Is Missing: Rethinking Dynamic Rank in LoRA
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA is governed by rank, which controls parameter budget and locally accessible task updates. Existing dynamic-rank methods mainly focus on capacity allocation, leaving unresolved whether the current adaptation space is sufficient for the task. We characterize the first-order information boundary of standard factor gradients, showing that their unobservable subspace coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold. Thus, factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the current space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach. This motivates a geometric view of rank evolution, where tangent information optimizes existing degrees of freedom and the normal spectrum quantifies the value of new ones. Under a local quadratic model, we show that leading normal singular directions yield the locally optimal rank expansion, with spectral energy determining its gain. Building on this characterization, we propose GEAR, which turns the tangent--normal decomposition into rank evolution through tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation for rank expansion, and task-induced geometric initialization. Across language and vision benchmarks, GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters. On LLaMA3-8B, it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.

AI.tldr: Proposes GEAR, a dynamic-rank LoRA method that splits the parameter space into tangent and normal parts of the low-rank manifold, refining existing directions in the tangent space and using the normal spectrum to decide where to add rank. It achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with fewer trainable parameters, raising the LLaMA3-8B commonsense average from 86.61 to 88.45 with 14.4M instead of 42.0M trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing dynamic-rank methods focus on capacity allocation and leave open whether the current adaptation space is sufficient, and factor gradients alone cannot distinguish under-optimization within the space from task-relevant directions beyond its first-order reach.
AI.method: The unobservable subspace of standard factor gradients coincides with the normal space of the low-rank manifold; under a local quadratic model, leading normal singular directions give the locally optimal rank expansion, which GEAR combines with tangent-space optimization, matrix-free normal-spectrum estimation and task-induced geometric initialization.
AI.result: Across language and vision benchmarks GEAR achieves the best average performance in all evaluated settings with substantially fewer trainable parameters; on LLaMA3-8B it raises the average commonsense score from 86.61 to 88.45 while reducing trainable parameters from 42.0M to 14.4M.
AI.conclusion: Rank evolution should be guided by the normal spectrum of the low-rank manifold, which quantifies the value of new degrees of freedom, giving a geometric route to efficient LoRA adaptation.

title: Asymptotic-Preserving Tensor Neural Networks for 3D High-Field Kinetic Equations with Applications to Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Kinetic equations in the high-field regime describe particle transport dominated by electric-field acceleration and collisional relaxation. These equations are widely used in simulations of plasmas and semiconductor devices. Typical models include the Vlasov--Poisson--Fokker--Planck (VPFP) and Boltzmann--Poisson systems. Their high dimensionality and multiscale nature pose two of the major challenges to accurate and efficient numerical solution. To address these challenges, we propose an asymptotic-preserving tensor neural network (APTNN) method. Specifically, to reduce high-dimensional computational costs and memory requirements, we adopt the canonical polyadic (CP) decomposition structure of TNNs to approximate their solutions. We show that the equation residuals retain this decomposition form, allowing high-dimensional loss integrals to be evaluated through combinations of one-dimensional integrals. The resulting computational and storage costs are reduced from exponential to polynomial growth with dimension. To improve the prediction accuracy in the high-field limit, we enhance the baseline AP loss by incorporating the first moment equation. The added loss term directly constrains the limiting flux closure to reduce its approximation error in the high-field regime. The enhanced AP loss can still be evaluated dimension-wise. Numerical results show that APTNN improves prediction accuracy in the high-field regime with significantly reduced computational costs and memory usage. For a 3D3V VPFP problem with multiple random inputs, training takes less than 30 minutes on a single GPU.

AI.tldr: Presents an asymptotic-preserving tensor neural network (APTNN) for three-dimensional high-field kinetic equations such as the Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck and Boltzmann-Poisson systems. It uses a CP-structured tensor network with an enhanced AP loss that adds the first moment equation, and trains a 3D3V VPFP problem with multiple random inputs in under 30 minutes on one GPU.
AI.motivation: High-field kinetic equations are high-dimensional and multiscale, which makes accurate and efficient numerical solution difficult, and accuracy in the high-field limit requires better constraint of the limiting flux closure.
AI.method: The CP decomposition of the tensor neural network keeps the equation residuals in decomposed form, so high-dimensional loss integrals reduce to combinations of one-dimensional integrals; the baseline AP loss is enhanced with the first moment equation and remains evaluable dimension-wise.
AI.result: APTNN improves prediction accuracy in the high-field regime with significantly reduced computational cost and memory, with costs growing polynomially rather than exponentially with dimension; the 3D3V VPFP problem with multiple random inputs trains in under 30 minutes on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: The approach makes high-dimensional, multiscale kinetic simulation with uncertainty quantification tractable at modest cost by exploiting the decomposition structure of the residuals.

title: CacheGraft: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Latent-Space Document Enrichment
comment: 5 pages. Third KEIR Workshop @ CIKM 2026. Work in progress
summary: Recent work in machine learning has demonstrated that transformer-based language model agents can communicate state not only through text, but also directly in latent space via key-value (KV) caches. In this paper, we argue that such cache-to-cache translation can provide utility beyond the original motivating application of real-time agent communication and can instead be utilized for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Building on the Cache-to-Cache (C2C) fusion framework, our proposed system CacheGraft encodes each corpus passage offline into a fused KV cache representation between a larger sharer model (4B parameters in our experiments) and a smaller receiver model (0.6B parameters) such that this cache can be injected into the receiver at query time with no need for the larger model. Across five QA benchmarks and two independent locally-run judges, CacheGraft improves answer quality over the text-only receiver baseline in 29 out of 30 comparisons, of which 17 of the 30 are statistically significant. Notably, these gains are zero-shot with respect to the fuser, which was never trained on retrieval data. These initial results suggest that latent-space document enrichment may be a promising avenue for enhancing the performance of RAG systems, particularly in compute-constrained settings where it is only feasible to deploy a small model at inference time.

AI.tldr: Proposes CacheGraft, which encodes each corpus passage offline into a fused KV cache between a 4B-parameter sharer model and a 0.6B-parameter receiver model, so the receiver can use the cache at query time without running the larger model. It improves answer quality over the text-only receiver in 29 of 30 comparisons across five QA benchmarks and two judges, 17 of them statistically significant.
AI.motivation: Language model agents can communicate through key-value caches rather than text, and this latent communication has been studied for real-time agent messaging, but its utility for retrieval-augmented generation had not been explored.
AI.method: Building on the Cache-to-Cache fusion framework, passages are pre-encoded into fused KV caches and injected into the small receiver at query time, and the fuser, which was never trained on retrieval data, is used zero-shot.
AI.result: Answer quality improves over the text-only receiver in 29 of 30 comparisons, 17 of which are statistically significant, across five QA benchmarks and two independent locally run judges.
AI.conclusion: Latent-space document enrichment may enhance RAG systems, particularly in compute-constrained settings where only a small model can be deployed at inference time.

title: Rigorously Certified Neural-Network Computation of Nonlinear Water Waves at Near-Machine Precision
summary: We present a computational framework that combines machine-learning-based discovery with rigorous computer-assisted numerical certification and formal verification for strongly nonlinear partial differential equations. We demonstrate the approach for periodic gravity-capillary traveling water waves. Physics-informed neural networks are used as a search mechanism, with the wave profile, wave speed and, in continuation experiments, surface tension learned directly from the governing equations without training data. Through a staged training and refinement procedure, the neural networks achieve near-machine-precision residuals of the governing equations, even in strongly nonlinear regimes. A single formulation recovers high-amplitude Stokes waves, Crapper waves and Wilton ripples. Continuation from a high-amplitude Wilton ripple in surface tension reveals new high-amplitude candidate solutions. We freeze one candidate as an explicit finite representation and rigorously certify a uniform bound on its governing-equation residual using interval arithmetic, accounting for floating-point roundoff, Fourier truncation, aliasing and grid-to-continuum errors. This independently validates the neural-network accuracy. We formalize the certification argument in Lean, which machine-checks the deductions from certified numerical bounds to the residual theorem. Both the interval certification and formalization were developed with substantial assistance from a large language model, while the validity of the result remains independent of the language model: the numerical bounds are rigorously enclosed by interval arithmetic and the subsequent mathematical deductions are checked by the Lean kernel. Together, these steps provide a pipeline from neural discovery to rigorous numerical certification and machine-checked verification with auditable mathematical guarantees.

AI.tldr: Presents a pipeline that uses physics-informed neural networks to find periodic gravity-capillary traveling water waves, then certifies one new high-amplitude candidate with interval arithmetic and machine-checks the deduction from the certified bounds to the residual theorem in Lean. The network residuals reach near machine precision.
AI.motivation: Strongly nonlinear PDEs need both the discovery of solutions and rigorous, machine-checkable guarantees, and neural solutions alone do not certify their own accuracy.
AI.method: Physics-informed neural networks, trained without data on the governing equations through a staged training and refinement procedure, search for wave profiles; continuation in surface tension reveals candidates, one of which is frozen as a finite representation and certified by interval arithmetic that accounts for roundoff, Fourier truncation, aliasing and grid-to-continuum errors.
AI.result: A single formulation recovers high-amplitude Stokes waves, Crapper waves and Wilton ripples; continuation from a high-amplitude Wilton ripple reveals new high-amplitude candidate solutions, and the certified uniform bound on the residual independently validates the network accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a pipeline from neural discovery to rigorous numerical certification and machine-checked verification with auditable guarantees, and the validity of the result does not depend on the language model that assisted with the code.

title: Truncated backpropagation through time induces a two-sided gradient turnpike property
summary: Truncated backpropagation through time reduces the computational burden of training recurrent models by restricting gradient computations to shorter temporal contexts. This induces two distinct boundary effects: missing past information perturbs the forward state evolution, while truncating the backward recursion omits future information. This motivates decoupling the interval over which gradient contributions are averaged for the parameter update from the surrounding temporal context over which they are computed. Under exponential decay of the state-transition Jacobians and mild regularity conditions, this leads to a two-sided gradient turnpike property: the error between truncated- and full-context gradient contributions decays exponentially with the distance from both context boundaries. We derive bounds for the averaged update gradient, yielding guarantees on gradient alignment and approximate full-context stationarity; under unbiased interval sampling and a Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, these further imply a bound on the resulting optimality gap. Numerical experiments on the Wiener-Hammerstein benchmark illustrate the role of past and future context and the trade-off between predictive performance and computational cost.

AI.tldr: Shows that truncated backpropagation through time has a two-sided gradient turnpike property: under exponential decay of the state-transition Jacobians, the error between truncated and full-context gradient contributions decays exponentially with distance from both context boundaries. This gives bounds on gradient alignment and approximate full-context stationarity, and an optimality-gap bound under a Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition.
AI.motivation: Truncated backpropagation through time reduces the training cost of recurrent models, but it causes two boundary effects, since missing past information perturbs the forward state evolution and truncating the backward recursion omits future information.
AI.method: The interval over which gradient contributions are averaged for the parameter update is decoupled from the surrounding temporal context over which they are computed, and the analysis uses exponential decay of the Jacobians, mild regularity conditions and unbiased interval sampling.
AI.result: Bounds on the averaged update gradient give guarantees on gradient alignment and approximate full-context stationarity, and with unbiased interval sampling and a Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition they imply a bound on the optimality gap; experiments on the Wiener-Hammerstein benchmark illustrate the role of past and future context and the trade-off between predictive performance and computational cost.
AI.conclusion: The truncation error is controlled by distance to the context boundaries, so the context length can be chosen to balance predictive performance against computational cost.

title: KOSMOS: Self-scheduling Persistent Kernels for Communication-Compute Overlap
summary: Tensor and sequence parallelism (TP+SP) and expert parallelism (EP) put collectives on the critical path of transformer layers. State-of-the-art fused kernels mitigate this with fixed roles or schedules, but this rigidity leaves large idle windows. Predicting a communication-computation split does not remove them either; a predetermined split cannot follow data readiness. We present KOSMOS, a library for self-scheduling persistent kernels whose workgroups use queues ordered by consumer demand to switch between communication and computation roles as data become ready, with no scheduler, per-call cost model, or tuned split. KOSMOS fuses every TP+SP collective of a transformer layer with its GEMM, and runs an entire expert layer, from router to fold, in one launch per direction. Evaluated on AMD Instinct MI350X and AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, KOSMOS speeds up TP+SP end-to-end training in Megatron-LM by 1.10-1.28x in BF16 and 1.10-1.25x in MXFP8. KOSMOS accelerates end-to-end training of DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxies by 1.29-1.83x over DeepEP.

AI.tldr: KOSMOS is a library of self-scheduling persistent kernels that let GPU workgroups switch between communication and computation roles as data becomes ready, overlapping collectives with GEMMs in transformer training. On AMD MI350X and MI355X GPUs it speeds up TP+SP training in Megatron-LM by 1.10-1.28x and end-to-end DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxy training by 1.29-1.83x over DeepEP.
AI.motivation: Tensor, sequence and expert parallelism put collectives on the critical path of transformer layers, and existing fused kernels with fixed roles or schedules leave large idle windows. A predetermined communication-computation split cannot follow data readiness.
AI.method: A self-scheduling persistent kernel design in which workgroups pull from queues ordered by consumer demand to switch between communication and computation roles, with no scheduler, per-call cost model or tuned split. Every TP+SP collective of a transformer layer is fused with its GEMM, and a whole expert layer from router to fold runs in one launch per direction.
AI.result: On AMD Instinct MI350X and MI355X GPUs, TP+SP end-to-end training in Megatron-LM improves by 1.10-1.28x in BF16 and 1.10-1.25x in MXFP8. End-to-end training of DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxies improves by 1.29-1.83x over DeepEP.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic role switching driven by data readiness recovers overlap that fixed or predicted splits cannot, giving a practical speedup for distributed transformer training on AMD GPUs.

title: OPRD-Imp: a dataset of experimentally observed impurities and side products in multi-step pharmaceutical syntheses
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Dataset available at this https URL
summary: Predicting reaction impurities is a critical yet persistently data-limited challenge in pharmaceutical process chemistry. While machine learning models for reaction outcome prediction have advanced rapidly, benchmarking their ability to predict impurities remains impractical due to the absence of curated, publicly accessible datasets. We present OPRD-Imp, a dataset of 229 organic reactions drawn from 62 publications in Organic Process Research & Development, each annotated with experimentally observed impurities and their mechanistic origins. A total of 784 impurity entries is provided, classified into four origin categories. Reactions are represented as reaction SMILES and impurities as individual SMILES strings, with multi-step synthetic route connectivity preserved. All data were manually extracted from the source publications by trained chemists following a standardized extraction protocol, with expert chemical validation and manual structure drawing. OPRD-Imp is intended to serve as a benchmark resource for evaluating models that predict reaction impurities, providing experimentally reported impurity annotations and mechanistic origin labels that are not systematically represented in conventional reaction datasets.

AI.tldr: OPRD-Imp is a curated dataset of 229 organic reactions drawn from 62 Organic Process Research & Development publications, annotated with 784 experimentally observed impurities and their mechanistic origins. It is intended as a benchmark for models that predict reaction impurities.
AI.motivation: Impurity prediction is data-limited in pharmaceutical process chemistry, and benchmarking reaction-outcome models on impurities is impractical without curated public datasets. Conventional reaction datasets do not systematically represent impurities or their origins.
AI.method: Reactions were manually extracted from source publications by trained chemists following a standardized protocol, with expert chemical validation and manual structure drawing. Reactions are stored as reaction SMILES and impurities as individual SMILES strings, with multi-step route connectivity preserved, and impurities are classified into four origin categories.
AI.result: The dataset contains 229 reactions and 784 impurity entries across four origin categories, drawn from 62 publications.
AI.conclusion: OPRD-Imp supplies experimentally reported impurity annotations with mechanistic origin labels as a benchmark resource for evaluating impurity prediction.

title: Statistical and Privacy Guarantees for Deep M-Regression via Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics
summary: In this article, we study deep nonparametric regression trained via stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD), a variant of stochastic gradient descent that injects carefully calibrated Gaussian noise during optimization. Using a PAC-Bayesian analysis tailored to deep ReLU networks, we establish an excess-risk bound that simultaneously accounts for network approximation error, statistical complexity, and the algorithmic cost accumulated along the SGLD trajectory. Under a Bernstein condition and within a stable SGLD regime, the excess-risk bound contains a stochastic term whose coefficient is inversely proportional to the variance of injected noise, while the estimator retains the optimal rate for nonparametric regression under the Hölder smoothness condition up to logarithmic factors. This result provides an approximation-error-aware, rate-optimal statistical perspective on the widely observed generalization benefits of moderate SGLD noise. For per-sample clipped SGLD, we further establish an exact f-DP guarantee and the corresponding asymptotic $\mu$-GDP guarantee for the proposed estimator. We establish statistical convergence rates and differential privacy guarantees for DNN estimators trained using SGLD, while explicitly accounting for both network approximation error and the effect of injected noise in the excess-risk bound. Extensive simulation studies and analyses of two real datasets examine the finite-sample predictive performance and privacy-utility behavior of the proposed procedure.

AI.tldr: The paper proves excess-risk and privacy guarantees for deep ReLU nonparametric regression trained with stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD). The excess-risk bound links its stochastic term to the injected noise variance, and per-sample clipped SGLD gets an exact f-DP guarantee and an asymptotic mu-GDP guarantee.
AI.motivation: The generalization benefits of moderate SGLD noise are widely observed but lack a theory that jointly accounts for network approximation error, statistical complexity and the algorithmic cost accumulated along the SGLD trajectory. Privacy guarantees for DNN estimators trained this way also need to be established.
AI.method: A PAC-Bayesian analysis tailored to deep ReLU networks yields an excess-risk bound under a Bernstein condition in a stable SGLD regime. For per-sample clipped SGLD, the analysis derives an exact f-DP guarantee and the corresponding asymptotic mu-GDP guarantee for the estimator.
AI.result: The excess-risk bound contains a stochastic term whose coefficient is inversely proportional to the injected noise variance, and the estimator keeps the optimal nonparametric rate under Holder smoothness up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and two real datasets examine finite-sample predictive performance and privacy-utility behavior.
AI.conclusion: The analysis gives an approximation-error-aware, rate-optimal perspective on why moderate SGLD noise helps generalization, and it supplies differential privacy guarantees for the same estimator.

title: ZYFA: Speed and Accuracy of FP8 FlashAttention on AMD CDNA4
summary: Attention is a core building block of frontier models and often dominates compute-bound prefill at long context. FP8 matrix instructions offer twice the peak throughput of BF16, but they accelerate only matrix multiplication, and the softmax between the two matrix multiplications of attention runs on vector units that FP8 does not accelerate. On the AMD Instinct MI355X, the vendor's AITER kernels reach 39% of peak FP8 matrix throughput at 32K tokens, compared with 49% in BF16. Attention is also more numerically sensitive to quantization than feed-forward layers, and unlike NVIDIA's Hopper and Blackwell GPUs, the MI355X does not track the completion of matrix instructions in hardware, so overlapping the softmax with the matrix multiplications depends on instruction order. We present ZYFA, prefill kernels for the MI355X built on three techniques: (1) computing each FP8 probability directly from its score with a multiply-add and an integer conversion instead of an exponential; (2) a ping-pong schedule in which one group of threads computes its softmax while another executes its matrix multiplications; and (3) scaling each block of probabilities up by a power of two before rounding, and normalizing by the sum of the rounded probabilities. On attention inputs captured from three models and timed at sustained clock speeds, ZYFA achieves 1.16-1.76x the throughput of AITER. On the Gaussian inputs of kernel benchmarks at 32K tokens, it achieves 1.26-1.37x at head dimension 128 and 1.99x for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention. The sustained clock of the MI355X depends on operand values, so throughput on random inputs does not reliably predict throughput on real model activations. At head dimension 128, ZYFA's numerical error is within a few percent of that of Composable Kernel and Triton and 62-78% lower than that of AITER's. The source code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ZYFA is a set of FP8 FlashAttention prefill kernels for the AMD MI355X that reach 1.16-1.76x the throughput of AITER on attention inputs captured from three models. At head dimension 128 its numerical error is within a few percent of Composable Kernel and Triton and 62-78% lower than AITER's.
AI.motivation: FP8 matrix instructions double peak throughput over BF16, but the softmax in attention runs on vector units that FP8 does not accelerate. AITER reaches only 39% of peak FP8 matrix throughput at 32K tokens, the MI355X does not track matrix-instruction completion in hardware, and attention is more sensitive to quantization than feed-forward layers.
AI.method: Three techniques: computing each FP8 probability from its score with a multiply-add and an integer conversion instead of an exponential; a ping-pong schedule in which one group of threads computes its softmax while another executes its matrix multiplications; and scaling each block of probabilities by a power of two before rounding, then normalizing by the sum of the rounded probabilities.
AI.result: On attention inputs captured from three models and timed at sustained clocks, ZYFA reaches 1.16-1.76x AITER throughput. On Gaussian kernel-benchmark inputs at 32K tokens it reaches 1.26-1.37x at head dimension 128 and 1.99x for DeepSeek-style multi-head latent attention. Throughput on random inputs does not reliably predict throughput on real activations, because the sustained clock depends on operand values.
AI.conclusion: FP8 attention on the MI355X can be sped up while keeping accuracy by reorganizing softmax and matrix work, and benchmarks should use real model activations because clock behavior depends on the data.

title: Coverage Hides Churn: Auditing and Preserving Conformal Decisions as VLM Label Registries Grow
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. Includes supplementary material
summary: Vision-language classifiers can learn new labels from text alone, so the label lists they serve keep growing. We show that this growth silently changes conformal decisions about old labels. Common softmax-based conformal scores compare each label with an average over all labels; adding labels changes that average, and with it the score of every old label, even when the model, the image, and the old calibration data stay the same. Recalibrating after the update keeps the coverage guarantee, yet across eleven settings it changes at least one old decision on 53-90% of new images. Coverage cannot reveal this, because it checks only the true label: in five controlled settings that keep the old calibration, so that only the normalizer changes, old-class coverage moves by at most 0.01 while 60-67% of images change. We propose a lifecycle audit that measures these changes alongside coverage and set size, and a simple fix, PrefixCP: each class keeps the label registry that existed when it was added. Its old decisions then never change, each class keeps exact class-conditional coverage under exchangeability, and one prefix scan computes all historical normalizers at once. PrefixCP recovers 40.9-58.5% of the set-size gap between never updating the reference and recalibrating, which gives smaller sets but changes old decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that adding labels to a vision-language classifier's label registry silently changes conformal decisions for old labels under softmax-based conformal scores, even when coverage is unchanged. It proposes a lifecycle audit and PrefixCP, which freezes each class's registry at the time the class was added so that its old decisions never change.
AI.motivation: Vision-language classifiers learn new labels from text, so label lists keep growing, and softmax-based conformal scores compare each label with an average over all labels. Coverage checks only the true label, so it cannot reveal changes to old decisions.
AI.method: A lifecycle audit that measures decision changes alongside coverage and set size, plus PrefixCP, in which each class keeps the label registry that existed when it was added. One prefix scan computes all historical normalizers at once.
AI.result: Across eleven settings, recalibrating after a label update changes at least one old decision on 53-90% of new images. In five controlled settings that keep the old calibration, old-class coverage moves by at most 0.01 while 60-67% of images change. PrefixCP recovers 40.9-58.5% of the set-size gap between never updating the reference and recalibrating.
AI.conclusion: Coverage alone is an incomplete audit for growing label registries, since it can stay stable while old decisions change, and PrefixCP keeps old decisions fixed while retaining exact class-conditional coverage under exchangeability.

title: Using Transformers to Generate 3-Manifold Triangulations
summary: Using dehydration signatures as an encoding, we train GPT-2-style transformers to generate triangulations of 3-dimensional manifolds. Our main runs each use approximately 3 exaFLOPs, spanning a 200 million parameter model trained on 60 million sphere triangulations to an 11 million parameter model trained on 1.1 billion sphere triangulations. The optimal model has 10 blocks, width 640 and generates dehydration signatures of closed manifolds of various topological types at a rate of 6.9%, 82% of which are spheres. To investigate how our method scales, we use the technique of IsoFLOP curves on 15-tetrahedron triangulations of the 3-sphere, over a compute range of 6 to 3000 petaFLOPs, and observe neural scaling behaviour. We extract a parameter scaling exponent of $\alpha = 0.49$ ($[0.48, 0.50]$ stat, $\pm 0.02$ syst), and an optimal ratio of 234 tokens per parameter for training. In addition, we present a number of smaller experiments, including evidence that transformers are able to learn to count degree-one edges near-perfectly, but get progressively worse when counting edges with higher degrees.

AI.tldr: GPT-2-style transformers trained on dehydration signatures generate triangulations of 3-manifolds, and the optimal model produces closed manifolds at a rate of 6.9%, 82% of which are spheres. Scaling experiments on 3-sphere triangulations give a parameter scaling exponent of 0.49 and an optimal ratio of 234 tokens per parameter.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether transformers can learn to generate triangulations of 3-dimensional manifolds from a compact encoding, and how the method scales with compute.
AI.method: Dehydration signatures serve as the encoding. Main runs use about 3 exaFLOPs each, from a 200 million parameter model trained on 60 million sphere triangulations to an 11 million parameter model trained on 1.1 billion sphere triangulations. Scaling is studied with IsoFLOP curves on 15-tetrahedron triangulations of the 3-sphere over 6 to 3000 petaFLOPs.
AI.result: The optimal model has 10 blocks and width 640 and generates dehydration signatures of closed manifolds of various topological types at a rate of 6.9%, 82% of which are spheres. The parameter scaling exponent is alpha = 0.49 (interval 0.48-0.50 statistical, plus or minus 0.02 systematic), with an optimal ratio of 234 tokens per parameter. Transformers learn to count degree-one edges near-perfectly but get progressively worse at counting edges of higher degree.
AI.conclusion: Transformers can generate 3-manifold triangulations and show neural scaling behavior on this combinatorial task, although their counting ability is uneven across edge degrees.

title: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
summary: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$, while time-average payments are of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/8})$.

AI.tldr: A mediator learns an unknown game and steers adaptive agents toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria using only trajectory feedback and nonnegative payments. The Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves directness and optimality gaps of O~(T^-1/4), with time-average payments of O~(T^-1/8).
AI.motivation: In multi-agent systems a mediator wants to influence strategic decisions, but she does not know the agents' utilities and receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback.
AI.method: Halving-type algorithms learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games. These are combined with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation and steering toward mediator-optimal EFCE.
AI.result: The learning procedures achieve sample complexity O~(eps^-2), matching worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. With high probability, Learn-Compute-Steer achieves directness and optimality gaps of O~(T^-1/4), while time-average payments are O~(T^-1/8).
AI.conclusion: A mediator with only outcome-level feedback and nonnegative payments can learn enough about agents' utilities to steer them toward her preferred equilibria, with the gaps shrinking as the number of rounds T grows.

title: TACT-KV: Tri-Axis Cosine Transform for Compressing Volumetric KV Caches in Medical VLMs
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) applied to 3D medical scans face a structural memory wall. A single CT or MRI volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, and the resulting key-value (KV) cache scales linearly with both batch and context. Existing KV compression methods operate on the cache's feature or token statistics, or apply 1D and 2D transforms, leaving the three-axis spatial structure in the cache unexploited. We propose TACT-KV (Tri-Axis Cosine Transform), a calibration-free KV compression method that exploits strong spatial correlations in visual KV states along all three anatomical axes of 3D scans. This correlation concentrates the KV cache energy under a frequency-domain transform. TACT-KV applies a separable 3D discrete cosine transform to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins via reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. We derive a close-form relation: the distortion reduction from adaptive bit allocation is dominated by the spectral concentration of the transformed cache. Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV achieves the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs in our main comparison. The same advantage reproduces on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks, indicating that the benefit of exploiting three-axis structure generalizes beyond medical imaging. At equal high-bandwidth memory (HBM), TACT-KV scales the decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to $8\times$.

AI.tldr: TACT-KV compresses the KV cache of medical VLMs that process 3D CT and MRI volumes by applying a separable 3D discrete cosine transform and allocating bits across frequency bins by reverse water-filling. It has the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs and scales decoding batch size by up to 8x at equal HBM.
AI.motivation: A single 3D volume produces tens of thousands of vision tokens, so the KV cache grows linearly with batch size and context. Existing KV compression methods use feature or token statistics or 1D and 2D transforms, and so leave the three-axis spatial structure unexploited.
AI.method: A calibration-free method that applies a separable 3D DCT to the KV cache, allocates a per-layer bit budget across frequency bins by reverse water-filling (more bits to high-energy components), and quantizes each bin with a fixed scalar codebook. A closed-form relation links the distortion reduction from adaptive allocation to the spectral concentration of the transformed cache.
AI.result: Across six medical VLMs and two 3D CT benchmarks, TACT-KV has the lowest 1-bit prediction-flip rate on eleven of twelve model and dataset pairs. The same advantage appears on four general-purpose VLMs evaluated on video tasks. At equal HBM it scales decoding batch size on a single GPU by up to 8x.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting three-axis structure in the visual KV cache reduces memory cost for 3D medical VLMs, and the abstract reports that the benefit also reproduces on general-purpose video VLMs.

title: Extracting Single-Mode Rayleigh--Taylor Instability dynamics from data via SINDy
summary: Rayleigh-Taylor instability (RTI) is of fundamental importance in fields such as inertial confinement fusion and supernova explosions, and its evolution is commonly described by potential--flow theory and buoyancy--drag models. However, both types of models struggle to accurately capture the overshoot behavior of bubble and spike velocities, as well as the subsequent reacceleration stage. To address these limitations, we develop a physics-constrained, data-driven framework based on the integral formulation of Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy), which extracts low-dimensional dynamical equations for bubble and spike evolution directly from data. By introducing the nondimensional initial amplitude $A_0 = k\eta_0$ as an explicit parameter, we identify distinct dynamical equations for the bubble and the spike based on data spanning multiple Atwood numbers and initial amplitudes. The resulting low-dimensional dynamical equations not only reproduce the overshoot behavior of the velocity with good accuracy, but also capture the reacceleration stage well, while maintaining high predictive accuracy at unseen values of the wavenumber, acceleration, and Atwood number. This work provides a physics-constrained, data-driven framework complementary to conventional potential-flow and buoyancy--drag models, accurately describing the dynamical evolution of the bubble and spike at high Atwood numbers, and provides a new perspective for directly extracting the dynamical equations of interfacial instabilities from data.

AI.tldr: The paper uses an integral formulation of SINDy to extract low-dimensional dynamical equations for bubble and spike velocities in single-mode Rayleigh-Taylor instability directly from data. The identified equations reproduce velocity overshoot and reacceleration and keep high accuracy at unseen wavenumber, acceleration and Atwood number values.
AI.motivation: Potential-flow theory and buoyancy-drag models both struggle to capture the overshoot of bubble and spike velocities and the subsequent reacceleration stage.
AI.method: A physics-constrained, data-driven framework based on the integral formulation of Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy), with the nondimensional initial amplitude A0 = k eta0 as an explicit parameter. Distinct equations are identified for the bubble and the spike from data spanning multiple Atwood numbers and initial amplitudes.
AI.result: The identified equations reproduce the velocity overshoot with good accuracy, capture the reacceleration stage well, and maintain high predictive accuracy at unseen values of the wavenumber, acceleration and Atwood number.
AI.conclusion: The framework complements potential-flow and buoyancy-drag models for bubble and spike dynamics at high Atwood numbers, and offers a route to extracting the dynamical equations of interfacial instabilities directly from data.

title: Randomized and Oracle-Based Feasible Directions Methods for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Constrained Optimization
summary: Minimizing nonsmooth nonconvex objectives over general convex sets using no derivatives of the objective, together with structural access to the constraint set, poses a fundamental geometric difficulty: at boundary points, the feasible direction cone may fail to be closed, preventing the construction of finite sets of search directions that capture all feasible descent directions. We develop a feasible-directions framework for problems structured as the difference between a continuously differentiable function and a convex function over a closed convex set, and access the objective without knowledge of its decomposition, through exact line searches along feasible segments. To address the geometric obstruction, we introduce $\eta$-feasible directions, which remain uniformly separated from the boundary of the feasible direction cone, enabling finite-direction search even in the presence of nonlinear constraints. We present two algorithmic realizations of this framework. The first assumes access to an $\eta$-direction oracle and extends feasible-directions methods from linear to general convex constraints. The second replaces the oracle by a noise-augmented randomization scheme that constructs spanning directions from the affine-hull inner normal and almost surely avoids nonsmooth boundary points when initialized outside that set. Under curvature bounds and Lipschitz continuity of the smooth component's gradient, we jointly control the spanning coefficients and feasible step lengths of the oracle construction. This yields finite-time approximate $d$-stationarity along every unit feasible direction admitting a prescribed positive step length. For both methods, we also establish a rate in the proximal directional minimization (PDM) measure, assuming uniformly bounded direction-set sizes. Randomized exploration ensures that, almost surely, every accumulation point is $d$-stationary.

AI.tldr: The paper develops derivative-free feasible-directions methods for minimizing nonsmooth nonconvex functions over general convex sets, using eta-feasible directions to handle the boundary geometry. It gives finite-time approximate d-stationarity and, for the randomized method, shows that almost surely every accumulation point is d-stationary.
AI.motivation: At boundary points the feasible direction cone may fail to be closed, which prevents building a finite set of search directions that captures all feasible descent directions.
AI.method: The objective is a continuously differentiable function minus a convex function over a closed convex set, accessed without knowledge of the decomposition through exact line searches along feasible segments. Two realizations are given: an eta-direction oracle that extends feasible-directions methods from linear to general convex constraints, and a noise-augmented randomization scheme that builds spanning directions from the affine-hull inner normal and almost surely avoids nonsmooth boundary points when initialized outside that set.
AI.result: Under curvature bounds and Lipschitz continuity of the smooth gradient, the oracle construction yields finite-time approximate d-stationarity along every unit feasible direction with a prescribed positive step length. Both methods have a rate in the proximal directional minimization measure, assuming uniformly bounded direction-set sizes.
AI.conclusion: The eta-feasible direction framework gives convergence guarantees for nonsmooth nonconvex constrained problems with general convex constraints, with randomization handling the boundary issue almost surely.

title: InfMasking: A Unified Variational Framework for Synergistic Multimodal Learning
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI). 16 pages; supplementary material provided as an ancillary file. Code: this https URL
summary: Multimodal models are expected to exploit synergistic information, that is, information available only when multiple modalities are observed together. In practice, however, a fusion module can fit the training objective by relying on a dominant modality or on information that modalities share, and the synergy between modalities is often left unused. We propose InfMasking, a unified multimodal learning framework based on Infinite Masking. Before fusion, InfMasking randomly masks the features of each modality; each sampled mask produces a different partial combination of cross-modal evidence and a fused representation of the corresponding modality interactions. All masked fused representations are required to remain consistent with a reference target: the unmasked fused view when training is unsupervised, and the class proxy of the task label when labels are available. Maintaining this consistency across diverse partial combinations discourages reliance on a dominant modality or on shared information alone, and drives the fusion module to learn cross-modal interaction patterns that remain meaningful under partial observations. Since the objective is an expectation over infinitely many masks, we model the masked fused representations as Gaussian and optimize closed-form variational bounds, whose population-moment gaps are controlled by the masking-induced covariance under this model. On the evaluated benchmarks, InfMasking improves predictive performance and yields higher mean PID estimates of task-label synergy in learned modality-specific representations, alongside higher InterSHAP interaction attribution in the trained predictors. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: InfMasking is a multimodal learning framework that randomly masks each modality's features before fusion and requires the fused representation under every mask to stay consistent with a reference target. Closed-form variational bounds under a Gaussian model make the expectation over infinitely many masks tractable, and the method improves predictive performance and synergy estimates on the evaluated benchmarks.
AI.motivation: A fusion module can fit the training objective by relying on a dominant modality or on information the modalities share, so the synergy between modalities often goes unused.
AI.method: Before fusion the features of each modality are randomly masked, and each mask yields a partial combination of cross-modal evidence and a fused representation. Masked fused representations must match a reference: the unmasked fused view when training is unsupervised, or the class proxy of the task label when labels are available. The masked representations are modeled as Gaussian and closed-form variational bounds are optimized, with population-moment gaps controlled by the masking-induced covariance.
AI.result: On the evaluated benchmarks, InfMasking improves predictive performance and yields higher mean PID estimates of task-label synergy in the learned modality-specific representations, along with higher InterSHAP interaction attribution in the trained predictors.
AI.conclusion: Keeping the fused representation consistent across diverse partial observations discourages reliance on a dominant or shared modality and pushes fusion toward cross-modal interaction patterns that stay meaningful under partial observation.

title: Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck for Multimodal Self-Supervised Learning
comment: 15 pages, 3-page supplementary material provided as an ancillary file. Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI)
summary: Multimodal self-supervised learning is challenged by heterogeneity, unequal informativeness, and complex information interactions across multimodal data sources such as images, text, audio, and tabular data. While contrastive methods effectively align shared semantics, they typically rely on strong multi-view redundancy assumptions, overlooking modality-specific and synergistic information, thus leading to suboptimal representations. We propose the Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck (MIIB), a principled framework grounded in Partial Information Decomposition that explicitly encodes redundant, unique, and synergistic information within multimodal interactions. MIIB employs a dual-path model architecture for modality-specific encoding and multimodal fusion, optimized using surrogate tractable entropy-based objectives that enforce minimal sufficient representations without requiring explicit mutual information estimation. By leveraging variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation, MIIB efficiently captures complex cross-modal interactions while suppressing superfluous information. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multimodal self-supervised methods. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MIIB is a Partial Information Decomposition-based framework for multimodal self-supervised learning that explicitly encodes redundant, unique and synergistic information with a dual-path architecture and tractable entropy-based objectives. The paper reports consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multimodal self-supervised methods across diverse benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Contrastive methods align shared semantics but typically rely on strong multi-view redundancy assumptions, so they overlook modality-specific and synergistic information when modalities are heterogeneous and unequally informative.
AI.method: A dual-path model separates modality-specific encoding from multimodal fusion and is optimized with surrogate entropy-based objectives that enforce minimal sufficient representations without explicit mutual information estimation. Variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation capture complex cross-modal interactions while suppressing superfluous information.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multimodal self-supervised methods. The abstract does not report specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The paper suggests that explicitly modeling redundant, unique and synergistic information can give better multimodal self-supervised representations than contrastive alignment that relies on redundancy alone.

title: Estimating Spectrum-Free Information Bounds for Generative Surrogates Beyond Conditional Collapse
summary: Conditional generative surrogates in high-energy physics, such as models that predict reconstructed jets from partons, are often evaluated on $1\text{D}$ marginal divergences among other metrics. Taken alone these metrics can reward conditional collapse. On a CMS simulation benchmark, a sampler that ignores the conditioner beats a trained Mixture Density Network (MDN) on all four target marginals under both KL and Wasserstein-1, and cannot be stably separated from a Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) model on two of the four. We instead score the models with the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS) from forecast verification, taking the exact marginal as the reference. We show how global skill depends on the evaluation spectrum, and we also report it within bins of a conditioning variable, where that dependence largely goes away. We then introduce a data-driven $k$-Nearest-Neighbor ($k$-NN) extrapolation that estimates the best CRPS the conditioning information allows. Both models agree with this estimate on all four targets, which suggests that current architectures have reached the information available in the conditioner, at least as far as these per-target scores can tell.

AI.tldr: The paper scores conditional generative surrogates for jet prediction with the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score against the exact marginal, and introduces a k-NN extrapolation that estimates the best CRPS the conditioning information allows. Both a trained Mixture Density Network and a Conditional Flow Matching model agree with this estimate on all four targets, which suggests current architectures have reached the information in the conditioner.
AI.motivation: One-dimensional marginal divergences can reward conditional collapse: on a CMS simulation benchmark, a sampler that ignores the conditioner beats a trained Mixture Density Network on all four target marginals under both KL and Wasserstein-1, and cannot be stably separated from Conditional Flow Matching on two of the four.
AI.method: The models are scored with the CRPSS, taking the exact marginal as the reference. Global skill is studied across evaluation spectra and also within bins of a conditioning variable. A data-driven k-NN extrapolation estimates the best CRPS that the conditioning information allows.
AI.result: Global skill depends on the evaluation spectrum, but within bins of the conditioning variable that dependence largely goes away. Both models agree with the k-NN estimate on all four targets.
AI.conclusion: Current architectures may have reached the information available in the conditioner, at least as far as these per-target scores can tell, so per-marginal metrics alone can mislead about conditional collapse.

title: Enhanced MRI brain tumor detection using deep learning in conjunction with explainable AI SHAP based diverse and multi feature analysis
comment: 15 pages. Published in Scientific Reports 15, 29411 (2025). Open access under CC BY 4.0
summary: Recent innovations in medical imaging have markedly improved brain tumor identification, surpassing conventional diagnostic approaches that suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure, and limited contrast. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is pivotal in precise and accurate tumor characterization owing to its high-resolution, non-invasive nature. This study investigates the synergy among multiple feature representation schemes such as local Binary Patterns (LBP), Gabor filters, Discrete Wavelet Transform, Fast Fourier Transform, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Gray-Level Run Length Matrix alongside five learning algorithms namely: k-nearest Neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier (SVC), and probabilistic neural network (PNN), and CNN. Empirical findings indicate that LBP in conjunction with SVC and CNN obtained high specificity and accuracy, rendering it a promising method for MRI-based tumor diagnosis. Further to investigate the contribution of LBP, Statistical analysis chi-square and p-value tests are used to confirm the significant impact of LBP feature space for identification of brain Tumor. In addition, The SHAP analysis was used to identify the most important features in classification. In a small dataset, CNN obtained 97.8% accuracy while SVC yielded 98.06% accuracy. In subsequent analysis, a large benchmark dataset is also utilized to evaluate the performance of learning algorithms in order to investigate the generalization power of the proposed model. CNN achieves the highest accuracy of 98.9%, followed by SVC at 96.7%. These results highlight CNN's effectiveness in automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: The study compares feature representations (LBP, Gabor, DWT, FFT, CNN features and GLRLM) with five classifiers for MRI brain tumor detection and finds that LBP with SVC or CNN gives the highest accuracy and specificity. On a large benchmark dataset CNN reaches 98.9% accuracy and SVC 96.7%.
AI.motivation: Conventional diagnostic approaches suffer from low resolution, radiation exposure and limited contrast, and MRI offers high-resolution, non-invasive tumor characterization. The paper asks which feature and classifier combinations detect brain tumors best and which features drive the classification.
AI.method: Multiple feature schemes are paired with five learning algorithms: k-nearest neighbor, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier, probabilistic neural network and CNN. Chi-square and p-value tests check the contribution of the LBP feature space, and SHAP analysis identifies the most important features.
AI.result: On a small dataset CNN reaches 97.8% accuracy and SVC 98.06%. On a large benchmark dataset CNN reaches 98.9% and SVC 96.7%.
AI.conclusion: The results point to CNN as an effective approach for automated, high-precision tumor diagnosis, with LBP features a promising basis for MRI-based tumor classification.

title: PlayGen2: Learning Real-Time Playable Worlds with Explicit 3D State
summary: Building a playable world requires more than generating plausible video: it demands responsive control, persistent spatial structure, and coherent interactions with dynamic entities. Using generated frames as the sole recurrent world representation ties these requirements to view-dependent appearance synthesis, making it difficult to maintain long-term spatial and temporal consistency in generation and interaction. We present PlayGen2, a real-time interactive world model that separates learned 3D state evolution from neural rendering. PlayGen2 maintains a persistent world memory comprising static geometry represented by a volumetric occupancy grid and identity-indexed 3D states for the player and other entities. Within a fixed-size local region, its world-state model jointly learns action-conditioned entity dynamics, geometry completion, and entity discovery, committing updates to a persistent world memory. A separate neural renderer synthesizes first-person observations from depth and semantic projections of the world state, without feeding generated images back into state prediction. Using Doom as a testbed, we demonstrate that the model successfully learns world dynamics including geometry-aware player motion and player--NPC interactions. The framework is computationally efficient, enabling the complete simulation and rendering pipeline to achieve approximately 160ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip. Beyond single-player interaction, we demonstrate zero-shot deployment on unseen Doom maps, multiplayer interaction through the composition of single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions. These capabilities demonstrate the transferability and extensibility of the learned game-world model. Code and pretrained model weights are publicly available.

AI.tldr: PlayGen2 is a real-time interactive world model that separates learned 3D state evolution from neural rendering, keeping a persistent volumetric occupancy grid and identity-indexed entity states. Using Doom as a testbed, it runs with about 160 ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip and supports zero-shot deployment on unseen maps.
AI.motivation: Using generated frames as the sole recurrent world representation ties playability to view-dependent appearance, which makes long-term spatial and temporal consistency hard to maintain in generation and interaction.
AI.method: A world-state model learns action-conditioned entity dynamics, geometry completion and entity discovery within a fixed-size local region, committing updates to a persistent world memory of static geometry (a volumetric occupancy grid) and 3D states for the player and other entities. A separate neural renderer synthesizes first-person observations from depth and semantic projections of the world state, without feeding generated images back into state prediction.
AI.result: The model learns geometry-aware player motion and player-NPC interactions in Doom. The full simulation and rendering pipeline reaches about 160 ms backend latency on a MacBook Pro with an M4 Pro chip. The paper also shows zero-shot deployment on unseen Doom maps, multiplayer interaction by composing single-player models, and programmable gameplay through rule-based state interventions.
AI.conclusion: Separating explicit 3D state from rendering gives a transferable and extensible route to learned game worlds, and the code and pretrained weights are public.

title: Which Signals of Code Correctness Survive Distribution Shift? Hidden-State and Causal Predictors of Program and Verdict Correctness
summary: Large language models increasingly judge code, yet without external feedback such judgments are unreliable, and verifying them by executing tests or by extended reasoning is costly. Instead, execution-free correctness predictors use signals from the model's output probabilities, sampled solutions, or hidden states to identify judgments that warrant further verification. However, these predictors may degrade under distribution shifts when generalizing across projects and languages. We compare six execution-free predictors from four families on Qwen3-Coder-30B and gpt-oss-20b under benchmark shift between LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench and language shift across Python, C++ and Java. We evaluate two targets: whether the model's own verdict on a program can be trusted, and whether the program itself is correct. Besides established approaches, we adapt two novel causal localization methods to code, which have been shown to be more robust out-of-distribution on natural language tasks. For verdict correctness, causal localization improves robustness to language shift. For Qwen3-Coder a probe on the causally localized subspace stays 0.09 AUROC ahead of output confidence under language shift (0.11 in distribution), significantly outperforming the best non-causal predictor by 0.04 AUROC on average. This advantage, however, does not generalize consistently to gpt-oss or to benchmark shift. For program correctness, predictors transfer more successfully between benchmarks, largely by identifying problems on which the model tends to fail. However, their ability to rank candidates within the same problem is limited.

AI.tldr: The paper compares six execution-free correctness predictors on Qwen3-Coder-30B and gpt-oss-20b under benchmark and language shifts. Causal localization helps verdict correctness under language shift for Qwen3-Coder but not consistently elsewhere, while program-correctness predictors transfer better across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Judging code with LLMs is unreliable without external feedback, and verifying judgments by executing tests or by extended reasoning is costly, so execution-free predictors are needed. Their reliability under distribution shift across projects and languages is uncertain.
AI.method: Six execution-free predictors from four families are compared under a benchmark shift between LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench and a language shift across Python, C++ and Java. Two causal localization methods, previously shown to be more robust out-of-distribution on natural language tasks, are adapted to code. Two targets are evaluated: whether the model's own verdict can be trusted, and whether the program is correct.
AI.result: For Qwen3-Coder, a probe on the causally localized subspace stays 0.09 AUROC ahead of output confidence under language shift (0.11 in distribution) and beats the best non-causal predictor by 0.04 AUROC on average. This advantage does not generalize consistently to gpt-oss or to benchmark shift. For program correctness, predictors transfer more successfully between benchmarks, largely by identifying problems the model tends to fail, but they rank candidates within the same problem poorly.
AI.conclusion: The robustness of execution-free predictors depends on the type of shift and the model, so causal localization is not a uniformly reliable fix, and program-level predictors mostly flag problems the model tends to fail rather than ranking candidates well.

title: Joint Modeling of Conditional Mean and Variability in Multilevel Functional Data: Application to Postprandial Glucose Trajectories in the AEGIS Study
summary: Functional data analysis provides a framework for studying time-varying associations between covariates and high-frequency biological signals.
