In digital health, participants often contribute repeated functional trajectories, yet existing multilevel regression methods largely focus on the conditional mean, overlooking variability and its role in biological heterogeneity. We propose a heteroskedastic functional mixed-effects regression framework that jointly models the conditional mean and variance of repeated trajectories, with participant-specific random effects in both components. We also develop a participant-level bootstrap to quantify uncertainty in estimated functional parameters. We apply the method to postprandial glucose trajectories from the AEGIS study. Premeal glucose, carbohydrate intake, and meal type show distinct time-dependent associations with glucose variability, whereas HbA1c is more strongly associated with the conditional mean than with variability. Substantial between-participant differences in residual variability remain even after accounting for observed covariates. These findings show that modeling conditional variability alongside the mean provides insights into glucose regulation and individual heterogeneity that mean-focused analyses may miss. More broadly, the proposed framework enables joint characterization of average responses, variability, and participant-specific heterogeneity in repeated biological signals.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a heteroskedastic functional mixed-effects regression that jointly models the conditional mean and variance of repeated glucose trajectories, with participant-specific random effects in both components. Applied to postprandial glucose data from the AEGIS study, it finds that covariates show time-dependent associations with glucose variability, while HbA1c is more strongly tied to the mean.
AI.motivation: Existing multilevel functional regression methods focus on the conditional mean and overlook variability and its role in biological heterogeneity.
AI.method: A heteroskedastic functional mixed-effects framework with participant-specific random effects in both the mean and the variance components, together with a participant-level bootstrap to quantify uncertainty in the estimated functional parameters.
AI.result: Premeal glucose, carbohydrate intake and meal type show distinct time-dependent associations with glucose variability. HbA1c is more strongly associated with the conditional mean than with variability. Substantial between-participant differences in residual variability remain after accounting for the observed covariates.
AI.conclusion: Modeling conditional variability alongside the mean reveals aspects of glucose regulation and individual heterogeneity that mean-focused analyses may miss.

title: KeHoSu: Keyed Homoglyph Substitution for Authenticated Text Provenance over Copy-Paste Channels
summary: Nowadays, large language models produce text at scale, and much of it is redistributed across platforms. A moderator who finds a suspicious comment, post or article may want to know which platform generated it and for which account. In this paper we study attribution over the channel through which such text actually travels, copy-paste, which discards document metadata but keeps Unicode code points. We present KeHoSu, which turns the confusable characters of homoglyph attacks into a keyed attribution channel: the variant chosen for each carrier letter encodes one bit of an identifier made of a platform field, a user field and a truncated authentication tag. Moreover, given that reshared text is often quoted in fragments, and the placement therefore keeps no positional state, we show that KeHoSu is invariant to sentence reordering up to a constant boundary layer and depends on a partial quotation only through the retained length. We characterize the code-point channel by its capacity, removability and detectability, and provide an achievable region that relates the three. We evaluate KeHoSu over a wide range of use cases and show that the mark survived copy-paste across 18 common platforms, attributing the majority of all excerpts to the correct account at 178 letters (about two sentences) on LLM-generated stories and 167 letters (about one sentence) on standard English prose.

AI.tldr: KeHoSu embeds a keyed attribution identifier in text by choosing homoglyph variants for carrier letters, so the mark survives copy-paste, which discards document metadata. It survived copy-paste across 18 common platforms and attributes most excerpts to the correct account at 178 letters on LLM-generated stories and 167 letters on standard English prose.
AI.motivation: A moderator who finds suspicious text may want to know which platform and account generated it, but copy-paste discards document metadata while keeping Unicode code points, so attribution has to live in the text itself.
AI.method: Confusable characters from homoglyph attacks become a keyed attribution channel: the variant chosen for each carrier letter encodes one bit of an identifier made of a platform field, a user field and a truncated authentication tag. The scheme is invariant to sentence reordering up to a constant boundary layer and depends on a partial quotation only through its retained length. The code-point channel is characterized by capacity, removability and detectability, with an achievable region relating the three.
AI.result: The mark survived copy-paste across 18 common platforms and attributed the majority of all excerpts to the correct account at 178 letters (about two sentences) on LLM-generated stories and 167 letters (about one sentence) on standard English prose.
AI.conclusion: Homoglyph-based marking at the code-point level gives a keyed, reordering-tolerant attribution channel for redistributed text, needing roughly one to two sentences of text in the evaluated settings.

title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. The resulting representation reduces memory footprint by storing a single shared dictionary per layer group, along with sparse layer-specific coefficients. On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. DictLLM compresses the original LLaMA-7B model by 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, achieving a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.

AI.tldr: DictLLM compresses LLMs after training by decomposing the weight matrices of grouped layers into a shared dictionary and sparse layer-specific coefficients, followed by aggressive quantization. It compresses LLaMA-7B 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.
AI.motivation: Deploying LLMs on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints, and post-training low-rank compression methods leave room to improve the trade-off between model size and performance.
AI.method: A four-step post-training optimization. SVD of input-scaled weight matrices gives shared dictionaries that amortize rank across grouped layers. Layer-specific coefficients are sparsified to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian, the dictionaries are refined given the sparse coefficients, and finally both components are quantized using factor-specific Hessian information (input covariance for the dictionaries, the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients).
AI.result: On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. On LLaMA-7B it gives 5.1x compression with a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity.
AI.conclusion: Shared dictionaries with sparse coefficients and factor-specific quantization offer a training-free route to much smaller LLMs at a modest perplexity cost.

title: Identifying Neural Dynamics Using Nonlinear Interventional State Space Models
summary: State-space models (SSMs) recover low-dimensional latent dynamics from high-dimensional observations, but latents are generally not identifiable from observational data alone. Interventional state-space models (iSSMs) use perturbations to break observational symmetries and identify parameters up to permutation, scaling, and shift. However, prior work restricts identifiability to linear latent dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions, excluding many behaviors characteristic of neural circuits. We extend iSSMs to a substantially broader model class: we prove that (i) affine identifiability holds under general injective emission functions and Gaussian latent transitions, and (ii) with interventions, identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift is preserved under general nonlinear latent dynamics. We validate our theory on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics, and then demonstrate two applications: adjudicating between competing models of decision-making; and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human neural recordings, with proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in the latter. Finally, simulations yield practical guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.

AI.tldr: The paper extends interventional state-space models to nonlinear latent dynamics and general injective emissions, proving identifiability up to permutation, scaling and shift under interventions. It validates the theory on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics and applies it to comparing decision-making models and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human recordings.
AI.motivation: Latent states of state-space models are generally not identifiable from observational data alone, and prior interventional identifiability results were restricted to linear latent dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions, which exclude many behaviors characteristic of neural circuits.
AI.method: The model class is extended in two steps. Under general injective emission functions and Gaussian latent transitions, affine identifiability is proved. With interventions, identifiability up to permutation, scaling and shift is shown to hold under general nonlinear latent dynamics.
AI.result: The theory is validated on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics. Applications include adjudicating between competing decision-making models and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human recordings, with proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in the human data. Simulations give practical guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.
AI.conclusion: The identifiability guarantees cover a much broader class of neural dynamics, and the work offers practical guidance for stimulation design, though the held-out-site generalization is reported only as proof of concept.

title: Detecting Silent Faults at the Environment-Trainer Boundary in Reinforcement Learning
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Everything Beneath the Policy. Code, specification, and every experiment's protocol, logs and findings: this https URL
summary: Robot reinforcement learning increasingly runs environments outside the trainer: in another process, on another machine, in another language. Many faults at this boundary raise no error. We make the boundary a wire protocol and ask what notices a fault in it. On Pendulum, HalfCheetah, Hopper and a 7-joint arm (Pusher), we injected up to 23 faults into what crosses the wire and 2 into the trainer's log, from one value to every value. Unless every value was wrong, a learning-curve threshold caught at most one run in ten, and a comparison with ten fault-free seeds at most 21%. A clean evaluation of all 1,060 final policies agreed with the curves: of the 728 boundary-fault runs both curve checks passed, 723 scored no more than three standard deviations below fault-free seeds, though nearly all ended on other weights and, for reward faults, logged other returns. Checks of the run itself, not of its outcome, saw every fault. A step ledger kept on both sides and compared step by step caught and located every fault that crossed, on Pendulum, Hopper and Pusher on one machine and on Pendulum across two, with no fault-free run and, on Pendulum, a median 3% more training time. An episode record kept at the environment caught the faults in the trainer's log. We list such faults found in practice, in Gymnasium 1.3 and our own code and, reported by others, in five multi-agent libraries, and recommend a step ledger and episode counts kept at the environment.

AI.tldr: The paper treats the environment-trainer boundary in robot reinforcement learning as a wire protocol and tests which checks notice injected faults. Learning-curve and fault-free-seed comparisons catch very few faults, while a step ledger kept on both sides catches and locates every fault that crosses the wire.
AI.motivation: Many faults at the boundary between a remote environment and the trainer raise no error, and it was unclear what would notice them.
AI.method: Up to 23 faults were injected into what crosses the wire and 2 into the trainer's log, on Pendulum, HalfCheetah, Hopper and a 7-joint arm (Pusher); the checks were a learning-curve threshold, comparison with ten fault-free seeds, a clean evaluation of 1,060 final policies, a step ledger compared step by step on both sides, and an episode record kept at the environment.
AI.result: Unless every value was wrong, a learning-curve threshold caught at most one run in ten and the seed comparison at most 21%; of 728 boundary-fault runs, both curve checks passed in all of them and 723 scored no more than three standard deviations below fault-free seeds in the clean evaluation. The step ledger caught and located every crossing fault on Pendulum, Hopper and Pusher on one machine and on Pendulum across two machines, with a median 3% more training time on Pendulum. The episode record caught the faults in the trainer's log.
AI.conclusion: Checks of the run itself, rather than of its outcome, caught every fault, so the authors recommend a step ledger and episode counts kept at the environment, and they list faults found in Gymnasium 1.3, in their own code and, as reported by others, in five multi-agent libraries.

title: AI-Native Task-Oriented Semantic Communications over a Relay: Benefits and Vulnerabilities
summary: Semantic communication (SemCom) using a relay node is considered, where the relay assists in conveying task-relevant information from a source to a destination, with meaning defined by classification labels. A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation, and destination decoders is developed to optimize both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality for image data. Relay-assisted schemes are shown to outperform direct transmission, with gains that become more pronounced in low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes across different relaying strategies. Alongside these performance benefits, however, a key security vulnerability introduced by the relay is identified, and a Byzantine attack is formulated in which the relay injects structured, learned perturbations into its transmitted signal. The attack operates on intermediate communication representations subject to channel effects, with perturbations generated through a learned mapping applied at test time. It is shown to significantly degrade semantic inference accuracy at the destination. These results reveal a clear trade-off between SemCom gains and security risks in relay-assisted systems, motivating the need for secure relay designs that account for insider threats.

AI.tldr: Relay-assisted semantic communication, where meaning is defined by classification labels, outperforms direct transmission, especially at low SNR. The same relay can mount a Byzantine attack that injects learned perturbations and significantly degrades semantic inference accuracy at the destination.
AI.motivation: A relay can help convey task-relevant information in semantic communication, but the security vulnerability it introduces as an insider threat had not been characterized.
AI.method: A joint end-to-end design of the source encoder, relay transformation and destination decoders for image data, optimizing both semantic inference accuracy and perceptual reconstruction quality; the Byzantine attack has the relay inject structured learned perturbations, generated by a learned mapping at test time, into intermediate representations subject to channel effects.
AI.result: Relay-assisted schemes outperform direct transmission across different relaying strategies, with gains larger in low SNR regimes; the attack is shown to significantly degrade semantic inference accuracy at the destination.
AI.conclusion: There is a clear trade-off between semantic communication gains and security risks in relay-assisted systems, which motivates secure relay designs that account for insider threats.

title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
comment: 30 pages, 6 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: World-action models adapt pretrained video generators, and vision-language-action models build on pretrained vision-language backbones; both tie policy architecture and inference cost to large transformers designed for generation rather than control. It remains unclear how much these generation-oriented choices affect control. In this work, we introduce Latent Action JEPA (La-JEPA), a compact world-action model whose policy transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. Following Fast-WAM, La-JEPA learns to predict future features jointly with actions during training and generates only actions at inference. Among policies without embodied pretraining, La-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art performance in clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes and on LIBERO-Plus with correct instructions, while using far fewer parameters than the strongest competing policies. It runs substantially faster than Fast-WAM at comparable performance and outperforms the closest JEPA-based methods, LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM, on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 without their pretrained policy backbones. On four real-robot tasks, its average success is comparable to pi0.5 and above non-embodied-pretrained baselines. Through a design study of the choices behind La-JEPA, we show that JEPA features outperform video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and that training-time future prediction choices significantly impact the policy even when future prediction is skipped at inference. We correct the LIBERO-Plus instructions, as the officially released evaluator corrupts them for most variants, and re-evaluate several strong open baselines. Without a generative pretrained policy backbone, La-JEPA is better and faster than far larger policies, suggesting that robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.

AI.tldr: La-JEPA is a compact robot world-action policy whose transformer is trained from scratch in the feature space of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder. Among policies without embodied pretraining it reaches state-of-the-art results with far fewer parameters, and it runs substantially faster than Fast-WAM at comparable performance.
AI.motivation: World-action and vision-language-action policies inherit large transformers built for generation, and it was unclear how much these generation-oriented choices affect control.
AI.method: Following Fast-WAM, the policy learns to predict future features jointly with actions during training and generates only actions at inference; a design study compares JEPA features with video VAE latents and examines future-prediction choices.
AI.result: Among policies without embodied pretraining it achieves state-of-the-art on clean and randomized RoboTwin 2.0 and on LIBERO-Plus with correct instructions, and it outperforms LeapBot-WA and JEPA-WAM on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0 without their pretrained backbones. Its average success on four real-robot tasks is comparable to pi0.5 and above non-embodied-pretrained baselines. JEPA features beat video VAE latents, most clearly out of distribution, and training-time future prediction choices significantly affect the policy even when prediction is skipped at inference. The authors corrected the LIBERO-Plus instructions, which the official evaluator corrupts for most variants.
AI.conclusion: Without a generative pretrained backbone La-JEPA is better and faster than far larger policies, suggesting robot foundation models may benefit from architectures designed for control rather than inherited from generation.

title: Improving Context-Shift Robustness of Convolutional Networks via Context-Regularized Cross-Entropy
summary: Image classification models often encounter objects in diverse and unpredictable contexts at test time, which may differ substantially from those seen during training. This phenomenon, termed context shift, exposes a key fragility in neural networks: when models rely on non-causal contextual cues for prediction, shifts in context can lead to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we propose a novel training framework to improve the robustness of convolutional neural networks under context shift. Our approach leverages spatial feature attribution to guide models toward making predictions that rely less on contextual regions and more on object-relevant features. As a first step, recognizing a theoretical limitation of existing feature attribution methods we introduce a new variant, ContrastiveCAMs, which produces more faithful attribution maps of model predictions. Building on ContrastiveCAMs, we further propose Context-Regularized Cross-Entropy (CR-CE), a modification of the standard cross-entropy loss that regularizes the model's attention by suppressing the influence of contextual regions, thereby improving robustness to context shift. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on several medium-to-large scale datasets (Waterbirds, Spawrious, ImageNet/ImageNet-BG, Hard-ImageNet), and report consistent improvements in context-shift robustness.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Context-Regularized Cross-Entropy (CR-CE), a modified cross-entropy loss that suppresses the influence of contextual regions on attention, together with a new attribution variant, ContrastiveCAMs. The authors report consistent improvements in robustness to context shift on several medium-to-large datasets.
AI.motivation: Convolutional networks that rely on non-causal contextual cues degrade when objects appear in unseen contexts at test time, and existing feature attribution methods have a theoretical limitation for guiding them away from context.
AI.method: ContrastiveCAMs is introduced as a variant that produces more faithful attribution maps; building on it, CR-CE regularizes the model's attention by suppressing contextual regions within the standard cross-entropy objective.
AI.result: Evaluated on Waterbirds, Spawrious, ImageNet/ImageNet-BG and Hard-ImageNet, with consistent improvements in context-shift robustness; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Steering attention toward object-relevant features during training improves the context-shift robustness of convolutional neural networks.

title: Patch Attention Wisely: Understanding Patch Length in Attention-Based Forecasting
summary: Attention-based time series forecasters commonly group consecutive observations into patches. Patch length is known to have a substantial impact on forecasting performance, yet its selection remains largely empirical. We develop a theoretical framework that explains why patch length matters for forecasting accuracy and provides a principled basis for its selection. For linear state-space models, we derive an exact factorization of the forecasting coefficient matrix that separates forecast dynamics from filtering dynamics. We show that dominance of a single forecast component at long horizons does not generally imply a rank-one representation. This explains why longer horizons alone need not reduce representational complexity. We combine the factorization with estimation bounds to develop a patch-selection criterion that balances representation and estimation errors under temporal dependence. Our analysis establishes conditions under which balanced patching is justified and clarifies how predictive structure, head count, training sample size, and long-run dependence enter the selection criterion.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework explaining why patch length matters for attention-based forecasting and derives a patch-selection criterion that balances representation and estimation errors. The analysis is exact for linear state-space models and holds under temporal dependence.
AI.motivation: Patch length strongly affects the accuracy of attention-based time series forecasters, yet its selection remains largely empirical.
AI.method: For linear state-space models the forecasting coefficient matrix is factored exactly, separating forecast dynamics from filtering dynamics; combined with estimation bounds, this gives a patch-selection criterion that accounts for temporal dependence.
AI.result: A single dominant forecast component at long horizons does not generally imply a rank-one representation, so longer horizons alone need not reduce representational complexity. The criterion shows how predictive structure, head count, training sample size and long-run dependence enter patch selection.
AI.conclusion: The analysis establishes conditions under which balanced patching is justified, giving a principled basis for choosing patch length in place of purely empirical tuning.

title: Regret Bounds for Profit Maximization in Bilateral Trade: Learning the Best Posted-Price Mechanism
summary: Bilateral trade models the task of intermediating between two strategic agents, a seller and a buyer, willing to trade a good for which they hold private valuations. We study this problem from the perspective of a profit-maximizing broker in a regret minimization framework. At each time step, a new seller and buyer arrive and the broker proposes a trading price to each agent. The trade happens if both agents accept, and the profit of the broker is the difference between the price received from the buyer and the one paid to the seller. At the end of each interaction, the learner only observes whether the trade occurred, and its goal is to achieve sublinear regret relative to the best fixed pair of prices in hindsight. We start by investigating the adversarial version of the problem, where buyer and seller valuations are generated by an adversary. In this setting, we construct a polynomial-time learning algorithm with a $\tilde O(T^{\frac 23})$ regret rate, which is nearly tight even if the valuations are drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions, thus matching the rate for one-sided pricing. Our adversarial algorithm combines a localized estimation procedure with an information-based minimax construction. We then consider valuations drawn i.i.d. from independent distributions satisfying the monotone-hazard-rate (MHR) property and provide a learning algorithm with nearly tight $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret. The algorithm combines localized estimation with a stochastic convex bandit routine applied to the negative logarithm of expected profit. Finally, we complement this result by showing a separation between MHR and regular distributions, proving that the minimax regret rate in the latter setting is $\tilde \Theta(T^{\frac 35})$. This last result contrasts with the $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound that can be obtained for one-sided pricing with regular distributions.

AI.tldr: The paper gives regret bounds for a profit-maximizing broker who learns the best fixed pair of posted prices from trade-or-not feedback in bilateral trade. Adversarial valuations give O~(T^{2/3}) regret, i.i.d. MHR valuations give O~(sqrt T), and regular distributions have minimax regret Theta~(T^{3/5}).
AI.motivation: The broker sees only whether each trade occurred, not the valuations, and the best achievable regret rates for this two-sided pricing problem under different valuation models were not settled.
AI.method: In the adversarial setting, a polynomial-time algorithm combines a localized estimation procedure with an information-based minimax construction; for i.i.d. MHR valuations, localized estimation is combined with a stochastic convex bandit routine applied to the negative logarithm of expected profit; a separation result compares MHR and regular distributions.
AI.result: Adversarial regret of O~(T^{2/3}), nearly tight even for i.i.d. independent valuations and matching the rate for one-sided pricing; regret of O~(sqrt T) under MHR, nearly tight; minimax regret Theta~(T^{3/5}) for regular distributions, in contrast with the O~(sqrt T) attainable for one-sided pricing with regular distributions.
AI.conclusion: The results separate MHR from regular distributions for two-sided posted-price learning, with regular distributions requiring substantially more regret.

title: Series-wise Cross-validation for Global Time Series Forecasting
summary: We consider the problem of cross-validation (CV) in time series forecasting, with a focus on global forecasting models based on deep learning. The prevailing CV strategy in forecasting is to partition data across time with the last part of each series used for testing. With global models trained on collections of time series, however, a fundamentally different approach becomes possible: partitioning across series and time. We formalize series-wise CV for global forecasting models and benchmark several instantiations, including K-fold CV, bootstrapping, and Monte Carlo CV, on 11 datasets with 10 neural network architectures. We evaluate CV procedures along five dimensions: performance estimation, overoptimism rate, model selection accuracy, regret, and downstream forecasting performance. We withhold a random fraction of series from training so that they appear only in the test set. This protocol simulates the emergence of new series not seen during training, a common scenario in global forecasting. Under this protocol, our results reveal a nuanced trade-off: series-wise CV yields better downstream forecasting accuracy by guiding model selection toward configurations that generalize across both time and series, while time-wise CV retains a slight advantage for estimating out-of-sample error.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes series-wise cross-validation for global deep forecasting models, partitioning data across both series and time, and benchmarks it against time-wise procedures. Series-wise CV gives better downstream forecasting accuracy, while time-wise CV retains a slight advantage for estimating out-of-sample error.
AI.motivation: The prevailing forecasting CV holds out the last part of each series, but global models trained on collections of series also allow partitioning across series, which can simulate new series unseen in training.
AI.method: K-fold CV, bootstrapping and Monte Carlo CV, both across series and across time, are benchmarked on 11 datasets with 10 neural network architectures; a random fraction of series is withheld from training so it appears only in the test set; procedures are evaluated on performance estimation, overoptimism rate, model selection accuracy, regret and downstream forecasting performance.
AI.result: Series-wise CV selects configurations that generalize across both time and series and yields better downstream forecasting accuracy, while time-wise CV retains a slight advantage for estimating out-of-sample error.
AI.conclusion: The choice of CV scheme involves a nuanced trade-off: series-wise CV is better for guiding model selection, and time-wise CV for error estimation.

title: DART: Domain-Agnostic Residual Transfer for Generalist Anomaly Detection
summary: Generalist Anomaly Detection (GAD) aims to detect anomalies in unseen domains using only a few reference samples. Recent normal-abnormal guided methods improve this setting by exploiting abnormal references, but their residuals often mix transferable anomaly cues with domain-specific appearance factors such as texture, geometry, and acquisition conditions. This residual domain entanglement limits cross-domain transfer and may produce spurious activations on novel domains. We propose DART, a plug-in framework for normal-abnormal guided GAD that learns to separate residuals into anomaly-relevant and domain-specific components. DART combines a Residual Disentanglement Module, which preserves anomaly-discriminative information while suppressing domain information, with Cross-Domain Meta-Training, which forms episodes across source domains to make the separation effective. The method is architecture-agnostic and can be inserted between residual computation and the detection head of existing GAD pipelines. Experiments on MVTec AD, VisA, and BraTS show consistent improvements over multiple base methods, with the largest gains under stronger domain shifts. this https URL

AI.tldr: DART is a plug-in framework for normal-abnormal guided generalist anomaly detection that separates residuals into anomaly-relevant and domain-specific components. It gives consistent gains over multiple base methods on MVTec AD, VisA and BraTS, with the largest gains under stronger domain shifts.
AI.motivation: Residuals in existing normal-abnormal guided methods mix transferable anomaly cues with domain-specific appearance factors such as texture, geometry and acquisition conditions, which limits cross-domain transfer and causes spurious activations on novel domains.
AI.method: A Residual Disentanglement Module preserves anomaly-discriminative information while suppressing domain information, and Cross-Domain Meta-Training forms episodes across source domains to make the separation effective; the method is architecture-agnostic and sits between residual computation and the detection head.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over multiple base methods on MVTec AD, VisA and BraTS, with the largest gains under stronger domain shifts.
AI.conclusion: Separating anomaly-relevant from domain-specific residual components improves cross-domain transfer in generalist anomaly detection.

title: Transformer-Based Trajectory Prescription for sEMG-Optimizing Robot-Mediated Rehabilitation
comment: Accepted for presentation and publication in the 2026 Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL). PMLR, 2026
summary: Robot-mediated rehabilitation has the potential to deliver high-intensity, individualized therapy, but existing systems (which have not consistently improved outcomes) typically prescribe kinematic trajectories rather than explicitly targeting the neuromotor activations thought to support recovery. To address this gap, and ultimately enable activation-optimizing rehabilitation robot behavior, we present a personalizable transformer-based model mapping individuals' muscle activations (as measured via surface electromyography) to prescribed contact force trajectories when interacting with an end-effector rehabilitation robot. The model uses a transformer encoder-decoder leveraging rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to generate a latent representation of trajectory-relevant and user-specific neuromotor factors, and augments trajectory prediction with flow matching to produce a distribution over plausible prescriptions biased toward the training distribution. Using data from 16 healthy participants completing 15 isometric trajectory tracking tasks, we evaluate generalization across held-out tasks and users, as well as the feasibility of user-specific fine-tuning within a therapy-session timescale. The model achieves mean trajectory prediction errors of <8% on held out tasks and users, with effectively instantaneous deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of trajectory distributions. An initial test using the model during live rehabilitation tasks demonstrates that, on average, participants reach the target neuromotor activations with just 15% error accumulated throughout the task. These results provide a proof of concept for data-driven, activation-targeted trajectory prescription in robot-mediated rehabilitation and establish a foundation for future validation in clinical populations. Data and code have been open-sourced as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK.

AI.tldr: A transformer encoder-decoder with rotary positional embeddings and flow matching maps surface EMG muscle activations to contact force trajectories for an end-effector rehabilitation robot. It predicts held-out trajectories with under 8% mean error and, in a live test, brought participants to their target activations with 15% accumulated error on average.
AI.motivation: Existing robot-mediated rehabilitation systems prescribe kinematic trajectories rather than explicitly targeting the neuromotor activations thought to support recovery, and they have not consistently improved outcomes.
AI.method: The model encodes trajectory-relevant and user-specific neuromotor factors in a latent representation and uses flow matching to produce a distribution over plausible prescriptions biased toward the training distribution; user-specific fine-tuning was tested within a therapy-session timescale.
AI.result: With data from 16 healthy participants over 15 isometric trajectory tracking tasks, mean trajectory prediction errors were below 8% on held-out tasks and users, with near-instant deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of distributions; in an initial test during live rehabilitation tasks participants reached target activations with 15% error accumulated throughout the task on average.
AI.conclusion: The results are a proof of concept for data-driven, activation-targeted trajectory prescription and a foundation for validation in clinical populations; data and code are open-sourced as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK.

title: RM-VLM: From Natural-Language Task Descriptions to Vision-Grounded Reward Machines
summary: Reward machines (RMs) have been proposed as a reward formulation in reinforcement learning (RL) to capture non-Markovian tasks where credit assignment depends on history. By representing reward functions as automata, RMs expose the task's temporal structure and allow such rewards to be handled within a Markovian framework. However, they assume a labelling function, a proposition-grounding oracle for observations, which must be manually engineered for each environment, limiting their wider applicability. In this work, we address this limitation by proposing RM-VLM, a novel approach in which a large language model (LLM) generates an RM from a natural-language task description, and a vision-language model (VLM) acts as the labelling function, grounding the RM's propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning. A VLM-based value function estimator is used to assess the agent's progress towards each RM transition and derive a dense reward signal. We evaluate RM-VLM on three domains covering non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection. Our experimental results show that RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.

AI.tldr: RM-VLM uses a large language model to generate a reward machine from a natural-language task description and a vision-language model as the labelling function over image observations. A VLM-based value estimator supplies a dense reward, and the method achieves higher task success than existing VLM-based reward methods in all tested domains.
AI.motivation: Reward machines need a manually engineered labelling function for each environment, which limits their wider applicability.
AI.method: An LLM generates the reward machine from the task description, a VLM grounds its propositions over image-based observations during RM-guided policy learning, and a VLM-based value function estimator assesses progress toward each RM transition to derive a dense reward signal.
AI.result: Evaluated on three domains, non-Markovian grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation and 3D object collection, RM-VLM consistently achieves higher task success rates than existing VLM-based reward methods across all tested domains.
AI.conclusion: Generating both the reward machine and its labelling function from language and vision removes the manual engineering that limited reward machines, and the method is shown to work across the three domains.

title: USB Gym: A Gymnasium Testbed for Closed-Loop Ultrasound View Matching
comment: 75 pages; supplementary material (62 pages) as an ancillary file. Submitted to Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine. Code: this https URL
summary: Background and Objective: Our main goal is ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. Published methods for each part of a guide are evaluated in separate simulators. We asked whether these methods, combined into one guide, are good enough. Methods: We built USB Gym, a testbed whose standard engine simulates ultrasound from public patient CT, with a network drawing organ textures from CT labels. Its guide has three replaceable parts (slots), an organ segmenter, a controller and a reward, which received 20 published methods, each run on the same 60 episodes of six held-out patients. In each slot, a published method replaced ours only if detectably better on these patients. The better of this combination and our original guide on 20 new CTs is the benchmark baseline. A pose oracle, reading the exact probe pose available only in simulation, set the reference. The results below are exploratory. Results: On these CTs, the probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view; the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm. Of the results known when the combination was fixed, only an image-similarity reward (SSIM) was slightly but detectably better, so the combination was our guide with that reward. This combination was the benchmark baseline, ending at 13.7 mm (16% of the oracle's progress). Conclusions: Combining untuned published methods with ours did not guide the probe near the target view; the task remains under-explored. The testbed accepts new methods; no guide was tested on hardware.

AI.tldr: USB Gym is a testbed for closed-loop ultrasound view matching in which 20 published methods were tried in each of three replaceable slots of a guide. The combined guide, using an SSIM reward, ended on average 13.7 mm from the target view, about 16% of the pose oracle's progress.
AI.motivation: Published methods for each part of ultrasound guidance were evaluated in separate simulators, so the authors asked whether they are good enough when combined into one guide.
AI.method: The simulator draws ultrasound from public patient CT with a network that generates organ textures from CT labels; each slot (organ segmenter, controller, reward) was filled by a published method only if detectably better on 60 episodes of six held-out patients, and the resulting baseline was tested on 20 new CTs against a pose oracle that reads the exact probe pose.
AI.result: The probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view and the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm; the baseline ended at 13.7 mm, 16% of the oracle's progress. Among results known when the combination was fixed, only an SSIM reward was slightly but detectably better.
AI.conclusion: Combining untuned published methods with the authors' own did not guide the probe near the target view, so the task remains under-explored; the testbed accepts new methods, and no guide has been tested on hardware. The results are labelled exploratory.

title: Unifying Central Flow, Rod Flow, and the Edge Coupling
summary: At the edge of stability, the iterates of gradient descent oscillate along the sharp directions of the Hessian. This poses a significant challenge for continuous-time models as the usual continuous-time approximation -- the gradient flow -- admits no oscillations. Several continuous-time models have been proposed to capture the behavior at the edge of stability, among them central flow and rod flow. Although both models can be interpreted as performing a coarse-graining in time, the connection between them remains poorly understood. Here we show that both flows can be derived from a third object, the edge coupling: a functional on consecutive iterates whose critical points are the fixed points and period-two orbits of gradient descent. It is revealed that the two flows correspond to coarse-grainings at different time scales. Rod flow coarse-grains over only the fastest time scale, while central flow coarse-grains over both the fast and intermediate time scales. Furthermore, using the edge coupling, we derive rod flows and central flows for momentum methods such as heavy ball and Adam. We verify the derived flows experimentally on representative neural network architectures, where they track the discrete iterates throughout all phases of training -- including the transition from the stable regime to the edge of stability.

AI.tldr: Central flow and rod flow, two continuous-time models of gradient descent at the edge of stability, are both derived from a single object, the edge coupling. The two flows coarse-grain over different time scales, and analogous flows are derived for heavy ball and Adam.
AI.motivation: Central flow and rod flow both model edge-of-stability oscillations by coarse-graining in time, but the connection between them was poorly understood.
AI.method: The edge coupling is a functional on consecutive iterates whose critical points are the fixed points and period-two orbits of gradient descent; both flows are derived from it, and the same object is used to derive flows for momentum methods such as heavy ball and Adam.
AI.result: Rod flow coarse-grains only the fastest time scale, while central flow coarse-grains both the fast and intermediate time scales; the derived flows track the discrete iterates through all training phases on representative neural networks, including the transition from the stable regime to the edge of stability.
AI.conclusion: The two flows are unified as coarse-grainings of one object at different time scales, and the same approach extends to momentum methods.

title: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
summary: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor--critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73\% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03\% vs. 0.63\%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.

AI.tldr: SHORE is an on-policy actor-critic for online 3D bin packing that combines a learned stability probability with an on-policy return conditioned on stability. In Isaac Gym it reaches 73% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, against about 1M for the same learner without stability modeling, and it reaches 0.734 utilization on the 60-box set against 0.588 for GOPT.
AI.motivation: Existing bin packing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, which limit how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation and placement.
AI.method: A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, and a discrete on-policy actor-critic uses the stability predictions in both its action values and its policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model; no extra search or simulation is needed at deployment.
AI.result: On the expanded 60-box set SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization against 0.588 for GOPT, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03% against 0.63%). Ablations suggest simulated alternatives give useful early supervision while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. The method is also demonstrated on a real robot.
AI.conclusion: SHORE learns faster and reaches higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set, trading more risk for greater packed volume.

title: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human-Humanoid Interaction
comment: CoRL 2026, Project page: this https URL
summary: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: Social Humanoid is a hierarchical system that generates socially responsive whole-body motion for a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. It is trained on a new 260-hour Human-Humanoid Interaction benchmark produced by a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents and cannot coordinate physically with human partners who anticipate and adjust to one another.
AI.method: A high-level policy models human and humanoid motion as sequences over a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive motion and anticipating the partner when occluded; a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion; the two-phase retargeting retargets one partner to the robot while morphing the other to preserve contact dynamics, reachability and relative body scale, across five motion-capture datasets.
AI.result: The system produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and in the real world. The abstract reports no quantitative comparison.
AI.conclusion: Socially responsive whole-body humanoid motion is achieved by this hierarchical design together with the retargeting pipeline used to build the new benchmark.

title: Network Effect Decomposition for Causal Effect Estimation under Network Interference
summary: Estimating causal effects from observational network data requires accounting for both individual treatment and neighborhood exposure. Existing outcome models commonly incorporate these intervention variables into a joint predictor and estimate causal effects through prediction contrasts, leaving the corresponding response components implicit. We propose the $\underline{N}$etwork $\underline{E}$ffect $\underline{D}$ecomposition $\underline{Net}$work (NEDNet), which parameterizes the conditional outcome response as a query-invariant pre-treatment baseline plus separate treatment- and exposure-response pathways. Path-specific neighborhood contextualization supplies local pre-treatment information to the two pathways. We characterize the fitted response through a unique reference-normalized decomposition, which is equivalent to a zero mixed treatment--exposure contrast. Experiments on semi-synthetic benchmarks derived from BlogCatalog and Flickr show that NEDNet achieves the lowest PEHE among the compared methods for individual, peer, and total effects across homogeneous and covariate-heterogeneous response settings.

AI.tldr: NEDNet decomposes the conditional outcome under network interference into a query-invariant pre-treatment baseline plus separate treatment and neighborhood-exposure pathways. On BlogCatalog and Flickr semi-synthetic benchmarks it achieves the lowest PEHE among the compared methods for individual, peer and total effects.
AI.motivation: Existing outcome models for causal effects under network interference fold individual treatment and neighborhood exposure into one joint predictor, which leaves the corresponding response components implicit.
AI.method: The response is parameterized as a query-invariant pre-treatment baseline plus separate treatment- and exposure-response pathways, with path-specific neighborhood contextualization supplying local pre-treatment information; the fitted response has a unique reference-normalized decomposition, equivalent to a zero mixed treatment-exposure contrast.
AI.result: NEDNet has the lowest PEHE among the compared methods for individual, peer and total effects, across homogeneous and covariate-heterogeneous response settings on the semi-synthetic benchmarks derived from BlogCatalog and Flickr.
AI.conclusion: Making the baseline, treatment and exposure components explicit gives a well-defined decomposition of the response for estimating causal effects under interference.

title: Double Machine Learning for Panel Data: Identification, Specification, and a Bank Regulation Effect
summary: This paper examines robustness and causal interpretation of panel estimates using double/debiased machine learning. The prototype treatment setup is the 2018 US banking regulation. Under common treatment timing, we characterize identification and nuisance restrictions and derive exact bank-level representations of specified "within" and "first-difference" scores. Simulations assess panel model transformation-induced specification bias and inference under weaker overlap. Empirically, estimates vary with asset-size classification and prior growth. Prior-growth adjustment reduces overlap-weighted estimates across four Machine Learners (ML); doubly robust estimates depend on the fitted propensity and concentrated weights. Both bank groups received relief, so we estimate differential exposure effects. The findings highlight specification issues and the relation between functional-form robustness and causal identification.

AI.tldr: The paper examines the robustness and causal interpretation of double/debiased machine learning estimates for panel data, with the 2018 US banking regulation as the prototype treatment. Estimates vary with asset-size classification and prior growth, and because both bank groups received relief, the authors estimate differential exposure effects.
AI.motivation: Panel estimates from double/debiased machine learning need careful checks of robustness and causal interpretation, and the 2018 US banking regulation provides a concrete setting.
AI.method: Under common treatment timing the authors characterize identification and nuisance restrictions and derive exact bank-level representations of "within" and "first-difference" scores; simulations assess transformation-induced specification bias and inference under weaker overlap, and the empirical analysis uses four machine learners.
AI.result: Prior-growth adjustment reduces overlap-weighted estimates across the four machine learners, and doubly robust estimates depend on the fitted propensity and concentrated weights; estimates change with the asset-size classification.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight specification issues and the relation between functional-form robustness and causal identification in panel DML analyses.

title: Neural Realized Measures: Forecast-Supervised Intraday Aggregation for Volatility Forecasting
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF 2026), Milan, Italy
summary: High-frequency volatility forecasting typically separates measurement from prediction: intraday observations are first compressed into a daily realized measure using a fixed aggregation rule, and the resulting statistic is then passed to a forecasting model. This conventional pipeline therefore treats measure construction as forecast-agnostic preprocessing. We ask whether the aggregation stage itself can instead be learned from the downstream forecasting objective while preserving the statistical structure of established realized measures. We propose Neural Realized Measures (NRM), a primitive-preserving, forecast-supervised aggregation framework that retains the original measure-specific intraday contributions but replaces uniform aggregation with positive, mean-normalized context-dependent weights. Uniform weights exactly recover the corresponding raw realized measure (RRM), so the classical construction is nested as a special case. Because NRM remains an explicit weighted sum of established primitive contributions, it also retains direct bar-level attribution. Across SF, HAR, and MIDAS forecasting specifications, NRM is evaluated against corresponding RRM specifications under controlled comparisons. In Heston simulations, NRM reduces RMSE for both contemporaneous and next-day latent integrated variance across all evaluated primitive--regime combinations. On six cryptocurrencies using five-minute data, NRM improves QLIKE in all 54 paired out-of-sample comparisons, with mean gains of 7.23\%, 8.15\%, and 9.22\% under SF, HAR, and MIDAS, respectively. Validation-selected NRM specifications also achieve the lowest mean QLIKE across the six assets among the evaluated approaches. Ablation and SHAP analyses reveal systematic time-of-day and nonlinear local-context effects in the learned allocation.

AI.tldr: Neural Realized Measures learns positive, context-dependent weights for intraday contributions to a realized volatility measure, supervised by the downstream forecasting loss. It nests the raw realized measure as the uniform-weight case and improves QLIKE in all 54 paired out-of-sample comparisons on six cryptocurrencies.
AI.motivation: Conventional pipelines compress intraday observations with a fixed aggregation rule, treating measure construction as forecast-agnostic preprocessing, and the authors ask whether this aggregation stage can be learned from the forecasting objective.
AI.method: The original measure-specific intraday contributions are kept, but uniform aggregation is replaced by positive, mean-normalized context-dependent weights, so the measure remains an explicit weighted sum with bar-level attribution; NRM is compared with corresponding raw realized measure specifications under SF, HAR and MIDAS forecasting models.
AI.result: In Heston simulations NRM reduces RMSE for both contemporaneous and next-day latent integrated variance across all evaluated combinations. On six cryptocurrencies with five-minute data it improves QLIKE in all 54 paired comparisons, with mean gains of 7.23%, 8.15% and 9.22% under SF, HAR and MIDAS; validation-selected specifications have the lowest mean QLIKE across the six assets. SHAP and ablation analyses reveal time-of-day and nonlinear local-context effects in the learned allocation.
AI.conclusion: Learning the aggregation stage from the forecasting objective, while preserving the measure's primitives, improves volatility forecasts and keeps the result interpretable through bar-level attribution.

title: Changepoint localization via nested exchangeability tests: from point estimates to confidence intervals
summary: We study distribution-free uncertainty quantification for a changepoint estimate in an offline setting. We observe a sequence with a single changepoint and are given an estimate of its location. The pre- and post-change segments are independent and each consists of i.i.d. (or, more generally, exchangeable) observations from arbitrary and unknown distributions. We introduce Changepoint LOcalization via Nested Exchangeability testing (CLONE), a novel method for constructing distribution-free confidence intervals around that estimate by testing exchangeability in nested windows centered at the reference estimate. Under these assumptions, CLONE provides finite-sample coverage for any black-box reference estimator. Using a geometrically shrinking radius grid, CLONE requires only $O(log n)$ permutation tests. We characterize optimal scores for the framework and provide practical recommendations that result in sharp confidence intervals. Under mild assumptions, CLONE confidence intervals have asymptotically vanishing normalized length. Simulations and experiments on image and text data support our theoretical findings.

AI.tldr: CLONE builds distribution-free confidence intervals around a single offline changepoint estimate by testing exchangeability in nested windows centred on it. It gives finite-sample coverage for any black-box reference estimator using only O(log n) permutation tests, with asymptotically vanishing normalized length under mild assumptions.
AI.motivation: Offline changepoint estimates lack distribution-free uncertainty quantification when the pre- and post-change segments come from arbitrary, unknown distributions.
AI.method: Nested windows centred on the reference estimate are tested for exchangeability over a geometrically shrinking radius grid; the optimal scores for the framework are characterized, and practical recommendations are given for sharp intervals.
AI.result: Finite-sample coverage holds for any black-box reference estimator, with O(log n) permutation tests and asymptotically vanishing normalized length under mild assumptions; simulations and experiments on image and text data support the theory.
AI.conclusion: The framework yields sharp, distribution-free confidence intervals for changepoint localization, with theoretical guarantees and practical guidance.

title: Identification and Bounding of Joint Expectation over Potential Outcomes
summary: The joint expectation of functions of potential outcomes $(Y_1,Y_0)$ is a fundamental quantity in causal inference, particularly when investigating the variation or heterogeneity of causal effects. This paper provides novel assumptions for their identification: comonotonicity and countercomonotonicity. These assumptions offer a unified framework for their identification across discrete, continuous, and mixed outcome variables. In the absence of these assumptions, we derive sharp bounds for two broad classes of functions, yielding new results for bounding moments of individual causal effects, which are central to measuring effect heterogeneity. We present corresponding estimation methods and illustrate them in simulation studies and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes comonotonicity and countercomonotonicity as assumptions for identifying the joint expectation of functions of potential outcomes, and derives sharp bounds for two broad function classes when they do not hold. The framework covers discrete, continuous and mixed outcomes.
AI.motivation: The joint expectation of functions of potential outcomes is a fundamental quantity for studying the variation and heterogeneity of causal effects, and the paper seeks identification and bounds for it.
AI.method: Comonotonicity and countercomonotonicity give a unified identification framework; in their absence, sharp bounds are derived for two broad classes of functions, and corresponding estimation methods are presented.
AI.result: The assumptions yield identification, and sharp bounds for two function classes give new bounds on moments of individual causal effects; the methods are illustrated in simulation studies and on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers a unified framework for identifying and bounding joint expectations of potential-outcome functions and, through them, moments of individual causal effects, which are central to measuring effect heterogeneity.

title: Doubly-robust causal inference for multi-valued treatment regimes with recurrent neural networks
comment: 33 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: We propose a doubly-robust method to estimate the causal effects of multi-valued treatment regimes on patient outcomes. A multi-valued treatment regime assigns personalized treatments from a set of competing options based on a patient's history. Existing methods for optimal treatment regimes are largely limited to binary or continuous treatments. We extend the longitudinal targeted minimum loss-based estimator (LTMLE) to accommodate multi-valued treatments by modeling treatment assignments with a multinomial model. We further integrate recurrent neural networks (RNNs) into the LTMLE framework as learners for the outcome, treatment, and censoring models, and compare this approach to ensemble machine learning. Simulation studies show that LTMLE with either ensemble machine learning or RNNs is approximately unbiased, with close to nominal coverage, whereas sequential g-computation with ensemble machine learning is substantially biased under a dynamic rule. A multinomial treatment model performs similarly to a series of binomial regressions with ensemble machine learning, but yields more stable inference when the treatment model is an RNN.

AI.tldr: The paper extends longitudinal targeted minimum loss-based estimation (LTMLE) to multi-valued treatment regimes with a multinomial treatment model and uses recurrent neural networks as learners. Simulations show LTMLE with ensemble machine learning or RNNs is approximately unbiased with near-nominal coverage, while sequential g-computation is substantially biased under a dynamic rule.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for optimal treatment regimes are largely limited to binary or continuous treatments, and do not cover multi-valued treatments personalized to a patient's history.
AI.method: LTMLE is extended by modeling treatment assignment with a multinomial model, and RNNs are integrated as learners for the outcome, treatment and censoring models, compared with ensemble machine learning.
AI.result: LTMLE with either ensemble machine learning or RNNs is approximately unbiased with near-nominal coverage, while sequential g-computation with ensemble machine learning is substantially biased under a dynamic rule. A multinomial treatment model performs similarly to a series of binomial regressions with ensemble machine learning, but gives more stable inference when the treatment model is an RNN.
AI.conclusion: The doubly robust LTMLE framework handles multi-valued treatment regimes with either RNN or ensemble learners, and RNN treatment models give more stable inference.

title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
summary: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

AI.tldr: The paper describes AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory and its functional analysis were autoformalized by AI agents, and argues that the remaining risk lies in whether formal statements match their intended meaning rather than in the proofs.
AI.motivation: A machine-checked proof only certifies the formal statement it proves, so the human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended; the authors report that the risks lie in the statements, and that established literature can contain such problems.
AI.method: The library is organized so that a reviewer compares formal statements with their natural-language counterparts without reading proofs, and simple automated tests are run on the statements to expose problems.
AI.result: Simple automated tests on the statements exposed problems even in established literature; a textbook theorem was found whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted.
AI.conclusion: Review effort for AI-formalized mathematics should focus on statement fidelity, and the authors invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

title: Batch-Conditioned Semantic Anchors for Robust Transductive Adaptation of Vision--Language Models
summary: Transductive adaptation improves vision-language models at test time by refining predictions on an unlabeled batch, but current methods face a key trade-off. Aggressive approaches exploit batch structure but can drift when batches are sparse, have prior shift, or cover little of the label space. Conservative methods better preserve CLIP text semantics, but fixed semantic references can under-adapt even when the batch provides strong corrective evidence. We propose JPTA (Joint Prior and Transport Adaptation), a prior-aware framework that casts transductive VLM adaptation as batch-conditioned semantic reference estimation. Instead of treating CLIP text prototypes as fixed priors or freely replaceable, JPTA views them as semantic references that shift toward image-side batch structure only under calibrated evidence. It estimates batch priors and soft image-side prototypes to form transported semantic references whose impact is scaled by batch reliability. Across standard benchmarks, low effective-class regimes, all-class evaluation, and online streams, JPTA consistently outperforms TransCLIP and StatA, with the largest gains on sparse and prior-shifted batches. Anchor-drift, active-support, and absent-class-mass diagnostics show that JPTA fixes effective-class mismatch without unconstrained transductive drift, indicating that robust transductive VLM adaptation should recalibrate semantic references using reliable batch evidence rather than choose between unrestricted transduction and fixed prototypes. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: JPTA is a prior-aware transductive adaptation framework for vision-language models that treats CLIP text prototypes as semantic references which shift toward batch structure only under calibrated evidence.
AI.motivation: Aggressive transductive methods drift when batches are sparse, prior-shifted or cover little of the label space, while conservative methods keep fixed CLIP text prototypes that under-adapt even when the batch provides strong corrective evidence.
AI.method: JPTA estimates batch priors and soft image-side prototypes to form transported semantic references, whose impact is scaled by batch reliability.
AI.result: JPTA consistently outperforms TransCLIP and StatA across standard benchmarks, low effective-class regimes, all-class evaluation and online streams, with the largest gains on sparse and prior-shifted batches; anchor-drift, active-support and absent-class-mass diagnostics support its behaviour.
AI.conclusion: Robust transductive VLM adaptation should recalibrate semantic references using reliable batch evidence rather than choosing between unrestricted transduction and fixed prototypes.

title: TraCE: Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Video understanding models often rely on motion, yet their explanations can obscure which motion sources support a prediction. We identify motion-source under-specification as a limitation of existing video XAI: region-centric explanations can be source-ambiguous, while motion vocabularies restricted to single-person pose sequences are source-incomplete. We propose TraCE (Trajectory-Aware Concepts for Explainable Video Understanding), a concept-based framework that discovers source-flexible motion concepts by clustering optical-flow trajectories from training videos. These concepts represent dynamic evidence from people, objects, and interactions, while object and scene concepts account for static context. The resulting typed trajectory/object/scene interface supports class prediction for action recognition and question-conditioned concept matching for video question answering (VQA). We evaluate TraCE across five random seeds on six benchmarks: NTU RGB+D Mutual, Chiral SSv2, UCF-101, KTH, TOMATO, and STAR. Relative to non-interpretable baselines, TraCE maintains competitive task performance, with an average accuracy drop of 1.0 points for action recognition and a nominal gain of 0.4 points for VQA. Motion perturbation and concept-removal tests provide complementary evidence of directional semantic alignment and decision faithfulness, while sample-level interventions illustrate targeted model debugging. Our project page is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TraCE is a concept-based explainable video understanding framework that clusters optical-flow trajectories into source-flexible motion concepts, combined with object and scene concepts, for action recognition and video question answering.
AI.motivation: Existing video explanations are region-centric and can be source-ambiguous, while motion vocabularies restricted to single-person pose sequences are source-incomplete.
AI.method: Trajectory-aware concepts are discovered by clustering optical-flow trajectories from training videos, forming a typed trajectory, object and scene interface that supports class prediction and question-conditioned concept matching.
AI.result: Across five random seeds on six benchmarks (NTU RGB+D Mutual, Chiral SSv2, UCF-101, KTH, TOMATO, STAR), TraCE has an average accuracy drop of 1.0 points for action recognition and a nominal gain of 0.4 points for VQA relative to non-interpretable baselines; motion perturbation and concept-removal tests support its faithfulness.
AI.conclusion: TraCE keeps competitive task performance while giving directionally aligned, decision-faithful explanations that also support targeted model debugging.

title: Gaussians Can Subtract: Neural Dissolve Fields for Hybrid Scene Rendering
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 16 pages including supplementary material, 11 figures, 8 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Hybrid Mesh-Gaussian rendering combines compact textured surfaces with flexible 3D Gaussian primitives, offering an efficient alternative to purely Gaussian scene representations for structured environments. Existing scene-reconstruction hybrids commonly follow an additive formulation, where Gaussian residuals compensate for errors left by the mesh. However, not every Mesh-Gaussian conflict is caused by missing content: residual geometry errors, occlusion mismatch, texture-projection artifacts, and view-dependent appearance can make the same mesh content consistent in one view but inconsistent in another. We therefore formulate hybrid rendering as a multi-view inconsistency problem and present Gaussolve, a subtract-and-refill framework that selectively dissolves inconsistent mesh content before residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions. We introduce a lightweight Neural Dissolve Field, parameterized by scalar spherical-harmonic Gaussians, to learn where and from which viewing directions mesh content should be dissolved. A continuous transmittance fusion rule progressively exposes residual Gaussians behind the dissolved mesh, preserving their reconstruction gradients and avoiding hard visibility discontinuities. Experiments on structured and semi-structured scenes demonstrate higher visual fidelity with fewer Gaussian primitives and faster rendering. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: Gaussolve is a hybrid mesh-Gaussian renderer that dissolves multi-view inconsistent mesh content with a Neural Dissolve Field, and lets residual Gaussians refill the revealed regions.
AI.motivation: Additive mesh-plus-Gaussian hybrids assume Gaussian residuals compensate for missing content, but many mesh-Gaussian conflicts come from residual geometry error, occlusion mismatch, texture-projection artifacts and view-dependent appearance.
AI.method: Hybrid rendering is formulated as a multi-view inconsistency problem, with a lightweight Neural Dissolve Field parameterized by scalar spherical-harmonic Gaussians and a continuous transmittance fusion rule that progressively exposes residual Gaussians.
