AI.conclusion: Surgical continual pretraining yields transferable representations that generalize across procedures, anatomical regions and task types, offering a scalable alternative to procedure-specific representation learning.

title: XM4D: 4D Reconstruction through Certifiable Geometric Optimization
summary: Accurate 4D reconstruction remains challenging: jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry, and non-rigid deformation entails highly nonconvex optimization, making global optimality difficult to guarantee. We present XM4D, a framework for accurate and efficient 4D reconstruction built upon certifiably globally optimal geometric optimization. By separating the estimation of camera motion from non-rigid deformation, we formulate both stages as structured quadratically constrained quadratic programs (QCQP) that admit semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations and verifiable global optimality certificates. For camera motion estimation, we lift static point tracks into 3D using foundational depth prediction models and formulate a scaled bundle adjustment problem that jointly estimates camera poses, depth scales, and static landmarks. By analytically eliminating translations and landmarks, we reduce the problem to a QCQP over scaled rotations. For non-rigid reconstruction, we represent dynamic motion using an embedded deformation graph (EDG) and show that its tracking, rigidity, and temporal regularization objectives similarly reduce to a rotation-only QCQP. Both problems admit SDP relaxations that we solve efficiently with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro solver based on Riemannian optimization. The recovered geometry further initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement. Extensive experiments across seven benchmarks demonstrate accurate camera motion estimation on both static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality.

AI.tldr: XM4D reconstructs 4D scenes by separating camera motion from non-rigid deformation and formulating each as a QCQP with SDP relaxations that yield verifiable global optimality certificates. It reports accurate camera motion and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering across seven benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Jointly estimating camera motion, scene geometry and non-rigid deformation is highly nonconvex, so global optimality is difficult to guarantee.
AI.method: Camera motion is estimated by a scaled bundle adjustment over depth-lifted static point tracks, with translations and landmarks eliminated analytically to give a rotation-only QCQP. Non-rigid motion is modeled with an embedded deformation graph whose objectives reduce to a similar rotation-only QCQP. Both are solved with a GPU-accelerated Burer-Monteiro Riemannian solver, and the recovered geometry initializes dynamic Gaussian splatting for photometric refinement.
AI.result: Accurate camera motion on static and dynamic scenes, efficient optimization that scales to thousands of frames, and state-of-the-art novel-view rendering quality across seven benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Certifiable geometric optimization can make 4D reconstruction both accurate and verifiable, and its output provides a strong initialization for Gaussian splatting.

title: StitchEdit: Stitching Depth Priors into Image Editors via Per-Layer Gradient Probing
summary: Text-guided image editing with diffusion models struggles with spatial edits (e.g. manipulating objects, changing viewpoints, manipulating occlusions) that depend on the 3D structure understanding of a scene. Marigold and follow-up work demonstrate that a pretrained diffusion backbone already harbors strong geometric priors that can be activated for depth estimation, yet how to redirect these priors toward editing remains unresolved. Through per-layer gradient probing, we discover that the editing and depth objectives are compatible in early transformer layers but actively conflict in late layers, explaining why naive depth-conditioned editing either ignores geometry or degrades visual quality. We present StitchEdit, which first activates the backbone's geometric capability via a lightweight depth-denoising adapter, then selectively fine-tunes this adapter for editing using a probe-guided per-layer learning rate schedule that preserves depth knowledge where it helps and prunes it where it conflicts. On the proposed StitchEditBench, a benchmark of 150 geometry-dependent edits spanning spatial transformation, occlusion manipulation, and viewpoint change, StitchEdit consistently surpasses both instruction-based and depth-conditioned baselines on perceptual quality and geometric fidelity.

AI.tldr: StitchEdit transfers the geometric priors of a pretrained diffusion backbone into text-guided image editing for geometry-dependent edits such as spatial transformation, occlusion manipulation and viewpoint change. It outperforms instruction-based and depth-conditioned baselines on perceptual quality and geometric fidelity.
AI.motivation: Diffusion image editors struggle with spatial edits that depend on 3D scene structure, and naive depth-conditioned editing either ignores geometry or degrades visual quality because the editing and depth objectives conflict.
AI.method: Per-layer gradient probing shows the editing and depth objectives are compatible in early transformer layers but conflict in late layers. StitchEdit first activates the backbone's depth capability with a lightweight depth-denoising adapter, then fine-tunes that adapter for editing with a probe-guided per-layer learning rate schedule that preserves depth knowledge where it helps and prunes it where it conflicts.
AI.result: On the proposed StitchEditBench of 150 geometry-dependent edits, StitchEdit consistently surpasses both instruction-based and depth-conditioned baselines on perceptual quality and geometric fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Routing depth priors layer by layer lets an image editor gain geometric awareness without sacrificing visual quality, and the proposed benchmark provides a test set for geometry-dependent edits.

title: Towards Scalable Diagnostic-Driven Whole-Slide Image Retrieval for Pathology Archives
summary: The growing adoption of digital pathology has rapidly expanded collections of hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images, yet efficient navigation through these archives remains challenging, as metadata is often inconsistent or unavailable. Content-based image retrieval addresses this challenge by identifying similar cases directly from visual representations instead of manual annotations or metadata. Existing retrieval systems have demonstrated promising performance but largely rely on handcrafted indexing pipelines and predefined sampling strategies, constraining scalability and generalization. Here, we present CLEAR-WSI (Constant-Length Embedding for Automatic Retrieval of Whole-Slide Images) as a scalable, diagnostic-driven slide-retrieval framework, validated on both public and clinical data. Using a fixed-length slide embedding, CLEAR-WSI refines retrieved candidates with either a predicted diagnostic label or the ground-truth label, depending on the retrieval setting. Newly processed cases are subsequently added to the expanding memory bank, allowing the retrieval archive to grow over time. On a comprehensive benchmark consisting of two public and one private clinical datasets representing four retrieval tasks, CLEAR-WSI improves Precision@5 over the strongest evaluated baseline, with gains on CAMELYON16 (3.10), BRACS-1 (2.75), BRACS-2 (1.95), and X-HER2 (3.75). Additional ablation and latency studies further examine the contribution of each component and highlight its potential for scalable deployment.

AI.tldr: CLEAR-WSI is a whole-slide image retrieval framework that uses a fixed-length slide embedding and refines candidates with a diagnostic label, either predicted or ground-truth depending on the retrieval setting. It improves Precision@5 over the strongest evaluated baseline on four retrieval tasks.
AI.motivation: Digital pathology archives are growing quickly, but existing retrieval systems rely on handcrafted indexing pipelines and predefined sampling strategies, which limit scalability and generalization.
AI.method: A fixed-length slide embedding supports retrieval, and candidates are refined with a predicted or ground-truth diagnostic label depending on the setting. Newly processed cases are added to an expanding memory bank so the archive grows over time.
AI.result: Across a benchmark of two public datasets (CAMELYON16 and BRACS) and one clinical dataset (X-HER2), CLEAR-WSI improves Precision@5 over the strongest baseline by 3.10 on CAMELYON16, 2.75 on BRACS-1, 1.95 on BRACS-2 and 3.75 on X-HER2. Ablation and latency studies are also reported.
AI.conclusion: A fixed-length, diagnosis-aware embedding with an expandable memory bank offers a scalable route to content-based retrieval over growing pathology archives.

title: WAM-Sim0.1: World Anchored Memory Meets Online RL for Consistent and Realistic Driving Simulation
summary: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: WAM-Sim is a driving world model with persistent hierarchical memory and online flow-matching RL post-training, aimed at long-horizon rollouts. It reaches FID 3.47 and FVD 25.72 on nuScenes and substantially mitigates structural and identity drift on minute-scale rollouts.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive driving world models suffer structural drift, identity drift and quality decay over long rollout horizons because their transient conditioning signals lack persistent state.
AI.method: Persistent context is organized at three scales: pose-aligned structural tokens for road topology, read-only scene tokens for geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens that keep traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. Self-generated rollouts are post-trained with flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge.
AI.result: On nuScenes WAM-Sim achieves FID 3.47 and FVD 25.72, with 24.16 mAP and 71.23 road mIoU in downstream perception. On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data it substantially reduces structural and identity drift while preserving scene similarity and subject identity coherence.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring generation in an invariant memory keeps RL from collapsing semantics or reward hacking, so online RL can add physical plausibility and visual sharpness to long driving rollouts.

title: IDPrior: Decoupling Identity Generation from Facial Image Synthesis
summary: Large-scale identity-labeled face datasets are essential for training modern face recognition models, yet collecting and annotating such data is costly and raises privacy and ethical concerns. Existing synthetic face generation methods typically derive identities from predefined class labels, unconditional image generation, or predefined latent sampling strategies, without explicitly modeling the underlying distribution of facial identities. In this paper, we propose IDPrior, a two-stage framework that decouples identity generation from image synthesis. We first learn a diffusion prior in the embedding space of a pretrained face recognition model to model the distribution of facial identities and generate novel identity embeddings. These embeddings are then used to condition a pretrained identity-conditioned diffusion model (DM), enabling the synthesis of multiple images of the same identity. This modular design provides a scalable approach to identity generation while remaining compatible with existing and future identity-conditioned DMs. Experiments indicate that IDPrior generates diverse and well-separated identities while maintaining a closer correspondence to the distribution of authentic identities. Face recognition models trained on datasets generated using IDPrior-generated identities achieve competitive or improved performance compared with existing synthetic-data-based methods across multiple face verification benchmarks. Code and generated datasets are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: IDPrior is a two-stage framework that decouples identity generation from image synthesis by learning a diffusion prior over face recognition embeddings and using the generated embeddings to condition a pretrained identity-conditioned diffusion model. Face recognition models trained on its synthetic datasets achieve competitive or improved verification performance.
AI.motivation: Identity-labeled face datasets are costly to collect and raise privacy concerns, while existing synthetic face methods derive identities from class labels, unconditional generation or predefined latent sampling without explicitly modeling the distribution of facial identities.
AI.method: A diffusion prior is learned in the embedding space of a pretrained face recognition model to generate novel identity embeddings, which then condition a pretrained identity-conditioned diffusion model to synthesize multiple images of the same identity. The modular design remains compatible with existing and future identity-conditioned models.
AI.result: IDPrior generates diverse and well-separated identities that correspond more closely to the distribution of authentic identities. Face recognition models trained on its generated data achieve competitive or improved performance over existing synthetic-data methods across multiple face verification benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Modeling the identity distribution directly in embedding space offers a scalable and modular route to synthetic identity datasets for training face recognition models.

title: Rotation Is Token-Blind: A Structural Criterion for Post-Training Quantization of Feed-Forward Geometry Transformers
summary: Feed-forward 3D models use Transformers to predict camera poses, depth, and structure in one pass, avoiding iterative multi-view optimization. Long sequences and deep attention incur high compute and memory costs, motivating Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) for deployment. Existing PTQ methods mainly suppress channel-wise outliers by smoothing or orthogonal rotation. Geometry Transformers introduce a different challenge: heterogeneous token types share one activation quantization grid. A few special tokens may exert high leverage over global outputs and be updated by only a subset of blocks. Token-blind transforms, which apply the same transformation to every token, reduce overall quantization error but cannot remove differentiated degradation across token types. We propose QMapAnything, a structure-aware PTQ framework. We cast floating-point-preserving rotation and smoothing as a token-blind reparameterization group, and prove that they yield common-mode gains while leaving relative token SNR unchanged. We introduce a statistic $\Gamma$ that combines a special token's quantization disadvantage and output leverage to predict whether differentiated bias correction is needed beyond rotation. Experiments on geometric benchmarks show that W4A8 closely matches full-precision performance. Under W8A8, peak memory falls by $2.2$--$3.1\times$ versus FP32, with up to $3.1\times$ speedup on real hardware. These results provide a principled and efficient approach to deploying feed-forward 3D reconstruction models in resource-constrained edges.

AI.tldr: QMapAnything is a structure-aware post-training quantization framework for feed-forward geometry Transformers that treats special tokens differently from ordinary ones. It keeps W4A8 close to full-precision performance and, under W8A8, cuts peak memory by 2.2 to 3.1 times versus FP32 with up to 3.1 times speedup on real hardware.
AI.motivation: Existing PTQ methods suppress channel-wise outliers with smoothing or orthogonal rotation, but in geometry Transformers heterogeneous token types share one activation quantization grid, and a few special tokens exert high leverage on global outputs, so token-blind transforms cannot remove differentiated degradation.
AI.method: Floating-point-preserving rotation and smoothing are cast as a token-blind reparameterization group, which is proven to give common-mode gains while leaving relative token SNR unchanged. A statistic Gamma that combines a special token's quantization disadvantage with its output leverage predicts whether differentiated bias correction is needed beyond rotation.
AI.result: On geometric benchmarks W4A8 closely matches full-precision performance. Under W8A8, peak memory falls by 2.2 to 3.1 times versus FP32, with up to 3.1 times speedup on real hardware.
AI.conclusion: Combining token-blind transforms with token-specific bias correction, guided by the Gamma statistic, offers a principled and efficient way to deploy feed-forward 3D reconstruction models on resource-constrained edge devices.

title: Bri3D: Bridging the Object-Scene Gap in Single-Image 3D Generation via Scene-Anchor
summary: Generating compositional 3D scenes from a single image requires recovering detailed object geometry and coherent spatial arrangements. Existing object-to-scene methods, including SAM3D and MIDI, extend object generation through image-context reasoning or inter-instance modeling. Coordinating objects remains challenging with limited scene-level supervision. Directly extending object-centric generators to entire scenes can degrade geometry and fail to preserve instance scale, orientation, and pose. We propose Bri3D, a framework bridging scene-level structural reasoning and object-level generative priors through instance-aware voxel scene anchors. Bri3D predicts a color-coded scene scaffold encoding coarse object geometry and spatial arrangements. Each instance is extracted as a scene anchor and refined into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible voxel support, enabling a frozen object generator to synthesize detailed textured geometry in the anchor-defined spatial reference. This coarse-to-fine design separates scene organization from object-scale detail synthesis, focusing scene-level training on spatial organization and anchor refinement while reusing pretrained object priors. Experiments demonstrate improvements in scene layout, object geometry, visual quality, and generalization. Bri3D predicts scene layouts efficiently; full scene generation is faster than SceneGen and SAM3D.

AI.tldr: Bri3D generates compositional 3D scenes from a single image by predicting a color-coded voxel scene scaffold and refining each instance into an anchor that conditions a frozen object generator. It improves scene layout, object geometry and visual quality, and full scene generation is faster than SceneGen and SAM3D.
AI.motivation: Object-to-scene methods such as SAM3D and MIDI struggle to coordinate objects with limited scene-level supervision, and directly extending object-centric generators to whole scenes degrades geometry and fails to preserve instance scale, orientation and pose.
AI.method: A color-coded scene scaffold encodes coarse object geometry and spatial arrangement. Each instance is extracted as a scene anchor and refined into a pose-preserving, prior-compatible voxel support, and a frozen object generator then synthesizes detailed textured geometry within the anchor-defined spatial reference, separating scene organization from object-scale detail.
AI.result: Experiments show improvements in scene layout, object geometry, visual quality and generalization, and layouts are predicted efficiently. Full scene generation is faster than SceneGen and SAM3D.
AI.conclusion: Splitting scene-level structural reasoning from object-level generation lets scene training focus on spatial organization while reusing pretrained object priors.

title: Reviving the Discarded High-Resolution Feature for Transformer-Based Tiny Object Detection
summary: Tiny object detection remains challenging because tiny instances occupy only a few pixels, and their fine-grained details are easily lost during feature downsampling. Although the highest-resolution feature preserves rich local details for tiny objects, DETR-like detectors often discard it due to its large computational cost, while directly reintroducing this feature also brings dense background noise. To address this problem, we propose ReDHF, a novel framework that Revives the Discarded High-resolution Feature for tiny object detection. ReDHF has three cooperative components. Cross-Scale Deformable Fusion (CSDF) first constructs a semantically enhanced highest-resolution feature and injects its fine-grained details into the shallow feature under a moderate cost. Ellipse-Guided Shallow Supervision (EGSS) then guides the enhanced feature to learn more reliable classification and localization priors by applying geometry-adaptive auxiliary supervision. Full-Scale Query Interaction (FSQI) further enables decoder queries to access both low-level details and high-level semantic information, allowing them to aggregate richer cues for tiny objects. Extensive experiments show that ReDHF consistently improves multiple baselines across different DETR variants and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated benchmarks. The best ReDHF variants surpass their baselines by +1.4 AP on AI-TOD-v2, +1.6 AP on VisDrone, and +1.5 AP on SODA-D, with especially notable gains on tiny and small objects.

AI.tldr: ReDHF revives the discarded highest-resolution feature for DETR-style tiny object detection through three cooperative components. Its best variants surpass their baselines by +1.4 AP on AI-TOD-v2, +1.6 AP on VisDrone and +1.5 AP on SODA-D.
AI.motivation: The highest-resolution feature preserves fine details of tiny objects, but DETR-like detectors discard it because of its computational cost, and reintroducing it directly brings dense background noise.
AI.method: Cross-Scale Deformable Fusion builds a semantically enhanced highest-resolution feature and injects its fine-grained details into the shallow feature at moderate cost. Ellipse-Guided Shallow Supervision applies geometry-adaptive auxiliary supervision to guide the enhanced feature toward more reliable classification and localization priors. Full-Scale Query Interaction lets decoder queries access both low-level details and high-level semantics.
AI.result: ReDHF consistently improves multiple baselines across different DETR variants and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated benchmarks, with especially notable gains on tiny and small objects.
AI.conclusion: Recovering high-resolution detail at moderate cost, with targeted supervision and cross-scale query access, is an effective way to improve tiny object detection in transformer detectors.

title: When GeoFMs Meet VHR: Benchmarking Foundation Models on Very High Resolution Earth Observation Imagery
summary: Geospatial foundation models are a widely adopted starting point for remote sensing tasks. Most are pretrained on Sentinel-1/2 and Landsat imagery at a ground sampling distance (GSD) of 10m or coarser. Many applications instead rely on very high resolution (VHR) imagery, where individual buildings, roads, and amenities are resolved. We study which pretraining regimes transfer well to this scale. We introduce VHR-Bench, a benchmark suite of ten datasets at 1.5m GSD or finer spanning five task families, eight application domains, and both satellite and aerial platforms. We evaluate twelve encoders in three pretraining tiers with frozen backbones at two training-data fractions. We find that both pretraining on large natural-image collections and VHR-specific pretraining transfer effectively to VHR tasks, with complementary strengths. SkySense leads when labels are scarce; at the full label fraction the web-pretrained DINOv3 ViT-L edges ahead, with the two close together there. Encoders pretrained only on Sentinel-scale imagery transfer least well under RGB input. Guided by these complementary results, we continue the self-supervised pretraining of DINOv3 ViT-L on 1.02 million held-out VHR tiles and evaluate the resulting encoder without changing the downstream protocol. The continued model gives a clear improvement over the released backbone when labels are scarce and a modest one at the full fraction, at no increase in inference parameters or compute. These findings support a generalize-then-specialize strategy: already strong, broad natural-image pretraining can be further improved by a short VHR continuation stage while preserving its general visual features.

AI.tldr: VHR-Bench is a benchmark of ten datasets at 1.5 m GSD or finer for evaluating geospatial foundation models on very high resolution Earth observation imagery. A short continued pretraining of DINOv3 ViT-L on 1.02 million VHR tiles improves the encoder without increasing inference parameters or compute.
AI.motivation: Geospatial foundation models are mostly pretrained on Sentinel and Landsat imagery at 10 m GSD or coarser, while many applications need VHR imagery where buildings, roads and amenities are resolved, and it is unclear which pretraining regimes transfer to this scale.
AI.method: Twelve encoders in three pretraining tiers are evaluated with frozen backbones at two training-data fractions across ten datasets spanning five task families, eight application domains and both satellite and aerial platforms. Guided by these results, DINOv3 ViT-L is further self-supervised on 1.02 million held-out VHR tiles and evaluated under the unchanged downstream protocol.
AI.result: Pretraining on large natural-image collections and VHR-specific pretraining both transfer effectively, with complementary strengths. SkySense leads when labels are scarce, while the web-pretrained DINOv3 ViT-L edges ahead at the full label fraction. Encoders pretrained only on Sentinel-scale imagery transfer least well under RGB input. The continued model improves clearly over the released backbone when labels are scarce and modestly at the full fraction.
AI.conclusion: A generalize-then-specialize strategy works: broad natural-image pretraining can be improved by a short VHR continuation stage while preserving its general visual features.

title: Deformable Contact-Aware 3D Object Placement
summary: Current language-guided 3D object placement typically predicts a rigid 6-DoF pose, ignoring the physical reality that indoor placements are dictated by contact. Consequently, predicted poses often float, interpenetrate supports, or fail to deform soft surfaces. We propose Deformable Contact-Aware Placement (DCAP), a framework that reframes placement as a drop-to-equilibrium process. Rather than predicting a static pose, DCAP constructs a semantic release state that specifies the drop location, object scale, and deformable components, allowing a coupled rigid-deformable simulator to settle the object under gravity and friction. This explicitly separates semantic intent from physical realization. Evaluated on a benchmark of 2,063 prompt-asset-scene cases, DCAP significantly outperforms static baselines. On standard placements, it improves VLM Physics & Naturalness by 21.2 points and human preference by 26.5 points over the strongest raw rigid baseline, while reducing mean penetration depth by 72.3%. Compared to simulated rollout baselines, DCAP reduces residual speed by 72.1%. Ultimately, our results prove that physically accurate 3D placement requires modeling semantic intent and physical realization as strictly separate processes.

AI.tldr: DCAP reframes language-guided 3D object placement as a drop-to-equilibrium process, in which a semantic release state is settled by a coupled rigid-deformable simulator under gravity and friction. On 2,063 prompt-asset-scene cases it significantly outperforms static rigid baselines on physical plausibility, naturalness, human preference and penetration.
AI.motivation: Language-guided placement typically predicts a rigid 6-DoF pose that ignores physical contact, so predicted objects float, interpenetrate supports or fail to deform soft surfaces.
AI.method: Instead of predicting a static pose, DCAP constructs a semantic release state that specifies the drop location, object scale and deformable components, and lets a coupled rigid-deformable simulator settle the object under gravity and friction. This explicitly separates semantic intent from physical realization.
AI.result: On a benchmark of 2,063 prompt-asset-scene cases DCAP significantly outperforms static baselines. On standard placements it improves VLM Physics and Naturalness by 21.2 points and human preference by 26.5 points over the strongest raw rigid baseline, and reduces mean penetration depth by 72.3%. Compared with simulated rollout baselines it reduces residual speed by 72.1%.
AI.conclusion: Physically accurate 3D placement requires modeling semantic intent and physical realization as strictly separate processes.

title: NutriVisRAG: Multimodal Exemplar Grounding for Nutrient Estimation with Vision-Language Models
summary: Diet is a major determinant of health, yet accurate dietary assessment from free-living meal images remains challenging. Existing retrieval-based Vision-Language Model (VLM) approaches to nutrient estimation typically rely on textual food representations, while, to our knowledge, direct grounding on visually similar annotated meals has not been investigated. We present NutriVisRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework that uses a vision encoder to retrieve similar meals with known nutritional annotations and provide them as multimodal in-context exemplars for VLM nutrient estimation at inference time, without task-specific fine-tuning. We evaluate NutriVisRAG across four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders, and two prompting strategies, including free-living meals from adults with insulin-treated diabetes, where carbohydrate estimates are compared against two dietitians' annotations. Across all 96 configurations (4 datasets x 4 VLMs x 3 retrieval encoders x 2 prompting strategies), NutriVisRAG reduced the primary estimation error in 56, with improvements more frequent under whole-meal (35/48) than per-item prompting (21/48). Across the evaluated configurations, the lowest NutriVisRAG error was below the best Vanilla error in 13 of 16 VLM--dataset pairs. For GPT-5.4-mini, under whole-meal prompting, the best-performing retrieval encoder for each dataset reduced the primary error on all four datasets relative to Vanilla, with reductions of 1.7--35.7%. Overall, our results show that grounding in multimodal exemplars comprising images and respective annotations can improve nutrient estimation at inference time without task-specific fine-tuning, although the benefits remain configuration-dependent.

AI.tldr: NutriVisRAG retrieves visually similar annotated meals and supplies them as multimodal in-context exemplars to vision-language models for nutrient estimation, without fine-tuning. It reduced the primary estimation error in 56 of 96 configurations, though the benefit depends on the configuration.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-based VLM approaches to nutrient estimation rely on textual food representations, and direct grounding on visually similar annotated meals has not been investigated.
AI.method: A vision encoder retrieves similar meals with known nutritional annotations, which are given to the VLM as multimodal in-context exemplars at inference time. The framework is evaluated with four datasets, four VLMs, three retrieval encoders and two prompting strategies, whole-meal and per-item.
AI.result: Across all 96 configurations NutriVisRAG reduced the primary estimation error in 56, more often under whole-meal prompting (35 of 48) than per-item prompting (21 of 48). The lowest NutriVisRAG error was below the best Vanilla error in 13 of 16 VLM-dataset pairs. For GPT-5.4-mini under whole-meal prompting, the best retrieval encoder reduced the primary error relative to Vanilla on all four datasets, by 1.7% to 35.7%.
AI.conclusion: Grounding VLMs in multimodal exemplars of images and annotations can improve inference-time nutrient estimation, but the benefits remain configuration-dependent.

title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics-Aware Industrial Anomaly Detection and Reasoning
comment: Accepted at IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027
summary: Industrial Anomaly Detection (IAD) is a long-established problem that aims to detect defects in industrial products during manufacturing for quality control. Most existing studies focus on static visual patterns as the basis for detection. However, in real manufacturing environments, many anomalies are dynamics-based, such as irregular movements that cannot be perceived from static cues alone. We observe that even recent Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based approaches fall short in identifying such dynamic anomalies due to limited temporal modeling capability. To address this, we introduce MUSTARD: MUltimodal SpatioTemporal Anomaly Reasoning and Detection, a framework that equips MLLMs with fine-grained spatiotemporal dynamics awareness for detecting and reasoning about dynamics-based defects. MUSTARD introduces optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities to capture critical motion irregularities through local motion patterns and global dynamic evolution. Its normal pattern-based reasoning pipeline requires only a few normal reference samples as the detection basis, avoiding any model updates. This enables efficient adaptation across various products and provides high decision interpretability. MUSTARD is the first MLLM-based framework for dynamics-based IAD. Experiments demonstrate its superior performance in detecting spatiotemporal anomalies and providing plausible explanations. The code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: MUSTARD equips multimodal large language models with spatiotemporal dynamics awareness for detecting dynamics-based industrial anomalies, using optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and a normal-pattern reasoning pipeline. It needs only a few normal reference samples and no model updates, and the abstract reports superior detection and explanation quality.
AI.motivation: Many manufacturing anomalies are dynamics-based, such as irregular movements that static cues cannot reveal, and even recent MLLM-based approaches fall short on them because of limited temporal modeling.
AI.method: Optical-flow-guided keyframe selection and augmented modalities capture motion irregularities through local motion patterns and global dynamic evolution. A normal pattern-based reasoning pipeline uses a few normal reference samples as the detection basis, avoiding any model updates.
AI.result: The experiments demonstrate superior performance in detecting spatiotemporal anomalies and in providing plausible explanations. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Dynamics-aware MLLM reasoning with few normal references enables efficient adaptation across products with high decision interpretability, and MUSTARD is presented as the first MLLM-based framework for dynamics-based industrial anomaly detection.

title: TerraMesh-Masks: Open-Vocabulary Segmentation for Earth Observation
summary: Open-vocabulary segmentation (OVS) enables models to segment a variety of concepts specified in natural language, removing the need for fixed label sets and fine-tuning. While recent OVS approaches have shown strong performance on natural images, they transfer poorly to Earth observation (EO) data due to differing semantics, scales, sensing modality, and geographic context. To date, large-scale EO-specific datasets and benchmarks for OVS remain scarce. We, therefore, introduce TerraMesh-Masks, a large-scale open-vocabulary segmentation dataset for EO, comprising 16 million binary masks aligned with nine million multimodal TerraMesh samples and annotated using OpenStreetMap and Overture-derived semantics. In addition, we provide an expert-reviewed evaluation set of 523 samples covering over 200 classes to enable robust evaluation. To demonstrate the impact of TerraMesh-Masks, we build an open-vocabulary version of TerraMind. Our results demonstrate significantly improved performance over general-purpose state-of-the-art models reaching 35.18% IoU versus 16.29% for this http URL and 11.33% for SAM-3. We release the dataset publicly under a permissive license at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TerraMesh-Masks is a large-scale open-vocabulary segmentation dataset for Earth observation, with 16 million binary masks aligned to nine million multimodal TerraMesh samples. An open-vocabulary TerraMind built on it reaches 35.18% IoU, against 16.29% for a general-purpose state-of-the-art model and 11.33% for SAM-3.
AI.motivation: Open-vocabulary segmentation transfers poorly to Earth observation data because of differing semantics, scales, sensing modality and geographic context, and large EO-specific datasets and benchmarks for it remain scarce.
AI.method: Masks are annotated with OpenStreetMap and Overture-derived semantics and aligned with nine million multimodal TerraMesh samples. An expert-reviewed evaluation set of 523 samples covering over 200 classes enables robust evaluation, and an open-vocabulary version of TerraMind is built to demonstrate the dataset.
AI.result: The open-vocabulary TerraMind reaches 35.18% IoU, versus 16.29% for a general-purpose state-of-the-art model and 11.33% for SAM-3, a significant improvement over general-purpose models.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale EO-specific mask data can substantially improve open-vocabulary segmentation over general-purpose models, and the dataset is released under a permissive license.

title: National-scale mapping of tree species composition in Switzerland from high-resolution aerial imagery and multimodal data
comment: 39 pages, 17 figures (11 in the main text, 6 in the supplementary material). Submitted to Remote Sensing of Environment
summary: Tree-species composition shapes forest productivity and how forests respond to climate disturbances such as drought, windthrow and insect outbreaks. Yet most national forest maps assign each pixel a single dominant species and cannot show the share of accompanying species. We mapped the basal-area shares of ten main tree species and a residual Other class across Switzerland at 30 m resolution. A deep-learning model combining 0.1 m aerial RGB imagery, airborne laser scanning (ALS), annual AlphaEarth satellite embeddings, and climate variables was trained on basal-area observations from 3,992 Swiss National Forest Inventory (NFI) sites. In spatial cross-validation, the model reached a macro-$R^2$ of 0.485 across the 11 classes. On an independent forest-reserve dataset, the map reached a macro-$R^2$ of 0.552 for individual 30 m pixels and 0.733 for plots, and identified the dominant class in 73.2% of pixels and 81.1% of plots. The map shows maple and ash as widespread minor components that dominant-class maps omit. It also reproduces the elevational sequence from broadleaved lowland stands through spruce to larch and Arolla pine near the treeline. By resolving the species mixture within each 30 m pixel, the map complements field inventory statistics with spatially continuous information that can support forest monitoring, the management of mixed stands, and climate-adaptation planning across Switzerland.

AI.tldr: The authors map the basal-area shares of ten main tree species plus an Other class at 30 m resolution across Switzerland, using a deep model that fuses 0.1 m aerial RGB imagery, airborne laser scanning, AlphaEarth satellite embeddings and climate variables. The map resolves the species mixture within each pixel, which dominant-class maps omit.
AI.motivation: Most national forest maps assign each pixel a single dominant species and cannot show the share of accompanying species, which affects forest productivity and how forests respond to climate disturbances.
AI.method: A deep-learning model combines 0.1 m aerial RGB imagery, airborne laser scanning, annual AlphaEarth satellite embeddings and climate variables, trained on basal-area observations from 3,992 Swiss National Forest Inventory sites.
AI.result: In spatial cross-validation the model reaches a macro-R2 of 0.485 across 11 classes. On an independent forest-reserve dataset the map reaches a macro-R2 of 0.552 for individual 30 m pixels and 0.733 for plots, and identifies the dominant class in 73.2% of pixels and 81.1% of plots. It shows maple and ash as widespread minor components and reproduces the elevational sequence from broadleaved lowland stands through spruce to larch and Arolla pine near the treeline.
AI.conclusion: Spatially continuous species-mixture maps complement field inventory statistics and can support forest monitoring, the management of mixed stands and climate-adaptation planning across Switzerland.

title: Towards Practical 20 kbps Generative Video Compression via Adaptive Tokenization and Entropy Modeling
summary: Video compression at ultra-low bitrates remains challenging due to the loss of perceptually important details under limited bit budgets. Recent generative video compression methods leverage pretrained video priors to improve perceptual quality and temporal coherence, but many follow a compress-then-generate paradigm, where generative priors are primarily exploited during reconstruction. Moreover, representations learned for generation and reconstruction are not inherently optimized for entropy coding. In this work, we propose \method, which adapts pretrained video representations into compression-oriented representations while preserving their reconstruction capability. Specifically, we adapt the pretrained causal video VAE of MiniMax-H3 into a discrete video tokenizer and develop a small autoregressive entropy model that captures local and global token dependencies, with grouped prediction for parallel decoding. To further improve coding efficiency, we jointly optimize the tokenizer and entropy model using a differentiable rate surrogate, allowing rate gradients to adapt token assignments toward lower coding costs while preserving reconstruction quality. Experiments on UVG, MCL-JCV, and HEVC Class B demonstrate superior perceptual rate--distortion performance, achieving BD-LPIPS savings of 82.2\%--87.5\% and BD-DISTS savings of 78.3\%--85.0\% relative to GLC-Video.

AI.tldr: The proposed method adapts a pretrained causal video VAE into a discrete video tokenizer and pairs it with a small autoregressive entropy model, jointly optimized with a differentiable rate surrogate for generative video compression at about 20 kbps. It achieves BD-LPIPS savings of 82.2% to 87.5% and BD-DISTS savings of 78.3% to 85.0% relative to GLC-Video.
AI.motivation: Ultra-low-bitrate video compression loses perceptually important detail, and generative compression methods typically follow a compress-then-generate paradigm that uses pretrained priors only during reconstruction, while representations learned for generation are not optimized for entropy coding.
AI.method: The pretrained causal video VAE of MiniMax-H3 is adapted into a compression-oriented discrete tokenizer while preserving its reconstruction capability. A small autoregressive entropy model captures local and global token dependencies with grouped prediction for parallel decoding, and the tokenizer and entropy model are optimized jointly with a differentiable rate surrogate so that rate gradients adapt token assignments.
AI.result: On UVG, MCL-JCV and HEVC Class B the method shows superior perceptual rate-distortion performance, with BD-LPIPS savings of 82.2% to 87.5% and BD-DISTS savings of 78.3% to 85.0% relative to GLC-Video.
AI.conclusion: Adapting pretrained video representations for compression, not only for reconstruction, yields strong perceptual rate-distortion gains at ultra-low bitrates.

title: ProtoGestalt: Interpretable Prototypes for Facial Phenotyping and Diagnosis of Rare Genetic Disorders
summary: Rare genetic disorders are difficult to diagnose due to their diversity and overlapping clinical features. Facial morphology can provide diagnostic clues, yet most diagnostic models offer limited interpretability and are not designed to support broad screening for undiagnosed disease. We present ProtoGestalt, an interpretable prototype-based framework for facial phenotyping, rare-disease screening, and syndrome identification. The method extends prototype learning by constraining learned visual features to select facial regions, allowing predictions to be explained through localized and additive evidence. We assess ProtoGestalt's ability to distinguish syndromic from unaffected faces on multiple control datasets and class prevalence values. We further evaluate it's diagnostic performance on syndromes observed during training. The learned prototype-based representations provide significant separation between syndromic and case-matched control images and retain useful performance as the proportion of controls increases. The framework also demonstrates the ability to differentiate among syndromes. Although reasonably accurate specialized models for facial classification of rare disorders already exist, ProtoGestalt offers an interpretable alternative that links predictions to anatomically meaningful facial regions, potentially supporting clinical decision-making and the discovery of phenotype-gene associations.

AI.tldr: ProtoGestalt is an interpretable prototype-based framework that links facial phenotype predictions to localized facial regions for rare genetic disorder screening and syndrome identification. It separates syndromic from case-matched control faces and differentiates among syndromes, and retains useful performance as the proportion of controls increases.
AI.motivation: Rare genetic disorders are hard to diagnose because of diverse and overlapping clinical features, and most facial diagnostic models offer limited interpretability and are not designed for broad screening for undiagnosed disease.
AI.method: The prototype learning approach is extended by constraining learned visual features to select facial regions, so that predictions are explained through localized and additive evidence.
AI.result: The learned prototype representations provide significant separation between syndromic and case-matched control images and retain useful performance as the proportion of controls increases. The framework also differentiates among syndromes observed during training.
AI.conclusion: Although specialized facial classifiers for rare disorders already exist, ProtoGestalt offers an interpretable alternative tied to anatomically meaningful facial regions that could support clinical decision-making and phenotype-gene association discovery.

title: FreeOcc: Decoupling Ego-Motion for Efficient 4D Occupancy Forecasting via Continuous Flow Matching
summary: Current 4D occupancy world models use heavy cross-attention or deep recurrence to disentangle ego-motion from scene dynamics. This requires significant computational capacity. However, this effort is largely redundant since the ego-vehicle's intended future motion is provided by the downstream motion planner. We present FreeOcc, a lightweight continuous-time world model that introduces explicit $SE(2)$ geometric decoupling into a conditional flow-matching framework. By mathematically factoring out self-motion, we create a purely dynamic feature space. This space supports attention-free temporal fusion and allows physics-constrained ODEs to operate strictly on residual agent kinematics. To maximize deployment efficiency, FreeOcc introduces an uncertainty-aware blending mechanism. This routes well-observed voxels to a single-pass decoder, reserving the ODE solver exclusively for ambiguous, high-uncertainty regions. Requiring only 28.3M parameters-roughly 40% of comparable models-our optimal ensemble mode (FreeOcc-E) runs at 27 FPS. On nuScenes, FreeOcc achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance with a 0.47 m Near Field Chamfer Distance (NFCD) and 32.1% mIoU. Furthermore, the model transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI. It also proves highly robust, retaining 92.8% of its ideal mIoU under significant sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.

AI.tldr: FreeOcc is a lightweight continuous-time 4D occupancy world model that factors out ego-motion via SE(2) geometric decoupling inside a conditional flow-matching framework. With 28.3M parameters and an ensemble mode running at 27 FPS, it reports a 0.47 m NFCD and 32.1% mIoU on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Existing 4D occupancy world models use heavy cross-attention or deep recurrence to disentangle ego-motion from scene dynamics, which demands significant compute even though the ego-vehicle's future motion is supplied by the downstream planner.
AI.method: Explicit SE(2) geometric decoupling removes self-motion, yielding a purely dynamic feature space that supports attention-free temporal fusion and lets physics-constrained ODEs operate on residual agent kinematics. An uncertainty-aware blending mechanism routes well-observed voxels to a single-pass decoder and reserves the ODE solver for ambiguous, high-uncertainty regions.
AI.result: On nuScenes FreeOcc achieves a Near Field Chamfer Distance of 0.47 m and 32.1% mIoU with 28.3M parameters, roughly 40% of comparable models, and its ensemble mode FreeOcc-E runs at 27 FPS. It transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI and retains 92.8% of its ideal mIoU under significant sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.
AI.conclusion: Removing ego-motion before forecasting lets a compact, efficient model reach state-of-the-art forecasting performance and stay robust to sensor degradation.

title: Describe Your Facial Expressions by Linking Image Encoders and Large Language Models
summary: This paper presents a novel task of describing human facial expressions of a facial image in natural language, which captures the nuances of facial actions and emotional states beyond traditional emotion categories or facial action units (AUs). To achieve the facial expression captioning model, we propose a three-stage training framework that trains a vision-to-language model using synthesized image-text pairs and the BLIP-2 pre-training techniques. To overcome the challenge of missing training image-text pairs for facial expression captioning, we propose a strategy that involves synthesizing and combining captions using GPT-3.5 and existing annotations on either emotion categories or AUs. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in generating captions that describe details of facial actions and emotions, as well as the inferential relationship between them, even when those emotions are not present in the training data. It is also demonstrated that the vision-to-language task enhances the performance of the intermediate visual features on both AU detection and emotion classification tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces facial expression captioning, which describes facial expressions in natural language, and trains a vision-to-language model with a three-stage framework using synthesized image-text pairs and BLIP-2 pre-training techniques. The captioning task also improves intermediate visual features for action unit detection and emotion classification.
AI.motivation: Natural-language descriptions of facial actions and emotional states go beyond emotion categories or action units, but training image-text pairs for facial expression captioning are missing.
AI.method: GPT-3.5 synthesizes and combines captions from existing emotion-category or action-unit annotations to create training pairs, and a three-stage framework trains a vision-to-language model following BLIP-2 pre-training techniques.
AI.result: The experiments show the method generates captions that describe facial actions, emotions and the inferential relationship between them, including for emotions absent from the training data. The vision-to-language task also enhances the performance of intermediate visual features on AU detection and emotion classification.
AI.conclusion: Captions synthesized from existing annotations can train expressive facial-expression captioning models, and captioning can serve as a useful auxiliary task for facial analysis.

title: Fault-Guided Cross-Layer Prediction for Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
comment: 20 pages including appendix; 4 figures and 21 tables. Preprint
summary: Feature reconstruction is widely used for unsupervised industrial anomaly detection in the single-class setting, where only normal images from one product category are available for training. We propose a single-class detector that asks what information one block can pass to another. We treat the depth of a frozen vision transformer as a sequence of discrete transitions. A directed predictor learns a block-to-block hidden-state transition pointwise over tokens. Adjacent-layer cosine similarity exposes four sharp fault lines in DINOv2 ViT-L, separating stable depth segments. The deepest blocks retain semantic context but lose local detail; a prediction from deep or shallow sources to sensitive targets therefore exposes the information that cannot be transported. The fault structure fixes the source and target roles, and the same rule transfers to ViT-B and RADIO-B. We use a bounded foreground prior calibrated solely on training images: it attenuates background evidence without also erasing defects outside the estimated foreground. Using one predictor architecture and a common training-only calibration protocol, image AUROC is 99.75 on MVTec-AD, 99.42 on VisA and 94.27 on Real-IAD. On Real-IAD the object-level AUROC is 96.26. At 256x256 pixel resolution, P-AUROC/P-AUPRO are 98.46/95.97 on MVTec-AD, 99.21/96.12 on VisA and 99.26/96.59 on Real-IAD.

AI.tldr: The method treats the depth of a frozen vision transformer as a sequence of discrete transitions and learns block-to-block predictors whose failures expose information that cannot be transported, for single-class unsupervised anomaly detection. It reports image AUROC of 99.75 on MVTec-AD, 99.42 on VisA and 94.27 on Real-IAD.
AI.motivation: Feature reconstruction for single-class unsupervised industrial anomaly detection has no principled rule for which blocks should predict which, and the deepest blocks retain semantic context but lose local detail.
AI.method: Adjacent-layer cosine similarity exposes four sharp fault lines in DINOv2 ViT-L that separate stable depth segments, and a directed predictor learns block-to-block hidden-state transitions pointwise over tokens, from deep or shallow sources to sensitive targets. A bounded foreground prior calibrated on training images attenuates background evidence without erasing defects outside the estimated foreground. The same rule transfers to ViT-B and RADIO-B.
AI.result: Using one predictor architecture and a common training-only calibration protocol, image AUROC is 99.75 on MVTec-AD, 99.42 on VisA and 94.27 on Real-IAD, and object-level AUROC on Real-IAD is 96.26. At 256x256 resolution, P-AUROC/P-AUPRO are 98.46/95.97 on MVTec-AD, 99.21/96.12 on VisA and 99.26/96.59 on Real-IAD.
AI.conclusion: The fault structure of a frozen ViT's depth fixes the source and target roles for cross-layer prediction, giving strong single-class anomaly detection and localization across three benchmarks.

title: MCUFlowNet: Hardware-Aware Neural Architecture Search for Optical Flow on Microcontrollers
comment: Submitted to IEEE ISCAS 2027 (under review). 5 pages
summary: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: PACE-NAS is a macro-to-micro neural architecture search that decouples memory from latency to find MCUFlowNet optical flow models for microcontrollers. The fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76 times faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at 1.6% higher EPE and reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of simulated forest flights versus 41.8%.
AI.motivation: Dense optical flow would help small drones avoid obstacles, but few dense flow networks are designed for microcontrollers with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution.
AI.method: PACE-NAS fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM in a macro design and searches operators and depths in a micro design to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. Profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head, which replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers by 18%, while two lightweight context modules lower EPE without raising the peak.
AI.result: On a Grove Vision AI V2 board with an Ethos-U55 NPU, the fastest variant MCUFlowNet-S runs 1.76 times faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at 1.6% higher EPE. In simulated forest flights at 2 m/s it reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials versus 41.8% for the baseline. A searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17 times faster at similar accuracy on semantic segmentation.
AI.conclusion: Fixing peak SRAM in the macro design removes the memory constraint from the search, so Pareto-optimal microcontroller models can be found efficiently, and the approach also applies to semantic segmentation.

title: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling
comment: Accepted at WACV 2027. Copyright 2027 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses
summary: Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at this http URL.

AI.tldr: MedHiVE is a 3D medical vision-language model that routes vision and text tokens through a two-level Soft Mixture-of-Experts hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, trained with contrastive learning on 25,000+ CT scans. It consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on segmentation, classification and detection.
AI.motivation: Medical 3D scans and reports are hierarchical with diagnostic cues tied to specific anatomical regions, but most medical vision-language models ignore this structure; prior work uses direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing.
AI.method: Local image and text features are routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations, with contrastive learning aligning anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in one space using report-derived anatomy-level alignment.
AI.result: Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on three tasks: segmentation, classification and detection.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate the importance of hierarchical modeling for 3D medical vision-language learning, with dynamic slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales.

title: SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes
summary: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint.

AI.tldr: SplatAnything proposes Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm) for feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting, canonicalizing a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to give a more consistent spatial reference for predicting Gaussian attributes. It reports state-of-the-art performance, especially under large scene-scale and viewpoint variation.
AI.motivation: Existing feed-forward 3DGS methods normalize Gaussian attributes by a radial-distance statistic, but the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers still varies across scene scales and camera configurations, causing systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets and ambiguous supervision.
AI.method: The authors replace radial-distance normalization with GSNorm, which normalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing, and evaluate with a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels and extrapolated viewpoints.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint; the abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Canonicalizing Gaussian spacing removes a source of ambiguous supervision in feed-forward 3DGS, improving robustness across arbitrary scenes.

title: Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds
summary: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.

AI.tldr: Interactive Visual Gym is a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and simulated human users. Its IVG-Bench has 315 scenarios, and evaluated VLMs show substantial limitations, with the best model completing only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit.
AI.motivation: Visual interaction models that assist users during physical tasks must be evaluated in closed loop, since assistant responses change user behavior and outcomes, yet existing benchmarks rely on offline replay and cannot capture these effects.
AI.method: The authors contribute three simulators for cooking, household manipulation and mobile-interface tasks with human-aligned action spaces, plus a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant and injects controlled execution errors and out-of-plan behaviors; these form IVG-Bench with 315 interaction scenarios.
AI.result: The best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, with weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance and latency that is often too slow to prevent errors. The interaction-quality metric agrees with participant preferences at 78.5% in a human study. In a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B in the cooking environment.
AI.conclusion: The environments provide useful learning signals as well as evaluation, and closed-loop assessment exposes limitations that offline benchmarks miss.

title: ManimCode: Learning Visual Self-Correction for Educational Animation
summary: Manim supports precise, programmatic video generation, but a successfully rendered educational animation can still have visual defects, missing explanations, or incorrect content. Rendering does not directly identify the code changes needed to correct these visual failures, so feedback-driven revision is needed. Existing agentic frameworks use iterative rendering and revision but typically rely on large models, often proprietary. Existing Manim datasets primarily contain final programs and often lack quality verification and the trajectories of feedback and revisions needed to learn this refinement process. We introduce ManimData and ManimCode, a data and training framework for feedback-driven educational animation generation. We construct ManimData through a render-guided pipeline that iteratively generates, executes, reviews, and revises Manim programs with retrieved API documentation. Its 24,034 render-verified, quality-filtered records preserve intermediate programs, execution errors, visual critiques, and corrective revisions. We use role-conditioned supervised fine-tuning on these trajectories to train ManimCode, a single 4B model, to write, review, and revise animation programs. To improve correction of errors that differ from those in the collected trajectories, we then train the Reviser with reinforcement learning on self-generated states, using rendering outcomes and reference-free quality feedback. ManimCode achieves 96.6% and 97.0% render success on ManimData-test and ManimBench, compared with 52.6% and 82.0% for the untrained 4B model under the same inference setup, while also improving video quality scores from 2.48 to 2.94 and from 3.00 to 3.44. Integrating ManimCode into two long-form educational video generation systems increases completed videos from 19/117 to 107/117 and from 53/239 to 239/239, alongside improvements in educational effectiveness and visual quality.

AI.tldr: ManimCode introduces ManimData, 24,034 render-verified Manim trajectories with errors, critiques and revisions, and a single 4B model trained on them to write, review and revise educational animation code. The model reaches 96.6% and 97.0% render success on ManimData-test and ManimBench, versus 52.6% and 82.0% for the untrained 4B model.
AI.motivation: A rendered Manim animation can still contain visual defects, missing explanations or incorrect content, and rendering alone does not identify the code changes needed; existing agentic frameworks rely on large proprietary models, and existing datasets contain final programs without verification or revision trajectories.
AI.method: ManimData is built with a render-guided pipeline that iteratively generates, executes, reviews and revises programs with retrieved API documentation; role-conditioned supervised fine-tuning trains a 4B model on these trajectories, and the Reviser is then trained with reinforcement learning on self-generated states using rendering outcomes and reference-free quality feedback.
AI.result: ManimCode reaches 96.6% and 97.0% render success on ManimData-test and ManimBench, compared with 52.6% and 82.0% for the untrained 4B model, and raises video quality scores from 2.48 to 2.94 and from 3.00 to 3.44. Integrated into two long-form educational video systems, completed videos rise from 19/117 to 107/117 and from 53/239 to 239/239.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-based training with rendering feedback lets a small model perform reliable feedback-driven correction of educational animation code, improving completion and visual quality in downstream video generation.

title: InstantHand: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting for Animatable Hand Avatar Reconstruction from a Single Image
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: Hand avatar reconstruction typically relies on multi-view capture or per-subject optimization, limiting its scalability. We introduce InstantHand, a feed-forward framework that constructs an animatable 3D Gaussian hand avatar from a single image using off-the-shelf MANO, camera, and mask estimates, without test-time optimization. Image-averaged losses provide insufficient supervision for alpha leakage, which thickens thin finger contours. To address this issue, we propose a Soft Alpha Band regularizer that concentrates supervision on silhouette boundaries. Furthermore, colors regressed from image features can drift toward a learned prior even in observed regions. Our Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer preserves observed appearance by transferring source colors according to each Gaussian's rendering contribution, while completing unobserved regions using the learned prior conditioned on global source identity. InstantHand constructs an avatar in 2.84 seconds and renders at 161 FPS, matching per-subject-optimized baselines on InterHand2.6M and remaining competitive in zero-shot evaluation on HanCo.

AI.tldr: InstantHand is a feed-forward framework that builds an animatable 3D Gaussian hand avatar from a single image without test-time optimization. It builds an avatar in 2.84 seconds, renders at 161 FPS, and matches per-subject-optimized baselines on InterHand2.6M.
AI.motivation: Hand avatar reconstruction usually needs multi-view capture or per-subject optimization, which limits scalability; image-averaged losses also give insufficient supervision for alpha leakage that thickens thin finger contours, and regressed colors can drift toward a learned prior even in observed regions.
AI.method: The method uses off-the-shelf MANO, camera and mask estimates, a Soft Alpha Band regularizer that concentrates supervision on silhouette boundaries, and a Reliability-gated Appearance Transfer that copies source colors according to each Gaussian's rendering contribution while completing unobserved regions with a learned prior conditioned on global source identity.
AI.result: InstantHand constructs an avatar in 2.84 seconds and renders at 161 FPS, matches per-subject-optimized baselines on InterHand2.6M, and remains competitive in zero-shot evaluation on HanCo.
AI.conclusion: Feed-forward single-image reconstruction can reach the quality of optimization-based hand avatars while being fast and scalable.

title: OraRefer: Segmentation-Guided Multi-Photograph Fusion for Oral Cancer Screening with Guaranteed Patient-Level Sensitivity
summary: Oral cancer and the oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMD) that can precede it are visible on the oral mucosa, which makes smartphone photographs a promising tool for screening. Deep learning models for this task classify individual photographs. However, screening refers patients, not photographs: a patient is usually photographed several times, and the referral decision must miss no more than a set share of patients with disease. We propose OraRefer, a patient-level screening model that reads each photograph with a segmentation-guided foundation model that conditions its class decision on the predicted lesion, combines all photographs of a patient with risk factors, and refers through a threshold with a finite-sample sensitivity guarantee. The model localizes the mouth itself, so inference needs no annotation. On 3000 photographs of 714 patients, patient-level fusion reaches an AUROC of 0.919 and outperforms attention-based multiple-instance learning. At a 90% sensitivity target, OraRefer detects 95% of patients with OPMD or cancer and misses 3 of 61 patients with cancer, at a specificity of 0.610. Because the threshold is calibrated without retraining, each clinic can set its own guaranteed operating point on a local calibration sample.

AI.tldr: OraRefer is a patient-level oral cancer screening model that fuses all smartphone photographs of a patient with risk factors and refers patients through a threshold with a finite-sample sensitivity guarantee. On 3000 photographs of 714 patients it reaches an AUROC of 0.919 and, at a 90% sensitivity target, detects 95% of patients with OPMD or cancer.
AI.motivation: Deep learning screening models classify individual photographs, but screening decisions concern patients, who are usually photographed several times, and referral must miss no more than a set share of patients with disease.
AI.method: OraRefer reads each photograph with a segmentation-guided foundation model that conditions the class decision on the predicted lesion, combines photographs of a patient with risk factors, and refers through a threshold with a finite-sample sensitivity guarantee; the model localizes the mouth itself, so inference needs no annotation.
AI.result: Patient-level fusion reaches an AUROC of 0.919 and outperforms attention-based multiple-instance learning. At a 90% sensitivity target, OraRefer detects 95% of patients with OPMD or cancer and misses 3 of 61 patients with cancer, at a specificity of 0.610.
AI.conclusion: Because the threshold is calibrated without retraining, each clinic can set its own guaranteed operating point using a local calibration sample.

title: Adaptive Low-Light Enhancement for Road Anomaly Detection: A Multi-Architecture Benchmark and Edge Deployment Study
summary: Road anomaly detection systems on autonomous vehicles must function reliably under degraded visual conditions including darkness, rain, and Harmattan dust haze. This paper benchmarks four object detection architectures, YOLOv8n, YOLOv12n, RT-DETR, and Faster R-CNN, under physically grounded lighting and weather degradation, and shows that uniform application of the SCI low-light enhancement network is actively harmful at dusk-level lighting (-16.1% to -30.7% mAP@50). We propose a lightweight, training-free luminance-adaptive router that selects between no enhancement, moderate SCI, and denoising plus strong SCI based on per-frame Rec. 601 luminance, recovering most of the dusk penalty while preserving low-light gains, and we validate the full pipeline on NVIDIA Jetson Nano edge hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks YOLOv8n, YOLOv12n, RT-DETR and Faster R-CNN under physically grounded lighting and weather degradation for road anomaly detection. It shows that uniform SCI low-light enhancement is harmful at dusk, and proposes a training-free luminance-adaptive router validated on Jetson Nano edge hardware.
AI.motivation: Road anomaly detection on autonomous vehicles must work in darkness, rain and Harmattan dust haze, but uniformly applying the SCI low-light enhancement network can hurt detection under dusk-level lighting.
AI.method: The authors propose a lightweight, training-free luminance-adaptive router that selects among no enhancement, moderate SCI, and denoising plus strong SCI based on per-frame Rec. 601 luminance.
