AI.result: Uniform SCI enhancement reduces mAP@50 by 16.1% to 30.7% at dusk-level lighting; the router recovers most of this dusk penalty while preserving low-light gains, and the full pipeline is validated on NVIDIA Jetson Nano edge hardware.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, per-frame selection of enhancement is needed for robust and deployable road anomaly detection under degraded visual conditions.

title: SM4RT: Cascaded Feed-forward Model for 4D Reconstruction
summary: We introduce SM4RT, a multi-task cascade feed-forward model for dynamic scene reconstruction from RGB videos. While existing feed-forward approaches typically address geometry reconstruction and motion estimation separately--and often predict motions in a single coordinate frame that must account for camera movement--SM4RT solves these tasks sequentially by first reconstructing 3D geometry and then bootstrapping motion estimation from the predicted structure. By expressing each pixel's 3D motion in its corresponding camera frame, SM4RT reduces ambiguity arising from camera motion. To address the sparsity of real-world motion labels, SM4RT further incorporates a weakly supervised loss that regularizes unlabeled point motions using labeled point positions at the other time step. We evaluate motion estimation on three dynamic-scene datasets--Kubric, Waymo, and Point Odyssey--and SM4RT achieves the best performance on most metrics compared with prior baselines. We additionally benchmark geometry reconstruction on five dynamic scene datasets and show that SM4RT achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Overall, our unified framework demonstrates that combining geometry reconstruction and motion estimation in a cascade not only avoids performance trade-offs but also enhances motion estimation through improved geometric reasoning.

AI.tldr: SM4RT is a cascaded feed-forward model that reconstructs dynamic scenes from RGB videos by first estimating 3D geometry and then bootstrapping motion from the predicted structure. It achieves the best motion estimation on most metrics across three datasets and competitive geometry reconstruction on five.
AI.motivation: Existing feed-forward approaches handle geometry and motion separately and often predict motion in a single coordinate frame that must account for camera movement, while real-world motion labels are sparse.
AI.method: SM4RT expresses each pixel's 3D motion in its corresponding camera frame to reduce ambiguity from camera motion, solves geometry before motion in a cascade, and adds a weakly supervised loss that regularizes unlabeled point motions using labeled point positions at the other time step.
AI.result: Motion estimation is evaluated on Kubric, Waymo and Point Odyssey, where SM4RT achieves the best performance on most metrics compared with prior baselines; geometry reconstruction on five dynamic scene datasets is competitive with state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining geometry reconstruction and motion estimation in a cascade avoids performance trade-offs and improves motion estimation through better geometric reasoning.

title: Edge-Assisted Crowdsensing for Explainable Cyclist Safety Perception
summary: Cyclist fatality rates remain high despite policy support for active travel, and autonomous vehicles add complexity to mixed traffic. Neither crash statistics nor multi-model detection pipelines scale to continuous monitoring of perceived safety along a route. We present an edge-assisted crowdsensing system: handlebar cameras supply street-level frames, a vision-language model (VLM) turns each frame into structured traffic attributes through a single prompt, and an explainable boosting machine (EBM) combines them with OpenStreetMap road infrastructure and on-bike kinematics to predict a crowdsourced 1-9 safety score. Extraction belongs at the network edge: the fastest self-hosted model needs 2.49 s per frame and scoring takes 0.4 ms on a CPU. On 1,362 annotated frames from two London routes, the EBM regressor reaches 72.2 percent binary accuracy and a mean absolute error of 1.011 under five-fold cross-validation. It is within one accuracy point of black-box ensembles. Its per-feature shape functions give exact attribution: physical lane separation is worth +0.97 rating points, a painted lane +0.70 and a construction site -0.65. Planners can therefore price an infrastructure change in rating points, and the results enter cost-benefit analysis directly. We also report inter-annotator agreement (alpha = 0.4695), an attribute audit, and a sensitivity analysis linking attribute error to accuracy. With re-encoding, a 20 s sampling interval serves 1,000 riders at 54 Mbit/s at a cost of 1.4 accuracy points, making continuous monitoring practical.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an edge-assisted crowdsensing system in which a VLM turns handlebar-camera frames into traffic attributes and an explainable boosting machine predicts a crowdsourced 1-9 cyclist safety score. On 1,362 annotated frames from two London routes it reaches 72.2% binary accuracy and a mean absolute error of 1.011.
AI.motivation: Crash statistics and multi-model detection pipelines do not scale to continuous monitoring of perceived cyclist safety along a route.
AI.method: Handlebar cameras supply street-level frames, a VLM extracts structured traffic attributes through a single prompt, and an explainable boosting machine (EBM) combines these with OpenStreetMap road infrastructure and on-bike kinematics; extraction runs at the network edge, with a 20 s sampling interval and re-encoding considered for bandwidth.
AI.result: The EBM regressor reaches 72.2% binary accuracy and a mean absolute error of 1.011 under five-fold cross-validation, within one accuracy point of black-box ensembles. The fastest self-hosted model needs 2.49 s per frame and scoring takes 0.4 ms on a CPU. Per-feature shape functions give physical lane separation +0.97 rating points, a painted lane +0.70 and a construction site -0.65. Inter-annotator agreement is alpha = 0.4695, and a 20 s interval serves 1,000 riders at 54 Mbit/s at a cost of 1.4 accuracy points.
AI.conclusion: The interpretable model lets planners price infrastructure changes in rating points for direct use in cost-benefit analysis, and makes continuous monitoring practical.

title: EgoGeneralist: Unifying Egocentric Action-Video Tasks through Video-Native Modeling
summary: Modern video models possess strong visual priors, yet do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space. We present EgoGeneralist, which adapts pretrained video generators to unify action-conditioned egocentric video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation. Our role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, making metric motion usable as both a spatial control signal and a recoverable generation target. Cross-stream action-video coupling establishes close correspondence between metric motion and visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior. Together, these designs establish a generalist framework spanning five action-video tasks. Despite adaptation only on controlled laboratory recordings, EgoGeneralist generalizes to diverse unseen scenes and interactions with effective action control and visual quality, bridging pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion.

AI.tldr: EgoGeneralist adapts pretrained video generators into a single framework for five action-video tasks, including action-conditioned egocentric video generation, pose estimation and joint action-video generation. It is adapted only on controlled laboratory recordings and generalizes to unseen scenes and interactions.
AI.motivation: Modern video models have strong visual priors but do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space.
AI.method: A role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, so metric motion serves both as a spatial control signal and as a recoverable generation target; cross-stream action-video coupling aligns metric motion with visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior.
AI.result: The abstract reports effective action control and visual quality on diverse unseen scenes and interactions, with no specific numbers stated.
AI.conclusion: The framework bridges pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion within one generalist model.

title: Where and Why is Grounded Reasoning Useful?
summary: Grounded reasoning, where a model outputs text coordinates of relevant locations in chain-of-thought reasoning, is a common strategy for solving complex visual reasoning problems. However, the benefits and limitations of grounded reasoning are understudied. We study where and why grounded reasoning is most useful. To do so, we introduce a chain-of-thought analysis method to measure how much a model uses its outputted grounding in its thinking trace and perform a detailed ablation study of a grounded reasoning training recipe. We find that grounded reasoning improves counting but shows no significant gain over baselines without coordinate grounding across a wide range of spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks. Using several synthetic tasks, we show that grounded reasoning is most useful when a task requires undescribable references, which are visual concepts that are difficult to describe in language. However, we observe that many existing visual reasoning benchmarks are solvable with only describable text references. To close this gap, we introduce BrickVision, a new benchmark that requires undescribable visual references to solve.

AI.tldr: The paper studies where grounded reasoning, in which a model outputs text coordinates in chain-of-thought, helps visual reasoning. It finds gains mainly on counting and on references that are hard to describe in language, and introduces BrickVision, a benchmark that requires undescribable visual references.
AI.motivation: The benefits and limitations of grounded reasoning are understudied, and many existing visual reasoning benchmarks can be solved with describable text references alone.
AI.method: The authors introduce a chain-of-thought analysis method that measures how much a model uses its own outputted grounding in its thinking trace, perform a detailed ablation of a grounded reasoning training recipe, run synthetic tasks, and build the BrickVision benchmark.
AI.result: Grounded reasoning improves counting but shows no significant gain over baselines without coordinate grounding across a wide range of spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks; it is most useful when a task requires undescribable visual references.
AI.conclusion: Grounded reasoning helps most for visual concepts that resist verbal description, so benchmarks that test it must require such references, which BrickVision provides.

title: Do You Miss the Nights We Spent Crafting Figures? Rethinking Teaser and Framework Figures in the Age of Generative AI
summary: Scientific figures give research ideas a visual form through choices of abstraction, composition, and emphasis. Generative AI offers new ways to realize these choices, raising questions about explanatory clarity and purposeful visual expression. We examine these questions through a visual retrospective of 371 motivation and framework figures from 200 papers. The corpus comprises a quota-based main sample of 160 papers spanning four temporal periods and a separate purposive style-contrast sample of 40 papers. A single multimodal judge evaluates six dimensions of communication and design, with three repeated judgments per figure. We attempt source-constrained revisions of all 371 figures, of which 369 pass the recorded fidelity checks. Original-figure ratings show no uniform decline across periods. Revisions increase mean clarity ratings by 0.428 points and decrease aesthetic coherence ratings by 0.111 points on a five-point scale. Gains in the six-dimension average are larger for main-sample motivation figures than for frameworks. Case analyses show that added explanation can clarify comparisons while leaving typographic hierarchy and visual economy unresolved. These model-based findings support researcher-led design, with AI assisting exploration and authors retaining responsibility for explanatory purpose, composition, and scientific relationships. The accompanying atlas and evaluation records are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: A visual retrospective of 371 motivation and framework figures from 200 papers finds that source-constrained generative AI revisions raise clarity ratings by 0.428 points but lower aesthetic coherence by 0.111 on a five-point scale. The authors argue that AI should assist exploration while researchers keep responsibility for explanatory purpose.
AI.motivation: Generative AI offers new ways to realize abstraction, composition and emphasis in scientific figures, raising questions about explanatory clarity and purposeful visual expression.
AI.method: A single multimodal judge rates six dimensions of communication and design, three times per figure, on a quota-based main sample of 160 papers across four temporal periods and a purposive style-contrast sample of 40 papers; the authors then attempt source-constrained revisions of all 371 figures.
AI.result: Of the 371 revisions, 369 pass the recorded fidelity checks. Original-figure ratings show no uniform decline across periods. Revisions increase mean clarity by 0.428 points and decrease aesthetic coherence by 0.111 points; six-dimension gains are larger for main-sample motivation figures than for frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Model-based findings support researcher-led design, with AI assisting exploration while authors keep responsibility for explanatory purpose, composition and scientific relationships, since added explanation can leave typographic hierarchy and visual economy unresolved.

title: Category differences in similarity between fixation density maps and psychological potential fields for sketches
summary: When an object comes into view, humans can instantaneously recognize it if known to them. However, assessing how this recognition takes place remains challenging. A few studies using simple sketches have reported varying degrees of image similarity between the fixation density map (FDM), which visualizes eye movements and durations, and the psychological potential field (PPF), which visualizes part of the visual cognition process, depending on the object category. This study reports how the similarity behaves across three categories---animal, non-animal, and meaningless shape---and under rotated presentation, which is known to increase cognitive load during object recognition. The similarity was quantified through area under the curve (AUC) measures, including a baseline-adjusted AUC that isolates the early rise in similarity from stimulus-dependent baseline levels. A variability score was introduced to assess individual differences, and linear mixed models were used to evaluate category and orientation effects. Results indicated that the baseline-adjusted AUC yielded significant differences among all three categories with large effect sizes, whereas the raw AUC did not distinguish between the animal and non-animal categories due to the influence of sketch representation. No significant Category $\times$ Orientation interaction was observed, indicating that rotated presentation did not produce a category-specific effect. The meaningless shape stimuli yielded consistently low similarity and variability scores, clearly separating them from the two meaningful object categories. These results characterize the behavior of the FDM--PPF similarity under free viewing and indicate that baseline adjustment is necessary to separate category-related variation from stimulus-dependent baseline levels.

AI.tldr: The study measures similarity between fixation density maps and psychological potential fields for sketches across animal, non-animal and meaningless shape categories, with and without rotation. A baseline-adjusted AUC separates all three categories with large effect sizes, while the raw AUC cannot separate animal from non-animal sketches.
AI.motivation: Previous studies using simple sketches reported varying similarity between eye-movement fixation density maps and psychological potential fields depending on object category, and it remains challenging to assess how recognition takes place.
AI.method: Similarity is quantified with area under the curve (AUC) measures, including a baseline-adjusted AUC that isolates the early rise from stimulus-dependent baseline levels; a variability score captures individual differences, and linear mixed models test category and orientation effects.
AI.result: The baseline-adjusted AUC gives significant differences among all three categories with large effect sizes, while the raw AUC does not distinguish animal from non-animal categories. No significant Category x Orientation interaction appears. Meaningless shapes yield consistently low similarity and variability scores, clearly separating them from the two meaningful categories.
AI.conclusion: Baseline adjustment is necessary to separate category-related variation from stimulus-dependent baseline levels when characterizing FDM-PPF similarity under free viewing.

title: An Evolutionary Hypothesis for White's Illusion: Constant Percentage Correction and Modern Individual Variation
comment: 12 pages and 7 figures. We may later send a shorter version to a conference
summary: White's illusion is a striking demonstration of context-dependent brightness and lightness perception. In earlier work, we developed a forward translucency-based formula capable of producing approximately constant perceived appearance across varying backgrounds. While validating that formulation, we observed a notable population-level pattern: individuals selected slightly different correction percentages for "constant perception," while the population average remained remarkably stable across experiments. In this paper, we propose an evolutionary hypothesis for this phenomenon. We suggest that a simple constant-percentage correction function could have emerged as an adaptive mechanism for maintaining useful material and reflectance judgments under variable illumination. Under this interpretation, the stability of the population mean may reflect a conserved perceptual mechanism, whereas individual differences may reflect learning, adaptation, or variation around a shared computational response. Using a modification of our previously published forward model, we show that White's illusion can be reproduced by applying a constant-percentage correction to background luminance. The model therefore provides a compact computational account of the observed population-level regularity and motivates a testable evolutionary interpretation of individual variation in contextual lightness judgments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an evolutionary hypothesis for White's illusion, in which a constant-percentage correction of background luminance could be an adaptive mechanism for stable material and reflectance judgments under variable illumination. A modification of the authors' forward model reproduces the illusion with this correction.
AI.motivation: Individuals choose slightly different correction percentages for constant perception, while the population average stays stable across experiments, and this population-level regularity needs an explanation.
AI.method: The authors use a modification of their previously published translucency-based forward model and apply a constant-percentage correction to background luminance to reproduce White's illusion.
AI.result: White's illusion can be reproduced by applying a constant-percentage correction to background luminance, providing a compact computational account of the stable population mean; the abstract reports no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The stable population mean may reflect a conserved perceptual mechanism while individual variation reflects learning, adaptation or variation around a shared response, which motivates a testable evolutionary interpretation.

title: FFMT: Frequency-Factorized Multi-Rate Tokenization for Music-to-Dance Generation
summary: Dance motion combines slowly varying body configurations with rapid local movements. We investigate how explicit temporal-frequency decomposition can guide the temporal resolution and codebook capacity of discrete motion representations. We introduce frequency-factorized motion tokenization (FFMT), which separates root-relative motion into a low-frequency choreographic scaffold and a complementary high-frequency residual. FFMT uses a lower token rate and a smaller codebook for the low-frequency component, and a higher token rate and a larger codebook for the high-frequency residual. This representation further induces a plan-then-articulate autoregressive factorization: low-frequency tokens establish coarse choreography, while high-frequency tokens realize local motion details conditioned on the generated plan and music. Experiments on AIST++ and FineDance show strong distributional fidelity while preserving realistic diversity and music--motion synchronization. Ablations consistently support frequency factorization, asymmetric temporal allocation, and low-to-high conditioning.

AI.tldr: FFMT factorizes root-relative dance motion into a low-frequency choreographic scaffold and a high-frequency residual, tokenizing each with its own token rate and codebook size. It uses a plan-then-articulate autoregressive generator for music-to-dance generation and shows strong distributional fidelity on AIST++ and FineDance.
AI.motivation: Dance motion combines slowly varying body configurations with rapid local movements, and discrete motion representations need temporal resolution and codebook capacity suited to each.
AI.method: Low-frequency tokens use a lower token rate and smaller codebook, high-frequency residual tokens use a higher rate and larger codebook, and high-frequency tokens are generated conditioned on the low-frequency plan and music.
AI.result: Experiments on AIST++ and FineDance show strong distributional fidelity while preserving realistic diversity and music-motion synchronization; ablations support frequency factorization, asymmetric temporal allocation and low-to-high conditioning.
AI.conclusion: Explicit temporal-frequency decomposition is an effective guide for discrete motion tokenization in music-to-dance generation.

title: Kinematic Hypothesis Context: Embodiment-Conditioned Learned Video Coding for Bandwidth-Limited Robot Policy Uplinks
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures. Preprint; supplementary material and code to be released upon formal publication
summary: Robots increasingly run large vision-language-action policies on remote servers, making the camera uplink the bottleneck. Existing video codecs spend bits on content the receiver could predict: the robot's own motion. We introduce the kinematic hypothesis context, a zero-rate conditioning signal that both ends build from joint states, the robot model and the camera calibration. Ego-motion homographies, per-link robot reprojections, an end-effector plane and a background memory warp the previous reconstruction into hypotheses that condition a learned video codec. We prove that history-only and global-pose conditioning with a limited receptive field cannot access this information under large motion, and that coding gains become task gains at the policy's success cliff. On LIBERO, the context saves 23.9% bit rate over a capacity-matched history-conditioned codec and 40-56% over x264, x265 and SVT-AV1, and needs 23.2% fewer bits than DCVC-RT at equal policy action deviation; trained to lower rates, it matches DCVC-RT in PSNR. In closed loop at equal rate, OpenVLA-OFT success nearly doubles from 22.8% to 43.1% at 6 kbps (72.6% with lower-rate training, 23.6 points above DCVC-RT), pi_0.5 success rises from 55.5% to 77.4%, and the gain grows under packet loss. The context transfers across three codec hosts and to real robot data.

AI.tldr: The kinematic hypothesis context is a zero-rate conditioning signal, built from joint states, the robot model and camera calibration, that lets a learned video codec skip robot self-motion when coding camera uplinks for remote VLA policies. It saves 23.9% bit rate over a capacity-matched history-conditioned codec and 40-56% over x264, x265 and SVT-AV1 on LIBERO.
AI.motivation: Robots increasingly run large vision-language-action policies on remote servers, making the camera uplink the bottleneck, and existing codecs spend bits on content the receiver could predict from the robot's own motion.
AI.method: Ego-motion homographies, per-link robot reprojections, an end-effector plane and a background memory warp the previous reconstruction into hypotheses that condition a learned video codec; the authors prove that history-only and global-pose conditioning with a limited receptive field cannot access this information under large motion.
AI.result: On LIBERO the context needs 23.2% fewer bits than DCVC-RT at equal policy action deviation. In closed loop at equal rate, OpenVLA-OFT success rises from 22.8% to 43.1% at 6 kbps (72.6% with lower-rate training) and pi_0.5 success rises from 55.5% to 77.4%, with larger gains under packet loss. The context transfers across three codec hosts and to real robot data.
AI.conclusion: Coding gains translate into task gains at the policy's success cliff, so embodiment-conditioned context is a practical route to bandwidth-limited robot policy uplinks.

title: MessyNav: Zero-Shot Navigation via Manipulation in Messy Environments
summary: Real-world environments are messy, with paths often blocked by everyday objects like chairs and toys, requiring robots to perform interactive navigation by manipulating obstacles to clear a path. Existing methods rely on extensive simulation-based learning or per-scene instructions specifying which objects to avoid or manipulate. They struggle to generalize across novel objects, diverse environments, and varied contexts such as a cart of fragile glassware that should be avoided while an empty one can be pushed. We formalize this problem as open-world interactive navigation and present MessyNav, a zero-shot framework based on vision-language models (VLMs). At its core, MessyNav performs explicit VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning to decide whether to swipe, pick up, or avoid an object and produce a high-level plan. Evaluated on a mobile manipulator across real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav improves success rate by 27 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials and achieves statistically significant gains in a larger-scale offline evaluation, without task-specific training.

AI.tldr: MessyNav is a zero-shot framework that lets mobile manipulators navigate by manipulating obstacles such as chairs and toys in messy environments. It performs VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning, and improves success rate by 27 percentage points over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials.
AI.motivation: Existing methods rely on extensive simulation learning or per-scene instructions and struggle to generalize to novel objects, diverse environments and context-dependent choices, such as avoiding fragile glassware while pushing an empty cart.
AI.method: The authors formalize open-world interactive navigation and use VLM-based affordance reasoning to decide whether to swipe, pick up or avoid each object before producing a high-level plan, without task-specific training.
AI.result: Evaluated on a mobile manipulator in real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav improves success rate by 27 percentage points over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials and achieves statistically significant gains in a larger offline evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Explicit affordance reasoning before planning enables zero-shot interactive navigation that generalizes across objects and environments.

title: FREE-LIVO: Physically Decoupled Yet Tightly Coupled LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry
summary: LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry (LIVO) integrates complementary LiDAR, camera, and IMU measurements to achieve robust state estimation. However, most existing methods assume a fixed relative pose and accurate time synchronization between sensors. Toward modular and heterogeneous robotic systems, this paper presents FREE-LIVO, a tightly coupled odometry method that requires neither a rigid LiDAR-camera rig nor LiDAR-camera time synchronization. The proposed method uses a pretrained image feature matcher to establish correspondences between a camera image and a dense LiDAR intensity image generated from a single LiDAR scan using a generative model. From the resulting 3D point-to-pixel correspondences, we construct reprojection factors that directly constrain LiDAR and camera poses at different acquisition times. These factors are jointly optimized in a single factor graph together with constraints from point cloud registration, visual feature tracking, and the IMU measurements associated with each sensor. On six sequences from the public M3DGR dataset, FREE-LIVO achieves an average absolute trajectory error (ATE) RMSE of 0.45 m without provided LiDAR-camera extrinsic parameters and exhibits minimal accuracy degradation under time synchronization errors of up to 0.5 s. Furthermore, experiments with the LiDAR and camera mounted on separate robots demonstrate that the method can jointly estimate the trajectories of independently moving sensors.

AI.tldr: FREE-LIVO is a tightly coupled LiDAR-inertial-visual odometry method that needs neither a rigid LiDAR-camera rig nor LiDAR-camera time synchronization. It reaches an average ATE RMSE of 0.45 m on six M3DGR sequences without provided extrinsics and tolerates time offsets of up to 0.5 s.
AI.motivation: Most LIVO methods assume a fixed relative pose and accurate time synchronization between sensors, which limits modular and heterogeneous robotic systems.
AI.method: A pretrained image feature matcher establishes correspondences between a camera image and a dense LiDAR intensity image generated from a single scan by a generative model; the resulting 3D point-to-pixel correspondences give reprojection factors that constrain LiDAR and camera poses at different acquisition times, optimized in one factor graph with point cloud registration, visual tracking and IMU constraints.
AI.result: On six M3DGR sequences the method achieves an average ATE RMSE of 0.45 m without provided LiDAR-camera extrinsic parameters, with minimal accuracy degradation under time synchronization errors of up to 0.5 s; experiments with sensors on separate robots jointly estimate their trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The method enables joint state estimation for independently moving LiDAR and camera sensors without rigid mounting or synchronization.

title: Learning Robotic World Models with Semantic and Visual Feedback
comment: 27 pages, including supplementary material. Project and code: this https URL . Data and weights: this https URL
summary: Robot world models predict action-conditioned future visual states to support robotic planning and decision making. However, visual reconstruction does not fully capture task progress, semantic evaluation alone provides limited constraints on fine-grained visual errors, and homogeneous predictions limit comparative feedback. We present RoboImagine, a framework for post-training autoregressive robotic world models through candidate-future comparisons with semantic and visual feedback. Diverse search promotes diversity among candidate trajectories under shared visual observations, action sequences, and task instructions. A frozen multimodal evaluator provides task-relevant semantic preferences through pairwise video comparisons in both presentation orders, complemented by pixel- and perceptual-level visual consistency feedback that constrains local structural and appearance errors. These signals drive policy optimization through group-relative advantages. Fixed initial context and branch-specific rolling histories support long-sequence generation with bounded context and consistent conditioning between candidate generation and policy optimization. Experiments with separately trained models on RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa cover real-world and simulated manipulation. On RT-1, under matched initialization, update counts, and evaluation protocols, RoboImagine improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning. Ablations show that diverse search improves prediction quality and that combined semantic and visual feedback yields higher external multimodal evaluation scores than visual feedback alone while maintaining comparable visual fidelity. Rolling histories further improve long-horizon prediction. These results support improving visual fidelity, task relevance, and long-horizon prediction through candidate comparison and complementary feedback.

AI.tldr: RoboImagine post-trains autoregressive robotic world models using candidate-future comparisons with semantic and visual feedback, combining a frozen multimodal evaluator with pixel and perceptual consistency signals. On RT-1 it improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Visual reconstruction does not fully capture task progress, semantic evaluation constrains fine-grained visual errors only weakly, and homogeneous predictions limit comparative feedback.
AI.method: Diverse search promotes diversity among candidate trajectories under shared observations, actions and instructions; a frozen multimodal evaluator gives pairwise semantic preferences in both presentation orders, complemented by pixel and perceptual consistency feedback; these signals drive policy optimization with group-relative advantages, and fixed initial context with branch-specific rolling histories supports long-sequence generation.
AI.result: On RT-1, under matched initialization, update counts and evaluation protocols, RoboImagine improves PSNR by 1.26 dB and reduces LPIPS by 11.93% relative to continued supervised fine-tuning. Ablations show diverse search improves prediction quality and combined semantic and visual feedback gives higher external multimodal evaluation scores than visual feedback alone, with comparable visual fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Candidate comparison with complementary feedback improves visual fidelity, task relevance and long-horizon prediction of robotic world models.

title: Reinforcing End-to-End Autonomous Driving Safety via Negative-Aware Planning in a Unified World-Action Model
summary: World-action models (WAMs) jointly model future traffic states and driving actions for end-to-end autonomous driving in intelligent transportation systems. However, their action learning remains dominated by expert-trajectory imitation, leaving unsafe alternatives close to expert trajectories insufficiently constrained. To improve WAM robustness in safety-critical scenarios, we propose NegWAM, a safety post-training framework for unified WAMs that learns explicit safety boundaries from near-expert failure trajectories. NegWAM constructs negative trajectories that are geometrically close to the expert trajectory yet carry safety risks, uses them as repulsive anchors to steer predictions away from dangerous behavior, and encodes them as scene-conditioned rider tokens to learn scene--trajectory compatibility. During training, NegWAM jointly optimizes the flow-matching and near-expert negative objectives, while the auxiliary rider branch is discarded at inference, incurring no additional overhead. On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1% relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and achieves 93.3 EPDMS on navtest. These results demonstrate that NegWAM achieves strong performance in safety-critical scenarios while preserving routine-driving performance. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM further demonstrates cross-benchmark generalization. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: NegWAM is a safety post-training framework for unified world-action models that learns explicit safety boundaries from near-expert failure trajectories used as repulsive anchors. It achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1% relative gain over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and 93.3 EPDMS on navtest on NAVSIM v2.
AI.motivation: World-action models learn action from expert imitation, which leaves unsafe alternatives close to expert trajectories insufficiently constrained in safety-critical driving scenarios.
AI.method: NegWAM builds negative trajectories geometrically close to the expert but carrying safety risk, encodes them as scene-conditioned rider tokens, and jointly optimizes the flow-matching objective with a near-expert negative objective; the rider branch is discarded at inference, adding no overhead.
AI.result: On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1% relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and 93.3 EPDMS on navtest. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM shows cross-benchmark generalization.
AI.conclusion: The approach achieves strong safety-critical performance while preserving routine-driving performance, at no extra inference cost.

title: Aligning Policy Encoders with a Shape Teacher
summary: 3D-aware representations can improve robotic manipulation by providing geometric information that is robust to changes in viewpoint, object position, and occlusion. However, using 3D inputs at deployment requires additional sensing and processing, making image-based policies more practical. We ask whether an image-based policy can acquire 3D shape information during training while retaining a purely image-based interface at deployment. We propose shape-teacher alignment, a training-time mechanism that uses a pretrained 3D shape representation as an alignment target for an image-based policy encoder. Specifically, we use Point-MAE features from individual objects as targets for corresponding image patches, transferring geometric structure to the policy without changing its deployment inputs or architecture. On LIBERO, shape-teacher alignment produces image representations that are more structured around object shape and corresponding parts, while substantially accelerating policy convergence and improving success rates. For pretrained policies, convergence is accelerated by 4.7x and 5.6x on the Object and Spatial suites, respectively, without requiring the shape teacher or depth input at deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes shape-teacher alignment, a training-time method that aligns an image-based policy encoder with Point-MAE 3D shape features, so the policy learns 3D shape structure while keeping an image-only interface at deployment. On LIBERO it yields more shape-structured representations, faster convergence and higher success rates.
AI.motivation: 3D-aware representations help robotic manipulation, but using 3D inputs at deployment needs extra sensing and processing, which makes image-based policies more practical; the open question is whether an image policy can acquire 3D shape information during training alone.
AI.method: Shape-teacher alignment uses features from a pretrained 3D shape model (Point-MAE), computed per individual object, as alignment targets for the corresponding image patches of the policy encoder, leaving deployment inputs and architecture unchanged.
AI.result: On LIBERO, the aligned encoders are more structured around object shape and parts and substantially accelerate policy convergence and improve success rates; for pretrained policies, convergence is 4.7x faster on the Object suite and 5.6x faster on the Spatial suite, without a shape teacher or depth input at deployment.
AI.conclusion: Geometric knowledge from a 3D teacher can be transferred into an image-only policy during training, giving some of the benefits of 3D perception without its deployment cost.

title: A Theoretical Analysis of a Bilevel Optimization Formulation for Combined Local-Global Optical Flow Models
comment: 31 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Mathematical Imaging and Vision. Python code in the ancillary files
summary: This paper analyzes a bilevel formulation for learning the regularization parameter of combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models. The lower-level problem computes the flow from a Lucas--Kanade data term and a quadratic or total variation (TV) regularizer, and the upper-level problem selects the parameter that minimizes the squared distance to a ground-truth flow. The setting is finite-dimensional, and a full-rank assumption makes the lower-level solution unique. For the quadratic model we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of an optimal parameter, for every optimal parameter to be positive, and for strict local optimality. For TV regularization an optimal parameter always exists, because the lower-level solution vanishes for large parameters, and we give a sufficient condition for positivity that accounts for the coupling of the two flow components through the local structure tensors. Synthetic examples illustrate the conditions, including cases in which they fail.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a theoretical analysis of a bilevel formulation that learns the regularization parameter of combined local-global (CLG) optical flow models with quadratic or total variation regularizers. It derives existence, positivity and local optimality conditions for the optimal parameter, illustrated on synthetic examples.
AI.motivation: Learning the regularization parameter of CLG optical flow models from ground-truth flow is posed as a bilevel problem, and its theoretical behaviour needs to be understood.
AI.method: The lower level computes the flow from a Lucas-Kanade data term and a quadratic or TV regularizer, with a full-rank assumption that makes the solution unique; the upper level selects the parameter that minimizes the squared distance to the ground-truth flow.
AI.result: For the quadratic model, sufficient conditions are derived for the existence of an optimal parameter, for every optimal parameter to be positive, and for strict local optimality; for TV, an optimal parameter always exists, and a sufficient positivity condition is given that accounts for coupling through local structure tensors. Synthetic examples illustrate the conditions, including cases where they fail.
AI.conclusion: The analysis clarifies when the learned parameter exists, is positive and is locally optimal, giving theoretical grounding for bilevel learning of CLG flow regularization in a finite-dimensional setting.

title: VisionSIM: Beyond Idealized Sensors - A Multi-Modal Simulator for Robot Perception
summary: Robotic perception increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensor suites combining cameras with emerging modalities (event, SPAD, iToF/dToF, and thermal). Yet existing simulators idealize these sensors, hiding critical modality-specific failure modes that limit real-world deployment. We present VisionSIM, a unified, physically grounded simulation platform that elevates sensor realism to a first-class concern by modeling the raw physical measurement process for diverse conventional and emerging modalities. We expose fine-grained control over physical sensor parameters, reproducing failure modes overlooked by general-purpose simulators: pileup and glare for LiDAR; phase wrapping, saturation, and motion artifacts for iToF; refractory drops for event cameras; and history-dependent emission for thermal cameras. This enables principled cross-modality comparison on identical scenes and trajectories. We release the platform and a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and rich ground-truth annotations.

AI.tldr: VisionSIM is a unified, physically grounded simulator that models the raw measurement process of conventional and emerging robot sensors (event, SPAD, iToF/dToF, thermal) instead of idealized sensing. It also releases a large indoor dataset with synchronized raw measurements and ground-truth annotations.
AI.motivation: Existing simulators idealize heterogeneous sensors, which hides modality-specific failure modes that limit real-world deployment of robot perception.
AI.method: The platform models the physical measurement process for diverse modalities and exposes fine-grained control over physical sensor parameters, so that failure modes such as LiDAR pileup and glare, iToF phase wrapping, saturation and motion artifacts, event-camera refractory drops, and history-dependent thermal emission can be reproduced.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative results; it states that the platform enables principled cross-modality comparison on identical scenes and trajectories and reproduces the listed failure modes that general-purpose simulators overlook.
AI.conclusion: Treating sensor realism as a first-class concern enables principled cross-modality comparison, and the released platform and dataset support perception research beyond idealized simulation.

title: MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
summary: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.

AI.tldr: MOMASPLAT is a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. It combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models and kinematics-based action retargeting.
AI.motivation: Imitation-learned visuomotor policies are highly sensitive to viewpoint changes, and existing novel-view synthesis augmentation assumes static scenes, so it cannot re-render the manipulated object during post-contact interaction.
AI.method: The framework reconstructs the static scene and the manipulated object separately from standard multiview mobile manipulation data, renders them from novel viewpoints, and generates geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions.
AI.result: Evaluated on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks with rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, with synthesized demonstrations validated against ground truth in simulation; it more than doubles the average success rate of the strongest baseline and keeps non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting demonstrations with dynamic novel-view synthesis improves robustness to unseen base poses and reduces the need for large-scale real-world data collection.

title: T3R: Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement Towards Efficient and Robust VLA Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable end-to-end robot control, but inference is increasingly expensive. Each decision processes hundreds of visual tokens, often across multiple cameras, leading to substantial computation while allowing irrelevant background content to distract action prediction under distribution shift. We argue that these issues stem from two complementary forms of redundancy: many visual tokens are spatially irrelevant, while attention over the remaining tokens is often misallocated. Based on this observation, we propose T3R, a Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement framework. In the first stage, segmentation-guided token pruning removes irrelevant visual patches to reduce computation and eliminate distracting context. In the second stage, saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention toward action-critical visual regions and language instructions within the retained tokens. Together, pruning produces a cleaner candidate set, while attention biasing further emphasizes the most decision-relevant evidence, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency frontier than either stage alone. On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate, and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations. The timing comparison attributes 7.8 ms per inference call to pruning and attention-bias application. As input resolution increases, LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3x speedup over the unpruned baseline. Evaluations across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones show the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings. These results demonstrate that training-free token refinement is a practical approach to efficient and robust VLA inference.

AI.tldr: T3R is a training-free two-stage token refinement method for VLA models: segmentation-guided pruning removes spatially irrelevant visual tokens, and saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention to action-critical regions and language instructions. It improves both the efficiency and the robustness of VLA inference.
AI.motivation: VLA inference is expensive because hundreds of visual tokens, often from multiple cameras, are processed per decision, and irrelevant background content can distract action prediction under distribution shift.
AI.method: Stage one prunes visual patches that are irrelevant to the task using segmentation guidance; stage two applies saliency-guided attention biasing over the retained tokens and language instructions, so that pruning yields a cleaner candidate set and biasing emphasises the most decision-relevant evidence.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations; pruning and attention biasing add 7.8 ms per inference call, and LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3x speedup at higher input resolution; evaluations span LIBERO, SIMPLER and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones.
AI.conclusion: Training-free token refinement is a practical route to efficient and robust VLA inference, with the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings.

title: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
summary: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

AI.tldr: VFlash speeds up visual planning for physical AI by predicting the coordinates of a whole visual primitive (point, box or trajectory) jointly in one forward pass with a lightweight drafter, instead of decoding one coordinate token at a time. It accepts structurally valid predictions without matching the autoregressive token sequence.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive vision-language models generate visual plans one coordinate token at a time, which makes richer spatial predictions costly.
AI.method: Flash Primitive Decoding exploits the known structure of visual primitives, and its layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality and length; the method trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement.
AI.result: VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks; preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate about 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting; a world action model conditioned on VFlash plans reaches 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, versus 62.6% for the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Joint primitive decoding makes visual planning faster and more accurate and improves downstream robot task success, without requiring the exact autoregressive token sequence.

title: KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
summary: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.

AI.tldr: KDASO continuously evolves an LLM skill library for liability adjudication through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent data, execution-aligned refinement and context-budgeted skill routing. It outperforms general-purpose and domain-specific baselines across three tasks.
AI.motivation: Skill libraries used by LLMs for liability adjudication go stale as scenarios evolve, skill descriptions suffer a semantic execution gap from the intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets, causing critical skill omission.
AI.method: Knowledge-data dual-driven skill optimization combines neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection.
AI.result: Experiments on ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination and logical reasoning judgment show significant gains over current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines; transfer to concept-similar scenarios yields an 8.96% improvement, and gains are maintained through continuous optimization.
AI.conclusion: The generated skills are highly transferable and stable, suggesting that continuously optimized skill libraries can keep LLM adjudication reliable as scenarios change.

title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement Learning Post-Training through Elastic Expert Parallelism
comment: 19 pages including references and appendices, 5 figures
summary: Reinforcement learning post-training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses is a major computational bottleneck. In mixture-of-experts models, workers that finish their assigned responses may remain occupied because their experts are still needed by workers processing longer responses. Consequently, approximately one-third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after local response generation finishes. Here we present FlexFloor, a system that enables earlier resource release during synchronous response generation while preserving the expert computation required by ongoing responses. FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers. It uses historical response lengths and memory constraints to guide batching and prompt placement, then progressively releases workers while maintaining expert availability and correct communication. Compared with the verl baseline, FlexFloor generates approximately 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied computing time and increases response generation throughput by 52.74%, with little observed variation in rollout reward. By making reinforcement learning post-training more efficient, FlexFloor supports faster development and iterative improvement of large language models and AI agents.

AI.tldr: FlexFloor speeds up synchronous RL post-training of mixture-of-experts LLMs by releasing workers early during response generation while keeping the experts needed by ongoing responses available. It reports about 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied compute time and 52.74% higher generation throughput than verl.
AI.motivation: In MoE RL post-training, workers that finish their responses stay occupied because their experts are still needed by workers handling longer responses, so about one-third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after local generation finishes.
AI.method: FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers, using historical response lengths and memory constraints to guide batching and prompt placement, and progressively releases workers while maintaining expert availability and correct communication.
AI.result: Compared with the verl baseline, FlexFloor generates about 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied computing time and raises response generation throughput by 52.74%, with little observed variation in rollout reward.
AI.conclusion: Earlier resource release during generation makes RL post-training more efficient, which supports faster iteration on LLMs and AI agents.

title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Models, and Systems of Record
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables. Code and synthetic data: this https URL
summary: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. A simulation with known ground truth shows the spine sustaining cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero, the reconciliation residual recovering planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors, and mid-flight gating cutting p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate. We propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Two-Ledger Model for attributing AI costs to business transactions across clouds, LLMs and systems of record, pairing a FOCUS-conformant settlement ledger with an invocation-grain attribution ledger built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A simulation with known ground truth shows high cost coverage, recovery of planted unmetered spend and a large reduction in p99 transaction cost from gating.
AI.motivation: Billing data is settlement-grain and cannot say what a single order, claim or case cost in AI, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries, and FOCUS remains settlement-grain even with AI token and requester attribution.
AI.method: The model joins a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records; a layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns records to transactions with recorded method and confidence, a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time, and period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice.
AI.result: In simulation, the spine sustains cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero; the reconciliation residual recovers planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors; mid-flight gating cuts p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate.
AI.conclusion: Costs can be reported per order, claim or outcome with agentic cost metrics, and the authors propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.

title: Autonomous AI Agents Systematically Diverge From Human Preferences in Proof Formalization
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have ushered in a new age of proof abundance, but helping humans understand these proofs requires new attention to the differences in how AI agents and humans pursue a proof-making task. We present "simulated collaboration", a methodology that allows us to examine two key questions: (1) the relative attention AI agents pay to surface syntax or, conversely, deeper underlying semantics, and (2) how and where AI agent preferences for what to do next diverge from human preferences. On a set of nine major human collaborations in Lean with 4.7M definitions across more than 6K commits, we find that, over the course of proof construction, AI agents (1) are far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps; (2) show a relative aversion to densely connected proof centers and to complex or surprising proof goals; and (3) are relatively attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to regularize toward baseline. Our results highlight important blind spots and potential interventions for future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.

AI.tldr: Using a "simulated collaboration" methodology on nine major human Lean formalization projects, the paper finds that AI agents diverge from humans in what they pursue during proof construction. Agents are strongly drawn to explicitly marked gaps and surprising proof bodies, and avoid densely connected proof centers and complex goals.
AI.motivation: Helping humans understand AI-produced proofs requires knowing how AI agents and humans differ in pursuing proof-making, in particular their attention to surface syntax versus deeper semantics and their preferences for what to do next.
AI.method: Simulated collaboration compares AI agent and human next-step preferences across nine major human collaborations in Lean, with 4.7M definitions over more than 6K commits.
AI.result: AI agents are far more strongly drawn than humans to explicitly marked gaps; they show relative aversion to densely connected proof centers and to complex or surprising proof goals; and they are relatively attracted to surprising proof bodies, which they tend to regularize toward baseline.
AI.conclusion: The divergences reveal blind spots in AI-assisted mathematics and suggest interventions for future human-AI collaboration in mathematics.

title: Trust Responsive Runtime Authorization for Agentic AI with Empirical Characterization of Policy Behavior and Parameter Sensitivity
summary: The policy that converts runtime estimates of an autonomous agent's condition into operational authority is rarely specified or measured. We empirically characterize the Trust Responsive Authorization Policy (TRAP), which maps an Authorization Readiness Score (ARS), a weighted combination of runtime trust, operational stability, and contextual risk, onto discrete authorization levels through an asymmetric rule: escalation requires consecutive observations above a band edge plus a margin, while a sharp drop in readiness restricts authority at once. On one matched set of 100 Monte Carlo traces, we compare TRAP with static, trust-only, risk-only, and symmetric policies. Under abrupt degradation, TRAP restricts at onset and re-escalates sooner after recovery than the symmetric policy, with the highest and, descriptively, least variable stability among the adaptive policies, although more of its post-recovery escalations occur below the selected trust threshold. Paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero for the remaining differences. In one-factor sweeps, recovery time rises with the escalation margin and run length, shifts with the score weights, and is unchanged by the restriction threshold. In an exploratory post-freeze experiment, when the same degradation is spread over 5-20 intervals, TRAP restricts only on the 4 traces that retain a single-interval drop above that threshold; averaged over all 100 traces, it holds authority above what readiness supports for 15.9-18.9 of the 20 degradation intervals, against 0.8 under abrupt degradation and about 10 for the symmetric policy. Its restriction advantage therefore depends on degradation being abrupt. All reported values are traceable to the publicly available, versioned research release.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically characterizes TRAP, an asymmetric policy that maps an Authorization Readiness Score (runtime trust, operational stability and contextual risk) to discrete authority levels. On 100 Monte Carlo traces, TRAP restricts quickly under abrupt degradation, but under gradual degradation it holds authority above what readiness supports.
AI.motivation: The policy that converts runtime estimates of an autonomous agent's condition into operational authority is rarely specified or measured.
AI.method: TRAP uses an Authorization Readiness Score, a weighted combination of runtime trust, operational stability and contextual risk; escalation requires consecutive observations above a band edge plus a margin, while a sharp drop in readiness restricts authority at once. It is compared with static, trust-only, risk-only and symmetric policies on a matched set of 100 Monte Carlo traces, with one-factor sweeps and an exploratory post-freeze experiment.
AI.result: Under abrupt degradation, TRAP restricts at onset and re-escalates sooner after recovery than the symmetric policy, with the highest and descriptively least variable stability among adaptive policies, though more of its post-recovery escalations occur below the trust threshold. When degradation is spread over 5-20 intervals, TRAP holds authority above readiness for 15.9-18.9 of the 20 intervals, against 0.8 under abrupt degradation and about 10 for the symmetric policy.
AI.conclusion: TRAP's restriction advantage depends on degradation being abrupt, so its benefit does not carry over to gradual degradation; all reported values trace to a public, versioned research release.

title: Adapting the Process of Adaptation: Darwinian, Lamarckian, and Agent-Directed Evolution in AI
summary: Evolution has shaped intelligence for billions of years. Artificial intelligence (AI) now raises a striking possibility: intelligence may begin to direct its own evolution. As AI agents become capable of modifying and evaluating their own behavior, how quickly could they improve, and how can that improvement remain safe? We develop a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian, and agent-directed evolution following environmental change. Darwinian evolution relies on natural selection, Lamarckian evolution adds inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution allows agents to generate and evaluate behavioral variants and choose how extensively to search. When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms exhibit progressively faster adaptation. Generating more variants accelerates adaptation, while optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty, and experimentation costs. However, an agent's ability to direct its improvement does not ensure that improvements are evaluated against the intended objective. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behavior, even as measured performance improves. In recursive self-improvement, such errors may persist across generations, posing challenges for AI safety. Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development. The central challenge is not simply to accelerate the evolution of intelligence, but to preserve humanity's ability to guide its direction, limit its speed, and intervene when necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework comparing Darwinian, Lamarckian and agent-directed evolution after environmental change. Effective learning and more generated variants speed adaptation, but when the evaluation target is misspecified, extra search converges toward the wrong behaviour, a safety concern for recursive self-improvement.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become able to modify and evaluate their own behaviour, it is unclear how quickly they could improve and how that improvement can remain safe.
AI.method: A theoretical framework compares Darwinian selection, Lamarckian evolution with inherited learning, and agent-directed evolution, in which agents generate and evaluate behavioural variants and choose how extensively to search.
AI.result: When learning is sufficiently effective, these mechanisms adapt progressively faster; generating more variants accelerates adaptation, and optimal search effort depends on learning ability, problem difficulty and experimentation costs. When the evaluation target is misspecified, additional search accelerates convergence toward the wrong behaviour even as measured performance improves.
AI.conclusion: Independent evaluation and oversight must keep pace with autonomous AI development, since the central challenge is to preserve humanity's ability to guide, limit and intervene in the direction of AI evolution.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration
summary: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.

AI.tldr: EFXPLORER is a constrained MARL exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint preserving task performance, solved with an epigraph reformulation and adaptive exploration budgets. It adds a successor-distance intrinsic reward and outperforms strong baselines on SMAX, VMAS and MPE.
AI.motivation: Naively combining intrinsic rewards with team objectives can distort the learning signal and compromise task performance, while cooperative behaviour in MARL is hard to discover by trial and error because of the combinatorial joint state-action space.
AI.method: The method separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility, using an epigraph reformulation with adaptive exploration budgets; a successor distance-based intrinsic reward captures long-horizon dependencies for diverse, temporally extended exploration.
AI.result: The method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across the SMAX, VMAS and MPE benchmark suites.
AI.conclusion: Constraining exploration by task feasibility lets intrinsic rewards aid the discovery of cooperation without sacrificing task performance.

title: When Verification Is Not Agreement: Cross-Agent LLM-to-Dafny Formalization
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding
summary: A verified Dafny postcondition certifies that a formula holds, but it does not guarantee that the result was reached through genuine independent reasoning. We introduce a cross-agent formalization protocol where a Specifier model translates clinical trial criteria into a Dafny predicate, and an Implementer model writes an operational method checked against it. A same-model control establishes that even with no capability gap, independent re-extraction from identical text agrees only 59.3% of the time. Evaluating four model configurations on 96 clinical trial documents, we find that agreement is highly sensitive to how model capability is allocated across the two roles: the GPT-4.1-nano/GPT-4.1-mini configuration achieves 53.0% agreement when the stronger model is the Implementer, but only 14.3% when the roles are reversed. The strongest tested configuration, GPT-5.6-luna/GPT-5.4-mini, improves agreement to 34.4% but remains below the same-model baseline and is dominated by direct contradiction (42.7%). We also detect a critical verification artifact in which a weaker Implementer satisfies the postcondition by invoking the Specifier's predicate directly; after structural auditing, corrected agreement falls from 14.3% to 13.2%. Our results show that verification success alone is insufficient evidence of independent cross-agent agreement, and that model capability does not guarantee agreement when formalizing the same source independently.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a cross-agent protocol in which a Specifier model writes a Dafny predicate from clinical trial criteria and an Implementer model writes a method checked against it, showing that a verified postcondition does not imply independent agreement. Agreement is low across configurations and is sensitive to how model capability is allocated between the two roles.
AI.motivation: A verified Dafny postcondition certifies that a formula holds but does not guarantee that the result was reached through genuine independent reasoning.
AI.method: A Specifier translates clinical trial criteria into a Dafny predicate and an Implementer writes an operational method checked against it; a same-model control measures agreement of independent re-extraction from identical text; four model configurations are evaluated on 96 clinical trial documents, with structural auditing of verification artifacts.
AI.result: Even same-model re-extraction agrees only 59.3% of the time; the GPT-4.1-nano/GPT-4.1-mini configuration reaches 53.0% agreement with the stronger model as Implementer but 14.3% when the roles are reversed; GPT-5.6-luna/GPT-5.4-mini reaches 34.4%, still below the same-model baseline and dominated by direct contradiction (42.7%); a weaker Implementer can satisfy the postcondition by invoking the Specifier's predicate, and after structural auditing corrected agreement falls from 14.3% to 13.2%.
AI.conclusion: Verification success is insufficient evidence of independent cross-agent agreement, and model capability alone does not guarantee agreement when the same source is formalized independently.

title: Robust Ranking of Port Impacts from Impending Tropical Cyclones: A Two-Stage Recommendation System
summary: When a tropical cyclone (TC) threatens several ports, preparedness planning depends on anticipating which ports are likely to be affected and where disruptions may last longest. Limited historical observations at individual ports and uncertainty in landfall location make these relative impacts difficult to estimate. We use a two-stage recommendation framework that first selects candidate ports based on their proximity to the expected landfall location and then ranks them by their estimated number of impact days.
