Using AIS-derived impact days for 37 ports and 31 TCs in the Gulf of Mexico study region, we compare three ways of representing port--cyclone interactions: pairwise feature interactions, tree-based feature combinations, and explicit feature crosses combined with learned embeddings. In tests on Hurricanes Nicole and Ian, the retrieval stage consistently identifies all observed affected ports under landfall uncertainty. Among the ranking models, Wide & Deep Learning achieves the closest agreement with the observed port rankings. Its mean ranking agreement exceeds that of the distance-based baseline by 85.5% for Nicole and 55.5% for Ian and is less sensitive to uncertainty in the landfall location. These rankings could help port authorities prioritize post-cyclone inspections and allocate recovery resources across ports threatened by the same event.

AI.tldr: A two-stage recommendation system ranks ports for tropical cyclone impact by first retrieving candidate ports near the expected landfall and then ranking them by estimated impact days. Wide & Deep Learning gives the closest agreement with observed port rankings and beats a distance-based baseline.
AI.motivation: Limited historical observations at individual ports and uncertain landfall location make the relative impacts of a threatening tropical cyclone hard to estimate, while preparedness requires anticipating which ports will be affected and where disruptions may last longest.
AI.method: The framework first selects candidate ports by proximity to the expected landfall location and then ranks them by estimated impact days; three representations of port-cyclone interaction are compared, namely pairwise feature interactions, tree-based feature combinations, and explicit feature crosses with learned embeddings, using AIS-derived impact days for 37 ports and 31 TCs in the Gulf of Mexico.
AI.result: On Hurricanes Nicole and Ian, the retrieval stage identifies all observed affected ports under landfall uncertainty; Wide & Deep Learning achieves the closest agreement with observed rankings, exceeding the distance-based baseline's mean ranking agreement by 85.5% for Nicole and 55.5% for Ian, and is less sensitive to landfall uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: The rankings could help port authorities prioritize post-cyclone inspections and allocate recovery resources across ports threatened by the same event.

title: SAVeR$^2$: Reasoning-based Safety Alignment for Large Reasoning Models via Verifiable Rewards
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance via explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet this process introduces critical safety risks. We formalize LRM safety objectives as requiring non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency, and explicit intent identification. We argue that existing alignment methods suffer from poor adversarial generalization, a significant ``safety tax'' on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards, primarily due to their neglect of the LRM's intrinsic reasoning capabilities for safety. To address these, we propose \textbf{SAVeR$^2$}, a novel \textbf{S}afety \textbf{A}lignment method via \textbf{R}ewards with \textbf{R}easoning capability. SAVeR$^2$ decomposes the safety objective into four fine-grained verifiable reward signals and utilizes a difficulty-aware data selection strategy to stabilize training. Crucially, we introduce a reasoning-preserving gradient projection mechanism that analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients, effectively eliminating the safety tax. Extensive experiments on models ranging from 1.5B to 671B demonstrate that SAVeR$^2$ achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates across multiple benchmarks without compromising general reasoning capabilities.

AI.tldr: SAVeR^2 aligns large reasoning models for safety by decomposing the safety objective into four verifiable reward signals and applying a reasoning-preserving gradient projection that resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients. Experiments on models from 1.5B to 671B parameters report better safety and lower over-refusal without losing reasoning ability.
AI.motivation: Explicit chain-of-thought reasoning in large reasoning models introduces safety risks, and existing alignment methods show poor adversarial generalization, a safety tax on reasoning, and unfaithful coarse-grained rewards because they neglect the model's reasoning capability for safety.
AI.method: The safety objective is decomposed into four fine-grained verifiable rewards covering non-malicious reasoning and answers, safety consistency and explicit intent identification; a difficulty-aware data selection strategy stabilizes training; and a reasoning-preserving gradient projection analytically resolves conflicts between safety and reasoning gradients.
AI.result: Across models from 1.5B to 671B parameters and multiple benchmarks, SAVeR^2 achieves superior safety performance and significantly lower over-refusal rates without compromising general reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The projection mechanism is presented as effectively eliminating the safety tax on reasoning, so safety alignment can be obtained without sacrificing reasoning.

title: DelegateEval: Evaluating Platforms for Personal External Service Agents
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Evaluation framework and experimental design
summary: AI agents that work for an individual over time may also help that individual serve external clients. We define a personal external service agent as an agent authorized and continuously managed by a specific individual to accept client requests, deliver work, and provide ongoing support using that person's knowledge, experience, professional methods, and service boundaries. Such agents could allow individuals to serve more clients with less direct involvement and generate economic value at scale. We propose DelegateEval, a platform-level evaluation framework for agent systems that may combine large language models, reusable skills, protocols such as MCP, and executable tool environments. It covers eight dimensions: ease of creation, service discovery and matching, delivery quality, expertise inheritance, service continuity, learning and improvement, reliability and governance, and efficiency and value. These dimensions assess whether a platform enables people with different backgrounds to turn their expertise into ongoing services that deliver verifiable work, develop capabilities through experience, and remain economically feasible. We present the framework and an experimental design. Complete datasets, executable environments, a unified scoring protocol, and cross-model results remain to be developed and empirically validated.

AI.tldr: DelegateEval proposes a platform-level evaluation framework with eight dimensions for personal external service agents, which serve clients on an individual's behalf using that person's expertise. The paper presents the framework and an experimental design, but datasets, environments, scoring protocol and cross-model results remain to be developed.
AI.motivation: Individuals could use AI agents to serve more external clients with less direct involvement, yet no framework evaluates whether agent platforms let people turn their expertise into ongoing services.
AI.method: The framework covers eight dimensions: ease of creation, service discovery and matching, delivery quality, expertise inheritance, service continuity, learning and improvement, reliability and governance, and efficiency and value, for agent systems that may combine LLMs, reusable skills, protocols such as MCP and executable tool environments.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results; complete datasets, executable environments, a unified scoring protocol and cross-model results remain to be developed and empirically validated.
AI.conclusion: The work is a proposed evaluation framework and experimental design whose empirical validation is still outstanding.

title: Graph learning-assisted logic-based Benders decomposition for distributionally robust in-station train rescheduling under disruptions
summary: Uncertainty in resource reopening times complicates train holding and rerouting decisions when resource closures coincide with arrival delays and processing-time extensions. We develop a rolling-horizon distributionally robust model that updates predictions of the remaining closure duration as observations of disruption resolution become available. The model jointly optimizes train routes, sequences, and timings. It minimizes the worst-case expected total completion delay over an ambiguity set of scenario probabilities. The solution algorithm, GNN-LBBD, uses logic-based Benders decomposition to coordinate routing and resource scheduling. Conditional cuts are constructed from resource-use patterns, and a graph neural network guides the order in which resource relaxation subproblems are solved. Across 28 test instances for a five-track station, GNN-LBBD achieved a mean total completion delay of 61.13 train-min. This was 16.63\% lower than tabu search and 20.06\% lower than variable neighborhood search, with a mean total computation time close to that of tabu search. Information comparisons on six representative instances showed that using observations of disruption resolution reduced mean total completion delay by approximately 21.7\%. Scenario-based and conditional-mean predictions produced similar overall results under the same information conditions. The benefits of information were more pronounced in some instances with alternative routes. This suggests a relationship between the use of observations, the station resource structure, and the scope for schedule adjustments.

AI.tldr: GNN-LBBD is a logic-based Benders decomposition algorithm for rolling-horizon, distributionally robust in-station train rescheduling under resource closure disruptions, in which a graph neural network guides the order of subproblems. It lowers mean total completion delay compared with tabu search and variable neighborhood search.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty in resource reopening times complicates train holding and rerouting decisions when resource closures coincide with arrival delays and processing-time extensions.
AI.method: A rolling-horizon distributionally robust model updates predictions of the remaining closure duration as disruption-resolution observations arrive and jointly optimizes routes, sequences and timings to minimize worst-case expected total completion delay over an ambiguity set of scenario probabilities; GNN-LBBD uses logic-based Benders decomposition with conditional cuts built from resource-use patterns, and a graph neural network orders the resource relaxation subproblems.
AI.result: Across 28 test instances for a five-track station, GNN-LBBD achieves a mean total completion delay of 61.13 train-min, 16.63% lower than tabu search and 20.06% lower than variable neighborhood search, with computation time close to that of tabu search; on six instances, using disruption-resolution observations reduces mean delay by about 21.7%, and scenario-based and conditional-mean predictions perform similarly.
AI.conclusion: The value of observations depends on the station's resource structure and is larger in instances with alternative routes, suggesting a link between information use and the scope for schedule adjustment.

title: Goal-Branching LaCAM: Temporary Goals as Search Branches in Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding
summary: LaCAM is a search-based solver for multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) that runs a depth-first search over joint configurations, using PIBT to generate successors and lazily adding single-agent constraints to explore alternatives. Although LaCAM is complete, it can struggle on dense, corridor-heavy instances because extracting blocking agents from deadlocks requires coordinated moves of several agents, often away from their goals, which PIBT's greedy one-step successors rarely propose and which LaCAM can only reach by enumerating constraints one agent at a time. This paper proposes Goal-Branching, where blocking agents are given temporary goals, each tried as an additional branch of LaCAM's search. We examine random and corridor-aware rules for choosing these temporary goals and show that completeness is preserved for any such rule. On dense instances (60-90% of free cells occupied) of three maze and room maps, Goal-Branching solves 89% of instances against 44% for LaCAM*, and, on instances both solve, it finds a first solution 10-14x faster on maze-32-32-2 and room-32-32-4, and nearly 200x faster in median time at 75% density on room-32-32-4. Solution cost increases by 15-22% on instances both solve, while on open maps and the full MovingAI benchmark its solutions cost no more than those of LaCAM* and it is at most 3% slower.

AI.tldr: Goal-Branching adds temporary goals for blocking agents as extra search branches in LaCAM, a complete MAPF solver, and shows that completeness is preserved for any such goal-selection rule. On dense instances it solves 89% against 44% for LaCAM*, and finds first solutions up to 10-14x faster on some maps.
AI.motivation: LaCAM can struggle on dense, corridor-heavy MAPF instances because extracting blocking agents from deadlocks needs coordinated moves away from their goals, which PIBT's greedy one-step successors rarely propose and which LaCAM reaches only by enumerating constraints one agent at a time.
AI.method: Blocking agents are given temporary goals, each tried as an additional branch of LaCAM's search; random and corridor-aware rules choose these temporary goals.
AI.result: On dense instances (60-90% of free cells occupied) of three maze and room maps, Goal-Branching solves 89% of instances versus 44% for LaCAM*; on instances both solve, it finds a first solution 10-14x faster on maze-32-32-2 and room-32-32-4 and nearly 200x faster in median time at 75% density on room-32-32-4, with solution cost 15-22% higher; on open maps and the full MovingAI benchmark its costs are no higher than LaCAM* and it is at most 3% slower.
AI.conclusion: Temporary goal branching improves LaCAM on dense instances at a cost in solution quality, while keeping its performance on open maps and the full benchmark.

title: CST-Bench: Benchmarking Counterfactual Spatial Transition Reasoning with Causal Transition On-Policy Self-Distillation
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables; includes technical supplementary material
summary: Spatial reasoning is a fundamental capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing benchmarks mainly focus on static scene understanding. When objects are moved or swapped, models must infer not only spatial relations but also how interventions change the scene state. To address this problem, we introduce CST-Bench, a benchmark for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CST-Bench contains 7,082 examples covering 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators, with dense causal annotations including intervention sources, affected relations, expected effects, invariant relations, and metric changes. We benchmark general-purpose MLLMs on CST-Bench and further compare post-training strategies on CST-Bench and standard spatial benchmarks. Results show that methods effective for ordinary spatial reasoning can still fail under counterfactual interventions. We further formulate counterfactual spatial reasoning as causal state-transition modeling and propose CT-OPSD, which uses CST-Bench annotations to guide a teacher model in learning counterfactual state transitions and causal reasoning chains. These chains are then distilled into a student model that reasons only from real observations. Overall, experiment results establish CST-Bench as a challenging benchmark and reusable supervision resource for counterfactual spatial reasoning. CT-OPSD further provides an initial demonstration of how its annotations can support model improvement.

AI.tldr: CST-Bench is a benchmark of 7,082 examples for counterfactual spatial reasoning, in which objects are moved or swapped and models must infer the resulting scene state. The paper also proposes CT-OPSD, which distills causal state-transition reasoning from a teacher guided by CST-Bench annotations into a student that reasons only from real observations.
AI.motivation: Existing spatial reasoning benchmarks focus on static scene understanding, whereas multimodal LLMs must also infer how interventions change the scene state.
AI.method: CST-Bench covers 6 intervention types and 12 transformation operators with dense causal annotations (intervention sources, affected relations, expected effects, invariant relations, metric changes); the task is formulated as causal state-transition modelling, and CT-OPSD uses a teacher guided by the annotations to learn counterfactual transitions and causal reasoning chains, which are then distilled into a student.
AI.result: General-purpose MLLMs are benchmarked on CST-Bench, and post-training strategies are compared on CST-Bench and standard spatial benchmarks; methods effective for ordinary spatial reasoning can still fail under counterfactual interventions; CT-OPSD gives an initial demonstration that the annotations can support model improvement.
AI.conclusion: CST-Bench is presented as a challenging benchmark and a reusable supervision resource for counterfactual spatial reasoning.

title: FlashOffloading: Low-Latency KV Cache Offloading for Long-Context LLM Serving
summary: In large language model (LLM) serving systems, the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length and concurrency, so long-context inference easily hits the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity wall and results in low concurrency. Offloading the KV cache to host dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) frees HBM space and raises concurrency, but the additional cache management and host-to-device (H2D) load overhead inflates inference latency, higher concurrency fails to translate into effective throughput. We present FlashOffloading, a host-DRAM-centric inference architecture that fully offloads the KV cache in both the prefill and decode phases. FlashOffloading builds rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute--load overlapped kernel, optimizing KV offloading latency across the entire pipeline and delivering throughput gains under a time-per-output-token (TPOT) service-level objective (SLO). In experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with multi-token prediction (MTP3) speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill--decode (PD)-disaggregated platform, FlashOffloading improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38\(\times\) and decode throughput by up to 1.91\(\times\) under a 30 ms TPOT constraint. FlashOffloading is integrated into an open-source serving framework: this https URL.

AI.tldr: FlashOffloading is a host-DRAM-centric LLM inference architecture that offloads the KV cache in both prefill and decode, raising throughput under a TPOT service-level objective. On GLM-5.2 with MTP3 speculative decoding on an Ascend910C prefill-decode disaggregated platform, it improves prefill throughput by up to 1.38x and decode throughput by up to 1.91x under a 30 ms TPOT constraint.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM serving hits the HBM capacity wall, and offloading the KV cache to host DRAM raises concurrency, but the added cache management and host-to-device load overhead inflates latency, so higher concurrency does not translate into effective throughput.
AI.method: A rolling HBM cache for prefill, a hot cache for decode, a reverse sparse index with zero extra miss-lookup overhead, and a compute-load overlapped kernel, which together optimize KV offloading latency across the whole pipeline.
AI.result: Under a 30 ms TPOT constraint, prefill throughput improves by up to 1.38x and decode throughput by up to 1.91x in experiments deploying GLM-5.2 with MTP3 on an Ascend910C PD-disaggregated platform.
AI.conclusion: Fully offloading the KV cache to host DRAM can turn higher concurrency into effective throughput under latency SLOs, and the design is integrated into an open-source serving framework.

title: Align Before Aggregation: Basis-Consistent Federated LoRA under Heterogeneous Ranks
summary: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) under heterogeneous client capacities is increasingly important, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) with heterogeneous ranks makes it practical. Existing server-side aggregators compose local matrix updates $\Delta W_i$ from client-specific LoRA factors $(A_i,B_i)$ before aggregating them. Although these matrix updates lie in the same weight space $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and can be averaged directly, the LoRA factors that generate them may expressed client-specific local basis. In the typical compose--aggregate--factorize--dispatch loop, this basis inconsistency can make the rank-$r_i$ reference prefix dispatched to lower-rank clients unstable after server-side refactorization. In this work, we propose \textbf{FedAbA}, a basis-consistent federated LoRA aggregation framework for heterogeneous ranks. FedAbA first extracts each client's local basis, aligns it to the corresponding prefix of the global reference basis, and constructs a basis-consistent reconstruction of each local matrix update before aggregation. It then aggregates these reconstructions with weights that combine client data size and consistency score, followed by exact coefficient-space SVD refactorization and gauge fixing before rank-prefix dispatch. Our theoretical analysis clarifies the role of basis consistency and supports the proposed consistency-aware aggregation mechanism. Extensive experiments show that FedAbA outperforms representative federated LoRA baselines, with the largest gains under the strongest rank heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: FedAbA is a basis-consistent aggregation framework for federated LoRA fine-tuning with heterogeneous client ranks. It aligns each client's LoRA basis to a global reference basis before aggregating the weight updates.
AI.motivation: Existing server-side aggregators compose client LoRA updates into full matrices and then refactorize them, but client-specific local bases make the rank prefixes dispatched to lower-rank clients unstable after refactorization.
AI.method: FedAbA extracts each client's local basis, aligns it to the corresponding prefix of the global reference basis, reconstructs a basis-consistent update, aggregates the reconstructions with weights combining client data size and a consistency score, then applies exact coefficient-space SVD refactorization and gauge fixing before rank-prefix dispatch.
AI.result: FedAbA outperforms representative federated LoRA baselines in the reported experiments, with the largest gains under the strongest rank heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Basis consistency matters for federated LoRA with heterogeneous ranks, and consistency-aware aggregation, supported by a theoretical analysis, is an effective remedy.

title: Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
summary: Agent harness evolution enables recursive self-improvement (RSI) without updating model weights. We examine whether higher benchmark scores yield reliable, efficient, and transferable improvement. We evaluate four methods across harnesses, general and coding tasks. Repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions, and admission replays reveal recurring patterns. All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing previously covered ones. In one general-task case, reliability rises by 5.2 points despite losing ten previously covered tasks. Most reliability gains also increase deployment cost. Specific changes usually outperform generic reminders, but their benefits can change when combined. The highest-scoring agent does not yield the largest mean improvement in any of our four pools, and stricter admission can discard useful alternatives. Transfer selectively preserves gains: coverage usually falls on the general-task target across both harness types and paradigms, but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness. These findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules, and explicit applicability conditions. As a constructive follow-up, EvoAudit turns these diagnostics into revisions of select, analyze, mutate, and gate, achieving the best performance.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates agent harness evolution as a route to recursive self-improvement without weight updates and finds that higher benchmark scores do not reliably mean reliable, efficient or transferable improvement. Its constructive follow-up, EvoAudit, revises the select, analyze, mutate and gate loop and achieves the best performance.
AI.motivation: Gains from evolving agent harnesses are usually judged by benchmark scores, but whether those gains are reliable, cost-effective and transferable had not been examined.
AI.method: Four harness-evolution methods are evaluated on general and coding tasks through repeated evaluations, controlled agent expansion, component interventions and admission replays.
AI.result: All sixteen evolved agents gain previously uncovered tasks while losing some previously covered ones; in one general-task case reliability rises by 5.2 points while ten covered tasks are lost; most reliability gains also raise deployment cost; the highest-scoring agent does not give the largest mean improvement in any of the four pools; transfer coverage usually falls on the general-task target but rises on the coding target with the outer-layer-only harness.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate preservation-aware evaluation, tested decision rules and explicit applicability conditions for harness evolution, and EvoAudit shows that such diagnostics can drive better revisions.

title: Redacting Personal Data: A Speed and Accuracy Comparison of Regex, Presidio and Hybrid Designs
summary: Many enterprise projects now pass free text to large language models (LLMs), and that text often contains personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, phone numbers, email addresses, home addresses and dates of birth. Once a prompt is sent, this data is copied into provider systems, application logs and observability traces. Redacting PII before the call is an obvious control, yet teams seldom have numbers on what it costs in latency or what it lets through. This paper compares four redaction designs that any LLM pipeline can adopt: a pure regular-expression (regex) redactor, Microsoft Presidio running on a spaCy model, a hybrid in which Presidio finds only person names while regex handles structured identifiers, and a fast hybrid that calls spaCy's named-entity component directly. All four share a known-entity rule, which removes the person the system already knows it is handling, and a consistent placeholder scheme, so the LLM can still tell one person from another after redaction. We evaluate the designs on a sample workflow, which we call ProfileAssist, that turns resumes into structured profiles, using 100 synthetic resumes (523 characters on average, with 900 PII values and 600 business terms that must survive). Regex ran at a 0.20 ms median but caught only 88.9% of PII, because it cannot find names that are not known in advance, such as the references listed in a resume. Presidio, hybrid and fast hybrid each caught 100% of PII and kept 100% of business terms, at median latencies of 37.59 ms, 30.23 ms and 13.48 ms. Measured against a 9,120 ms median LLM call, even the slowest option adds only 0.41% to the request. We therefore recommend the fast hybrid as a default for LLM pipelines that handle personal data, with regex kept as a safety net rather than as the only control.

AI.tldr: The paper compares four PII redaction designs for LLM prompts (regex, Presidio, a Presidio-plus-regex hybrid, and a fast hybrid using spaCy named-entity recognition) on speed and accuracy. It recommends the fast hybrid as the default for LLM pipelines that handle personal data, with regex kept as a safety net.
AI.motivation: Teams send free text containing PII to LLMs, yet they seldom measure the latency cost of redaction or how much PII gets through.
AI.method: All four designs share a known-entity rule and a consistent placeholder scheme, and are evaluated on ProfileAssist, a resume-to-profile workflow, using 100 synthetic resumes with 900 PII values and 600 business terms that must survive.
AI.result: Regex had a 0.20 ms median latency but caught only 88.9% of PII, since it cannot find names not known in advance. Presidio, the hybrid and the fast hybrid each caught 100% of PII and kept 100% of business terms, at median latencies of 37.59 ms, 30.23 ms and 13.48 ms. Against a 9,120 ms median LLM call, even the slowest option adds only 0.41%.
AI.conclusion: Redaction adds little latency relative to an LLM call, so the fast hybrid with regex as a safety net is a practical default for personal data.

title: Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable, and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems
comment: 51 pages, 26 figures. Code repository and benchmarks available at this https URL
summary: Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. In practice, this burns massive context windows, inflates API bills, and produces brittle agents that fail unpredictably in production. In this work, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and capability registry that formally separates what an agent wants to do from how that task is executed. Instead of prompting models with loose text instructions or markdown files baptized as 'skills', Skillware equips them with modular, versioned software capability bundles. Much like skill hotkeys in video games that execute deterministically under fixed world rules, each bundle combines a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets, and automated unit tests. In-process adapters translate these capabilities into native tool declarations for any model, from frontier cloud APIs to local open-weight runtimes with zero network latency. Evaluating 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions, we show that small local models (3B to 8B parameters) equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows. They cut token usage by up to 84.8%, slash inference costs by up to 97.3%, and eliminate parameter errors entirely. True agent reliability does not come from larger models or longer prompts, but from equipping logical systems with verified, deterministic software. Finally, we articulate the trajectory of capability bundles across an invariant continuum of information processing systems: from digital logical systems today, to IoT, drones, and embodied robotics tomorrow, establishing a foundation for auditable, real-time capability execution.

AI.tldr: Skillware is an open architectural framework that equips LLM agents with versioned, deterministic software capability bundles instead of prompting them to write code or follow text skills. Across 23 models and 368 benchmark conditions, small local models with Skillware outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents that write code, guess API payloads and memorize constraints through prompting burn context windows, inflate API bills and fail unpredictably in production.
AI.method: Each capability bundle combines a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets and automated unit tests, and in-process adapters translate bundles into native tool declarations for any model.
AI.result: Small local models (3B to 8B parameters) equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows, cutting token usage by up to 84.8%, inference costs by up to 97.3%, and eliminating parameter errors entirely.
AI.conclusion: Agent reliability comes from equipping systems with verified deterministic software rather than from larger models or longer prompts, and the authors propose extending capability bundles to IoT, drones and embodied robotics.

title: PharmAgents2: Towards Autonomous End-to-End Drug Discovery
summary: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space. We introduce PharmAgents2, an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with organized large-scale exploration. Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and, together with expert-developed skills, supports research decisions. Self-Scaling Discovery expands exploration through parallel agents inheriting research context and decision-making capabilities across targets, scientific hypotheses, and discovery strategies. We introduce PharmAgents-Bench v0.1, comprising 121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks assessed with expert-defined process rubrics. PharmAgents2 outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies, autonomous investigations generated findings subsequently supported by human-executed experiments. For LpxH, PharmAgents2 hypothesized a previously unreported allosteric site and screened compounds against it, identifying a novel inhibitor scaffold with experimentally confirmed inhibitory activity and binding. For JAK1, it prioritized a covalent inhibition strategy and nominated compounds with experimentally demonstrated activity. Starting from a known bioactive molecule, Self-Scaling Discovery explored candidate targets across the proteome and identified a new binding target, with the interaction subsequently confirmed experimentally. PharmAgents2 represents a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, marking a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.

AI.tldr: PharmAgents2 is an autonomous system for end-to-end drug discovery that combines knowledge-enhanced decision-making with large-scale parallel exploration. It outperforms evaluated baselines in most decision categories on PharmAgents-Bench v0.1 and produces experimentally confirmed findings in three real-world studies.
AI.motivation: Drug discovery requires continuous scientific decision-making across a vast research space, which calls for transferable decision knowledge and organized large-scale exploration.
AI.method: Paper2Skill extracts transferable scientific decision knowledge from public sources and combines it with expert-developed skills, and Self-Scaling Discovery runs parallel agents that inherit research context and decision capabilities across targets, hypotheses and discovery strategies.
AI.result: On PharmAgents-Bench v0.1 (121 questions across nine decision scenarios and three end-to-end tasks), PharmAgents2 outperforms baselines in most decision categories and achieves the highest process scores on all three end-to-end tasks. In three real-world studies it proposed a previously unreported allosteric site for LpxH and found a novel inhibitor scaffold, prioritized a covalent strategy for JAK1 with experimentally demonstrated activity, and identified a new binding target for a known bioactive molecule, confirmed experimentally.
AI.conclusion: The system is presented as a prototype of a virtual pharmaceutical company, a step toward autonomous end-to-end drug discovery.

title: Who Should Know What? Empirical Information Design for Multi-Agent LLM Economies
summary: The performance of multi-agent LLM systems depends not only on the capabilities of the underlying models but also on information-sharing policies, which govern what information each agent observes and at what level of detail. But does providing AI agents with more detailed information always improve collective outcomes, or can transparency paradoxically degrade efficiency? To investigate this, we introduce empirical information design, an experimental framework that systematically compares disclosure policies across economic markets populated by LLM agents, while holding interaction rules and models fixed. We evaluate ten frontier LLMs in multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions, using ground-truth utilities to decouple identified opportunities from realized outcomes. We find that finer information disclosure yields highly model-dependent results. In trade, revealing exact valuations rather than ordinal preference rankings reduces realized gains for GPT-6 Sol (from 98% to 91% of maximum) yet increases them for Claude Sonnet 5 (from 72% to 86%). In bargaining, exact information leads Grok 4.7 to produce less balanced agreements, whereas Claude Opus 5.5 divides gains symmetrically. In double auctions, full disclosure inflates price demands, triggering market breakdown and lowering welfare for Gemini 3.1 Pro (97% to 78%), Claude Opus 5.5 (94% to 64%), and Grok 4.7 (97% to 62%). Overall, these results suggest that model selection and information design must be co-optimized, as LLMs vary in how their strategic responses to information impact system objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces empirical information design and shows across LLM-agent markets that finer information disclosure has model-dependent effects, sometimes helping and sometimes degrading collective outcomes. It concludes that model selection and information design must be co-optimized.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether giving LLM agents more detailed information always improves collective outcomes, or whether transparency can paradoxically degrade efficiency in multi-agent economies.
AI.method: An experimental framework compares disclosure policies in multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining and double auctions with ten frontier LLMs, holding interaction rules and models fixed and using ground-truth utilities to separate identified opportunities from realized outcomes.
AI.result: In trade, revealing exact valuations rather than ordinal rankings reduces realized gains for GPT-6 Sol (98% to 91% of maximum) but increases them for Claude Sonnet 5 (72% to 86%). In bargaining, exact information leads Grok 4.7 to less balanced agreements, while Claude Opus 5.5 divides gains symmetrically. In double auctions, full disclosure inflates price demands and causes market breakdown, lowering welfare for Gemini 3.1 Pro (97% to 78%), Claude Opus 5.5 (94% to 64%) and Grok 4.7 (97% to 62%).
AI.conclusion: LLMs vary in how they respond strategically to information, so model selection and information design must be co-optimized rather than chosen separately.

title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction. We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone. We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MCPHallu is a benchmark of 358 tasks for diagnosing hallucination-prone failures of LLM agents in Model Context Protocol environments along reasoning, execution and memory axes. Fourteen frontier agents average 0.642 on a 0 to 1 scale, with failures concentrated on Unreachable Goal tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing MCP benchmarks mainly measure task completion and diagnose failures only after execution, rather than building specific reasoning, execution and memory failure risks into task construction.
AI.method: Tasks run on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers, and each task has a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes (Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, Context Forgetting) the dominant failure risk, which enables subtype-level analysis.
AI.result: Fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors were evaluated on 5,012 trajectories, averaging 0.642. On Unreachable Goal tasks the average drops to 0.458 and 23.2% of runs pass; a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes; Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models (r = -0.12).
AI.conclusion: Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, often continuing to issue tool calls or claiming success rather than recognizing infeasible goals, so subtype-level evaluation is needed.

title: Towards Generalist Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
summary: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) aims to identify graphs that deviate significantly from the majority. While recent advances have achieved competitive performance, existing approaches mainly follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring substantial in-domain data and training cost when applied to new application scenarios. This limits their scalability and practicality in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce and diverse domains are continuously emerging. In this paper, we investigate the problem of generalist GLAD, which seeks to learn a single unified model capable of detecting anomalous graphs across multiple domains with minimal supervision on the target data. This problem introduces key challenges, including learning transferable patterns from heterogeneous graph datasets and effective adaptation under limited supervision. To address these challenges, we propose GenGLAD, a generalist GLAD approach that leverages discriminative subgraph extraction as the core mechanism to learn transferable anomaly knowledge and enable efficient adaptation to new domains. Specifically, GenGLAD employs a graph neural network-based discriminative subgraph extraction model to learn the anomaly-discriminative substructures that distinguish anomalous and normal graphs across diverse domains. During the test-time adaptation phase, multi-dimensional discrepancies between the extracted subgraph and multi-level contextual information are calculated to characterize anomalies from multiple perspectives. For efficient adaptation, a lightweight scoring module is introduced to automatically decide the most informative signals, improving robustness against misleading patterns. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong performance, superior generalization ability, and improved data efficiency compared to existing methods.

AI.tldr: GenGLAD is a generalist approach to graph-level anomaly detection that learns one model across multiple domains and adapts to new domains with minimal target supervision, using discriminative subgraph extraction as its core mechanism.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-level anomaly detectors follow a dataset-specific paradigm that needs substantial in-domain data and training cost for each new application, which limits scalability when labels are scarce and domains keep emerging.
AI.method: A GNN-based discriminative subgraph extraction model learns anomaly-discriminative substructures across diverse domains; at test time, multi-dimensional discrepancies between the extracted subgraph and multi-level contextual information characterize anomalies, and a lightweight scoring module selects the most informative signals.
AI.result: The abstract reports strong performance, superior generalization and improved data efficiency compared with existing methods on diverse benchmark datasets, without giving specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A single unified model that transfers subgraph-based anomaly knowledge and adapts with lightweight scoring offers a practical route to generalist graph-level anomaly detection.

title: Pediatric ECG foundation model via adult-to-pediatric fine-tuning: downstream tasks and clinical evaluation
summary: Pediatric electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation is complicated by age-dependent electrophysiological changes that limit direct transfer of adult AI models. We asked whether an adult ECG foundation model could be adapted to pediatric ECGs. Using 339,563 12-lead ECGs from 238,189 children, we compared direct application, pediatric fine-tuning, and training from scratch under an identical architecture. Direct transfer was poor (mean AUC 0.8256). Fine-tuning reached 0.9695, above de novo training (0.9661), and attained 0.9079 using only 1% of training data. On 10,999 external ECGs, fine-tuning achieved a mean AUC of 0.9385 across 30 labels. It generalized to age regression (MAE 1.12 years) and congenital heart disease classification (AUC 0.9562). Across 17 clinicians and 100 cases, diagnostic accuracy rose from 56.8% to 65.4% (p < 0.001) and did not decline when AI erred. Adult ECG foundation models require pediatric adaptation; fine-tuning offers a data-efficient route to scalable pediatric ECG AI.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning an adult 12-lead ECG foundation model on pediatric ECGs gives a data-efficient route to pediatric ECG AI, reaching a mean AUC of 0.9695 against 0.8256 for direct transfer. It also raises clinician diagnostic accuracy.
AI.motivation: Age-dependent electrophysiological changes limit the direct transfer of adult ECG AI models to pediatric ECGs, and it was unclear whether an adult foundation model could be adapted to children.
AI.method: Using 339,563 12-lead ECGs from 238,189 children, the authors compared direct application, pediatric fine-tuning and training from scratch, all under an identical architecture.
AI.result: Direct transfer gave a mean AUC of 0.8256; fine-tuning reached 0.9695, above training from scratch (0.9661), and reached 0.9079 with only 1% of the training data. On 10,999 external ECGs, fine-tuning achieved a mean AUC of 0.9385 across 30 labels, age regression with MAE 1.12 years, and congenital heart disease classification with AUC 0.9562. Across 17 clinicians and 100 cases, diagnostic accuracy rose from 56.8% to 65.4% (p < 0.001) and did not decline when the AI erred.
AI.conclusion: Adult ECG foundation models require pediatric adaptation, and fine-tuning offers a data-efficient route to scalable pediatric ECG AI.

title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery
summary: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.

AI.tldr: RIVER is a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme-reaction retrieval that identifies reactions a given enzyme may catalyze and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction, assembling and validating evidence from LLMs, biochemical tools and knowledge resources.
AI.motivation: Existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme-reaction pairs, which makes it hard to integrate biochemical evidence over large candidate spaces and to retrieve among highly similar members of an enzyme family.
AI.method: RIVER coordinates LLMs, specialized biochemical computational tools and external knowledge resources to gather evidence on reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms and database annotations; validation modules examine evidence gaps and conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records.
AI.result: On public benchmarks RIVER achieves the highest success rates in enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation, outperforms baselines in family-specific retrieval on the selected datasets and metrics, and achieves the best retrieval results on E. coli tasks built from recent literature, substantially outperforming Claude Code, Codex and Phylo Max with both closed-source and open-source model configurations.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme-reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.

title: The Intrusion Pathway: How Non-Evidential Context Degrades Language Model Performance
comment: 32 pages, 25 figures, 29 tables. Dikshant Kukreja and Gautam Gupta contributed equally. Website: this https URL Code: this https URL
summary: Language models lose accuracy when a prompt contains non-evidential context: irrelevant statements from unrelated domains, or random off-distribution tokens, with no competing answer and no semantic overlap with the query. Such noise pervades retrieval-augmented, tool-using, and long-context deployments, yet the failure has lacked a mechanistic account. We trace the corruption to the Intrusion Pathway, which starts with MLPs enriching both query-subject and irrelevant-token representations, parroting heads carry prefix-token content to the prediction position, and relational readers largely avoid unrelated sources. Nevertheless, preserved subject enrichment and selective reading do not prevent intrusion in the broader computation. We then localize part of this interference to a sparse set of attention heads, which we call intrusion heads. Their prefix-derived writes promote distractor-related content, while their reduced support for the correct answer arises primarily from weaker non-prefix contributions rather than direct suppression by the prefix. The same heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence, enabling a class-conditional intervention. Replacing the corrupted last-token residual with its clean counterpart, an oracle probe that requires a matched clean forward pass, recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks. A deployable mask level knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of the model's attention heads, recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that irrelevant, non-evidential context degrades LLM accuracy through an Intrusion Pathway, and that a sparse set of intrusion heads carries much of the interference. A deployable knockout of about ten heads, roughly 1% of attention heads, recovers 57% of the drop at bounded cost to helpful context.
AI.motivation: Language models lose accuracy when prompts contain irrelevant statements or random off-distribution tokens, a failure common in retrieval-augmented, tool-using and long-context deployments that had lacked a mechanistic account.
AI.method: The authors trace the corruption through MLPs, parroting heads and relational readers, localize part of the interference to a sparse set of intrusion heads, and test a class-conditional intervention, including an oracle probe that swaps the corrupted last-token residual for its clean counterpart and a deployable mask-level knockout.
AI.result: The oracle probe recovers 97.6% on average of the distractor-induced drop across four downstream tasks, and the deployable knockout of about ten heads recovers 57% at bounded cost to helpful context. The intrusion heads transfer across tasks and distractor types and are largely weight-disjoint from the heads that integrate relevant contextual evidence.
AI.conclusion: Interference from non-evidential context is localized to a small, transferable set of attention heads, which enables a targeted and deployable intervention.

title: FARR: Forecast-Aware Residual Refinement with Matched Endpoint Evidence for Long-Horizon Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Large language models use auxiliary conditioning to incorporate additional information into time-series forecasts. However, auxiliary conditioning does not consistently improve accuracy and can increase forecasting error when its influence is poorly matched to the observed temporal context. We propose Forecast-Aware Residual Refinement (FARR), which learns to correct forecasts using endpoint evidence. FARR obtains a valid forecast under the standard condition and a null forecast under a predefined null condition. Their difference reveals how conditioning changes the prediction. A shared residual refiner combines this endpoint evidence with historical features to estimate the remaining error of the valid forecast. Horizon-wise gating then controls the contribution of the predicted residual to the final output. Experiments on four long-horizon forecasting benchmarks show that FARR achieves the best dataset-average MSE and MAE among the compared methods. Code will be released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FARR corrects long-horizon time-series forecasts from LLMs by learning residual corrections from endpoint evidence, the difference between a standard-condition forecast and a null-condition forecast. It achieves the best dataset-average MSE and MAE on four long-horizon benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Auxiliary conditioning is meant to add information to LLM time-series forecasts, but it does not consistently improve accuracy and can increase forecasting error when its influence is poorly matched to the observed temporal context.
AI.method: FARR obtains a valid forecast under the standard condition and a null forecast under a predefined null condition; a shared residual refiner combines their difference with historical features to estimate the remaining error, and horizon-wise gating controls how much of the predicted residual enters the final output.
AI.result: On four long-horizon forecasting benchmarks, FARR achieves the best dataset-average MSE and MAE among the compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Matching the influence of conditioning to the temporal context through endpoint evidence can make auxiliary conditioning useful for forecasting, and the code is to be released.

title: Responsible GenAI Use During Active Armed Conflict: Evidence from Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms
summary: Armed conflict can increase the value of Generative AI (GenAI) while undermining the conditions required for its responsible use. Yet the perspectives of community-based humanitarian responders working under these conditions remain underrepresented in responsible AI research. We examine GenAI use in Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs), a community-led humanitarian network, through an exploratory survey of 89 respondents and 15 semi-structured interviews with GenAI users and non-users. War reconfigures GenAI's role, making it most useful where its outputs are hardest to verify. ERR responders turned to GenAI when conflict made human expertise difficult or dangerous to reach. However, participants cautioned that GenAI could not independently establish rapidly changing local conditions, and that relying on its outputs could lead to harmful decisions when human verification was difficult. Risks arose before GenAI was used. For some volunteers, carrying a phone or accessing the internet could expose them to danger. Others were concerned that sharing sensitive beneficiary or operational information with GenAI could put people at risk. Participants feared that AI-assisted reports could undermine their credibility with donors, whose funding sustains the food and medical aid ERRs provide. Access to GenAI was uneven, and volunteers using it sometimes relied on colleagues with relevant expertise or local knowledge to verify its results. Our findings show that responsible use of GenAI during conflict depends not only on model performance or individual adoption, but also on whether responders can safely access these tools, verify their outputs against local conditions, and recognize when limiting or avoiding GenAI is the more responsible choice.

AI.tldr: An exploratory study of Sudan's community-led Emergency Response Rooms finds that GenAI is most useful where its outputs are hardest to verify, and that responsible use during armed conflict depends on safe access, verification and knowing when to refrain. The study draws on a survey of 89 respondents and 15 interviews.
AI.motivation: Community-based humanitarian responders working under armed conflict are underrepresented in responsible AI research, and conflict both raises the value of GenAI and undermines the conditions for its responsible use.
AI.method: An exploratory survey of 89 respondents and 15 semi-structured interviews with GenAI users and non-users in Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms.
AI.result: Responders turned to GenAI when conflict made human expertise hard to reach, but participants cautioned that it could not establish rapidly changing local conditions. Risks arose before use: carrying a phone or accessing the internet could endanger volunteers, sharing sensitive beneficiary information could put people at risk, and AI-assisted reports could undermine credibility with donors. Access was uneven, and volunteers sometimes relied on colleagues to verify outputs.
AI.conclusion: Responsible GenAI use during conflict depends on safe access, verifying outputs against local conditions, and recognizing when limiting or avoiding GenAI is the more responsible choice.

title: When Bigger Becomes Brittle: Why Compression Hurts More as Language Models Scale
summary: Quantization and pruning reduce the cost of deploying language models, but their effects are usually reported as benchmark scores. Such scores record only the loss that remains at the output. Inside the model, compression damages some components more than others, and the rest of the network can partly compensate. The observed loss therefore reflects both the damage and this compensation, which benchmark scores cannot separate. How the two combine, and whether their balance changes with model size, remains unclear. We study this compensation for in-context retrieval, a capability carried by a small, identifiable set of attention heads. To separate the two, the expected loss from ablating these heads is decomposed exactly into the part restored by the rest of the network, attributed to the components responsible, and the part that reaches the output. This decomposition is then compared across model sizes. For damage of comparable size, smaller models restore most of the loss, whereas larger models retain most of it, because the compensating responses offset less of it as models grow. Compressing the heads produces the same pattern. Compression that is nearly harmless in small models can therefore be costly in large ones.

AI.tldr: Quantization and pruning damage language models more as they scale, because larger models restore less of the lost in-context retrieval capability through compensation by the rest of the network. Compression that is nearly harmless in small models can therefore be costly in large ones.
AI.motivation: Benchmark scores of compressed models record only the output loss, which mixes the damage with the compensation by other components, and how the two combine as model size changes remained unclear.
AI.method: For in-context retrieval, a capability carried by a small set of attention heads, the expected loss from ablating those heads is decomposed exactly into the part restored by the rest of the network, the part attributed to responsible components, and the part that reaches the output; this decomposition is compared across model sizes, and compressing the heads produces the same pattern.
AI.result: For damage of comparable size, smaller models restore most of the loss, whereas larger models retain most of it, because the compensating responses offset less of the damage as models grow.
AI.conclusion: Compression that is nearly harmless in small models can be costly in large ones, so benchmark scores alone can mislead about the safety of compressing larger models.

title: GuidedWAM: Training-Free Energy Guidance for World Action Models in Autonomous Driving
summary: World action models (WAMs) for autonomous driving couple the driving policy and the visual world model in a single generative network whose objectives are fixed post-training. Conditioning on a new driving objective requires retraining. We study energy guidance as a general mechanism and present GuidedWAM, a model-agnostic framework for injecting driving objectives into frozen WAMs at sampling time. Our framework constructs each objective as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization, and velocity-bounded correction. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released WAMs by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than 10% to the sampling time per step. These results position energy guidance as a practical post-training control channel for WAMs.

AI.tldr: GuidedWAM injects driving objectives into frozen world action models for autonomous driving at sampling time through energy guidance, with no retraining. On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split it improves three frozen, publicly released models by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS.
AI.motivation: World action models couple the driving policy and the visual world model in a single generative network whose objectives are fixed after training, so conditioning on a new driving objective normally requires retraining.
AI.method: Each objective is built as differentiable energies on the sampler's intermediate clean-action estimate, which needs only forward access to the frozen model, and is stabilized by sampling-time guidance scheduling, per-energy normalization and velocity-bounded correction.
AI.result: On the NAVSIM v2 hard-split, guidance improves all three frozen, publicly released world action models by 1.8 to 3.6 EPDMS, averaged over three sampler seeds, and adds less than 10% to the sampling time per step.
AI.conclusion: Energy guidance is presented as a practical post-training control channel for world action models.

title: Adaptive Semantic Branching: Disagreement-Localized Cross-Trajectory Regeneration for Reasoning Candidate Expansion
summary: Reasoning trajectories generated for the same problem often arrive at conflicting answers. These disagreements reveal alternative intermediate decisions that can be reused to explore new solutions. We introduce Adaptive Semantic Branching (ASB), a training-free inference procedure that turns cross-trajectory disagreement into targeted candidate generation. ASB first groups independently sampled trajectories by extracted final answer, selects a representative from each group, and aligns their reasoning steps with a monotonic dynamic program. A persistent-divergence objective identifies the point at which initially similar reasoning paths develop different continuations. For each selected directed pair, ASB retains the source trajectory's textual prefix, extracts a short reasoning window from a competing donor trajectory, and generates a fresh solution conditioned on both. A diversity-aware policy allocates up to three additional generations according to the answer-cluster structure. In a 500-problem MATH evaluation with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, ASB increases oracle candidate coverage from 445/500 (89.0%) with seven initial samples to 455/500 (91.0%), recovering correct candidates for 10 of the 55 initially uncovered problems. The method uses 576 additional generation calls across the evaluation set, averaging 8.152 calls per problem. We provide a precise specification of the branching operator, alignment objective, generation policy, and experimental configuration.

AI.tldr: Adaptive Semantic Branching is a training-free inference procedure that turns disagreement between reasoning trajectories into targeted new candidate solutions. On a 500-problem MATH evaluation with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, it raises oracle candidate coverage from 89.0% to 91.0%.
AI.motivation: Reasoning trajectories for the same problem often reach conflicting answers, and these disagreements reveal alternative intermediate decisions that could be reused to explore new solutions.
AI.method: Trajectories are grouped by extracted final answer, a representative is selected from each group, and their steps are aligned with a monotonic dynamic program; a persistent-divergence objective locates where paths diverge, and for each directed pair the source prefix is kept, a reasoning window from a competing donor is inserted, and a fresh solution is generated, with a diversity-aware policy allocating up to three extra generations.
AI.result: On the 500-problem MATH evaluation, oracle coverage rises from 445/500 (89.0%) with seven initial samples to 455/500 (91.0%), recovering correct candidates for 10 of the 55 initially uncovered problems, using 576 additional generation calls and averaging 8.152 calls per problem.
AI.conclusion: Cross-trajectory disagreement is a usable signal for targeted candidate generation, at a cost of 576 additional generation calls across the evaluation set.

title: How Finite Brains Generalize Without Bound: Spatial Memory as a Universal Computer
summary: A child who learns to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace the difference to what a learner reads when it decides. A position, a count or a time keeps taking new values as the input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine is at least 99% correct, on average over lengths 41 to 500, on nine of fifteen benchmark tasks, five of them tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves; given new cycles after training it reverses strings of 15,015 symbols without error and fails beyond that on the curve the theory predicts; and its controllers run unchanged on neurons.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that a learner which reads positions as coordinates and decides only by coincidences can generalize to inputs of any length, and reports a cycle-based machine that is at least 99% correct on lengths 41 to 500 on nine of fifteen benchmark tasks.
AI.motivation: LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones, whereas people generalize addition and grammar to any length; the paper seeks to explain this difference through what a learner reads when it decides.
AI.method: A generalizing memory must be made of cycles (grid modules), with cells that detect return (place cells), records (hippocampal index) and a prefrontal controller that moves the cycles; the resulting machine is trained on strings up to 40 symbols and its controllers run unchanged on neurons.
AI.result: Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine is at least 99% correct on average over lengths 41 to 500 on nine of fifteen benchmark tasks, five of which no LSTM or Transformer solves; with new cycles after training it reverses strings of 15,015 symbols without error and fails beyond that on the curve the theory predicts.
AI.conclusion: Finite brains can generalize without bound under this theory, and the cycle machine's controllers run unchanged on neurons.

title: ChemE-as-Code: An Open-Source Platform for Agentic AI in Chemical Engineering
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables; Supporting Information (28 pages) appended. Submitted to AIChE Journal. Code and data: this https URL
summary: ChemE-as-Code provides an open-source environment in which AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) can carry out chemical engineering work and engineers can check it. Its calculation tools range from catalysis through process simulation to plant layout, HAZOP and life cycle assessment, and skills tell a general-purpose agent how to use them. Engineering files are linked, machine-readable and versioned in Git; calculations run outside the LLM, each value records its origin, and automated checks report inconsistencies and out-of-date results by file and line. In an illustrative ammonia case, agents developed a written task into a preliminary basic-engineering package (simulation files, P&IDs, layout, HAZOP, datasheets, relief) for USD 224 of API cost in the design sessions. Planted faults and engineering changes show that the checks find what their rules cover and miss the rest, so they guide human review rather than replace it. No independent engineer has reviewed the design.

AI.tldr: ChemE-as-Code is an open-source platform in which LLM agents carry out chemical engineering work that engineers can check, with calculations run outside the LLM and automated consistency checks. In an illustrative ammonia case, agents produced a preliminary basic-engineering package for USD 224 of API cost.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI for chemical engineering needs work that engineers can trace and check, rather than LLM outputs that cannot be verified.
AI.method: Calculation tools span catalysis, process simulation, plant layout, HAZOP and life cycle assessment, and skills tell a general-purpose agent how to use them; engineering files are linked, machine-readable and versioned in Git, each value records its origin, and automated checks report inconsistencies and out-of-date results by file and line.
AI.result: In the ammonia case, agents developed a written task into a preliminary package (simulation files, P&IDs, layout, HAZOP, datasheets, relief) for USD 224 of API cost. Planted faults and engineering changes show that the checks find what their rules cover and miss the rest.
AI.conclusion: The checks guide human review rather than replace it, and no independent engineer has reviewed the design.

title: Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, evaluating the correctness of their responses is crucial for reliable use. However, such evaluation is challenging because reference answers are rarely available in practice. Existing reference-free methods mainly rely on output signals, which may assign high scores to incorrect responses and thus do not necessarily reflect correctness. This motivates exploring the model's internal computation for complementary correctness signals. Recent studies exploit internal states, but they mainly analyze hidden-state trajectories across layers, which record only the combined updates of attention and feed-forward networks (FFNs) and overlook how these components interact. We therefore propose Circe, a training-free self-evaluation method that assesses a response using both internal and external signals, without reference answers or repeated sampling. For internal signals, we first introduce component interaction consistency (CIC), which measures the directional alignment between attention updates in earlier layers and attention-induced FFN output changes in later layers. We further incorporate representation geometry (RG) to characterize normalized displacement and angular changes along layerwise hidden-state trajectories. For the external signal, we convert the mean negative log-likelihood of generated tokens into a bounded likelihood confidence (LC) score. Finally, we fuse CIC, RG, and LC into a unified correctness score. Experiments on five LLMs and six benchmarks across four domains show that our method distinguishes correct from incorrect responses more effectively than existing baselines, and generalizes to multilingual, multimodal, and open-world settings.

AI.tldr: Circe is a training-free LLM self-evaluation method that scores response correctness from internal component interaction consistency, representation geometry and likelihood confidence, without reference answers or repeated sampling. It separates correct from incorrect responses more effectively than existing baselines across five LLMs and six benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Reference answers are rarely available in practice, reference-free output signals can assign high scores to incorrect responses, and hidden-state trajectory analyses overlook how attention and FFN components interact.
AI.method: Component interaction consistency measures the directional alignment between attention updates in earlier layers and attention-induced FFN output changes in later layers; representation geometry characterizes normalized displacement and angular changes along hidden-state trajectories; the mean negative log-likelihood of generated tokens becomes a bounded likelihood confidence score; the three signals are fused into one correctness score.
AI.result: Across five LLMs and six benchmarks in four domains, Circe distinguishes correct from incorrect responses more effectively than existing baselines and generalizes to multilingual, multimodal and open-world settings.
AI.conclusion: Internal component interactions give complementary correctness signals, making training-free self-evaluation a practical option when reference answers are unavailable.

title: Secure Formal Raising: Protecting the Development of AI through Executable Properties
summary: Model raising revisits Turing's developmental view of machine intelligence. Formal Raising (FR) has recently been proposed to complement this view with explicit behavioral properties. This paper extends that proposal to the security of the raising environment. Secure Formal Raising (SFR) models policy integrity, authorization, and confidential data flow using four-valued evidence that preserves unknown and inconsistent assessments. We prove six security invariants and show that they force admission to accept only confirmed evidence. A plain-C reference implementation satisfies the invariants in a bounded exhaustive exploration, which also exposes a confused-deputy gap for tool calls that a provenance requirement closes.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Formal Raising to the security of the raising environment, proposing Secure Formal Raising (SFR), which uses four-valued evidence and six security invariants so that admission accepts only confirmed evidence. A plain-C reference implementation satisfies the invariants in a bounded exhaustive exploration and exposes a confused-deputy gap for tool calls that a provenance requirement closes.
AI.motivation: Formal Raising complements Turing's developmental view of machine intelligence with explicit behavioral properties but does not address the security of the raising environment, which covers policy integrity, authorization and confidential data flow.
AI.method: SFR models policy integrity, authorization and confidential data flow using four-valued evidence that preserves unknown and inconsistent assessments, and defines six security invariants that force admission to accept only confirmed evidence.
AI.result: A plain-C reference implementation satisfies the six invariants in a bounded exhaustive exploration, and this exploration exposes a confused-deputy gap for tool calls that a provenance requirement closes.
AI.conclusion: Explicit security invariants and a provenance requirement can keep the AI raising environment from admitting unconfirmed or improperly authorized evidence, extending formal raising to security.

title: When Imperfect Automated Fact-Checking Backfires: Social Learning in the Presence of Misinformation
summary: Automated fact-checking tools, cheap and fast but imperfect, are increasingly available on social platforms. We study when such tools can backfire in a sequential social learning model of misinformation. Agents observe an article's reliability and their predecessors' actions, which indicate whether they liked or disliked the article. They may also pay to fact-check it.
