We examine how welfare, defined as the probability of a correct cascade, changes when a free, error-prone automated tool supplements costly but perfectly accurate manual fact-checking. Two opposing effects arise. Broader use of fact-checking helps agents escape wrong cascades. At the same time, errors from the automated tool can mislead agents who would otherwise have verified the article perfectly, reducing the likelihood of correct cascades. We prove that adding the tool strictly lowers welfare for articles of intermediate reliability when truthful articles are not too informative and manual checking is sufficiently costly. Simulations show that the tool can help on either side of the intermediate range, and that it improves on manual-only checking on average only above a threshold accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a sequential social learning model of misinformation in which a free but error-prone automated fact-checking tool supplements costly, perfectly accurate manual checking, and shows that adding the tool can strictly lower welfare, defined as the probability of a correct cascade, for articles of intermediate reliability.
AI.motivation: Automated fact-checking tools are cheap and increasingly available on social platforms, but their imperfection may mislead agents, and it is unclear when such tools help or backfire in social learning.
AI.method: Agents observe an article's reliability and the actions of predecessors, which reveal whether they liked or disliked the article, and may pay for manual fact-checking. The welfare effect of adding a free, error-prone automated tool to manual checking is analyzed through two opposing effects, combined with theoretical proofs and simulations.
AI.result: The authors prove that adding the tool strictly lowers welfare for articles of intermediate reliability when truthful articles are not too informative and manual checking is sufficiently costly. Simulations show the tool can help on either side of the intermediate range and improves on manual-only checking on average only above a threshold accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Imperfect automated fact-checking can backfire, so deploying such tools benefits social learning only when their accuracy exceeds a threshold, and their effect depends on article reliability and the cost of manual checking.

title: MUSS: A Multi-scale and Sequence-based Model for Single-cell Gene Regulation
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures; includes references, appendices, and the NeurIPS checklist
summary: Modeling gene regulation in single cells requires jointly representing DNA sequence, chromatin accessibility, and gene expression across regulatory scales. Sequence-based models capture DNA-level regulatory grammar but often lack cell-level resolution, whereas many single-cell omics models represent genes and peaks as fixed-vocabulary tokens without their underlying sequence. Here, we present MUSS, a sequence-based multi-scale model for single-cell gene regulation that preserves both DNA-level and cell-level resolution. MUSS derives peak- and gene-level representations from DNA using a frozen pre-trained sequence encoder and integrates them through peak-peak self-attention and distance-biased peak-gene interactions. Peak masked language modeling followed by training on paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq aligns these representations with cell-specific regulatory states. Across gene expression prediction, enhancer-gene linking, motif-guided regulatory prioritization, and zero-shot cell clustering, MUSS achieves strong performance against sequence-based and single-cell omics baselines. It further predicts expression for genes and peaks unseen during task training. These results support sequence-grounded, multi-scale representations for decoding cell-type-specific regulatory programs. Code, datasets, and model checkpoints are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MUSS is a sequence-based multi-scale model for single-cell gene regulation that derives peak- and gene-level representations from DNA using a frozen pre-trained sequence encoder and aligns them with scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data, achieving strong performance across several regulatory tasks.
AI.motivation: Sequence-based models capture DNA-level regulatory grammar but lack cell-level resolution, while many single-cell omics models represent genes and peaks as fixed-vocabulary tokens without their underlying sequence.
AI.method: MUSS derives peak- and gene-level representations from DNA with a frozen pre-trained sequence encoder and integrates them through peak-peak self-attention and distance-biased peak-gene interactions. It is trained with peak masked language modeling, followed by training on paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data.
AI.result: MUSS achieves strong performance against sequence-based and single-cell omics baselines on gene expression prediction, enhancer-gene linking, motif-guided regulatory prioritization and zero-shot cell clustering. It also predicts expression for genes and peaks unseen during task training.
AI.conclusion: Sequence-grounded, multi-scale representations can decode cell-type-specific regulatory programs, preserving both DNA-level and cell-level resolution.

title: Create Your Own Work Stack: Deploying Self-hosted AI and Tooling in a Tech Startup
comment: Accepted for poster presentation at the Thirty-Ninth Annual Conference on Innovative Applications of Artificial Intelligence (IAAI-27), February 18-20, 2027
summary: Self-hosting AI is often presented as a way to reduce inference costs and increase control, but deployment introduces its own costs. We report our experience deploying a hybrid AI stack at Grayhat Developers, a small software company with an AI-intensive development workflow. Our initial motivation was to counter the growing cost of commercial AI usage: Claude/Codex incurred approximately \$325 per month, with more than 25.93 billion recorded tokens. We experimented with local open-source models as replacements for commercial coding agents, but after learning that their performance and inference speed were insufficient, we adopted a hybrid approach in which commercial agents remained responsible for complex tasks while local models handled lower-complexity tasks, organizational information retrieval, and synchronization with self-hosted tools including Outline, Plane, and ERPNext. We estimated that approximately 30--40\% of our commercial AI workload was associated with context transfer, documentation synchronization, task management, and related operational coordination. By moving this work to local models, we estimate that approximately 90\% of this coordination workload could be handled without commercial inference, corresponding to an estimated 27--36\% reduction in overall commercial-AI workload or cost-equivalent usage. Our first internal deployment nevertheless failed to achieve adoption because it introduced UX friction. Replacing it with a centrally configured deployment substantially improved feedback and adoption. We conclude that local inference is most useful not as a wholesale replacement for commercial AI, but as part of a hybrid architecture that assigns tasks according to their capability requirements, cost, context demands, and operational sensitivity.

AI.tldr: The authors report deploying a hybrid AI stack at a small software company, where commercial agents handle complex tasks and local open-source models handle lower-complexity coordination work. They estimate this could cut commercial AI workload or cost-equivalent usage by 27 to 36 percent.
AI.motivation: Commercial AI usage was costly, with Claude/Codex incurring about $325 per month and more than 25.93 billion recorded tokens, and self-hosting is often presented as a way to reduce costs and increase control, although deployment introduces its own costs.
AI.method: The company first tried local open-source models as replacements for commercial coding agents, found their performance and inference speed insufficient, and then adopted a hybrid approach in which local models handle lower-complexity tasks, organizational information retrieval and synchronization with self-hosted tools including Outline, Plane and ERPNext. A first internal deployment was replaced by a centrally configured one.
AI.result: The authors estimate that 30 to 40 percent of the commercial AI workload was associated with context transfer, documentation synchronization, task management and related coordination, and that about 90 percent of this coordination workload could be handled locally, corresponding to an estimated 27 to 36 percent reduction in overall commercial-AI workload or cost-equivalent usage. The first deployment failed to achieve adoption because of UX friction, while the centrally configured deployment substantially improved feedback and adoption.
AI.conclusion: Local inference is most useful as part of a hybrid architecture that assigns tasks by capability requirements, cost, context demands and operational sensitivity, rather than as a wholesale replacement for commercial AI.

title: A Generative Foundation Model for Multimodal Tokamak Tasks
summary: Tokamak experiments record diverse measurements, including waveforms, profiles, fields, and scalars, which are used to reconstruct the plasma, forecast its evolution, recover associated control signals, and estimate disruption risk. Most models are built separately for one task and a fixed set of inputs and outputs, and each relies on a prescribed subset of diagnostics rather than structuring the full multimodal observation set to extract global, cross-signal information about the discharge. These limitations motivate a reusable foundation model that adapts to each task's input-output schema and models heterogeneous target signals jointly, rather than retraining a separate model for every configuration. In this work, we extend the TokaMark benchmark with two groups of tasks for actuator action inversion and disruption prediction, yielding 20 MAST tasks in six groups with explicit schemas and evaluation protocols. Then, we introduce GenToka, a generative tokamak foundation model that jointly generates schema-selected targets through a shared conditional diffusion Transformer, with signal-specific codecs preserving native time series, profiles, fields, and scalars; foundation pretraining and task-specific adaptation transfer cross-signal structure across all six groups. Evaluation on MAST measurements shows that GenToka reduces macro-average normalized root mean squared error relative to TokaMind by 4.7% on Groups 1-4 and by 17.7% on Group 5, and improves macro-average window-level F1 on Group 6 by 8.4% at a common validation-selected threshold. GenToka provides a reusable, generative, and multimodal pathway for experimental tokamaks, linking plasma-state reconstruction, actuator inference, and disruption warning from shared measurements to support more integrated, data-driven fusion plasma prediction and control research.

AI.tldr: GenToka is a generative tokamak foundation model that jointly generates schema-selected targets with a shared conditional diffusion Transformer and signal-specific codecs. Evaluated on MAST measurements across an extended TokaMark benchmark of 20 tasks in six groups, it reduces normalized RMSE relative to TokaMind and improves window-level F1 on the disruption prediction group.
AI.motivation: Tokamak models are usually built separately for one task and a fixed set of inputs and outputs, and each relies on a prescribed subset of diagnostics rather than the full multimodal observation set, which motivates a reusable foundation model.
AI.method: The authors extend the TokaMark benchmark with two groups of tasks for actuator action inversion and disruption prediction, yielding 20 MAST tasks in six groups with explicit schemas and evaluation protocols. GenToka jointly generates schema-selected targets through a shared conditional diffusion Transformer, with signal-specific codecs preserving native time series, profiles, fields and scalars, and uses foundation pretraining followed by task-specific adaptation.
AI.result: On MAST measurements, GenToka reduces macro-average normalized RMSE relative to TokaMind by 4.7 percent on Groups 1-4 and by 17.7 percent on Group 5, and improves macro-average window-level F1 on Group 6 by 8.4 percent at a common validation-selected threshold.
AI.conclusion: GenToka offers a reusable, generative and multimodal pathway linking plasma-state reconstruction, actuator inference and disruption warning from shared measurements, supporting more integrated data-driven plasma prediction and control research.

title: PCBRouteAgent: How Close Are LLM Agents to Becoming PCB Routing Engineers?
summary: Automating printed circuit board (PCB) routing requires coordinating board-level connectivity decisions with geometric execution under strict design rules. Although recent agents can interact with native routing tools, reliable routing on complex boards remains challenging. We present PCBRouteAgent, a multimodal PCB routing agent inspired by how human engineers coordinate global strategy with local execution. A Global Routing Planner combines board images and structured electrical and geometric information to specify connection topology, routing order, corridors, and layer transitions. A Detailed Routing Executor realizes these guides through KiCad's native routing engine and performs bounded local recovery. Unresolved failures are returned as structured feedback, enabling targeted guide revisions while preserving accepted routes. We evaluate PCBRouteAgent on 247 synthetic and real-world boards from four PCBWorld-Bench test splits. It achieves clean-pass rates of 100%, 94.9%, 100%, and 40% on D2, D3-A, D3-B, and D3-C, respectively. On the three real-world subsets, PCBRouteAgent outperforms the best evaluated baseline in clean-pass rate by 13.9, 36, and 10 percentage points, respectively.

AI.tldr: PCBRouteAgent is a multimodal PCB routing agent that pairs a Global Routing Planner with a Detailed Routing Executor built on KiCad's native routing engine. It reaches clean-pass rates of 100 percent, 94.9 percent, 100 percent and 40 percent on four PCBWorld-Bench test splits, and outperforms the best evaluated baseline on three real-world subsets.
AI.motivation: Automating PCB routing requires coordinating board-level connectivity decisions with geometric execution under strict design rules, and reliable routing on complex boards remains challenging for existing agents that interact with native routing tools.
AI.method: A Global Routing Planner combines board images with structured electrical and geometric information to specify connection topology, routing order, corridors and layer transitions. A Detailed Routing Executor realizes these guides through KiCad's native routing engine and performs bounded local recovery, while unresolved failures return as structured feedback that drives targeted guide revisions and preserves accepted routes.
AI.result: Evaluated on 247 synthetic and real-world boards from four PCBWorld-Bench test splits, PCBRouteAgent achieves clean-pass rates of 100 percent on D2, 94.9 percent on D3-A, 100 percent on D3-B and 40 percent on D3-C. On the three real-world subsets it outperforms the best evaluated baseline in clean-pass rate by 13.9, 36 and 10 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating global strategy with local execution, and feeding failures back as structured guidance, makes LLM agents substantially more capable at PCB routing, although performance on the hardest split remains low.

title: BabyTheorist: A Benchmark for Learning to Theorize the World from Observation Alone
summary: How would we know whether a machine truly understands the world? We argue that one key capability is \textit{observational theory learning}: acquiring reusable theories from pure observations and applying them to new situations. Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus primarily on the latter, presenting each task as a few-shot puzzle grouped by a common rule. We introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark for controlled training and evaluation of observational theory learning. BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs; during training, learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities, or support sets. To support theory learning and evaluation, BabyTheorist controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms, and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.

AI.tldr: BabyTheorist is a benchmark for observational theory learning, in which learners acquire reusable theories from before-after visual observations generated by hidden compositional programs without labels. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances.
AI.motivation: Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus on applying a rule to few-shot puzzles rather than on acquiring reusable theories from pure observation, which the authors argue is a key capability for understanding the world.
AI.method: BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs. During training learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities or support sets. The benchmark controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping.
AI.result: Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, and the gap widens as the curriculum advances.
AI.conclusion: BabyTheorist isolates observational theory learning, a capability that current program-learning approaches do not yet address.

title: Signals, Evidence, and Context: User Scrutiny in Real-World LLM Conversations
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often present synthesized answers without making their supporting evidence easy to inspect. We study how features of these answers relate to users' subsequent accepting, checking, and challenging in 489,283 assistant-user response pairs from ShareChat and WildChat. Broad attribution language appears in 31.9% of qualifying responses, compared with explicit URLs in 1.33%, revealing a gap between claims of grounding and preserved inspectable support. Attribution, uncertainty, and other response cues generally accompany both checking and challenging; only uncertainty shows a small statistically distinguishable pooled association favoring checking. Within Technical Help, uncertainty favors checking relative to challenging; refusals and reasoning traces favor challenging in Seeking Information. Scrutiny is concentrated in some conversations, while its apparent turn-to-turn persistence becomes much smaller when conversation-level differences and response ordering are examined separately. These results suggest that supporting verification requires attention to what evidence can be inspected, which question a user is trying to resolve, and the history of the interaction.

AI.tldr: Using 489,283 assistant-user response pairs from ShareChat and WildChat, the paper finds that broad attribution language is common while explicit URLs are rare, and that attribution, uncertainty and other response cues generally accompany both checking and challenging by users rather than predicting one of them.
AI.motivation: LLMs often present synthesized answers without making supporting evidence easy to inspect, so it is unclear how features of answers relate to users' accepting, checking and challenging.
AI.method: The authors analyze 489,283 assistant-user response pairs from ShareChat and WildChat, relating response features such as attribution language, explicit URLs, uncertainty, refusals and reasoning traces to subsequent user behavior, and examine conversation-level differences and response ordering within conversations and by task type.
AI.result: Broad attribution language appears in 31.9 percent of qualifying responses, compared with explicit URLs in 1.33 percent. Attribution, uncertainty and other cues generally accompany both checking and challenging, and only uncertainty shows a small statistically distinguishable pooled association favoring checking. Within Technical Help, uncertainty favors checking over challenging, and refusals and reasoning traces favor challenging in Seeking Information. Apparent turn-to-turn persistence of scrutiny becomes much smaller when conversation-level differences and response ordering are examined separately.
AI.conclusion: Supporting verification requires attention to what evidence can be inspected, which question the user is trying to resolve, and the history of the interaction, since claims of grounding often exceed the inspectable support actually provided.

title: Value-oriented policy distillation for interpretable wind farm power control
summary: Wind farm power control can help the system maintain balance and avoid blackouts. In Europe, this can be achieved through implicit balancing, where a wind farm adjusts its power setpoint in anticipation of the imbalance price using information published by the Transmission System Operator. Thereby, the wind farm helps restore system balance while also reducing its own imbalance costs resulting from forecast errors. However, implicit balancing is a challenging problem since the settlement price is unknown in advance and can be impacted by the pursued control strategy. Reinforcement learning methods could help to solve this problem, but lack the interpretability needed to be deployed on real wind farms. Therefore, we propose a policy distillation framework using explainable boosting machines (EBMs), a variant of generalized additive models, to obtain a transparent control policy. To increase the value captured by the EBM model, we introduce a value-oriented perspective to policy distillation inspired by research in the field of energy forecasting. Furthermore, we suggest to include expert knowledge during model design, such that the control strategy is also justifiable to stakeholders. Using real data of the Belgian grid and an offshore wind farm, we find that our value-oriented and expert-based controller can reduce imbalance costs by 82%, while outperforming a price threshold controller as well as a policy distillation baseline using decision trees.

AI.tldr: The paper distills a reinforcement learning wind farm controller into an interpretable explainable boosting machine (EBM) with a value-oriented objective and expert knowledge, which reduces imbalance costs by 82 percent on real Belgian grid and offshore wind farm data while outperforming a price threshold controller and a decision-tree distillation baseline.
AI.motivation: Implicit balancing lets a wind farm adjust its power setpoint in anticipation of imbalance prices, but the settlement price is unknown in advance and depends on the control strategy. Reinforcement learning can address this but lacks the interpretability needed for deployment on real wind farms.
AI.method: The authors propose a policy distillation framework using explainable boosting machines, a variant of generalized additive models, to obtain a transparent control policy. They add a value-oriented perspective to policy distillation, inspired by energy forecasting research, and include expert knowledge during model design so the strategy is justifiable to stakeholders.
AI.result: Using real data of the Belgian grid and an offshore wind farm, the value-oriented and expert-based controller reduces imbalance costs by 82 percent, outperforming a price threshold controller and a policy distillation baseline that uses decision trees.
AI.conclusion: A transparent, value-oriented and expert-informed distilled policy can match or beat both simple rules and a decision-tree distillation baseline, making interpretable wind farm control a practical option for deployment.

title: LeanContext: Disentangling Mathematical Resources from Local Formal Context in Lean Whole-Proof Generation
summary: Neural theorem proving increasingly uses retrieved premises and project context to support proof generation. Evaluating these resources requires measuring the advantage of target-selected declarations over comparable alternatives and how this advantage depends on training. We introduce LeanContext, a benchmark of 129,826 Lean whole-proof generation problems, to investigate these questions. We group selected complete preceding mathematical declarations as Mathematical Context (MC) and the remaining selected local source commands as Environment Context (EC). Four aligned input views support crossed training and inference evaluations with shared targets and original Lean verification environments. For both diffusion- and autoregressive-based models, selected declarations outperform comparable alternatives by a larger margin when training includes MC. Final-input audits identify omitted declarations referenced by the target. Prioritizing these dependencies improves Pass@32 by 1.40% and 1.70% for LLaDA and Llama, respectively, on 2,000 targets. The selection experiment operates without access to target reference proofs and holds checkpoints, EC, and inference budgets constant. The code and dataset are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: LeanContext is a benchmark of 129,826 Lean whole-proof generation problems that separates mathematical context from local environment context. Prioritizing dependencies omitted from the input improves Pass@32 by 1.40 percent for LLaDA and 1.70 percent for Llama on 2,000 targets.
AI.motivation: Neural theorem proving uses retrieved premises and project context, but evaluating these resources requires measuring the advantage of target-selected declarations over comparable alternatives and how that advantage depends on training.
AI.method: The authors group selected complete preceding mathematical declarations as Mathematical Context (MC) and the remaining selected local source commands as Environment Context (EC). Four aligned input views support crossed training and inference evaluations with shared targets and original Lean verification environments, applied to diffusion-based and autoregressive models. Omitted declarations referenced by the target are identified by final-input audits and prioritized without access to reference proofs, holding checkpoints, EC and inference budgets constant.
AI.result: For both diffusion- and autoregressive models, selected declarations outperform comparable alternatives by a larger margin when training includes MC. Prioritizing dependencies referenced by the target improves Pass@32 by 1.40 percent for LLaDA and 1.70 percent for Llama on 2,000 targets.
AI.conclusion: Mathematical context matters more when models are trained with it, and auditing and prioritizing the declarations a target depends on can improve whole-proof generation without changing the models.

title: A Generative Model of Contextual Integrity: Appropriate vs. Inappropriate Information Sharing
comment: Accepted as a main conference paper at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Contextual integrity (CI) holds that appropriate information flow depends on context-specific norms. The same disclosure may be appropriate in one context and inappropriate in another. We build a generative model of contextual integrity to study information sharing through simulated conversations. Two actors played by large language models exchange messages, with one holding private information and the other seeking it. We examine how sharing and refusal vary with the situation, the holder's decision logic, disposition, and the underlying language model. Actors shared information with the rightful recipients when it was needed, but also disclosed it to people who were not entitled to receive it. The model provides a way to study how disclosure and refusal develop through conversation as the situations and the actors vary.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a generative model of contextual integrity in which two LLM-played actors exchange messages, one holding private information and the other seeking it, to study when information is shared or refused. Actors shared information with rightful recipients when needed but also disclosed it to people not entitled to receive it.
AI.motivation: Contextual integrity holds that appropriate information flow depends on context-specific norms, so the same disclosure may be appropriate in one context and inappropriate in another, but this is hard to study directly.
AI.method: Two actors played by large language models exchange messages in simulated conversations, with one holding private information and the other seeking it. The authors vary the situation, the holder's decision logic, disposition and the underlying language model, and examine how sharing and refusal develop through conversation.
AI.result: Actors shared information with the rightful recipients when it was needed, but also disclosed it to people who were not entitled to receive it.
AI.conclusion: The generative model offers a way to study how disclosure and refusal develop through conversation as situations and actors vary, and it reveals inappropriate sharing that norm-aware behavior should prevent.

title: First-Token Attraction in Mamba Dynamics
summary: We study token dynamics in deep Mamba models, with a particular focus on the attracting role of the first token. Unlike attention mechanisms, where token interactions are governed by positive scalar coefficients, Mamba dynamics involve full matrix-valued interaction coefficients with no positivity or definiteness guarantees. This structural difference makes Mamba dynamics substantially harder to analyze and prevents the direct application of existing techniques for attention-based models. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a new analytical framework based on a high-dimensional invariant box and a sharp exit-time argument, which together recover an effective form of sign-definiteness. Using this framework, we characterize the possible limit points of token trajectories and prove explicit exponential convergence rates. Our analysis reveals that the first token has privileged dynamics: its limiting direction attracts subsequent tokens, inducing token clustering and attention-sink phenomena in deep Mamba models. We further show that this attraction mechanism extends to broader sequence dynamics, including state-space models, causal attention, and classical time-series models. Experiments on Falcon-Mamba-7B validate our predictions, showing that concentration on the first token increases with depth and dominates in later layers.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that in deep Mamba models the first token has privileged dynamics whose limiting direction attracts subsequent tokens, inducing token clustering and attention-sink phenomena. Experiments on Falcon-Mamba-7B show that concentration on the first token increases with depth and dominates in later layers.
AI.motivation: Unlike attention, where token interactions use positive scalar coefficients, Mamba dynamics involve full matrix-valued interaction coefficients with no positivity or definiteness guarantees, so existing techniques for attention-based models do not directly apply.
AI.method: The authors introduce an analytical framework based on a high-dimensional invariant box and a sharp exit-time argument, which together recover an effective form of sign-definiteness. They use it to characterize possible limit points of token trajectories and prove explicit exponential convergence rates.
AI.result: The analysis shows the first token attracts subsequent tokens, and the attraction mechanism extends to state-space models, causal attention and classical time-series models. Experiments on Falcon-Mamba-7B validate the predictions, with concentration on the first token increasing with depth and dominating in later layers.
AI.conclusion: The first-token attraction explains token clustering and attention-sink behavior in deep Mamba models, and the mechanism is not specific to Mamba but extends to broader sequence dynamics.

title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures, 10 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that when a coding agent is exposed to benchmark success criteria, it produces code that overfits to the verifier rather than the instructed task, because the advantage disappears when criteria change slightly. The authors propose instruction-faithful criteria that better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.
AI.motivation: Several recent embodied self-improvement works expose benchmark success criteria to the learning agent, a practice the authors call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria were written to verify imitation-learned policies and often demand more than the language instructions, so verifier scores may not reflect task completion.
AI.method: The authors run controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE and compare its success rate under the given criteria, then change the criteria slightly without departing from the original instructions and measure transfer of the skills the agent develops across tasks. They then propose instruction-faithful criteria.
AI.result: With CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly. Skills developed under CE transfer poorly across tasks, and instruction-faithful criteria better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark scores under exposed criteria can overstate embodied agents' ability, so evaluation should use criteria faithful to the instructions, since high scores may reflect learning the verifier rather than the task.

title: Enhancing Local and Global Structure in Compressed AI Agent Memory
summary: AI agents store text as embedding vectors and compress them at scale. A compression is accepted when each item's nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete, and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. We evaluate both ends with two label-free fidelities from our prior work: the local fidelity $L$ at 10 neighbors and the global fidelity $G$ at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach an $L$ of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme; PCA with 8-bit codes, at an $L$ of 0.77, moves 1.7 percent. Rescoring leaves the stored codes, and thus $G$, unchanged. We prove that across the $G$ band, $1-\nu_k$ is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, and that this rate follows the distance noise of the compression (correlation 0.979). Our locality-aware quantization (LAQ) turns the bound into a hinge objective on the codebooks of an OPQ index, keeping its bytes, rotation, and search. To our knowledge, LAQ is the first quantizer whose objective comes from a proven bound on the far end. Reconstruction alone raises $G$ in 0 of 52 held-out runs; the far hinge raises it in all 52. LAQ raises $G$ in all 52 ($p=8.5\times 10^{-4}$ over 13 memory-encoder groups), including the external FinDER memory, has the highest $G$ of seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scales to a million passages, and keeps evidence recall.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes locality-aware quantization (LAQ), which turns a proven bound on the far end of memory geometry into a hinge objective for the codebooks of an OPQ index, raising global fidelity G in all tested runs while keeping bytes, rotation and search unchanged.
AI.motivation: Compressed AI agent memories are accepted when each item's nearest neighbors survive, but agents also consolidate, delete and compare memories, tasks that depend on which items lie far apart. Local compression fidelity alone does not guarantee global structure.
AI.method: The authors evaluate two label-free fidelities: local fidelity L at 10 neighbors and global fidelity G at 30 to 50 percent of the memory. They prove that across the G band, 1 minus nu_k is at most 2 to 2.18 times the square root of the near-far rank-violation rate, which follows the distance noise of the compression. LAQ adds a far hinge objective to the codebooks of an OPQ index.
AI.result: At 96 bytes per passage, rescored binary codes reach L of 0.97 yet move 10.1 percent of passages to another theme, while PCA with 8-bit codes at L of 0.77 moves 1.7 percent. Reconstruction alone raises G in 0 of 52 held-out runs, whereas the far hinge raises it in all 52. LAQ raises G in all 52 runs (p = 8.5e-4 over 13 memory-encoder groups), has the highest G of seven equal-size quantizers in all 12 Multi-Doc-2025 runs, scales to a million passages and keeps evidence recall.
AI.conclusion: Local neighbor preservation does not ensure global memory structure, and a quantizer whose objective comes from a proven far-end bound preserves it, making LAQ the first quantizer the authors know of with such an objective.

title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Evaluations and Datasets Track
summary: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

AI.tldr: NPCBench is a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma with 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort. Across 30 evaluated models, strong individual-task performance does not guarantee jointly correct diagnostic and care answers, and strict CarePath success reaches at most 23 percent among 21 multimodal models.
AI.motivation: Medical benchmarks usually test isolated factual questions, single-image tasks or static case vignettes, which reveal little about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition across a course of care.
AI.method: NPCBench mirrors specialist training through guideline and foundational knowledge, case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway, supplemented by paired controls and physician calibration.
AI.result: Across 30 evaluated models the authors observe a composition gap, where strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23 percent.
AI.conclusion: NPCBench extends medical AI evaluation beyond static question answering to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

title: Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care
summary: Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates modeling how patient states evolve and generate care demands. However, conventional approaches typically tailor compact state transitions to a single policy question and omit history-dependent dynamics, thus requiring the redefinition of states and transitions when there is a new question that entails different clinical information. We propose to learn a patient world model from longitudinal EHRs using a neural network to provide a shared clinical representation of patient trajectories that can serve simulation questions across scenarios. Taking ICU operations as an example, we train the model on MIMIC-IV, freeze it, and couple its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues via scenario-specific mappings, so that one model renders admission demand, care tasks, and discharge proposals across simulations evaluating ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. Experiments show that our model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies. It also reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, the learned representation captures a 24-h recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points), a contrast missed by compact state models, which propagates into distinct simulated care demand, queue burden, and bed use. These results indicate that a learned world model of patient dynamics has the potential to replace question-specific state models, allowing new care policies to be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without model rebuilding.

AI.tldr: The paper learns a patient world model from longitudinal MIMIC-IV EHRs and couples its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources and queues, so one frozen model can serve different simulation questions. It matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional policy responses, and captures a 24-hour recovery difference that compact state models miss.
AI.motivation: Health system simulation usually tailors compact state transitions to one policy question and omits history-dependent dynamics, so new questions with different clinical information require redefining states and transitions.
AI.method: A neural network is trained on MIMIC-IV, then frozen and coupled through scenario-specific mappings to shared ICU calendars, resources and queues. It renders admission demand, care tasks and discharge proposals across simulations of ICU bed capacity, care dispatch and post-ICU transfer capacity.
AI.result: The model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies, and reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, it captures a 24-hour recovery difference of -6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points, a contrast missed by compact state models.
AI.conclusion: A learned patient world model has the potential to replace question-specific state models, letting new care policies be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without rebuilding the model.

title: The Gold Rush in AI4Math, II: What are signatures of AI-assisted Proofs?
summary: The growing use of AI in mathematics raises a question: can we detect AI involvement in proofs, separately from AI assistance with writing? Historical arXiv papers, recent papers disclosing substantive AI use, and manuscripts released by OpenAI provide a rich empirical basis for studying this question. However, several challenges remain: lack of matched case-control pairs; potential incompleteness of disclosure; and lack of ready-to-use features designed to capture signals of AI involvement in proofs. To address these challenges, we construct five cohorts comprising 8,281 papers by combining existing manuscripts with those we produced using generative AI. These cohorts span different levels of AI involvement and include matched pairs of papers addressing the same research problems. We then introduce ProofTrace, a framework that represents each paper as a graph of immediate proof support (GIPS) and extracts interpretable features of mathematical organization. Our study yields three discoveries. First, principal-component projections of our features reveal a qualitative gradient of AI involvement, where AI-reworded papers remain close to human papers, the two AI-generated cohorts depart in broadly shared directions, and papers disclosing substantive AI use occupy intermediate positions which shifts toward AI-generated cohorts over time. Second, we identify recurring signatures of AI-generated proofs, such as fewer externally cited results, greater reliance on intermediate conclusions, and altered graph connectivity; many of these signatures persist under controls for research field, manuscript length, or graph size. Finally, in a separate detection experiment, ProofTrace distinguishes human-written papers from those disclosing substantive AI use. Its performance remains stable under AI rewording, whereas the performance of state-of-the-art text-based detectors declines sharply.

AI.tldr: ProofTrace represents papers as graphs of immediate proof support and extracts features that separate human-written papers from those disclosing substantive AI use, with performance that stays stable under AI rewording while text-based detectors decline sharply. Across 8,281 papers in five cohorts, AI-generated proofs show recurring structural signatures.
AI.motivation: Detecting AI involvement in mathematical proofs, separately from AI-assisted writing, is challenging because of a lack of matched case-control pairs, potentially incomplete disclosure and a lack of features designed to capture AI signals in proofs.
AI.method: The authors build five cohorts of 8,281 papers by combining existing manuscripts with papers produced using generative AI, spanning different levels of AI involvement and including matched pairs on the same research problems. They represent each paper as a graph of immediate proof support (GIPS) and extract interpretable features of mathematical organization for principal-component analysis and a detection experiment.
AI.result: Principal-component projections reveal a gradient of AI involvement, with AI-reworded papers close to human papers, two AI-generated cohorts departing in broadly shared directions, and papers disclosing substantive AI use in intermediate positions that shift toward AI-generated cohorts over time. AI-generated proofs show fewer externally cited results, greater reliance on intermediate conclusions and altered graph connectivity, many persisting under controls for research field, manuscript length or graph size. ProofTrace's detection performance remains stable under AI rewording, whereas state-of-the-art text-based detectors decline sharply.
AI.conclusion: Proof structure carries interpretable signals of AI involvement that persist under controls and rewording, offering a detection approach more robust than text-based detectors.

title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
summary: Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958). We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves. More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce continuous validation for agentic benchmarks and apply it to Terminal-Bench 2.0, finding issues in roughly 30 percent of the tasks and releasing repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. The repairs raise accuracy by over 10 percentage points and shift leaderboard positions by up to three ranks, while the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958).
AI.motivation: Even carefully validated benchmarks become stale as models find valid solutions that verifiers reject and as changes to evaluation infrastructure invalidate task assumptions, creating a growing gap the authors call benchmark maintenance debt.
AI.method: The continuous-validation workflow combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks and human-gated repairs. The authors apply it to Terminal-Bench 2.0, which had undergone extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release, and evaluate how resource budgets such as fixed wall-clock time shape agent performance.
AI.result: The audit identifies issues in roughly 30 percent of the benchmark, and the repairs raise accuracy by over 10 percentage points, with leaderboard positions moving by up to three ranks. Fixed wall-clock limits materially change results: extending the time limit closes a 20 pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp.
AI.conclusion: Resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside tasks, and as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need revalidation.

title: The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI
summary: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes meta access, giving an LLM assistant a structured, permissioned view of the chat interface and its workspace, and describes a ladder of levels with the Meta Chat prototype in the Chat AI client. It argues this can turn chat into a control layer for the whole workspace while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection and trust.
AI.motivation: The model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it, and general agentic harnesses can change their own settings, so meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary.
AI.method: The authors propose a ladder of meta access levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages with confirmed mutation; and full orchestration. They ground this in the Meta Chat prototype, which builds bounded context from summaries, settings and relevant messages, links references, supports confirmed reversible changes, offers a tutorial library and recommends personas as user-started conversations.
AI.result: The paper reports the design and capabilities of the Meta Chat prototype, including bounded context construction, linked references, confirmed and reversible changes, a browsable tutorial library and persona recommendations, and argues that structured application state can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. No quantitative evaluation is stated in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface, so that chat becomes a control layer without surrendering user control.

title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
summary: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

AI.tldr: ReproBridge builds refined reproducible ML artifacts, with a codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers and a reproduction guide, and shows on ReproBridge-Bench that these artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4 percent to 92.6 percent across four models while reducing downstream API spending by 19.7 percent on average.
AI.motivation: Reproducing ML experiments requires reconstructing procedures scattered across papers, released code and supporting artifacts, so coding agents' success depends on filling in missing details rather than on released artifacts alone.
AI.method: The authors define a standardized artifact design and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow that constructs refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts, and a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. An ablation removes each component.
AI.result: Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4 percent to 92.6 percent and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7 percent on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models above 90 percent mean success. Removing any component reduces success, with the largest losses from removing code and environment.
AI.conclusion: Preserving recovered execution knowledge in artifacts helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
summary: LLM-guided evolutionary search uses AI agents to improve programs for mathematical and computational problems by iteratively refining solutions and combining high-scoring methods. However, the process is often slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity. We present SwarmEvolve, a framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round work in swarms, reason in latent space without decoding to text, and share information by passing KV caches. Each swarm studies the problem from a different angle. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by directly measuring the distances between the agents' hidden state vectors. Crossover of ideas happens naturally in latent space, as a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members. On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve gets the highest average score and needs a median of only 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. On several problems, SwarmEvolve with Qwen3 8B improves on the solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs. Our work shows that agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

AI.tldr: SwarmEvolve is an LLM-guided evolutionary search framework in which hundreds of low-cost agents per round reason in latent space and share KV caches instead of generating long textual chains of thought. On 21 problems it has the highest average score and reaches the best scores of other state-of-the-art frameworks in a median of 3 to 8 minutes, versus 60 minutes for those frameworks.
AI.motivation: LLM-guided evolutionary search is slow because the LLM generates a long textual chain of thought for each round and must repeat this generation many times to maintain population diversity.
AI.method: Agents work in swarms, each studying the problem from a different angle, and reason in latent space without decoding to text, sharing information by passing KV caches. A novelty filter keeps the most distinct agent ideas by measuring distances between their hidden state vectors, and crossover happens in latent space when a summarizer agent receives the combined KV caches of all swarm members.
AI.result: On 21 problems in mathematical discovery and scientific computing, SwarmEvolve has the highest average score and needs a median of 3 to 8 minutes to reach the best scores that other state-of-the-art frameworks reach in 60 minutes. With Qwen3 8B it improves on some solutions that AlphaEvolve first found with frontier LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Agent swarms that communicate in latent space offer a fast, low-cost approach to program search for scientific problems.

title: A minimal dynamical model of human-AI cognitive coevolution
summary: The rapid deployment of generative AI raises the question of whether pervasive cognitive offloading drives a measurable, potentially irreversible decline in unassisted human reasoning. We examine this question with a phenomenological dynamical model based on the Cattell-Horn-Carroll distinction between fluid intelligence ($G_f$) and crystallized intelligence ($G_c$). Starting from the discrete-time Bivariate Latent Change Score formalism used in cognitive-aging research, we derive its continuous-time linear counterpart and introduce a fast third variable representing composite machine-intelligence capability. The machine variable enters the human subsystem through Hill-function modifications of the self-feedback and cross-coupling coefficients. We emphasize that our phenomenological model captures both the positive and negative effects of AI on human cognition. By formalizing the qualitative concepts of positive and negative impacts, we introduce definitions for AI-induced cognitive decline and AI-induced cognitive augmentation. A singular-perturbation reduction, justified via Tikhonov's theorem, collapses the resulting three-dimensional system onto a two-dimensional slow manifold. On this manifold we locate two bifurcations of the equilibrium. In one parameter regime, weakening the contribution of fluid reasoning to crystallized knowledge produces a saddle-node bifurcation that eliminates the stable positive equilibrium. In another, reversing the contribution of crystallized knowledge to fluid reasoning creates opposing feedback; increasing fluid self-feedback then reduces damping and produces a supercritical Hopf bifurcation with a stable periodic orbit. We discuss limitations and future directions, interpret our results as a phenomenological account of a coupled socio-technical system, and state the conditions under which each dynamical regime applies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a phenomenological continuous-time dynamical model of human-AI cognitive coevolution, built on the Cattell-Horn-Carroll distinction between fluid and crystallized intelligence. It finds two bifurcations of the equilibrium: a saddle-node that eliminates the stable positive equilibrium in one regime, and a supercritical Hopf bifurcation with a stable periodic orbit in another.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether pervasive cognitive offloading to generative AI drives a measurable, potentially irreversible decline in unassisted human reasoning, and it needs a model that captures both the positive and the negative effects of AI on human cognition.
AI.method: The discrete-time Bivariate Latent Change Score formalism from cognitive-aging research is converted into a continuous-time linear counterpart with a fast third variable for composite machine-intelligence capability. This variable enters the human subsystem through Hill-function modifications of the self-feedback and cross-coupling coefficients. A singular-perturbation reduction, justified via Tikhonov's theorem, collapses the system onto a two-dimensional slow manifold, and definitions of AI-induced cognitive decline and augmentation are introduced.
AI.result: On the slow manifold, weakening the contribution of fluid reasoning to crystallized knowledge produces a saddle-node bifurcation that eliminates the stable positive equilibrium. Reversing the contribution of crystallized knowledge to fluid reasoning creates opposing feedback, and increasing fluid self-feedback then produces a supercritical Hopf bifurcation with a stable periodic orbit.
AI.conclusion: The model is a phenomenological account of a coupled socio-technical system, with its limitations discussed, and it states the conditions under which each dynamical regime applies.

title: ApproxBrain: Certified Sufficiency Frontiers in Connectome-Constrained Neural Systems
summary: Background. A connectome specifies the substrate available to a nervous system, not how much of it a given computation requires. Reported compact sufficient circuits are point estimates: one subset, one task, one fidelity threshold, one parameterisation. Methods. We formalise computational sufficiency as a cost-indexed family of neuron subsets conditioned on a task and a tolerance pair (permitted degradation epsilon, permitted failure fraction rho), separate task adequacy from phenotype fidelity, and certify candidates on held-out parameter draws with one-sided bounds rather than reporting a single minimum. We measure three quantities a single circuit cannot express: non-decomposability, degeneracy, and an intervention-derived role taxonomy. Results. On a released walking simulator, the published 148-neuron circuit is certified sufficient with margin (mean Dtask = 0.017 over 32 held-out draws, no failure), no 146- or 147-neuron subset of it is sufficient, and removing any one of its three interneurons destroys adequacy. Complement splitting recovers the published set exactly in three of seven seeds and reaches its size in five, within 66-97 evaluations, against 221 neurons for the bundle hierarchy at the same budget. Varying only the task changes which neurons are needed: our best-found solutions retain 155 and 149 neurons and share only 3 of 11 searchable neurons. Relaxing the tolerance reveals alternative sufficient circuits, and the whole-CNS interface alone fails every replicate while 93 search-chosen neurons give a certified solution. Conclusions. Sufficiency is set-valued and conditioned jointly on task and tolerance, and no single search strategy dominates across regimes. A frontier is interpretable only alongside its interface-only baseline, its tolerance and its budget. Every result here is model-relative.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes computational sufficiency in connectome-constrained neural systems as a cost-indexed family of neuron subsets, certified on held-out parameter draws with one-sided bounds. On a released walking simulator it certifies the published 148-neuron circuit as sufficient, and it shows that sufficiency depends jointly on the task and the tolerance.
AI.motivation: Reported compact sufficient circuits are point estimates, with one subset, one task, one fidelity threshold and one parameterization, so they cannot express how much of a connectome a given computation actually requires.
AI.method: Computational sufficiency is defined as a cost-indexed family of neuron subsets conditioned on a task and a tolerance pair (permitted degradation epsilon, permitted failure fraction rho). Task adequacy is separated from phenotype fidelity, candidates are certified on held-out parameter draws with one-sided bounds, and three quantities are measured: non-decomposability, degeneracy, and an intervention-derived role taxonomy. Complement splitting is compared against a bundle hierarchy at the same budget.
AI.result: On a released walking simulator, the published 148-neuron circuit is certified sufficient with margin (mean Dtask 0.017 over 32 held-out draws, no failure), no 146- or 147-neuron subset of it is sufficient, and removing any one of its three interneurons destroys adequacy. Complement splitting recovers the published set exactly in three of seven seeds, within 66 to 97 evaluations, against 221 neurons for the bundle hierarchy at the same budget. Changing only the task changes which neurons are needed: the best-found solutions retain 155 and 149 neurons and share only 3 of 11 searchable neurons.
AI.conclusion: Sufficiency is set-valued and conditioned jointly on task and tolerance, no single search strategy dominates across regimes, and a frontier is interpretable only alongside its interface-only baseline, its tolerance and its budget. All results are model-relative.

title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNs for Flexible Working Memory
summary: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

AI.tldr: Recurrent neural networks trained with adaptation on sequence working memory tasks with variable delays spontaneously develop oscillatory phase coding, in which item identity is carried by oscillation amplitude and serial order by phase. A neural circuit model with content units and an adaptive time ring reproduces this coding.
AI.motivation: Oscillatory phase coding is widely observed in neural systems and implicated in memory and sequence processing, but its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear.
AI.method: Recurrent neural networks with adaptation are trained on sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. Ablation studies identify three required elements (adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information), and neuron-type and recurrent connectivity analyses examine the content and time cells that emerge.
AI.result: Oscillatory phase coding emerges spontaneously in the trained network: memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm. Content and time cells emerge and process item identity and sequence order separately. Time cells are connected in a phase-organized way, and digit-selective content-cell groups have structured internal connections.
AI.conclusion: The study shows how oscillatory phase coding arises from network structure and task demands, offers insight into its implementation and computational mechanisms in biological systems, and motivates computational models of human-like cognitive functions.

title: From Maps to Metabolism: Historical Precedents and a Unified Critique of Computationalism
summary: Alexander Lerchner's recent work on the 'abstraction fallacy' argues that computational functionalism confuses physical processes with abstract descriptions, and that symbolic computation alone cannot instantiate consciousness. Yet these claims were anticipated by Korzybski's map-territory distinction, Searle's critique of strong artificial intelligence, Floridi's levels of abstraction, Spencer et al.'s observer-relativity arguments, Winograd and Flores's account of computation as socially grounded practice, and Nasuto and Bishop's biological arguments. Synthesizing these contributions, this paper advances a form of non-computational physicalism: consciousness depends upon intrinsically organized, metabolically grounded physical dynamics rather than abstract computation, whilst leaving open the possibility of artificial consciousness. An objection is that this critique targets an outdated computationalism. Mechanistic computationalism, associated with Milkowski, Piccinini, Craver, Bechtel, and Kaplan, treats computation as a property of physically realized mechanisms rather than substrate-independent formalism. Although this represents an important advance, it does not dissolve the abstraction fallacy. Computational attributions remain dependent upon choices of state individuation, system boundaries, and interpretive mapping that are not determined by physical facts alone. Kaplan and Craver's 'model-to-mechanism mapping' constrains computational descriptions without eliminating their dependence upon an external observer. Grounding computation in neural mechanisms does not confer intrinsic significance or the normativity explored by Bickhard and Nasuto and Bishop. The abstraction fallacy persists wherever computational descriptions are treated as constitutive of, rather than descriptive of, physical reality.

AI.tldr: The paper synthesizes historical critiques of computation to argue for a non-computational physicalism in which consciousness depends on intrinsically organized, metabolically grounded physical dynamics rather than abstract computation. It argues that mechanistic computationalism does not dissolve the abstraction fallacy.
AI.motivation: Lerchner's recent abstraction-fallacy argument holds that computational functionalism confuses physical processes with abstract descriptions and that symbolic computation alone cannot instantiate consciousness. The paper also addresses the objection that this critique targets an outdated computationalism.
AI.method: The paper draws on earlier contributions, including Korzybski's map-territory distinction, Searle's critique of strong AI, Floridi's levels of abstraction, observer-relativity arguments, Winograd and Flores's account of computation as socially grounded practice, and Nasuto and Bishop's biological arguments. It then tests the critique against mechanistic computationalism, associated with Milkowski, Piccinini, Craver, Bechtel and Kaplan.
AI.result: The abstract reports no empirical results; it is an argumentative synthesis. It contends that computational attributions still depend on choices of state individuation, system boundaries and interpretive mapping that physical facts alone do not determine, and that Kaplan and Craver's model-to-mechanism mapping constrains computational descriptions without removing dependence on an external observer.
AI.conclusion: The abstraction fallacy persists wherever computational descriptions are treated as constitutive of, rather than descriptive of, physical reality, while the possibility of artificial consciousness is left open.

title: KG-AST for Cheaper CI/CD: Budgeted Test Selection and AI Bug Review
summary: Continuous integration and AI-assisted review spend the same budget on every commit, although few commits introduce bugs. We study KG-AST, which scores each commit risk from git history and code-graph features before heavy tests or AI review run, so the budget goes to the riskiest commits first, and which hands the AI reviewer only a graph slice around the change. On 155 open-source projects in 11 languages, a single cross-language model trained on other projects ranks commits so that heavy testing of the riskiest 20% covers 49-64% of bug-introducing commits depending on the language, against 20% for random selection and 40-55% for testing the biggest change first. Every language beats the biggest-change baseline, by 3.8 to 13.2 points. In 20 Java projects the gain at a 20% budget is 15.1 points (64.6% vs 49.5%, 95% interval +11.6 to +18.4), and the model wins in 19 of the 20 projects. About twelve training projects suffice; richer features, tuning and cleaner labels did not help. An AI reviewer that sees only a commit's diff finds 26% of later-fixed defects exactly (32% with graph context), and about half of its findings that did not match a later fix were judged real by independent AI judges. A static call-graph selector runs about 8% of a test suite while including a test written for the fix in 85% of 67 fix commits. The Poincare embedding used in our retrieval work adds nothing measurable here: commit-risk AUC, bug review and severity ranking are unchanged or worse. The labels are noisy and the budget metric assumes a heavy test catches the bug it covers; no CI minutes were measured.

AI.tldr: KG-AST scores each commit's bug risk from git history and code-graph features, so heavy tests and AI review are spent on the riskiest commits first, and the AI reviewer receives only a graph slice around the change.
