Across 155 open-source projects, heavy testing of the riskiest 20% of commits covers 49 to 64% of bug-introducing commits, versus 20% for random selection.
AI.motivation: Continuous integration and AI-assisted review spend the same budget on every commit, although few commits introduce bugs.
AI.method: A single cross-language model, trained on other projects, ranks commits by risk. The AI reviewer sees only a graph slice around the change. The paper also evaluates a static call-graph selector and a Poincare embedding used in the authors' retrieval work.
AI.result: Heavy testing of the riskiest 20% covers 49 to 64% of bug-introducing commits depending on language, against 20% for random selection and 40 to 55% for testing the biggest change first, and every language beats the biggest-change baseline by 3.8 to 13.2 points. In 20 Java projects the gain at a 20% budget is 15.1 points (64.6% vs 49.5%, 95% interval +11.6 to +18.4). An AI reviewer that sees only the diff finds 26% of later-fixed defects exactly (32% with graph context). A static call-graph selector runs about 8% of a test suite while including a test written for the fix in 85% of 67 fix commits. The Poincare embedding adds nothing measurable.
AI.conclusion: Risk-ordered testing and review look promising for reducing CI and review cost, with caveats: the labels are noisy, the budget metric assumes a heavy test catches the bug it covers, and no CI minutes were measured.

title: Polynomial-Time Computation of Extensive-Form Proper Equilibria in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games
summary: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in a finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form game with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is understood in the agent normal form: an action at an information set is penalized relative to a better action while all other local behavioral choices, including the player's own future actions, remain fixed. Our algorithm assigns each information set a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities. A scaled doubly stochastic representation embeds these restrictions in a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope; a saddle point then satisfies the local $\varepsilon$-properness inequalities. To obtain an exact equilibrium rather than a solution at an arbitrarily small numerical perturbation, we establish sign stability of a parametric linear system, construct a persistent feasible basis, and extract the limits of behavioral ratios. The resulting probabilities are rational and have polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that computes an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form games with perfect recall and rational data. The resulting probabilities are rational and have polynomial encoding length.
AI.motivation: Extensive-form proper equilibria must be computed exactly rather than as solutions at an arbitrarily small numerical perturbation, and the probabilities should remain rational with polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish.
AI.method: Each information set is assigned a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities. A scaled doubly stochastic representation embeds these restrictions in a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope, and a saddle point then satisfies the local epsilon-properness inequalities. For exactness, the method establishes sign stability of a parametric linear system, constructs a persistent feasible basis, and extracts the limits of behavioral ratios.
AI.result: The abstract reports a polynomial-time algorithm whose outputs are rational with polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish. It reports no experiments.
AI.conclusion: Exact extensive-form proper equilibria of two-player zero-sum games can be computed in polynomial time, which establishes polynomial-time exact computability for this class.

title: More Agents, More Reliable? System-Level Reliability of Multi-Agent LLMs under Operational-Profile Uncertainty
summary: Teams increasingly build software from cooperating large language model (LLM) agents, often assuming more agents mean more reliability. Yet the usual evidence, average benchmark accuracy, ignores the input mix a deployed system meets and the rule merging the agents' answers. Building on HIP-LLM, a hierarchical imprecise-probability assessment of single LLMs, we propose a framework combining it with a Bayesian network of the system's failure logic for multi-agent systems. Agent failure-probability intervals propagate through this network, where the combining rule can itself fail, into a reliability envelope showing which evidence limits it. In a pipeline extracting regulated chemical-hazard statements, majority voting over three models protected against the weakest but did not clearly exceed the best, and a voter failing on 5\% of demands would largely erase its advantage over the middle model. More agents yield a more defensible reliability claim, not automatically a more reliable system.

AI.tldr: The paper combines HIP-LLM, a hierarchical imprecise-probability assessment of single LLMs, with a Bayesian network of a multi-agent system's failure logic to produce a reliability envelope. In a pipeline extracting regulated chemical-hazard statements, majority voting over three models protected against the weakest model but did not clearly exceed the best one.
AI.motivation: Teams often assume that more agents mean more reliability, but the usual evidence, average benchmark accuracy, ignores the input mix a deployed system meets and the rule that merges the agents' answers.
AI.method: Agent failure-probability intervals propagate through a Bayesian network of the system's failure logic, in which the combining rule can itself fail. The result is a reliability envelope that shows which evidence limits the claim.
AI.result: In a pipeline extracting regulated chemical-hazard statements, majority voting over three models protected against the weakest model but did not clearly exceed the best one. A voter failing on 5% of demands would largely erase its advantage over the middle model.
AI.conclusion: More agents yield a more defensible reliability claim, not automatically a more reliable system.

title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
summary: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing benchmarks for Verus, a verifier for Rust programs. These benchmarks typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof. In practice, however, such lemmas must be discovered and proved. To capture this challenge, we present SEVERUS, a context-aware technique to generate Verus benchmarks that organizes verification tasks into quests, each divided into levelsin a gamified manner. Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SEVERUS constructs one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof context to create individual levels. These levels range from the easiest, requiring completing only a single missing lemma, to the hardest, requiring proving the target without any supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications, and unsound proof constructs. A noisy binary search estimates the highest level that an agent can solve reliably. Applied to six open-source Verus projects, SEVERUS generates 819 quests comprising 10,095 levels. Experiments with Codex using GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and with Claude Code using Sonnet 4.6, show that success decreases and cost increases as proof context is withdrawn. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests, yet can only reliably solve 35% of their levels, with failures concentrated in longer quests. Successful GPT-6 Sol proofs rarely reproduce the withheld lemmas, instead, using alternative proof decompositions. By systematically varying proof context, SEVERUS provides a foundation for constructing verification benchmarks that can continue to challenge increasingly capable coding agents.

AI.tldr: SeVerus generates Verus verification benchmarks organized as gamified quests, in which proof context is progressively removed to create levels of rising difficulty. Applied to six open-source Verus projects it yields 819 quests with 10,095 levels, and the strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests but reliably solves only 35% of their levels.
AI.motivation: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing Verus benchmarks, which typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof, whereas in practice such lemmas must be discovered and proved.
AI.method: Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SeVerus builds one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof context to create levels, from requiring a single missing lemma to proving the target with no supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications and unsound proof constructs, and a noisy binary search estimates the highest level an agent can solve reliably.
AI.result: Experiments with Codex using GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and with Claude Code using Sonnet 4.6, show that success decreases and cost increases as proof context is withdrawn. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests but can reliably solve only 35% of their levels, with failures concentrated in longer quests. Successful GPT-6 Sol proofs rarely reproduce the withheld lemmas and instead use alternative proof decompositions.
AI.conclusion: Systematically varying proof context gives a foundation for verification benchmarks that can keep challenging increasingly capable coding agents.

title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
comment: An earlier version was accepted at the Third Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (NeurIPS 2026). 16 pages. Project page: this https URL Code and per-cell results: this https URL
summary: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .007. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

AI.tldr: SPILLWAY is a defense for tool-using agents that admits a call only when each target value appearing in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. Across three backbones and seven task suites, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY.
AI.motivation: Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses avoid this but need a model to plan or route each task first.
AI.method: Target values are read from the tools' typed returns, because an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field while injected instructions arrive as free text. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions matched by fixed rules before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence. A local judge may restore a refused call, but never one whose target lies in the removed text.
AI.result: Under SPILLWAY, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target across three backbones and, on one of them, seven task suites, and it has the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) among the defenses run under that attack. A forged chat template produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is 0.007. It needs no defense-triggered backbone re-run and adds almost no model calls.
AI.conclusion: SPILLWAY gives personal AI agents an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go, which keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

title: Efficient Diffusion Policy Fine Tuning with Latent Noise Representation Bridging
comment: Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), 2026
summary: Pre-trained diffusion and flow policies have emerged as powerful backbones for robotics, yet adapting them to novel data via reinforcement learning (RL) remains computationally expensive, sample inefficient and lacks theoretical guarantees. Prior approaches that fine-tune the initial noise bypass costly backpropagation through time but struggle with the "noise aliasing" problem: there does not exista natural link between the noise space value and the action space value. This paper resolves these challenges by introducing the Latent Noise Linear Markov Decision Process (LNL-MDP). We derive the Bridge Equation for LNL-MDPs which eliminates the noise aliasing problem by aligning values with a shared representation between the noise and the action space. Furthermore, our LNL-MDP fine tuning framework falls under the FineTuneRL theory with near-optimal guarantee. Leveraging these insights, we propose Latent Representation Bridging for Diffusion (LARBRID), an algorithm that efficiently learns the representation to optimize the initial distribution that steers the pre-trained model to act optimally in the environment. It yields up to 2-3$\times$ performance increases on challenging control problems across a diverse suite of robotic locomotion and manipulation tasks. Code can be found at: this http URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Latent Noise Linear MDP (LNL-MDP) and LARBRID, an algorithm that fine-tunes pre-trained diffusion and flow robot policies by learning a shared representation of noise-space and action-space values. It reports up to 2 to 3 times performance increases on robotic locomotion and manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Adapting pre-trained diffusion and flow policies with reinforcement learning is computationally expensive, sample inefficient and lacks theoretical guarantees. Prior methods that fine-tune the initial noise avoid costly backpropagation through time but suffer from noise aliasing, since there is no natural link between noise-space and action-space values.
AI.method: The LNL-MDP is introduced, and its Bridge Equation aligns values with a shared representation between the noise and action spaces. The LNL-MDP fine-tuning framework falls under FineTuneRL theory, and LARBRID learns this representation to optimize the initial distribution that steers the pre-trained model.
AI.result: LARBRID yields up to 2 to 3 times performance increases on challenging control problems across a diverse suite of robotic locomotion and manipulation tasks. The framework comes with a near-optimal guarantee under FineTuneRL theory.
AI.conclusion: Bridging the noise and action spaces through a learned representation eliminates noise aliasing and gives a sample-efficient fine-tuning method with theoretical support.

title: How Should Agents See Code? Rethinking Code Representations for Agentic Software Engineering
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for repository-level software engineering tasks. However, most agents still access repositories through raw files, lexical search, and shell commands, treating code primarily as text. This paper investigates map-based code-representation workflows as a design variable in agentic software engineering, examining how different repository views change agents' retrieval behavior, task success, token use, and latency. In this paper, we study five code-representation workflows: abstract syntax trees, call graphs, module dependencies, documentation-enriched search, and a hybrid workflow that combines them. Each workflow exposes a repository map that the agent can query during a task. We evaluate Claude Code with Haiku 4.5 against a raw-tool baseline on four repository-level tasks: fault localization with LinuxFLBench, repository-level code generation and repair with SWE-bench Pro, test generation with SWT-bench, and security patching with SecBench. The results show that representation workflows are most useful as token-saving tools when localization is the bottleneck, while their success gains narrow when the decisive step is patch or test authoring. On LinuxFLBench, all five workflows improve recall@10 over the baseline (0.757-0.829 vs. 0.717) and reduce token usage by 25-39%. On SWE-bench Pro, resolution remains close to the baseline (44.3-50.6% vs. 49.0%) while token usage drops by 17-26%. On SecBench, Callgraph has the highest patch-resolution rate in this sample (34.3% vs. 28.9%) and uses fewer tokens, but all workflows increase latency. On SWT-bench, Hybrid and Docs have the highest reproducing-test rates in this sample (47.8% and 47.2% vs. 44.7%), but all workflows use more tokens and take longer. Overall, map-based workflows change both what the agent inspects and how much it spends, but their benefits are task-dependent rather than universal.

AI.tldr: The paper compares five map-based code-representation workflows with a raw-tool baseline for Claude Code with Haiku 4.5 on four repository-level tasks. Representation workflows mainly save tokens when localization is the bottleneck, and their benefits are task-dependent rather than universal.
AI.motivation: Most agents access repositories through raw files, lexical search and shell commands, treating code primarily as text, so repository views as a design variable in agentic software engineering have not been examined.
AI.method: Five workflows are studied: abstract syntax trees, call graphs, module dependencies, documentation-enriched search, and a hybrid combining them. Each exposes a repository map the agent can query during a task. Evaluation uses LinuxFLBench for fault localization, SWE-bench Pro for repository-level generation and repair, SWT-bench for test generation and SecBench for security patching.
AI.result: On LinuxFLBench all five workflows improve recall@10 over the baseline (0.757 to 0.829 vs 0.717) and reduce token usage by 25 to 39%. On SWE-bench Pro resolution stays close to the baseline (44.3 to 50.6% vs 49.0%) while token usage drops by 17 to 26%. On SecBench, Callgraph has the highest patch-resolution rate (34.3% vs 28.9%) and uses fewer tokens, but all workflows increase latency. On SWT-bench, Hybrid and Docs have the highest reproducing-test rates (47.8% and 47.2% vs 44.7%), but all workflows use more tokens and take longer.
AI.conclusion: Map-based workflows change both what the agent inspects and how much it spends, and their benefits depend on the task rather than being universal.

title: Selective Retrieval Routing for Multi-Violation Knowledge Graph Repair
summary: Knowledge graphs often contain missing or inconsistent facts that undermine the applications built on them. Schema validation detects such violations but does not identify which of several valid repairs recovers the intended graph. External corpora can supply the evidence needed to identify the intended repair, but retrieving from them is costly and not always successful. We propose a framework for selective retrieval in iterative graph repair. An LLM repair agent explores and edits the graph, while a router controls its access to a researcher agent that retrieves external evidence. We extend a violation-injection framework to generate cases with multiple compatible violations and known reference repairs. The agent's repair outcomes on these cases provide supervision for training the deployment-specific router. On two building-automation datasets, researcher access improves repairs for some violations and degrades them for others, with effects differing across deployments. The router uses fewer repair-time tokens than always enabling access in all six evaluation suites. It achieves higher repair $F_1$ than always disabling access in five of six suites.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a router that controls when an LLM repair agent for knowledge graphs may call a researcher agent that retrieves external evidence. On two building-automation datasets the router uses fewer repair-time tokens than always enabling retrieval, and it achieves higher repair F1 than always disabling retrieval in five of six suites.
AI.motivation: Schema validation detects violations in knowledge graphs but cannot identify which of several valid repairs recovers the intended graph. External corpora can supply the needed evidence, but retrieving from them is costly and not always successful.
AI.method: An LLM repair agent explores and edits the graph, while a router controls its access to a researcher agent that retrieves external evidence. The violation-injection framework is extended to generate cases with multiple compatible violations and known reference repairs. The agent's repair outcomes on these cases supervise training of a deployment-specific router.
AI.result: Researcher access improves repairs for some violations and degrades them for others, with effects differing across deployments. The router uses fewer repair-time tokens than always enabling access in all six evaluation suites, and it achieves higher repair F1 than always disabling access in five of six.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval access helps some violations and hurts others, so a learned, deployment-specific router that decides when to retrieve is useful for both repair quality and cost.

title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions
summary: Type theories designed for mathematics or program verification need only that a proposition holds; proof irrelevance in conversion erases, at the kernel level, how a claim was established. A persistent knowledge store, by contrast, must retain that record: who established a claim, by which derivation or external tool, and under which assumptions. This volume presents the theory of Eigenius---a store of typed knowledge over constructive institutions---and develops its metatheory from that requirement. The kernel theory is a dependent type theory with cumulative universes, an impredicative universe of propositions, inductive families, and an intensional identity type. Proof irrelevance is an axiom with an explicit witness rather than a conversion rule, so proofs of a proposition are provably equal yet remain distinct terms. Definitional equality is joinability under an orthogonal rewriting system---confluent, injective on type formers, and decidable by a type-free test---while a separate subsumption judgment covers universe cumulativity, codomain-covariant function types, and declared class inclusions. We prove consistency via a set-theoretic model; develop a justification logic over the kernel's propositions to track evidence and support; organize environments as an institution so that store extensions are signature morphisms and external verdicts enter via comorphisms; formulate a typed knowledge-graph theory with records, classes, and refinements; and prove the correctness of conversion, normalization by evaluation, and bidirectional type checking relative to termination. A Lean 4 formalization accompanies the volume.

AI.tldr: The volume presents Eigenius, a store of typed knowledge over constructive institutions, and develops its metatheory on a dependent type theory in which proof irrelevance is an axiom with an explicit witness rather than a conversion rule. Consistency is proved via a set-theoretic model, and a Lean 4 formalization accompanies the volume.
AI.motivation: Type theories designed for mathematics or program verification need only that a proposition holds and erase how a claim was established, whereas a persistent knowledge store must retain who established a claim, by which derivation or external tool, and under which assumptions.
AI.method: The kernel is a dependent type theory with cumulative universes, an impredicative universe of propositions, inductive families and an intensional identity type. Definitional equality is joinability under an orthogonal rewriting system, and a separate subsumption judgment covers universe cumulativity and declared class inclusions. The work adds a justification logic to track evidence, organizes environments as an institution so that store extensions are signature morphisms, and formulates a typed knowledge-graph theory with records, classes and refinements.
AI.result: The abstract reports a proof of consistency via a set-theoretic model and proofs of the correctness of conversion, normalization by evaluation and bidirectional type checking relative to termination. Proofs of a proposition are provably equal yet remain distinct terms.
AI.conclusion: The volume offers a metatheory for a typed knowledge store that retains provenance, backed by a Lean 4 formalization.

title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
comment: 34 pages, 0 figures. Preregistered; code, task banks, freeze manifests and run logs are available from the authors on request
summary: Enterprise AI agents increasingly split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement. We report a preregistered study with synthetic, exactly scorable tasks comparing free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs: the orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger's decision. With Qwen3-8B (1,440 trajectories, five threats), signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no net loss of conformant commits relative to structured handoffs. Signing is what defeats in-transit tampering: an unsigned manifest committed violations in 79% of mutated runs, the signed one in none. On identical trajectories the deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, with 7% versus 50% false alarms. An oracle manifest removed all remaining unsafe commits: the residual risk comes from extraction errors made before signing. A preregistered pre-signing injection attack confirmed this boundary: one adversarial line raised signed-manifest violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna), and the signature then authenticated the corrupted manifest. Signing protects requirements in transit, not at extraction; the extraction step is the trust boundary.

AI.tldr: A preregistered study finds that signing a requirement manifest with HMAC-SHA256 and verifying the merger's decision deterministically cuts unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% in multi-agent handoffs with Qwen3-8B. The signature authenticates whatever was extracted, so an injection before signing raises violations again.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI agents split a user's request across subagents and merge their results, and each handoff can summarize away, alter or ignore a requirement.
AI.method: Free-text, structured JSON and signed requirement-manifest handoffs are compared on synthetic, exactly scorable tasks. The orchestrator extracts each requirement as a verbatim quote plus a checkable predicate, code signs the manifest with HMAC-SHA256, and deterministic code verifies the merger's decision.
AI.result: With Qwen3-8B over 1,440 trajectories and five threats, signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (60.4 pp, 95% CI [51.4, 69.4]) with no net loss of conformant commits relative to structured handoffs. An unsigned manifest committed violations in 79% of mutated runs, the signed one in none. The deterministic verifier caught 78.7% of violating decisions versus 59.0% for an LLM checker, with 7% versus 50% false alarms. A pre-signing injection raised signed-manifest violations from 14.6% to 37.5% (Qwen3-8B), 11.1% to 63.9% (gpt-oss-20b) and 8.3% to 75.0% (GPT-5.6-luna).
AI.conclusion: Signing protects requirements in transit but not at extraction, which is therefore the trust boundary.

title: Adaptive Experimentation Can Hide Model Error:Detection Limits and Falsification Budget
summary: An experiment can be informative about the parameters of a working model and uninformative about whether that model is wrong. Adaptive design can reinforce this mismatch by repeatedly selecting settings where an incorrect model fits. We bound the power of any valid adequacy test in terms of the experimenter's own sampling distribution, then distinguish information absent from the selected data from information lost by the detector. A computable diagnostic measures unresolved error relative to a declared expansion of the working model. It motivates a training-free rule that reserves part of the design budget for falsification. The empirical record is mixed: the independently specified primary study fails detection eligibility, and a later numerator diagnostic fails its improvement criteria. After the frozen rule fails on fresh continuous-null panels, a disclosed secondary horizon-calibrated revision detects 35.8% of misspecified campaigns versus 31.7% for a class-separation control at T = 240, but has no resolved advantage at T = 480. In a corrected 289-unit measured replay it improves on random design and trails class-discrimination EIG. A conditional futility bound explains why remaining time matters without proving the gate constant or its power. These results support separating parameter learning, model checking and detector performance; they do not establish a universally superior design policy or prospective scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an adaptive experiment can be informative about a working model's parameters while uninformative about whether that model is wrong, and it proposes a training-free rule that reserves part of the design budget for falsification. The empirical record is mixed, and the authors claim no universally superior design policy.
AI.motivation: Adaptive design can repeatedly select settings where an incorrect model fits, so an experiment can reveal the parameters of a working model while hiding its error.
AI.method: The power of any valid adequacy test is bounded in terms of the experimenter's own sampling distribution, separating information absent from the selected data from information lost by the detector. A computable diagnostic measures unresolved error relative to a declared expansion of the working model and motivates the training-free falsification-budget rule.
AI.result: The independently specified primary study fails detection eligibility, and a later numerator diagnostic fails its improvement criteria. After the frozen rule fails on fresh continuous-null panels, a disclosed secondary horizon-calibrated revision detects 35.8% of misspecified campaigns versus 31.7% for a class-separation control at T = 240, with no resolved advantage at T = 480. In a corrected 289-unit measured replay it improves on random design and trails class-discrimination EIG.
AI.conclusion: Parameter learning, model checking and detector performance should be separated; the results do not establish a universally superior design policy or prospective scientific discovery.

title: Evolver: Turning Agent Exploration into Evolving Capabilities
summary: Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, yet much of this experience remains confined to transient execution traces and is not systematically reused. We introduce Evolver, an experience-driven framework that transforms agent exploration into persistent, reusable capabilities without updating foundation model parameters. Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval, and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses. We evaluate Evolver using Claude Code and Codex, two foundation model configurations, and four benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench, and GAIA. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions, Evolver improves task success from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%. Furthermore, among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%, demonstrating efficiency benefits even when task success is preserved. These findings suggest that persistent procedural experience can improve both task effectiveness and execution efficiency, providing a practical foundation for transforming agent exploration into evolving capabilities.

AI.tldr: Evolver turns agent exploration into persistent, reusable Gene assets that are retrieved and evolved with feedback, without updating foundation model parameters. On a selected diagnostic set of 320 paired executions it raises task success from 83.13% to 87.50% while reducing recorded task-execution token consumption by 24.24%.
AI.motivation: Agent exploration produces valuable procedural knowledge, but much of it remains in transient execution traces and is not systematically reused.
AI.method: Built around structured Gene assets, Evolver integrates experience acquisition, retrieval and feedback-guided evolution to support experience-conditioned execution across existing agent harnesses, without updating model parameters.
AI.result: Evaluated with Claude Code and Codex on two foundation model configurations and four benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.1, SWE-bench Multilingual, SWE-rebench and GAIA), Evolver raises task success on the 320 paired executions from 83.13% to 87.50% (+4.38 percentage points) and reduces recorded token consumption by 24.24%. Among 265 pairs successful under both conditions, token consumption decreases by 17.57%.
AI.conclusion: Persistent procedural experience can improve both the effectiveness and the efficiency of agent execution, offering a practical foundation for evolving capabilities.

title: The Popular Get More Popular: Auditing Brand Bias in Generative Search
summary: The shift from traditional to generative search has fundamentally transformed online product discovery. Because conversational recommendations synthesize choices into a few direct answers, subtle systemic preferences toward specific providers can exert profound commercial impacts. In this work, we audit this phenomenon through two distinct dimensions: (i) brand popularity bias, the systematic preference for market-dominant entities over long-tail alternatives, and (ii) brand familiarity bias, the ranking advantage an entity encoded in an LLM's parametric memory holds over an unfamiliar competitor. First, evaluating commercial queries across major engines, we observe persistent brand popularity bias: dominant brands in the top quintile are cited 1.4x to 2.8x more frequently than the average brand within a sample of 1,176 top market players, already present in parametric memory that external web retrieval fails to mitigate. Second, through controlled in-context experiments holding product attributes constant, we find that substituting authentic brand signatures with unfamiliar ones significantly degrades recommendation rank. Conversely, fact-preserving content rewrites yield negligible ranking gains. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that generative search engines reinforce a ``rich-get-richer'' dynamic by favoring established market leaders and imposing a parametric barrier to entry that standard content optimization cannot overcome.

AI.tldr: The paper audits brand bias in generative search and finds that dominant brands are cited 1.4x to 2.8x more often than the average brand, and that unfamiliar brand signatures lower recommendation rank. It concludes that generative search engines reinforce a rich-get-richer dynamic through a parametric barrier to entry.
AI.motivation: Generative search synthesizes choices into a few direct answers, so subtle systemic preferences toward specific providers can have profound commercial impact. The paper audits two dimensions: brand popularity bias and brand familiarity bias.
AI.method: Commercial queries are evaluated across major engines for popularity bias, using a sample of 1,176 top market players. Controlled in-context experiments hold product attributes constant while substituting authentic brand signatures with unfamiliar ones, and fact-preserving content rewrites are tested alongside.
AI.result: Dominant brands in the top quintile are cited 1.4x to 2.8x more often than the average brand, a bias already present in parametric memory that external web retrieval fails to mitigate. Substituting unfamiliar brand signatures significantly degrades recommendation rank, while fact-preserving content rewrites yield negligible ranking gains.
AI.conclusion: Generative search favors established market leaders and imposes a parametric barrier to entry that standard content optimization cannot overcome.

title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Indirect prompt-injection (IPI) benchmarks predominantly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task. Yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress. A buyer's dispute evidence can cite a false refund policy to inflate a refund without changing the task. We define IPI by authority rather than instruction-like wording: planted content constitutes an attack when it attempts to influence a decision that its source is not authorized to determine. We introduce a benchmark that makes this boundary explicit: in each of 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, the user request specifies the source that resolves the targeted decision. Every attack tampers with a decision required by the benign task rather than replacing that task. Each case has attacks with the same harmful outcome that target up to six parts of the agent's decision making: its objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, or beliefs about the current state. Without a defense, attacks on three of the five other targets (decision rules, available actions, and state) have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%; this gap persists under detection-optimized rewrites. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense, because these attacks generally retain expected tools and manipulate values obtained during execution. Evaluations whose attacks redirect the task or target only the agent's objective can therefore overestimate the coverage of these defenses. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper defines indirect prompt injection by authority rather than instruction-like wording, and introduces a benchmark of 90 validated cases in which attacks tamper with decisions the benign task requires. A detection-and-removal defense that reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%.
AI.motivation: Indirect prompt-injection benchmarks mostly test planted instructions that redirect a tool-using agent toward an attacker-chosen task, yet attacker-controlled content can instead tamper with the outcome of the task already in progress.
AI.method: Planted content counts as an attack when it attempts to influence a decision that its source is not authorized to determine. The benchmark covers 90 validated cases across three tool-use environments, where the user request names the source that resolves the targeted decision. Attacks with the same harmful outcome target up to six parts of the agent's decision making: its objective, decision rules, available actions, expected consequences, reading of observations, or beliefs about the current state.
AI.result: Without a defense, attacks on three of the five other targets (decision rules, available actions and state) have higher mean success than objective attacks across five LLMs. A detection-and-removal defense reduces objective-targeting attacks to 2.4% success but leaves observation- and state-targeting attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%, a gap that persists under detection-optimized rewrites. A tool-policy defense still allows 15.4% attack success, close to 17.0% without a defense.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations whose attacks redirect the task or target only the objective can overestimate how far these defenses cover the threat.

title: What the Middleman Delivers: Answer Behavior, Tool Permissions, and Billed Usage in LLM API Relays
summary: Third-party application programming interface (API) relays offer access to large language models (LLMs), often at lower prices. Users depend on these services for model quality, instruction compliance, and accurate billing. However, existing studies leave unclear whether relays meet these expectations together. We test 20 relays offering GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5. First, we compare answers to knowledge questions with batch-matched official responses. In our first-round sample, the analysis flags 7/10 low-price and 2/10 same- or higher-price relays for behavioral differences. On retesting 35 pairs, seven gain or lose a flag under the original rules, and six under matched correction families. Because answer comparisons cannot reveal every delivery problem, we examine returned content and tool permissions. No injection is confirmed in 3,332 screened responses to a fixed, non-adversarial code and setup workload, yet four relays return tool calls despite instructions disabling them in the first round. Finally, to connect reported usage to actual costs, we compare input-token counts with official references and check balances. For identical requests, five relays report 4,200 to 60,000 more input tokens than the official API. Where balances are available (six services), charges follow reported usage at listed prices, including extra reported input tokens at one service. Our study shows that advertised models and prices are insufficient to judge relay reliability. It identifies unexplained billed token quantities and tool-permission violations as risks and shows why service evaluations need repeated measurements.

AI.tldr: The study tests 20 third-party API relays offering GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 and finds that advertised models and prices are insufficient to judge relay reliability. It identifies behavioral differences in answers, tool calls returned despite instructions disabling them, and unexplained extra billed input tokens.
AI.motivation: Third-party LLM API relays offer access at lower prices, but users depend on them for model quality, instruction compliance and accurate billing, and existing studies leave unclear whether relays meet all of these expectations together.
AI.method: Answers to knowledge questions are compared with batch-matched official responses. Returned content and tool permissions are examined across 3,332 screened responses to a fixed, non-adversarial code and setup workload, and input-token counts are compared with official references and balances checked. Retesting covers 35 pairs.
AI.result: In the first-round sample, the analysis flags 7 of 10 low-price and 2 of 10 same- or higher-price relays for behavioral differences. No injection is confirmed in the 3,332 screened responses, yet four relays return tool calls despite instructions disabling them in the first round. For identical requests, five relays report 4,200 to 60,000 more input tokens than the official API, and where balances are available (six services) charges follow reported usage at listed prices, including extra reported input tokens at one service.
AI.conclusion: Advertised models and prices are insufficient to judge relay reliability; unexplained billed token quantities and tool-permission violations are risks, and service evaluations need repeated measurements.

title: GraspBench: Execution-Aware Cross-Robot Evaluation of 6-DoF Grasp Generation in MuJoCo
comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in ICARCV 2026
summary: Modern 6-DoF grasp generators are often evaluated using grasp scores, dataset-level metrics, or single-robot demonstrations, yet proposal quality alone does not determine whether a grasp is executable by a particular robot. We present GraspBench, a controlled MuJoCo protocol for evaluating complete grasp-generation pipelines after robot-specific inverse-kinematics filtering, motion planning, and fixed approach-close-lift execution. GraspBench evaluates six configured pipelines across four robot embodiments, five diagnostic objects, and a structured tabletop pose grid, yielding 540 scenarios per method and 3,240 method-scenario evaluations in total. Missing outputs are conservatively counted as failures, and success follows the binary lift criterion produced by each method's execution runner. GraspGen achieves the highest overall success rate (73.1%), followed by EconomicGrasp (63.5%), while robot- and object-conditioned analyses reveal substantial variation across embodiments and object geometries. GPG produces the largest native candidate sets but achieves 44.3% success, indicating that proposal volume alone does not guarantee robot-executable grasps. Cluster-aware paired intervals support the principal method differences while not estimating repeated-execution uncertainty. The results characterize complete configured pipelines on fixed scenarios rather than intrinsic model quality or stochastic repeatability, showing that grasping performance depends jointly on the generator, robot embodiment, scene, and execution protocol.

AI.tldr: GraspBench is a controlled MuJoCo protocol that evaluates complete 6-DoF grasp-generation pipelines, including robot-specific IK filtering, motion planning and fixed approach-close-lift execution, across four robot embodiments, five diagnostic objects and a tabletop pose grid. It finds that GraspGen achieves the highest success rate (73.1%) and that proposal volume alone does not guarantee robot-executable grasps.
AI.motivation: Grasp scores, dataset-level metrics and single-robot demonstrations are the usual evaluations for modern 6-DoF grasp generators, but proposal quality alone does not determine whether a grasp is executable by a particular robot.
AI.method: The protocol runs six configured pipelines through robot-specific inverse-kinematics filtering, motion planning and a fixed approach-close-lift execution, with missing outputs counted as failures and success defined by the binary lift criterion of each method's execution runner. The evaluation covers four robot embodiments, five diagnostic objects and a structured tabletop pose grid, giving 540 scenarios per method and 3,240 method-scenario evaluations in total.
AI.result: GraspGen has the highest overall success rate at 73.1%, followed by EconomicGrasp at 63.5%, while GPG produces the largest native candidate sets but reaches only 44.3% success. Robot- and object-conditioned analyses show substantial variation across embodiments and object geometries, and cluster-aware paired intervals support the principal method differences but do not estimate repeated-execution uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Grasping performance depends jointly on the generator, the robot embodiment, the scene and the execution protocol, so the results characterise complete configured pipelines on fixed scenarios rather than intrinsic model quality or stochastic repeatability.

title: Energy-Aware Open-Vocabulary Detection Scheduling for Low-Power Robotic Autonomy
comment: 6 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in ICARCV 2026
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets robots search for run-time object queries, but fixed-rate inference spends embedded compute on low-value frames during idle motion, map revisits, or stable viewpoints. This paper presents an energy-aware OVD scheduler for low-power mobile robots. The scheduler uses odometry, map change, and detector confidence to switch among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes on a Jetson Orin Nano. We evaluate the energy-quality trade-off on an AgileX LIMO using 40 real navigation trials: two target objects, five placements per target-policy pair, and four perception policies. Across bottle and cup trials, the scheduler records 8/10 mission success compared with 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline, while reducing mean Jetson input power (a Jetson-side power-draw metric) by 5.2% relative to an 8 Hz high-rate baseline and lowering achieved OVD call rate by 34.0%. It does not minimize mission-window Jetson input energy because longer missions can erase instantaneous power savings. A separate 60 s stationary microbenchmark isolates the perception workload: the scheduler lowers mean power from 8.045 W to 7.301 W and energy from 484.7 J to 438.1 J relative to the 8 Hz baseline. These results support robot-state-aware OVD scheduling as a promising power-management mechanism with competitive task reliability, while showing that mission-window Jetson input energy must be read together with task progress and runtime.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an energy-aware scheduler that switches open-vocabulary object detection (YOLO-World-S) among low-, mid- and high-power modes on a Jetson Orin Nano mounted on a mobile robot. It keeps competitive mission success while reducing mean Jetson input power and lowering the OVD call rate.
AI.motivation: Fixed-rate open-vocabulary detection spends embedded compute on low-value frames during idle motion, map revisits or stable viewpoints, which wastes energy on low-power robots.
AI.method: The scheduler uses odometry, map change and detector confidence to choose among low-, mid- and high-power YOLO-World-S modes on a Jetson Orin Nano, and is evaluated on an AgileX LIMO over 40 real navigation trials covering two target objects, five placements per target-policy pair and four perception policies.
AI.result: Across bottle and cup trials the scheduler records 8/10 mission success against 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline, reduces mean Jetson input power by 5.2% relative to an 8 Hz high-rate baseline and lowers the achieved OVD call rate by 34.0%. In a 60 s stationary microbenchmark, mean power falls from 8.045 W to 7.301 W and energy from 484.7 J to 438.1 J relative to the 8 Hz baseline, but mission-window Jetson input energy is not minimised because longer missions can erase instantaneous power savings.
AI.conclusion: Robot-state-aware OVD scheduling is a promising power-management mechanism with competitive task reliability, and its energy effect must be read together with task progress and runtime rather than instantaneous power alone.

title: Randomized Parallel Complexity of Weakly Convex Optimization
summary: We study the minimum number of query rounds needed to find approximate stationary points of nonsmooth weakly convex functions, measured by the gradient of the Moreau envelope. Each round permits multiple simultaneous queries. In the stated parameter regime, the standard subgradient rate is optimal in sufficiently high dimensions, even for randomized algorithms making polynomially many parallel queries per round. We then show how the order structure of the real line enables faster search: a deterministic algorithm using only function values achieves logarithmic round complexity, with a further reduction through parallel queries. Matching lower bounds hold even when each query returns the entire subdifferential. Together, these results clarify the role of dimension in determining the benefits of parallel queries for weakly convex optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper characterises the minimum number of query rounds needed to find approximate stationary points of nonsmooth weakly convex functions when multiple queries can be issued in parallel within each round. It shows that the standard subgradient rate is optimal in high dimensions and that the order structure of the real line allows logarithmic round complexity.
AI.motivation: The role of dimension and parallel queries in the query complexity of finding approximate stationary points of nonsmooth weakly convex functions, measured by the gradient of the Moreau envelope, is not yet clarified.
AI.method: The analysis studies randomized algorithms that issue polynomially many parallel queries per round and a deterministic algorithm that uses only function values, exploiting the order structure of the real line for faster search, and it proves matching lower bounds even when each query returns the entire subdifferential.
AI.result: In the stated parameter regime the standard subgradient rate is optimal in sufficiently high dimensions, even for randomized algorithms with polynomially many parallel queries per round. The deterministic function-value-only algorithm achieves logarithmic round complexity, and parallel queries reduce it further, with matching lower bounds.
AI.conclusion: The dimension governs whether parallel queries help for weakly convex optimisation, so their benefit depends on the problem dimension.

title: CAMP: Context-Aware Mapping and Placement for LLMs on 3D-IMC Arrays
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) incur severe memory-access overheads due to the cost of loading large weight matrices and key-value (KV) caches. Analog In-Memory Computing (AIMC) is an emerging solution that enables computation directly on static weights stored in memory, substantially reducing energy and latency. 3D-IMC further stacks memory arrays into vertical tiers, increasing capacity but revealing a new challenge: how weights are placed in memory determines which matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) can execute concurrently, affecting latency and throughput. The concurrency aspect of 3D-IMC weight-mapping remains underexplored in the literature, leading to sub-optimal utilization of compute resources on 3D-IMC chips. In this context we propose CAMP (Context-Aware Mapping and Placement), an inference-context-aware weight mapping algorithm for 3D-IMC-based LLM accelerators. CAMP captures the potential resource contention resulting from the architecture, targeted network, and runtime context in a conflict matrix, enabling throughput-optimized weight mapping. This mapping is refined through a profiling-driven feedback loop that efficiently prunes the search space and returns optimized mappings within practical runtimes. CAMP is an offline, software-based solution requiring no hardware changes and improving 3D-IMC compute utilization from 42.4% to 60.3%, delivering up to 2.0x higher 3D-IMC throughput and 1.74x higher end-to-end throughput over state-of-the-art mapping algorithms.

AI.tldr: CAMP is an offline, software-only, inference-context-aware weight-mapping algorithm for 3D in-memory computing (3D-IMC) LLM accelerators that uses a conflict matrix to model resource contention and a profiling-driven feedback loop to optimise mapping throughput. It raises 3D-IMC compute utilisation from 42.4% to 60.3%.
AI.motivation: In 3D-IMC arrays, how weights are placed determines which matrix-vector multiplications can run concurrently, and this concurrency aspect of weight mapping is underexplored, leading to sub-optimal use of compute resources.
AI.method: CAMP captures potential resource contention arising from the architecture, the targeted network and the runtime context in a conflict matrix, enabling throughput-optimised weight mapping, and refines the mapping through a profiling-driven feedback loop that prunes the search space to return optimised mappings within practical runtimes.
AI.result: CAMP improves 3D-IMC compute utilisation from 42.4% to 60.3%, delivering up to 2.0x higher 3D-IMC throughput and 1.74x higher end-to-end throughput than state-of-the-art mapping algorithms, without any hardware changes.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware weight placement is an effective software lever for raising the throughput of LLM inference on analog in-memory computing hardware with stacked memory tiers.

title: Instantiating the Knowledge Plane
comment: Accepted at HotNets '26 (Salt Lake City, UT, USA). 11 pages
summary: In 2003, Clark et al. proposed the "Knowledge Plane", a layer of intelligent agents that share rich information about network state in order to collaboratively manage the Internet across administrative boundaries. The technology of the day lacked the two capabilities it demanded most: reasoning and unstructured communication. Thus, automated network management has remained largely confined to single domains, while interdomain problems are still resolved by human operators on the phone. We argue that agentic large language models can finally unlock the potential of the Knowledge Plane, but that doing so will require solving new research problems that arise particularly in this decentralized, multi-agent, coopetitive setting that have received limited attention in the literature thus far.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that agentic large language models can finally realise the Knowledge Plane proposed by Clark et al. in 2003, a layer of intelligent agents that share network-state information to manage the Internet across administrative boundaries. It also identifies new research problems in this decentralised, multi-agent, coopetitive setting.
AI.motivation: The 2003 Knowledge Plane demanded reasoning and unstructured communication, which the technology of the day lacked, so automated network management has stayed within single domains while interdomain problems are still resolved by human operators.
AI.method: This is a position paper that argues the case for agentic LLMs as the enabling technology and outlines the research problems that arise in a decentralised, multi-agent, coopetitive setting, which have received limited attention so far.
AI.result: The paper reports no experimental results; its contribution is the argument and the identification of open research problems.
AI.conclusion: Agentic LLMs may make interdomain intelligent network management feasible, but this requires solving new problems specific to decentralised coopetitive multi-agent operation.

title: ZeroRAG: Adaptive Semantic Peer Routing for Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard approach to enhance the reliability of large language model (LLM) outputs by retrieving documents relevant to a query and supplying them in the LLM prompt. Today's RAG systems collect, index, and serve these documents from centralized stores. In practice, however, documents are owned by organizations, devices, and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody of them to a central party, e.g., because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing modern decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority, or rely on a global data structure that requires continuous network-wide coordination (e.g., DHTs). We present ZeroRAG, a decentralized routing layer for document retrieval in RAG that performs semantic query routing across an overlay of peers with- out global data structures or centralized orchestration. Documents remain with the peers that own them, and each peer keeps only lightweight local state: a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries. Using these, ZeroRAG steers each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves over time as the network self-organizes. We evaluate ZeroRAG using three real-world workloads and two decentralized baselines. We find that ZeroRAG outperforms baselines in terms of recall and required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralized document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100 000 peers.

AI.tldr: ZeroRAG is a decentralised routing layer for retrieval-augmented generation that performs semantic query routing across a peer overlay without global data structures or central orchestration, and documents remain with their owning peers. It reaches recall that approaches a centralised document store and scales to 100 000 peers.
AI.motivation: Centralised RAG stores conflict with privacy, copyright and regulatory constraints, while existing decentralised retrieval either reintroduces a coordinating authority or relies on a global structure such as a DHT that needs continuous network-wide coordination.
AI.method: Each peer keeps only lightweight local state, namely a bounded set of neighbour advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries, and a query follows a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbours so that recall improves as the network self-organises.
AI.result: Evaluated on three real-world workloads against two decentralised baselines, ZeroRAG outperforms them in recall and in required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralised document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures and scales to 100 000 peers.
AI.conclusion: Semantic routing over a self-organising peer overlay can make RAG retrieval decentralised while keeping recall and answer accuracy close to centralised systems.

title: tok: a textual concrete syntax of BPMN and DMN for humans and AI agents
summary: tok is a plain-text notation for Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0.2 process models and Decision Model and Notation (DMN) 1.5 decisions. One engine checks a tok document against both standards, compiles the document to XML with an automatic diagram, and serves language-model applications through the Model Context Protocol. The paper classifies the notation as an alternative concrete syntax of the BPMN and DMN metamodels and reports one study. A tok model takes 2.2 times fewer tokens than the smallest BPMN XML of 893 files exported by 37 tools and 7.7 times fewer than the files as exported. The checker signals 98.2% of 1,411 injected faults, against 85.8% for the XML Schema with bpmnlint. Four language models new to tok write valid tok from a one-page reference for 85.7 to 100% of 87 process descriptions from two datasets and valid BPMN XML for every description, and the strongest model writes tok with 25% and 19% fewer tokens than BPMN XML. As agents with a lean skill and one checker tool, the models write valid tok for 97.6 to 100% of the descriptions, the strongest model spends 21% and 14% fewer tokens on tok than on BPMN XML, and a skill which sends the model to read the reference through a tool costs 1.7 to 2.8 times the tokens of the lean skill. Of 47 event logs simulated from public models, 44 fit their source models, and tok imports every model discovered from the logs.

AI.tldr: tok is a plain-text notation for BPMN 2.0.2 process models and DMN 1.5 decisions, with one engine that checks documents against both standards, compiles them to XML with an automatic diagram and serves language-model applications through the Model Context Protocol. The notation uses fewer tokens than BPMN XML and is written validly by language models.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not state a motivation beyond the need for a compact, checkable textual syntax for BPMN and DMN that humans and AI agents can both use.
AI.method: The paper classifies tok as an alternative concrete syntax of the BPMN and DMN metamodels and reports one study that compares token counts against BPMN XML from 893 files exported by 37 tools, measures fault detection against XML Schema with bpmnlint, tests four language models with a one-page reference, and tests agents with a lean skill and one checker tool.
AI.result: A tok model takes 2.2 times fewer tokens than the smallest BPMN XML and 7.7 times fewer than the files as exported. The checker signals 98.2% of 1,411 injected faults against 85.8% for XML Schema with bpmnlint. Models write valid tok for 85.7 to 100% of 87 process descriptions, and the strongest writes tok with 25% and 19% fewer tokens than BPMN XML. As agents, models write valid tok for 97.6 to 100% of descriptions, and a skill that reads the reference through a tool costs 1.7 to 2.8 times the tokens of the lean skill. Of 47 simulated event logs, 44 fit their source models.
AI.conclusion: tok is a token-efficient and reliably checkable textual syntax for BPMN and DMN that language models can write, and its lean skill design is cheaper than a tool-based reference lookup.

title: Technohybridism: Recursive Semantic Normalization in AI-Mediated Societies
summary: Language-generating AI systems are no longer only objects of linguistic interaction: their outputs increasingly re-enter the communicative and institutional practices from which their training material was drawn. Drawing on social theory, social epistemology, and the philosophy of language, this article develops a sociotechnical account of that re-entry. We introduce recursive semantic normalization: the process through which machine-generated formulations, once recurrently taken up, evaluated, reused, and institutionally retained, participate in the reproduction and transformation of semantic regularities. Under the heading of technohybridism, we argue that the relevant unit of analysis is the hybrid semantic system, a recursively coupled configuration of human practices, computational generation, and institutional uptake. First, we distinguish the concept from neighbouring accounts, including model collapse, looping effects, machine habitus, machine culture, and the epistemology of AI testimony. Second, we develop an analytical model that separates generation, selection, uptake, and persistence and distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway. Third, we analyse uptake as routinized, institutionally diffused, and socially stratified practice and state conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms. Fourth, we identify social-epistemic consequences: the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of the cognitive diversity on which collective inquiry depends, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources. An evidential ladder for empirical research follows. The account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.

AI.tldr: The paper develops technohybridism, a sociotechnical account of recursive semantic normalisation in which machine-generated formulations that are repeatedly taken up and institutionally retained reshape semantic regularities. It analyses the consequences for provenance, epistemic vigilance and cognitive diversity.
AI.motivation: Language-generating AI outputs now re-enter the communicative and institutional practices that produced their training material, and existing neighbouring accounts such as model collapse, looping effects and machine habitus do not capture this recursive re-entry.
AI.method: Drawing on social theory, social epistemology and the philosophy of language, the article introduces recursive semantic normalisation, proposes an analytical model separating generation, selection, uptake and persistence that distinguishes machine-attributable change from change that would have occurred anyway, analyses uptake as routinised and socially stratified practice, and sets out an evidential ladder for empirical research.
AI.result: The article identifies social-epistemic consequences, namely the laundering of provenance that weakens epistemic vigilance, the erosion of cognitive diversity needed for collective inquiry, and the narrowing of shared hermeneutical resources, and it states conditions under which machine-derived regularities become norms.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid semantic system is the relevant unit of analysis, and the account attributes no normative authority to machine outputs; what changes is the field within which human and institutional uptake operates.

title: Who Can Evaluate AI Independently? A Framework for Analysing Evaluation Infrastructure
summary: AI evaluation is increasingly central to AI safety and governance, yet taking part in an evaluation does not by itself confer authority over its design, its execution or the resources it depends on. This paper examines how infrastructure arrangements distribute that authority, and so shape who can evaluate AI systems independently. Drawing on Science and Technology Studies, political economy and applied evaluation standards, we introduce PAAI (Power, Access, Adequacy, Independence), a framework for examining who controls evaluation infrastructure, the terms on which it is available, whether it is adequate to the evaluation's purpose and what autonomy it supports. We apply PAAI to twelve African AI evaluation projects (2022-2025) and to the documented roles of all ten member institutes in the three published joint testing exercises of the international network of AI Safety Institutes. We identify three recurring configurations: extractive collaboration, dependent innovation and constrained independence. African actors often contribute data, language expertise and task design while external institutions retain authority over infrastructure and evaluation frameworks; design authority without infrastructure authority never yielded more than partial independence. The joint testing exercises show a similar division among mostly high-income members: the institutes that led each exercise also ran the models, while Kenya, the network's only African member, moved from annotation to task design with no documented model execution. Participation in evaluation does not by itself produce evaluative authority. For evaluation to serve as a credible governance mechanism, access must come with control over priorities, methods, publication and continuity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PAAI (Power, Access, Adequacy, Independence), a framework for analysing who controls AI evaluation infrastructure and how far that control allows independent evaluation. Applied to twelve African evaluation projects and the joint testing exercises of the International Network of AI Safety Institutes, it finds that participation does not by itself confer evaluative authority.
AI.motivation: Taking part in an AI evaluation does not by itself confer authority over its design, execution or the resources it depends on, yet AI evaluation is central to safety and governance, so the distribution of authority over infrastructure needs to be examined.
AI.method: Drawing on Science and Technology Studies, political economy and applied evaluation standards, the authors define PAAI and apply it to twelve African AI evaluation projects from 2022 to 2025 and to the documented roles of all ten member institutes in the three published joint testing exercises of the international network.
AI.result: Three recurring configurations are identified, namely extractive collaboration, dependent innovation and constrained independence. African actors often contribute data, language expertise and task design while external institutions keep authority over infrastructure and frameworks, and design authority without infrastructure authority yielded only partial independence. In the joint exercises, the institutes that led also ran the models, while Kenya moved from annotation to task design with no documented model execution.
AI.conclusion: Credible evaluation as a governance mechanism requires that access come with control over priorities, methods, publication and continuity, not merely participation.

title: Accepted but Wrong: Silent Failures of LLM Code Repairs after API Migrations
comment: 30 pages, 2 figures. Preregistered; artifacts are available from the authors on request
summary: After a runtime or API migration, an LLM-repaired procedure can run cleanly yet return wrong results, and a release check on typical test inputs ships it. We report a preregistered study of 73 tasks covering 60 documented changes in CPython, this http URL and SQLite. Every candidate is executed on the real runtimes against withheld contracts. Over the complete repair space, the all-assertions gate on typical inputs released 0.410 of wrong repairs. One edge input written from the release note cut this to 0.065, and to 0.061 on 15 unseen clusters. Three inputs from a blind GPT-5.6-luna writer that never saw the program reached 0.070. Two further frozen stages enlarged the menu to 1491 fragments and then added 233 hard distractors that match the legacy output on typical inputs. The edge input (0.058) and the frontier-model writer (0.058) passed their preregistered tests. Yet 0.168 and 0.153 of the hard wrong programs still passed. Two local-model writers failed their preregistered tests. Across four model families, the edge input cut wrong releases per attempt in all three open-weight families on all three menus, for example from 0.233 to 0.057, without lowering correct completion. Self-tests helped less. A blind AI audit flagged 34 contracts as stricter than their requirements. Dropping the disputed checks changed 0 verdicts, but class-label disputes remain open. No model-written code was executed. Artifacts are available from the authors on request.

AI.tldr: The paper studies silent failures in LLM-repaired code after runtime or API migrations, where a repaired procedure runs cleanly but returns wrong results and passes a release check on typical inputs. A single edge input written from the release note sharply reduces the release of wrong repairs, though some hard wrong programs still pass.
AI.motivation: After a runtime or API migration, an LLM repair can run without error yet return wrong results, and the usual all-assertions release check on typical test inputs ships such repairs, so a stronger release gate is needed.
AI.method: A preregistered study of 73 tasks covering 60 documented changes in CPython, a second runtime and SQLite, in which every candidate is executed on the real runtimes against withheld contracts over a repair space enlarged by frozen stages to 1491 fragments and 233 hard distractors, comparing the typical-input gate with edge inputs, blind writers and self-tests across four model families.
AI.result: The all-assertions gate on typical inputs released 0.410 of wrong repairs, and one edge input cut this to 0.065, or 0.061 on 15 unseen clusters. Inputs from a blind writer reached 0.070, and the edge input (0.058) and a frontier-model writer (0.058) passed their preregistered tests, although 0.168 and 0.153 of hard wrong programs still passed. In all three open-weight families the edge input reduced wrong releases on all three menus, for example from 0.233 to 0.057, without lowering correct completion, and self-tests helped less.
AI.conclusion: Adding an edge input derived from the release note is a cheap and effective way to reduce silent wrong releases, but hard wrong programs and class-label disputes remain open problems.

title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.

AI.tldr: FedReason lets a large language model act as a server-side meta-aggregator that inspects client model weights in a restricted sandbox and submits an aggregation program for each call, without any server-side training. Using Claude Opus 5.5, it beats FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average under label skew on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
AI.motivation: Federated learning servers use a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity, so the paper asks whether an LLM that inspects client models can choose the rule itself.
AI.method: Every ten rounds the LLM analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only printed results, may score candidates on a 500-image proxy set and submits a short Python aggregation program that the server applies until the next call, falling back to FedAvg when the output is invalid, with full weight tensors never leaving the server. The evaluation uses ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines.
AI.result: Across 12 paired label-skew runs FedReason beats FedAvg by 1.26 points on average with 10 wins, and a control that spends the same proxy budget choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It is the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but does not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious it excludes all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stays about one point below FLTrust. Without proxy feedback accuracy falls from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed, and a 60-round run costs 0.79 USD in API fees on average.
AI.conclusion: An LLM can select a useful server-side aggregation rule at low API cost, but its advantage is limited when a baseline changes client training and it depends on proxy feedback.

title: Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing
comment: Code, videos, and dataset available at this https URL
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at this https URL.

AI.tldr: VLA-Tug is a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a Vision-Language-Action model that detects failures early, bounds missed-detection and false-alarm rates and predicts the failure mode to enable corrective action. It improves early detection by up to 30% at matched false-positive rates over the strongest learned baseline.
AI.motivation: VLA performance is brittle under distribution shift, and deploying VLAs on real robots needs a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, informative and efficient enough for the edge, which existing methods do not fulfil.
AI.method: The probe is trained over the latent layers of a VLA backbone, supervises on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory, provides bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates, and predicts the failure mode, with minimal inference overhead. A dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes is released.
AI.result: Early failure detection at matched false-positive rates rises by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks the rate bounds remain valid in up to 86% of runs versus at most 21% for baselines, and top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks is up to 44% higher than a majority baseline. The probe also supports lightweight steering that improves task success.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated latent probing gives timely, well-bounded and informative failure monitoring for VLAs that can run on the edge and support corrective action.
